1.1 Scope
2
This technical report provides the threat model and risk assessment for the Non-RT-RIC.  The report identifies threats and risks and recommends potential security controls to
3
protect against those threats through safeguards or mitigation.
4
The steps of the threat modelling process are as follows:
5
1.
Identify assets: Identify the assets of the Non-RT-RIC that must be protected.
6
2.
Identify threats: Identify the threats that could adversely impact the Non-RT-RIC and threats that can use the Non-RT-RIC to adversely impact other components of the
7
O-RAN system.
8
3.
Identify the attack surface and attack vectors: Identify the points in the Non-RT-RIC where an attacker could gain entry, exploit a vulnerability or misconfiguration,
9
and compromise the system or its data.
10
4.
Measure risk: The extent to which confidentiality, integrity, or availability is threatened, based upon the impact level resulting from an attack and the likelihood of
11
occurrence.
12
5.
Recommend controls: The management, operational, and technical controls for an information system to protect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of the
13
Non-RT-RIC and its information
14
15
1.2 Considerations
16
The attack surface of the Non-RT-RIC includes its interfaces, functions, and data.  Data-at-rest, Data-in-motion, and Data-in-use must be considered.
17
The O-RAN Alliance is pursuing a zero-trust architecture (ZTA) for its specifications.  A ZTA assumes that the adversary is already inside the network and makes no
18
assumption of implicit trust based upon asset ownership, network location, or physical location.  This has the effect of increasing the likelihood scoring.
19
Security controls are recommended for specifications of the Non-RT-RIC, which is the responsibility of

19

1.4.1 Definitions
13
For the purposes of the present document, the terms and definitions provided in O-RAN.WG1.O-RAN-Architecture-Description-v06.00 apply:
14
A1: Interface between non-RT RIC and Near-RT RIC to enable policy-driven guidance of Near-RT RIC applications/functions, and support AI/ML workflow.
15
A1 policy: Type of declarative policies expressed using formal statements that enable the non-RT RIC function in the SMO to guide the near-RT RIC function, and hence the
16
RAN, towards better fulfilment of the RAN intent.
17
A1 Enrichment information: Information utilized by near-RT RIC that is collected or derived at SMO/non-RT RIC either from non-network data sources or from network
18
functions themselves.
19
Near-RT RIC: O-RAN Near-Real-Time RAN Intelligent Controller: A logical function that enables near-real-time control and optimization of RAN elements and resources via
20
fine-grained data collection and actions over E2 interface. It may include AI/ML (Artificial Intelligence / Machine Learning) workflow including model training, inference and
21
updates.
22
Non-RT RIC: O-RAN Non-Real-Time RAN Intelligent Controller: A logical function within SMO that drives the content carried across the A1 interface.  It is comprised of the
23
Non-RT RIC Framework and the Non-RT RIC Applications (rApps) whose functions are defined below.
24
Non-RT RIC Applications (rApps): Modular applications that leverage the functionality exposed via the Non-RT RIC Framework’s R1 interface to provide added value services
25
relative to RAN operation, such as driving the A1 interface, recommending values and actions that may be subsequently applied over the O1/O2 interface and generating
26
“enrichment information” for the use of other rApps.  Th

added value services
25
relative to RAN operation, such as driving the A1 interface, recommending values and actions that may be subsequently applied over the O1/O2 interface and generating
26
“enrichment information” for the use of other rApps.  The rApp functionality within the Non-RT RIC enables non-real-time control and optimization of RAN elements and
27
resources and policy-based guidance to the applications/features in Near-RT RIC.
28

Non-RT RIC Framework: That functionality internal to the SMO that logically terminates the A1 interface to the Near-RT RIC and exposes to rApps, via its R1 interface, the
1
set of internal SMO services needed for their runtime processing.  The Non-RT RIC Framework functionality within the Non-RT RIC provides AI/ML workflow including model
2
training, inference and updates needed for rApps.
3
SMO: A Service Management and Orchestration system
4
R1 Interface: Interface between rApps and Non-RT RIC framework via which R1 Services can be produced and consumed.
5

6
R1 Services: A collection of services including, but not limited to, service registration and discovery services, authentication and authorization services, AI/ML workflow
7
services, and A1, O1 and O2 related services.

2.1 Architecture
2
The primary goal of non-RT RIC is to support non-real-time intelligent radio resource management, higher layer procedure optimization, policy optimization in RAN, and
3
providing AI/ML models to near-RT RIC and other RAN functions. The A1 interface supports communication & information exchange between non-RT RIC and near-RT RIC,
4
key objective of A1 interface is to support policy-based guidance of near-RT RIC functions/use-cases, transmission of enrichment information in support of AI/ML models into
5
near-RT RIC, and basic feedback mechanisms from near-RT RIC.
6

3 Threats
1
3.1 Threat Model
2
For identifying threats, we are using STRIDE:
3
1. S - Spoofing identity. An application or program can masquerade as another to gain advantages not typically
4
allowed for that program.
5
2. T - Tampering with data. This involves the malicious modification of data, including making unauthorized
6
changes to a database and alteration of data as it flows between computers.
7
3. R - Repudiation. A user or program refuses the authenticity of a good or reasonable command or action.
8
4. I - Information disclosure. This involves the exposure of information to individuals with unauthorized access to
9
it. For example, users gain the ability to read a file that they normally would not have been granted access to, or
10
an intruder can read data in transit between computers.
11
5. D - Denial of service. These attacks deny service to valid users, such as making a website unavailable or unusable
12
by flooding it with illegitimate requests to keep legitimate users without access.
13
6. E - Elevation of privileges. An unauthorized user gains privileged rights to access previously no granted to
14
compromise or destroy the system, such as a change in membership.

4.2 rApps Threats
1
rApps have the ability to manipulate behavior of a certain cell, a group of UEs, and a specific UE. A malfunctioning rApp could
2
potentially be used to track or impact service for a certain UE-Id or degrade service in an area.
3
Threat ID
T-rAPP-01
Threat title
Conflicting rApps unintentionally or maliciously impact O-RAN system functions to degrade performance or
trigger a DoS
Threat
description
rApps in the Non-RT RIC can be provided by different vendors. For example, one vendor can provide the rApp
for Carrier license scheduling and another vendor provide the rApp for energy saving, etc.
This creates the risk that different rApps will take conflicting decisions at the same instance in time for the same
user. Such conflicts between rApps include:
•
Direct conflicts: different rApps request change for the same parameter.
•
Indirect conflicts: different rApps request change to different parameters that will create opposite
effects.
•
Implicit conflicts: different rApps request change to different parameters that are not creating any
obvious opposite effect but result in an overall network performance degradation, instabilities, etc.
These conflicts are difficult to mitigate since dependencies are impossible to observe.
Threat type
Denial of Service
Impact type
Availability
Affected
Asset
rApps

6 Risk Assessment
1
This section provides risk assessment tables for each of the identified assets: Non-RT RIC, R1 interface, A1 interface,
2
and rApps.  These tables list the assets, threats, impacts, and possible security controls.
3
A malicious actor may be a nation-state adversary, cybercriminal, or employee.  Risk scoring includes Likelihood and
4
Impact.
5
Likelihood scoring is based upon current security controls.  Likelihood scoring does not consider security controls that
6
may be potentially specified in the future.
7
Likelihood scoring considers a zero trust architecture which protects against internal threat actors.  Likelihood scores
8
are higher for a zero trust architecture (ZTA) because internal threats must be considered in addition to external threats.
9
In a ZTA it cannot be assumed that perimeter defenses are sufficient.  As a result, scored Likelihood = Medium, at a
10
minimum.   Reconnaissance type attacks can be scored Likelihood = High while damaging/availability attacks can be
11
scored Likelihood = Medium.  The reason is that threat actors are less likely to perform damaging attacks that are
12
quickly and easily detected. Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) typically move laterally in anonymous fashion to
13
prevent detection while providing reconnaissance.
14
Zero trust architecture removes the ability to assume perimeter security is sufficient.  The Non-RT RIC must be
15
protected from untrusted external sources attempting to have access, while also assuming the adversary is already inside
16
the network with access to its functions.  As a result, the Non-RT RIC cannot have its security posture founded on the
17
assumption the SMO is secure.

7 Recommendations
1
The Security Analysis presented in this technical report used the following process:
2
1. Asset identification -> 2. Threat identification -> 3. Threat analysis -> 4. Risk analysis -> 5. Recommend
3
Security Controls
4
The Non-RT RIC Reference Architecture is a logical architecture, not an implementation architecture.  The Non-RT
5
RIC can be monolithic or multiple disaggregated functions.  The Non-RT RIC Framework may be considered an asset
6
for which security controls can be applied.  Other critical assets that are part of the Non-RT RIC Framework are rApps,
7
the R1 interface, and the A1 interface, which are considered assets for this security analysis.
8
Recommendation 1: SFG should update the Security Threat and Remediation document [8] to include the assets
9
identified in this security analysis technical report.  A CR will be generated.
10
20 threats were identified, which are categorized as 3 Non-RT RIC threats, 7 rApps threats, 7 R1 threats, and 3 A1
11
threats.  In addition, 6 threats for the protocol stack of the R1 and A1 interfaces were identified.
12
Recommendation 2: SFG should update the Security Threat and Remediation document [8] to include the threats
13
and threat tables created for this security analysis technical report.  A CR will be generated.
14

15
Risk analysis included impact-likelihood scoring.  All 20 of the identified threats were score either high-medium or
16
high-high.  Likelihood scoring was influenced by the consideration of a zero trust architecture (ZTA), which is a
17
publicly expressed goal of the O-RAN Alliance.  ZTA is built on the foundational principles that perimeter defenses are
18
insufficient to secure a network as internal external threats pose risk to a network.  There are two guidelines for
19
designing a network and its network functions for a ZTA:
20
1. There is no implicit trust granted to an asset based upon ownership, physical location, or network location [13].
21
2. Assume the adversary is already inside the network [20].
22
Recommendation 3: The Non-RT RIC should be protected from untrusted external sources attempting to have
23
access.  Specific requirements will be formed as this SFG work item continues.
24
Recommendation 4: The Non-RT RIC should have security controls implemented to protect its functions and
25
interfaces from internal threats, consistent with a ZTA. Specific requirements will be formed as this SFG work item
26
continues.
27

28
14 security controls were identified for securing the Non-RT RIC to provide protection from confidentiality, integrity,
29
and availability attacks.
30
Recommendation 5: The SFG should update its Security Requirements Specifications document [7] and Security
31
Protocols Specifications document [9] to provide guidance for use of the suggested security controls.  Requirements
32
for these security controls will be developed as this SFG work item continues.  The security controls recommended
33
in the Risk Analysis tables in section 6 for the R1 and A1 interfaces should be considered by WG2.
34
Recommendation 6: Consistent with a ZTA architecture the Non-RT RIC should be secure by design in which its
35
security posture does not assume that the SMO is secure and will provide perimeter protection for the Non-RT-RIC.
36
A new SFG work item should address security of SMO and Non-RT RIC integration.
37

38
Non-RT-RIC has additional attack vectors that have broader scope across O-RAN. These additional attack vectors that
39
are not exclusive to the Non-RT-RIC include secure application on-boarding and lifecycle management of rApps,
40
certificate management, key management, implementation of a secure protocol stack on the A1 and R1 interfaces,
41
security configuration validation, cloud security best practices, ML/AI security, logging security, and secure software
42
development, including secure use of open source software.
43

Recommendation 7: SFG should address each of these non-exclusive attack vectors mentioned above as work
1
items to be studied in collaboration with the relevant working group of the O-RAN Alliance.  In some cases, the
2
SFG itself may be the relevant working group.
3

Terms

Circular economy [ITU-T L.1020]: A circular economy is restorative and regenerative by design, and aims to
keep products, components, and materials at their highest utility and value at all times while reducing waste
streams. A concept that distinguishes between technical and biological cycles, the circular economy is a
continuous, positive development cycle. It preserves and enhances natural capital, optimises resource yields,
and minimises system risks by managing finite stocks and renewable flows, while reducing waste streams.

Circular economy on network equipment
Based on ITU-T L.1023 recommendation, there is a three-step methodology to identify an information and
communication technology (ICT) good´s circularity in three dimensions via three circularity aspects: first, the
ICT good durability, second, the ICT good ability to be recycled, repaired, reused and upgraded; and third,
the manufacturers ability to recycle, repair, reuse and upgrade the ICT good put into the market. The three
asppects are then divided into indicators for circular product design.
In this document the circularity indicators are then assessed at three levels, applicability identification on
network equipment (O-CU, O-DU and O-RU), how well circularity has been achieved and priority level
according to the effect (for customer, environment etc) of the indicator at hand.
Table 1 – Circularity Aspects – contains a list of circular principles that put all the indicators into different
aspects. The description of each aspect is as follows:
1. Product durability (PD): It included indicators related to promoting the life span and durability of
products by adapting their design and upgrading software to a new version and service support by
ensuring the product can be used for as long as possible by the first user or subsequent users.
2. Ability to recycle, repair, reuse, upgrade (3Rue) – equipment level: It includes indicators related to
the product´s structure and access to its priority parts for repair, connecting, systems to facilitate
disassembly and reassembly, spare parts, diagnostic and information availability. It relates to:
a. Possibilities to refurbish the ICT good;
b. Possibilities to reuse product parts and components within the ICT good (after first use) in
refurbishment of similar or other ICT goods;
c. Facili

diagnostic and information availability. It relates to:
a. Possibilities to refurbish the ICT good;
b. Possibilities to reuse product parts and components within the ICT good (after first use) in
refurbishment of similar or other ICT goods;
c. Facilite the identification, separation and recycling of materials. Addresses separate
collection of products for better recycling and development of designated recycling
technologies.
3. Ability to recycle, repair, reuse, upgrade (3Rum) – manufacturer level: It includes indicators related
to the manufacturer ability (on company level) to facilitate recycling, repair, reuse, and upgrade.
These requirements are not directly connected to the equipment, but to the infrastructure and
support to be developed or supported by the manufacturer. It relates to:
a. Availability of service support in terms of information, infrastructure, and spare parts.

In terms of network equipment circularity aspects and indicators and based on the latest publication of ITU-

In summary, each group contains a set of indicators that directly address the group's topic. The proposed
table is in principle unlimited regarding the number of groups and indicators. For example, new indicators

Following the second level of assessment of this document, below is described definition and contribution
cases to circular economy of each indicator per aspect:
1. Product durability

1.1. Software and data support: Availability of software and firmware updates & upgrades (according
to EN 45554).
•
The most contributing variable to the circularity of the equipment: Software and firmware
updates & upgrades availability can be categorized as long-term (class A, i.e., for a duration
of time that reflects the expected maximum useful life of the product, cf. EN 45554).
•
Does not contribute to the circular economy of the equipment: No information on duration
of availability (class D, cf. EN 45554) is provided on software and firmware updates &
upgrades availability.

1.2. Scratch resistance: Resistance of housing parts subject to be scratched (resistance regarding ASTM
D3363 – 05 (2011) e2 standard.)
•
The most contributing variable to the circularity of the equipment: Plastic scratch resistance
equal or greater than 2H.
•
Does not contribute to the circular economy of the equipment: Plastic scratch resistance
lower or equal to B.

1.3. Maintenance support: Availability of consumables, wear-out parts expected to be replaced
periodically and availability of maintenance infrastructure (according to EN 45554).
•
The most contributing variable to the circularity of the equipment: Consumables and wear-
out parts expected to be replaced periodically can be categorized as publicly available (class
A in EN 45554) or as available to independent maintenance service providers (class B in EN
45554).
•
Does not contribute to the circular economy of the equipment: Consumables and wear-out
parts expected to be replaced periodically can be categorized as not available (class E in EN
45554). No maintenance infrastructure are offered by manufacturer.

1.4. Robustness: Refers to the ability of the equipment to tolerate or resist perturbations that may affect
its functional body. If the equipment is robust, it has greater durability and is therefore better from
a circular economy point of view.
•
The most contributing variable to the circularity of the equipment: The product's design
features have better characteristics than the minimum requirements for the environmental
class in which the product is intended to be used and comply to the enhanced requirements
(Example: a product intended to be used in non-weather protected location and satisfies
the requirements of class 4.1E (extended severity level) of [b-EN 300 019-1-4] instead of
class 4.1 (minimum severity level) and complies to the enhanced requirements of ITU-T
K.20/21/45).
•
Does not contribute to the circular economy of the equipment: The product's design
features characteristics do not comply to several of the minimum requirements for the
environmental class in which the product is intended to be used.

2. Recycle, repair, reuse, upgrade – Equipment level

2.1. Fasteners and connectors: Fasteners, connectors and tools used to disassemble parts that are likely
to need replacement during the expected lifetime of the product are reusable/removable per EN
45554.
•
The most contributing variable to the circularity of the equipment:  Fasteners and
connectors can be categorized as reusable (class A) and using no tools, basic tools or product
specific tools (classes A-C as defined in EN 45554).
•
Does not contribute to the circular economy of the equipment: Fasteners and connectors
can be categorized as neither removable nor reusable (class C).

2.2. Diagnostic support: Facilitate the identification of problems or defects. Relates to the type of
interface available and how intuitive it is for fault detection, parameter reset or default upgrade. An
accessible diagnostic and reset interface facilitate further repair, reuse and upgrade. Diagnostic
support classification by necessary interface.
•
The most contributing variable to the circularity of the equipment: Interface can be
categorized as an intuitive interface (Class A) - cf. EN 45554.
•
Does not contribute to the circular economy of the equipment: Diagnostic is not possible
with any type of interface (Class E) - cf. EN 45554.

2.3. Material recycling compatibility - Plastic parts: Materials compatibility for joint recycling.
•
The most contributing variable to the circularity of the equipment: All of the following
requirements shall be fulfilled;

________________________________________________________________________________________________
10
a) Plastic parts >25g do not contain metal inlets or fasteners that are molded, heat or
ultrasonically inserted or glued-in and cannot be separated by breaking off from the
plastic part or with commonly available tools.
b) Plastic parts >100g do not have an adhesive, coating, paint or finish that is not compatible
with recycled. NOTE: Plastic parts with >25% post-consumer recycled content and
printed-circuit boards are exempt. Requirement does not apply to parts where such
measures are required for safety, legal or technical requirements.
c) Plastic parts >25g are comprised of a single resin or combination of resins compatible for
recycling and are separable by hand or with commonly available tools from other plastic
parts >25g and not compatible for joint recycling. NOTE: Printed circuit boards, wires and
cables, connectors, electronic, optical, acoustic, ESD and EMI components are excluded.
•
Does not contribute to the circular economy of the equipment: None of the requirements
specified is fulfilled.

2.4. Material recycling compatibility - Metal parts: Materials compatibility for joint recycling.
•
The most contributing variable to the circularity of the equipment: All of the following
requirements shall be fulfilled.
a) In metal parts with weight > 25 g, metals are kept separable for easy recycling,
particularly the materials intended for different end-of-life treatment.
b) Data on used alloys is available.
c) Metal parts with weight > 25 g do not have such adhesive, coating, paint, or finish that is
not compatible with recycling.
•
Does not contribute to the circular economy of the equipment: None of the requirements
specified is fulfilled.

2.5. Recycled/renewable plastics: Use of pre- or post-consumer recycled plastics. NOTE: Refers to
plastics used in the ICT good itself.
•
The most contributing variable to the circularity of the equipment: Total content of recycled
and biobased plastics 75-100%.
•
The less contributing variable to the circularity of the equipment: Total content of recycled
and biobased plastics 0-25%.

2.6. Recycled metals: Use of recycled metals.
•
The most contributing variable to the circularity of the equipment: Combined total recycled
metals content in at least two predominant metals by mass is 75-100%.
•
Does not contribute to the circular economy of the equipment: Combined total recycled
metals content in at least two predominant metals by mass is 0-25%.

2.7. Material identification: Identification and marking of the materials contained in the equipment. The
identification and marking of materials facilitate the subsequent recycling of the equipment.
Materials identification according to ISO 11469.
•
The most contributing variable to the circularity of the equipment: Markings to identify base
materials as per ISO 11469, ISO 1043-1 (plastics), ISO 1629 (rubbers) ISO 18064
(thermoplastic elastomers), as well as fillers and reinforcing materials (ISO 1043-2),
plasticizers (ISO 1043-3) and flame retardants (ISO 1043-4)
•
Does not contribute to the circular economy of the equipment: No markings to identify
materials on any part.

________________________________________________________________________________________________
11
2.8. Hazardous substances (Bromine and Chlorine): Reduction of bromine and chlorine in plastic parts
(The flame retardant used in plastic parts may contain these hazardous substances).
•
The most contributing variable to the circularity of the equipment: Each plastic part in the
product exceeding 0.5 g shall not contain greater than 1000 ppm chlorine or greater than
1000 ppm bromine at the homogeneous level [b-IEEE1680]. Test methods such as IEC
62321-3-1 and 62321-3-2 are recommended. [b-IEEE1680]. NOTE: Parts which exceed 25%
post-consumer recycled content may contain a maximum of 5000 ppm chlorine and a
maximum of 5000 ppm bromine [b-IEEE1680].  Power cords - in jurisdictions where PVC-
free power cords have not been approved by safety agencies for use in the product - are
exempted. [b-IEEE1680].
•
Does not contribute to the circular economy of the equipment: The bromine and chlorine
based substances content is unknown.

2.9. Critical Raw Materials: Declaration of Critical Raw Materials Content. NOTE: CRMs are different for
each region. Examples of defined CRM include L.1100 and the list of CRM for the EU [b-EU-CRM].
Each product has to choose the appropriate CRM list.
•
The most contributing variable to the circularity of the equipment: Based on the CRM
content assessment, the location of the CRM in the ICT good is available to improve
recyclability.
•
Does not contribute to the circular economy of the equipment: The CRM content is
unknown.

2.10. Packaging recycling: Material recycling aspects included in the primary packaging.
•
The most contributing variable to the circularity of the equipment: All the aspects of
material efficiency are considered for the packaging, by fulfilling all of the following five
requirements:
a) Elimination of elemental chlorine as a bleaching agent used to bleach virgin or recovered
fibers subsequently used in product packaging.
b) Elimination of the use of expanded polystyrene in product packaging.
c) Packaging is designed in a way that it allows reuse, recycling or recovery.
d) Sum of the concentrations of intentionally added lead, cadmium, mercury and hexavalent
chromium present in primary packaging shall not exceed 100 ppm by weight.
e) Minimum used 30% recycled content by mass of plastic and fibre-based materials.
•
Does not contribute to the circular economy of the equipment: None of the requirements
for packaging material recycling are fulfilled.

2.11. Technical performance product mass-based materials efficiency: Technical performance per
product mass.
•
The most contributing variable to the circularity of the equipment: Technical performance
per product mass used improved > 15% in between product at hand and previous
corresponding product model.
•
Does not contribute to the circular economy of the equipment: Technical performance per
product mass not improved in between product at hand and previous corresponding
product model.

3. Ability to Recycle, Repair, Reuse, upgrade - Manufacturer level

________________________________________________________________________________________________
12
3.1. Service offered by manufacturer: Duration of Repair, Reuse, upgrade services (according to EN
45554).
•
The most contributing variable to the circularity of the equipment: Repair, Reuse and
upgrade service availability can be categorized as long-term (class A). NOTE: Expected
durability is the time a customer (the user of the ICT good) can expect the product to last.
•
Does not contribute to the circular economy of the equipment: No Repair, Reuse and
upgrade service availability is offered.

3.2. Spare parts distribution: Availability of spare parts to different categories of persons/ organisations
to facilitate equipment repairability (according to EN 45554).
•
The most contributing variable to the circularity of the equipment: Spare parts are publicly
available or available to independent repair service providers (Class A and Class B, as defined
in EN 45554).
•
Does not contribute to the circular economy of the equipment: Spare parts are not available
(Class E, as defined in EN 45554).

3.3. Spare parts availability: Duration of spare parts availability (according to EN 45554). The longer the
availability of spare parts, the greater the circularity.
•
The most contributing variable to the circularity of the equipment: Spare parts availability
can be categorized as long-term (class A, i.e., a repair, re-use or upgrade process, for which
the required spare part(s) is/are available for a duration of time that reflects the expected
durability of the product category, cf. EN 45554)
•
Does not contribute to the circular economy of the equipment: No information on duration
of availability is provided for spare parts (class D, i.e., repair, re-use or upgrade process, for
which the required spare part(s) is/are available at the time of sale, but for which the
duration of availability cannot be determined, cf. EN 45554).

3.4. Disassembly information: Classification of information availability by comprehensiveness
(according to EN 45554).
•
The most contributing variable to the circularity of the equipment: Information is publicly
available (class A, i.e., repair, re-use or upgrade process, for which the relevant information
is available to all interested parties, cf. EN 45554).
•

the manufacturer only (class D, i.e., repair, re-use or upgrade process, for which the relevant

•
The most contributing variable to the circularity of the equipment: A designated collection
program for refurbish, remanufacturing, repair and a designated selective, recycling
program for specific parts of ICT goods (e.g., specific recycling process able to recover
Germanium from optical fiber, Tantalum from Tantalum capacitors or Indium from
LCD/OLED displays, etc.) is available.
•
Does not contribute to the circular economy of the equipment: Neither designated
collection nor designated recycling program is available.

environmental footprint.

This document defines the End to End (E2E) testing framework for comprehensive E2E testing and validation of the Open
2
RAN (O-RAN) Systems ensuring robust interoperability and operate with high performance as intended in real-world
3
deployments.

System.

testing framework will therefore need to take into consideration the Operators’ O-RAN deployment variants given its

influence on the scope of E2E testing.

Group (TIFG) focuses on the definition of the E2E testing framework based on addressing the needs of these most
21
common and probable deployment scenarios.

23
Deployment Blueprints and testing practices respectively, to assist O-RAN Alliance with developing comprehensive E2E
24
testing methodologies and test cases. These inputs are included in this specification for referencing purposes.

interfaces between the O-RAN network functions. These O-RAN network functions and open interfaces are mapped to a

list of the most con

Chapter 4 O-RAN Deployment Blueprints
1
4.1  Introduction
2
This chapter provides the high-level definition of the O-RAN Deployment Blueprint template which contains the
3
necessary descriptors to build the underlying O-RAN Deployment Blueprints.
4
The O-RAN Deployment Blueprint is defined as the set of inputs used to describe a specific O-RAN deployment from
5
several aspects. These aspects include the specification of the O-RAN deployment at the System level (e.g. architecture,
6
performance metrics) as well as Subsystem level and the Open Interfaces between the specified Subsystems. This would
7
then allow definition and documentation of the testing methodology and the test cases using the blueprint specification.
8
Each of the O-RAN Deployment Blueprints can be described with
9
1. A single System Profile
10
2. Two or more Subsystem Instance Profiles
11
3. One or more Subsystem Pair Interoperability Profile(s)
12

13
Figure 4-1 shows the relationship between Deployment Blueprint and its associated set of Profiles.
14

15
Figure 4-1: Deployment Blueprint and the associated Profiles
16
4.2  System Profiles
17
The purpose of the System Profile is to describe the O-RAN Deployment Blueprint from the E2E system perspective.
18
A System Profile consists of System Architecture information and a set of System Profile parameters.
19
Figure 4-2 shows the scope of the System Profile in relation to the O-RAN Deployment Blueprint.
20

6
Hybrid models. Refer to [6][7] for more details.

8

9
1. Subsystems involved
10
2. Type of implementation of each Subsystem (e.g. as a Physical (PNF), Virtual (VNF) or Cloud-Native Network
11
Function (CNF))
12
3. Location where each of the Subsystems are expected to be deployed (e.g. Cell site, Edge site, Regional site,

Core/Central site as appropriate)

4. Interconnections and Cardinality between the Subsystems

QoE Optimization, Massive MIMO Beamforming Optimization, RAN Sharing among others – refer to [8] for

more details)

3. Use Cases E2E Performance requirements of the Application, Services (e.g. data rate, latency, reliability,

availability, deterministic networking including transmission latency etc.)

4. Indoor or Outdoor deployment

Chapter 5 O-RAN End-to-End (E2E) Testing Framework
1
This chapter describes the E2E testing methodology for the holistic testing and evaluation of the O-RAN Deployment
2
Blueprints ensuring that these Blueprints can be robustly tested and optimized, ensuring consistent high quality and
3
performance in a deterministic, repeatable and reproducible manner across the entire technology lifecycle.
4
Figure 5-1 shows the major phases of the technology lifecycle which will require testing and optimization.
5
In this version of the specification, the focus will be on the Lab Verification phase.
6

7
Figure 5-1: Major Stages of the Technology Lifecycle
8
The proposed testing methodology involves Subsystem testing, Subsystem Pairing and Open Interfaces Interoperability
9
testing and E2E System testing.
10
5.1  Stages and Sequence of Testing
11
Figure 5-2 shows the stages and sequence of testing which can be performed on the O-RAN Deployment Blueprint
12
1. Perform Subsystem Testing on each of the Subsystems defined in the Blueprint
13
2. Perform Interoperability testing with pairs of Subsystems which have passed the Subsystem Testing stage
14
3. Perform E2E System Testing after all Subsystem Pairs passed the Subsystem Pair Interoperability Testing stage
15

16

________________________________________________________________________________________________

23

1
Figure 5-2: Stages and Sequence of Testing to be performed on the O-RAN Deployment Blueprint
2
These various stages of testing can be performed (or repeated) for any modifications to the O-RAN Deployment Blueprint
3
which can include one or more of the following conditions
4
1. New Subsystem vendors
5
2. New releases of the software, firmware and/or hardware in any of the Subsystems
6
3. Configuration changes to the software, firmware and/or hardware in any of the Subsystems
7

8
The modifications may or may not be accompanied with corresponding updates in the System profile, Subsystem Instance
9
profiles, Subsystem Pair and Open Interfaces Interoperability profiles and therefore the test cases, performance
10
measurements and KPIs.
11
The modifications are required to be thoroughly reviewed to be able to evaluate the impacts of these modifications to the
12
corresponding modified Subsystem Instance and the Subsystems Pair and E2E System associated with the modified
13
Subsystem Instance. The impact evaluation can then be applied to the design and selection of test cases within each of
14
the Test Stages needing to be executed due to the modifications.
15
For example, a new release can be labelled as a major or minor release but it is only through detailed analysis of the
16
modifications in this new release can help to determine the specific impacts and therefore test cases within each of the
17
Test Stages needing to be executed for this new release.
18
Subsystem Replacement Testing is an implementation variant of E2E System Testing with one of Subsystems replaced
19
in the E2E System Test environment while keeping the other Subsystems and all the test configurations the same.
20
Subsystem Replacement Testing methodology is further discussed in Section 5.4.1.
21
Test Automation will be required to make the testing procedure extremely efficient as the Test Automation framework
22
can be designed and used to handle repetitive, time-consuming tests which are required to be executed when any part of
23
the Blueprint has been modified. This results in improved accuracy as automated tests perform the same steps precisely
24
every time they are executed and create detailed reports. Test Automation is expected to be applied to all Stages of Testing

One of the key objectives of Subsystem testing is to validate the functionality of production grade DUT when the DUT
23
is not operating in test mode and in few cases in standardized test mode as when required. One example of standardized

13

1. Subsystem Profiles for all the Subsystems (e.g. xApp supporting Dynamic Traffic Steering)
6
2. Subsystem Pair IOT Profile for all the Subsystem Instance Pairs (e.g. OFH between the O-DU and O-RU)
7
3. System Profile for the entire O-RAN Deployment Blueprint
8

9
Recommendations and considerations for E2E System Testing test cases and KPIs are further detailed in Chapter 6.
10
5.4.1  Subsystem Replacement Testing
11
One variant of the E2E System Testing which can be considered is the Subsystem Replacement Testing approach when
12
the E2E System Testing is performed.
13
Subsystem Replacement Testing approach involves replacing one of Subsystems in the E2E System Test environment
14
with the other Subsystems and all the test configurations remaining the same.
15
The Subsystem Replacement Testing approach can be useful for testing the following scenarios within the E2E System
16
Testing environment as it is important to evaluate the compatibility and impact of such changes of the Subsystem to the
17
entire E2E System specified per the O-RAN Deployment Blueprint
18
1. Testing multiple vendors offering the same Subsystem (instance)
19
2. Testing upgrades (software/firmware/hardware) to a Subsystem (instance)
20
3. Testing major parameters changes to a Subsystem (instance) which have been either determined or needing to
21
be evaluated for potential System-wide impacts (e.g. expiry value of a certain timer which may have cascaded
22
impact through the E2E system as per defined in the O-RAN Deployment Blueprint)
23

24
Subsystem Replacement Testing can be applied when a reduced scope of testing and set of test cases can be performed
25
depending on the Subsystem replaced for any of the above listed scenarios. Scope reduction for the testing and test cases
26
are typically determined through detailed impact analysis of the Subsystem (to be replaced) and scenarios.
27
In this case, prior to performing E2E System Testing (described in section 5.4), the Subsystem (to be replaced) must
28
successfully complete both Subsystem Testing (described in section 5.2) and Subsystem Pair and Open Interfaces
29
Interoperability Testing (described in section 5.3) based on the determined scope of testing and set of test cases.
30

________________________________________________________________________________________________

36
Figure 5-9 shows the wrap around testing setup for E2E System under Test with one of the Subsystems replaced. In this
1
example, the O-DU subsystem is replaced as part of the E2E System Testing setup. Multiple vendors’ O-DUs can be
2
tested in the same E2E System Testing environment with the other Subsystems in the E2E test environment remaining
3
the same.
4

5
Figure 5-9: Wrap around testing setup for E2E System under Test (SUT) with one Subsystem Replaced
6
OFH indicated in Figure 5-9 includes WG4 CUS and M plane implementation and for M-Plane both Hierarchical and
7
Hybrid models. Refer to [6][7] for more details.
8

9

________________________________________________________________________________________________

37
Chapter 6 O-RAN E2E Test Cases and KPIs
1
6.1  Introduction
2
The O-RAN E2E testing framework aims to evaluate the entire O-RAN Deployment Blueprint holistically as a System
3
under Test (SUT) based on a set of well-defined E2E Test Cases and Key Performance Indicators (KPIs).
4
The purpose of this Chapter is to outline the key considerations along with information to help guide testing and validating
5
the O-RAN Deployment Blueprints with the relevant E2E Test Cases and KPIs.
6
The following considerations will be discussed in further details in the next sections in this Chapter
7
1. Use Cases and Services Requirements
8
2. O-RAN Deployment Blueprint dependencies
9
3. Relevance of 3GPP KPIs
10
4. Relevance of NGMN 5G Test Cases and KPIs defined in [10]
11
5. Test Conditions to be considered
12
6. Test Scenarios and KPIs to be considered
13

14
6.2  Use Cases and Services Requirements
15
The selection of the E2E Test Cases and KPIs are determined mainly by 2 factors
16
1. Use Cases and Services
17
2. O-RAN Deployment Blueprint which are optimized according to the Use Cases and Services requirements
18

19
Figure 6-1 shows a few examples for each of the major categories of use cases and services which are supported by 3GPP
20
and O-RAN compliant networks.
21

22
Figure 6-1: Examples of Use Cases/Services supported by 3GPP compliant and O-RAN RIC-enabled networks
23
To convince an operator to invest in O-RAN infrastructure, 3GPP and Operators’ Services which can be supported with
24
3GPP compliant networks must be well supported with O-RAN compliant networks.
25
It can therefore be expected that operators will require comprehensive system testing and evaluation to be performed on
26
the O-RAN Deployment Blueprints using the E2E Test Cases and KPIs which are defined for the 3GPP and Operators’
27
Services that are of interest to them.
28
O-RAN Alliance has specified a set of prioritized use cases which can be only supported by O-RAN RIC-enabled
29
networks. These use cases leverage the O-RAN architecture and demonstrates its unique benefits. Key benefits of O-RAN
30
architecture include the ability to utilize machine learning systems and artificial intelligence back end modules to
31
empower network intelligence through open and standardized interfaces / feeds in a multi-vendor network.
32
Operators will require guidance on the E2E Test Cases and KPIs which can be used to test and evaluate the performance
33
for each of these RIC-enabled use cases in order to be able to quantify the benefits of implementing these use cases using
34
O-RAN RIC-enabled networks as compared to networks without O-RAN RIC capabilities.
35

38

1
6.3  O-RAN Deployment Blueprint dependencies
2
An O-RAN Deployment Blueprint can consist of multiple Subsystems from possibly multiple vendors. The KPIs can be
3
measured as E2E KPIs across any combinations of vendors and as well as Subsystems and Subsystems Pairs KPIs for the
4
different Subsystems and the Open interfaces between the Subsystems respectively.
5
The specific Performance Measurements, KPIs and their respective values defined for Subsystem Testing, Subsystem
6
Pair and Open Interfaces Testing and E2E System Testing will be dependent on the O-RAN Deployment Blueprints.
7
For example, from the E2E System Testing perspective, the beam forming system performance gain KPIs specified for
8
outdoors macro cells would not be applicable for indoors small cells which may not require beam forming capabilities.
9
Similarly, the beam forming performance gain measurements specified for the O-RUs which are designed and optimized
10
for outdoors macro cells systems would not be applicable for O-RUs which are designed and optimized for indoors small
11
cells.
12
It is therefore important to ensure that testing is performed for each of the
13
1. Subsystem Instances with their defined Subsystem Instance profiles and associated KPIs
14
2. Subsystem Instances pairs with their defined Subsystem Pairs Interoperability profiles and associated KPIs
15
3. System Deployment Blueprints with the defined E2E System KPIs
16

chunks.section_title: 3GPP KPIs defined for network monitoring, assessment, analysis,
chunks.text:
17
6.4  Relevance of the 3GPP KPIs
18
As highlighted in Section 6.2, operators will require validation of the O-RAN Deployment Blueprints that the overall
19
3GPP System characteristics is as expected.
20
In general, 3GPP defines two categories of RAN KPIs
21
1. Performance data for technology tests, trials, and evaluation such as in 3GPP TR 38.913.
22
2. Performance data for network monitoring, assessment, analysis, optimization, and assurance which will be
23
further discussed in Section 6.4.1.
24

metadata.section_title: 3GPP KPIs defined for network monitoring, assessment, analysis,

chunks.section_title: 3GPP KPIs defined for network monitoring, assessment, analysis,
chunks.text:
25
The same set of E2E KPI categories and KPIs which are defined for 3GPP compliant networks and services will be
26
directly applicable for O-RAN compliant networks.
27
Additional considerations for the application of 3GPP defined KPIs for O-RAN Deployment Blueprint testing and
28
verification will be discussed in Section 6.4.2.
29
6.4.1  3GPP KPIs defined for network monitoring, assessment, analysis,
30
optimization and assurance
31
From the 3GPP system perspective, the E2E KPIs defined for network monitoring, optimization and assurance are
32
typically defined for the following categories
33
1. Availability (e.g. cells ready to service connections)
34
2. Accessibility (e.g. connection establishment rates, attempts/failures, latency)
35
3. Integrity (e.g. throughput, latency, jitter, retransmission rates)
36
4. Mobility (e.g. intra/inter RATs handover rates, interruption times for control / user planes)
37
5. Reliability (e.g. amount of sent packets which are successfully delivered to the destination within the time
38
constraint required by the target service, divided by the total number of sent packets)
39
6. Retainability (e.g. drop rates for PDN/PDU sessions, call session)
40
7. Utilization (e.g. resources utilization based on certain traffic conditions and profiles such as fronthaul, compute)
41
8. Energy Efficiency (e.g. power consumption based on certain traffic conditions and profiles)
42

43

39
3GPP TS 28.554 [9] has defined a set of E2E KPI for the 5G System (5GS) and network slicing including the NR RAN
1
and 5G Core (5GC).
2

3
6.4.2  Applicability to RAN, RAN Slices, Users and Services
4
3GPP KPIs are typically defined for 3GPP networks (RAN and Core), E2E network slices and 3GPP hosted services such
5
as 3GPP voice services with VoLTE, EPS Fallback, VoNR and others.
6
Additional important KPIs dimensions which are required to be considered for O-RAN Deployment Blueprint testing and
7
verification include
8
1. RAN Slices even though 3GPP has not yet standardized RAN slicing, this is one of the O-RAN use cases
9
2. Users and Services QoS to be evaluated for Accessibility, Integrity, Mobility, Retainability
10
3. Users and Services QoE to be evaluated
11

6.5  Relevance of the NGMN 5G Test Cases and KPIs
13
NGMN has developed a set of E2E Test Cases and KPIs which are designed to evaluate the performance of 3GPP 5G NR
14
networks [10] with its work on the definition of the testing framework for NGMN’s Pre-Commercial 5G networks trials
15
initiative.
16
The current published version of this NGMN document focuses on outdoors field testing of the 5G NR system configured
17
in NSA EN-DC mode, which includes validation of the 5G NR radio interface, E2E KPIs and features which require E2E
18
validation such as the E2E latency and E2E network slicing.
19
This set of NGMN defined E2E Test Cases and KPIs can be leveraged to a large extent for testing and validating the O-
20
RAN Deployment Blueprints in both the lab and field-testing environments.
21
Table 6-1 lists the E2E Test Cases and KPIs documented in [10] which should be referred to for more details.

1
6.6  Test Conditions to be considered
2
As highlighted in the earlier sections, the E2E System Test Cases and KPIs which are defined by 3GPP will be directly
3
applicable for testing and validating the O-RAN Deployment Blueprints, while those defined by NGMN in [10] can be
4
leveraged to a large extent for similar purpose.
5
However, it is important to take into considerations the following aspects when testing and validating O-RAN Deployment
6
Blueprints
7
1. Multi-vendors interoperability
8
2. Functional, Performance including normal and abnormal conditions
9
3. Radio channel variations and impacts on the overall system performance and Quality of Experience (QoE)
10
4. Management, Orchestration and Network Automation
11
5. Additional considerations related to practical deployment aspects
12

13
6.6.1  Multi-vendors interoperability
14
As the O-RAN Deployment Blueprint can consist of multiple Subsystems from possibly multiple vendors, additional
15
considerations for O-RAN focused system test scenarios, conditions and KPIs will be required to validate and evaluate
16
the performance of multi-vendors interoperability in accordance to the O-RAN Deployment Blueprint definition.
17
For example if the O-RUs, O-DUs and O-CU-CPs/O-CU-UPs in an O-RAN Deployment Blueprint are provided by
18
different vendors, then it would be important to ensure that the E2E KPIs are evaluated with the appropriate E2E test
19

________________________________________________________________________________________________

41
cases and test scenarios which can be used to validate multi-vendors interoperability between these O-RAN network
1
functions.
2
6.6.2  Functional, Performance including normal and abnormal conditions
3
Multi-vendors interoperability testing typically includes functional validation for handling normal conditions.
4
However, similar to how the 3GPP Radio Access Networks are expected to be tested and optimized for Performance and
5
Abnormal conditions handling, operators would be expecting the O-RAN Deployment Blueprints to be tested and
6
optimized in the same manner.
7
O-RAN Deployment Blueprints consisting of Subsystems from multiple vendors will therefore require Multi-vendors
8
interoperability testing to include testing for Performance and Abnormal conditions handling.
9
Performance testing can be used to evaluate how well each individual Subsystem, each pair of Subsystem Instances and
10
all the Subsystems in the O-RAN Deployment Blueprint inter-operate to achieve the best in class cost-performance ratio.
11
This can include quantifying the O-RAN Deployment Blueprint when Subsystems from multiple vendors inter-operate
12
under Performance test conditions through
13
1. Performing testing using the same set of KPIs, for example examining if the latency figures can be achieved in
14
performance testing conditions.
15
2. Measuring resources utilization efficiency for example with Radio resource blocks, Open Fronthaul and xHaul
16
transport, O-Cloud computing / networking / storage and power consumption / energy efficiency.
17

18
Abnormal testing will in some cases be required to be performed to validate fault management and zero-touch network
19
automation techniques such as self-healing functions.
20
6.6.3  Radio channel variations and impacts on the overall system
21
performance and QoE
22
Radio access networks should be tested with close to real-world radio channel conditions, variations of the channel
23
conditions and mobility patterns in the lab environment for a proper evaluation of the overall system performance of the
24
RAN and QoE of the services handled by the RAN.
25
For example testing key 3GPP RAN functions such as Radio resource, Beam / Cell level mobility management and
26
advanced use cases defined by O-RAN such as Traffic Steering and Massive MIMO Beamforming Optimization will
27
require the test environment to be setup with the appropriate network and slices topology, radio channel conditions, UEs
28
distributions and mobility patterns, which otherwise these functions and use cases cannot be properly tested and evaluated.
29
Testing O-RAN Deployment Blueprints consisting of Subsystems from multiple vendors under the appropriate radio
30
channel conditions and mobility patterns will be required to validate how well the multi-vendors Subsystems inter-operate
31
under these test conditions.
32
6.6.4  Management, Orchestration and Network Automation
33
In general, operators require the Management & Orchestration (MANO) and Network Automation capabilities of their
34
networks to be robustly validated.
35
In order for operators to be able to deploy O-RAN networks and network slices which can consist of Subsystems from
36
multiple vendors, multi-vendors interoperability testing will be required for validating the management and orchestration
37
functions of all the Subsystems de

e able to deploy O-RAN networks and network slices which can consist of Subsystems from
36
multiple vendors, multi-vendors interoperability testing will be required for validating the management and orchestration
37
functions of all the Subsystems defined in the O-RAN Deployment Blueprints.
38
O-RAN Alliance has specified a set of prioritized use cases for O-RAN orchestration of virtualized RAN and the interfaces
39
used for management and orchestration, in particular the O1 interface between the service management and orchestration
40
framework and the RAN managed functions and the O2 interface between the service management and orchestration
41
framework and the O-Cloud Infrastructure Management Services/Deployment Management Services that controls
42
resource assignment for Virtualized Network Functions.
43

________________________________________________________________________________________________

42
Operators will require guidance on the E2E Test Cases and KPIs which can be used to test and evaluate the functionality
1
and performance for each of these orchestration use cases in order to be able to quantify the feasibility and benefits of
2
deploying O-RAN compliant networks.
3
6.6.5  Additional considerations related to practical deployment aspects
4
In addition to performing testing based on 3GPP, ITU-T, IEEE specified functionalities, it is important as well to take
5
into considerations the practical deployment aspects which operators will need to consider and therefore tested as part of
6
the E2E Testing framework. These considerations include
7
1. Performance Evaluation and Monitoring
8
2. Robustness, Resilience, Reliability, Security
9
3. Troubleshooting and Root Cause Analysis (RCA)
10
4. Practical Network Operating Conditions such as fronthaul transport loading and non-zero variable delays
11
5. FCAPS including fault, configuration, accounting, performance, and security management
12
6. System Deployment lifecycle (installs, upgrades)
13
7. Virtualization, interaction with O-Cloud (NFVi), Management and Orchestration (MANO)
14
8. Evolution towards Zero Touch Automation network management
15

16
System Deployment lifecycle (installs, upgrades) involves multiple phases of the System Deployment lifecycle which
17
will include new installs and as well as future field upgrades scenarios such as
18
1. Performing software or firmware upgrades of the existing installed O-RAN Network Functions (e.g. increased
19
performance, enhanced capabilities such as dynamic spectrum sharing, bug fixes and others)
20
2. Installing new O-RAN Network Functions which are required to interoperate with existing installed O-RAN
21
Network Functions (e.g. adding new O-RUs from a new vendor to the field operational O-DU currently serving
22
O-RUs from the current vendor, new xApp to be installed onto the current near-RT RIC)
23
3. Installing new or Replacing existing hardware (or O-Cloud) to support existing installed O-RAN Network
24
Functions (e.g. adding, replacing storage, networking, computing resources)
25

26
It is therefore important to define testing templates ensuring that the essential testing is performed for the specific
27
Subsystem Instances, Subsystem Instances Pairs and Open Interfaces and System Deployment Blueprint which are
28
affected by the System Deployment lifecycle scenarios.
29
6.7  Test Scenarios and KPIs to be considered
30
A few examples of Test Scenarios and KPIs which are needing to be considered for testing O-RAN Deployment Blueprint
31
consisting of Subsystems from multiple vendors are shared in more details in this section.
32
1. Mobility management
33
2. Deployability
34

35
6.7.1  Mobility Management
36
Mobility management test cases may need to consider test scenarios which involve testing multi-vendors interoperability
37
between Subsystems provided from multiple vendors.
38
Test scenarios can include intra O-RU (inter beams for intra cell and inter cells), inter O-RUs (intra O-DU), inter O-DUs
39
(intra O-CU-CP/O-CU-UP), inter O-CU-CP/O-CU-UPs, Intra vs Inter RATs handovers in Idle and Connected modes.
40
Figure 6-2 shows an example of a test scenario which can be used to verify the interoperability aspects of mobility
41
management in a multi-vendors O-RAN Deployment Blueprint test setup.
42

43

________________________________________________________________________________________________

43

1

In this test scenario

4

The Mobility KPIs including handover attempts/success rates, interruption time (aka latency) to control, user plane and
9
services plane, services performances such as packet losses, jitter and latency should be measured in order to validate that
10
the services SLAs can be met while executing the test sequences.
11
6.7.2  Deployability
12
One of the key considerations for dis-aggregated RAN deployments is the requirements for the underlying transport
13
network which will be dependent on the requirements of the Services and dis-aggregated RAN functions which will be
14
required to interwork over the transport network segments.
15
These requirements are typically simulated, estimated, tested, measured, and validated for dis-aggregated RAN transport
16
planning purposes.
17
O-RAN Deployment Blueprints will be required to go through similar process with the additional complexity that the
18
Subsystems in the same O-RAN Deployment Blueprint may be provided by different vendors which may have different
19
levels of influences on the transport requirements therefore needing to be tested and validated with test setup
20
considerations outlined in Section 6.6.
21
The Integrity and Utilization KPIs including transport capacity/throughput, packet losses, jitter and latency should be
22
measured during the testing process taking into considerations the following aspects
23
1. Capacity/throughput for Open fronthaul interface for transport planning purposes, which can vary depending on
24
test scenarios and key factors such as radio conditions among others outlined in Section 6.6.3.
25
2. Latency for transport planning purposes and delay management interoperability which can vary dependent on
26
the transport options and can be impacting performance and users-services experiences

onditions among others outlined in Section 6.6.3.
25
2. Latency for transport planning purposes and delay management interoperability which can vary dependent on
26
the transport options and can be impacting performance and users-services experiences.
27
3. Resources Utilization based on test profiles which should include networking, computing, storage resources.
28

Methodology

This annex provides an overview on the O-RAN Software Community (OSC) work and its current software releases and

B.1 O-RAN Software Community
6
The O-RAN Software Community (OSC) is an open source software development project aimed at providing an open
7
source implementation of an end-to-end RAN system following O-RAN Alliance architecture and specifications.  The
8
OSC is hosted by the Linux Foundation and funded by the O-RAN Alliance.
9
The OSC is led by a 12-member Technical Oversight Committee (TOC) with its current members representing AT&T,
10
China Mobile, Deutsche Telekom, Ericsson, Nokia, NTT DOCOMO, Orange, Radisys and Verizon.
11
The working effort of the OSC is organized into the following development projects:
12
•
Operations and Maintenance (OAM)
13
•
Non-Realtime RAN Intelligent Controller (NONRTRIC)
14
•
Near-Realtime RAN Intelligent Controller Platform (RIC)
15
•
Near-Realtime RAN Intelligent Controller Applications (RICAPP)
16
•
O-RAN Central Unit (OCU)
17
•
O-RAN Distributed Unit High (ODUHIGH)
18
•
O-RAN Distributed Unit LOW (ODULOW)
19
•
Simulations (SIM)
20
•
Infrastructure (INF)
21
•
Documentation (DOC)
22
•
Integration and Testing (INT)
23
and subcommittee(s)
24
•
Requirements and Software Architecture Committee (RSAC)
25

26
The OSC conducts its business on open communication and development platforms including Zoom teleconferencing
27
bridge, Groups.io mailing lists, Confluence wiki, and Git/Gerrit source code repositories.  All O-RAN SC information
28
and O-RAN SC developed software can be accessed via resources listed in Annex B.6.
29
B.2 OSC Development Cycles
30
The OSC developed software is released on a bi-annual schedule, first in May/June time frame and the second in
31
November/December.   The naming scheme of releases follows color names in alphabetical order, with individual release
32
names selected by community member voting.  The first four releases are named Amber, Bronze, Cherry, and Dawn.  The
33
OSC delivered its first release, Amber release, in November 2019.
34
The high-level objectives and use cases for the next release are usually selected by the RSAC during the later portion of
35
the current release cycle.  The first several weeks of each release cycle typically are for the design and planning phase
36
where the high-level release objectives are designed into implementable features and tasks, which are distributed to the
37
OSC development projects.  Following the planning phase is the development phase, during which the development
38
projects and teams implement the agreed-upon features.  This phase is divided into three-week sprints where each sprint
39
has its own more manageable implementation and testing goals.  Finally, prior to the release of the software, it is the
40
testing phase, during which the integrated system testing and end-to-end use case testing are conducted, and the viability
41
and quality of the software are verified and evaluated.
42

________________________________________________________________________________________________

55
After each release, the OSC also institutes a maintenance window for the new release during the design and planning
1
phase of the next release cycle.  Normally this time window is used only for fixing major problems discovered after the
2
release.
3

The OSC projects are set up based on the O-RAN Alliance architecture.

B.5 OSC Testing
25
OSC testing effort is divided into five levels
26
1. Unit testing (UT)
27
o
UT is performed by the developers by implementing test cases using programming language specific
28
unit testing and static code analysis framework.
29

57
o
UT is triggered automatically every time when there is source code change submitted into the code
1
repository for review.
2
o
At OSC level the INT project team provides support for unit test and code scan (i.e. static code analysis)
3
integration into Linux Foundation Continuous Integration flow, and result reporting into the SONAR
4
Cloud platform.  Using the reports, TOC sets quality gates such as percentage of code covered by unit
5
test cases, no major issues discovered, etc.
6
2. Project level integrated testing (PIT)
7
o
Each development project is expected to conduct project level integrated testing, where all software
8
components developed by the project are deployed into a single system for testing internal flows.
9
o
PIT is expected to be conducted by individual project teams, at the end of each development sprints or
10
other development milestones.
11
o
At OSC level the INT project team organizes sprint demonstration fests regularly where development
12
project teams gather and demonstrate achieved features in the previous sprint, using project level system
13
deployment in project team’s own testing and demonstration environment.
14
o
The INT project team is also working with individual development projects on Robot testing
15
framework-based testing flows that are to be integrated into Linux Foundation Continuous Integration
16
flow.  Such test flows serve as regression tests for implementation updates and can be triggered
17
automatically by the CI system on a regular basis (e.g. daily) or upon new code submission.
18
3. Project pairwise testing (PPT)
19
o
For projects that deliver O-RAN architectural components that interact with each other, PPT is
20
conducted to ensure communication compatibility.
21
o
PPT sessions are organized by the INT proje

submission.
18
3. Project pairwise testing (PPT)
19
o
For projects that deliver O-RAN architectural components that interact with each other, PPT is
20
conducted to ensure communication compatibility.
21
o
PPT sessions are organized by the INT project team, using either community testing lab or self-arrange
22
testing facilities by involved projects.
23
4. System integrated testing (SIT)
24
o
SIT is whole OSC software testing where all OSC development components are deployed into a single
25
system.  SIT focuses on overall system health, inter-project communication and application
26
compatibility, overall system deployment flow, and resource requirements.
27
o
SIT is conducted by the INT project team using OSC community testing lab.
28
o
SIT is conducted during the testing phase of each release cycle.
29
o
Robot test framework-based health check test flows used as automated regression test.
30
5. Use case testing (UCT)
31
o
UCT is whole OSC software testing where all OSC development components are deployed into a single
32
system.  UCT tests OSC deployment that has passed SIT.
33
o
UCT is conducted by the INT project team using OSC community testing lab.
34
o
UCT is conducted during the testing phase of each release cycle.
35
o
UCT uses Open Testing Framework (OTF), a test flow definition and orchestration tool that is
36
developed as a sub-project under the INT.

O-RAN-WG1 Information Model and Data Models v01.00
Chapter 3. O-RAN Information Model
1
3.1 A general view of an Information Model
2
In general, an Information Model is an abstract but formal representation of entities including their properties,
3
relationships and the operations that can be performed on them.  In includes a representation of concepts and the
4
relationships, constraints, rules, and operations to specify data semantics for a chosen domain of discourse:
5
•
Things (Modeled as Classes) with Definitions
6
•
Class Properties (Attributes); Class Relationships
7
•
Association Types (Simple Association, Aggregation, Composition, Inheritance)
8
•
Multiplicity and Direction
9
•
Operations/Behaviors (optional)
10
•
Represented on a Collection of Class Diagrams
11
•
Implementation Independent
12
•
Interfaces – Operations, Attributes (in, out, return)
13
3.2 Modeling approach, Unified Modeling Language (UML)
14
Modeling is the designing of software applications before coding. Modeling is an essential part of large software
15
projects, and helpful to medium and even small projects as well. A model plays the analogous role in software
16
development that blueprints and other plans (site maps, elevations, physical models) play in the building of a
17
skyscraper.
18
Models raise the level of abstraction by hiding or masking details, bringing out the “big picture,” or by focusing on
19
different aspects of a prototype.
20
The Information Model within O-RAN uses the Unified Modeling Language™ (UML®) from the Object Management
21
Group (OMG) with an open source Model-Based Engineering tool, Eclipse Papyrus.
22
3.3 IISOMI (Informal Inter-SDO Open Model Initiative) guidelines
23
The information model is split into a structural part and a behavioral part; i.e., data model

3.3 IISOMI (Informal Inter-SDO Open Model Initiative) guidelines
23
The information model is split into a structural part and a behavioral part; i.e., data model (structural/static) is decoupled
24
from operations model (behavioral/dynamic).
25
The following guidelines are sourced from a Technical Recommendation developed within IISOMI (Informal Inter-
26
SDO Open Model Initiative) and originally published by the ONF:
27
•
UML 2.5 (Unified Modeling Language) is used for specifying the model
28
•
The model shall be management/control protocol-neutral, i.e., not reflect any middleware protocol-specific
29
characteristics (like e.g., CORBA, HTTP, JMS)
30
•
The model shall be map-able to various protocol-specific interfaces (it is recommended to automate this mapping
31
supported by tools)
32
•
It shall be possible to separate UML artifact properties which are only required for interface related (purpose
33
specific) models.
34
•
Traceability from each modeling construct back to requirements and use cases shall be provided whenever possible.
35

4.5 YANG Conventions
4
This section describes the recommended conventions to be used in the O-RAN Alliance when writing YANG models.
5
In particular, because the creation and maintenance of YANG models is expected to be distributed across  different
6
working groups, this guide is intended to ensure that the way the models are organized and presented will be consistent
7
across the entirety of the O-RAN Alliance.
8
4.5.1 Naming
9
MODULE FILE NAMING: M-Plane YANG modules should have filenames of the form “o-ran-xxx.yang” (for O1 the
10
file naming is TBD)
11
MODULE NAMESPACE: YANG modules should have a namespace defined of the form namespace "urn:o-
12
ran:xxx:version"; where version represents an increasing numerical integer value and where the value used in all newly
13
defined models is "1". The module namespace version will be incremented when any non-backwards compatible
14
changes are introduced into a model.
15
PREFIX NAMING: Each module requires a prefix statement with a prefix that other dependent modules will use (also
16
used in path references within the same module). Prefixes should be short and clear, with abbreviations as appropriate.
17
Module prefixes should be of the form: o-ran-xxx, or or-xxx, and must be unique regardless of over which interface the
18
YANG module is exposed (ex. O1 or Open FrontHaul M-Plane).
19
4.5.2 Revision Statement
20
The revision statement in all YANG models includes a reference statement used to cross-reference to the version of a
21
particular O-RAN publication where the corresponding functionality was initially introduced. The revision statement of
22
the YANG models also includes a description that is used to track the versioning of the YANG model. All revision
23

O-RAN-WG1 Information Model and Data Models v01.00
statement descriptions will begin with version a.b.c, where a, b and c are used to reflect the version of the YANG
1
model, where        ‘a’ corresponds to the first digit of the O-RAN specification version where the corresponding
2
description was first introduced; ‘b’ is incremented when errors in the YANG model have been corrected; ‘c’ is
3
incremented only in working versions of the YANG model indicating incremental changes during the editing process.
4
Hence, all published versions of O-RAN alliance YANG models should have this value set to zero.
5
4.5.3 Indents
6
O-RAN Alliance YANG models should use two-space tab indents.
7
4.5.4 YANG Language Usage
8
YANG VERSION: All models should use YANG data modeling language version 1.1 [1] (RFC 7950) and follow the
9
Guidelines for Authors and Reviewers of YANG Data Model Documents [RFC 6087].
10
TOP-LEVEL DATA NODE: There should only be one top-level data node defined in each YANG module, if any data
11
nodes are defined at all.
12
NMDA (Network Management Datastore Architecture): No O-RAN YANG models should prevent the use of NMDA
13
[RFC 8342].
14
KEY-LESS LISTS OF OPERATIONAL STATE: Although permitted in YANG, the use of a list that consists of
15
operational-state without a defined key should be avoided.
16
VALIDATION: All YANG modules should be validated / compiled with pyang tool using the following flag: pyang --
17
lint <module>. Note, successful compilation with pyang does not guarantee a working model, as xPATH expressions
18
aren't evaluated and forbidden operational data dependencies in the configuration may not generate appropriate errors.
19
NETCONF ACCESS CONTROL: Sensitive data within models should be tagged with an appropriate "nacm:default"
20
statement.

aren't evaluated and forbidden operational data dependencies in the configuration may not generate appropriate errors.
19
NETCONF ACCESS CONTROL: Sensitive data within models should be tagged with an appropriate "nacm:default"
20
statement. O-RAN makes use of NACM (NETCONF Access Control Model RFC 8341) rules to define the privileges
21
associated with user groupings. An O-RAN NETCONF server should hard code these restrictions into the server. The
22
defined NACM rules are therefore unmodifiable, with the rules being used to provide an "external indication" of such
23
restrictions.
24
CONSTRAINTS: Generally, O-RAN systems should strive to consider a blank configuration to be a valid config.
25
4.5.5 Cross Working Group Co-ordination
26
Models that are likely to be applicable to more than one O-RAN Alliance working group should provide clear
27
delineation between separate working groups configuration and/or state. The use of feature and if-feature is
28
recommended to ensure that NETCONF servers are not required to implement the entire data model, e.g., when aspects
29
of such relate to the individual working group defined use cases. The feature name should indicate which working
30
group the capabilities have been defined by.

3 GoB / L3 Mobility
1
3.1 Overview
2
Grid of Beam Optimization (GoB) provides an automated beam forming configuration tailored to the topology of the cell,
3
the physical environment, as well as the distribution of users and traffic in a cell (e.g. wide beams might cover low-density
4
areas while narrow beams might cover high-density areas). Beam-based Mobility Robustness Optimization (bMRO) is
5
an autonomous self-optimizing algorithm that improves beam-based inter-cell mobility performance by applying beam-
6
specific Cell Individual Offsets (CIO) on the handover triggers between neighbor cells, based on the analysis of beam-
7
AI/ML assisted network-wide (multi-gNB/TRP) optimizations framework proactively and autonomously infers optimal
8
configuration per gNB/TRP for SS Burst Set, DMRS and CSI-RS based on available measurements, observations, and
9
PIs at different nodes of the 3GPP NR and/or O-RAN access and core network elements.
10

metadata.section_title: Problem Statement, Solution and Value Proposition

chunks.section_title: Problem Statement, Solution and Value Proposition
chunks.text:
11
3.2 Solution 1: Grid-of-Beams Beamforming (GoB BF) Optimization
12
3.2.1 Problem Statement, Solution and Value Proposition
13
Massive MIMO (mMIMO) is among the key methods to increase performance and QoS in 5G networks. Capacity
14
enhancement is obtained by means of beamforming of the transmitted signals, and by spatially multiplexing data streams.
15
Beamforming can increase the received signal power and simultaneously decrease the interference generated for other
16
users, hence resulting in higher SINR and higher user throughputs. Grid-of-Beams (GoB) with the corresponding beam
17
sweeping has been introduced to allow beamforming of the control channels used during initial access as well as for data
18
transmission and reception, mainly for high frequency (but can be used also for the sub-6 GHz band) MIMO operation.
19
The physical properties of the antenna array and its possible configurations characterize the span of the beams, namely
20
the horizontal and vertical aperture in which beamforming is supported, and therefore the coverage area and the shape of
21
the cell. mMIMO can be deployed in 5G macrocell clusters as well as in heterogeneous networks, where macro-cells and
22
small cells co-exist and complement each other for better aggregated capacity and coverage. In order to obtain optimal
23
beamforming and cell resources (Tx power, PRB) configuration, one will have to look at a multi-cell environment instead
24
of a single cell. Moreover, different vendors may have different implementations in terms of the number of beams, the
25
horizontal/vertical beam widths, azimuth and elevation range, to achieve the desired coverage. In a multi-node/multi-
26
vendor scenario, centralized monitoring and control is required to offer optimal coverage, capacity and mobi

metadata.section_title: Problem Statement, Solution and Value Proposition

chunks.section_title: Problem Statement, Solution and Value Proposition
chunks.text:
ber of beams, the
25
horizontal/vertical beam widths, azimuth and elevation range, to achieve the desired coverage. In a multi-node/multi-
26
vendor scenario, centralized monitoring and control is required to offer optimal coverage, capacity and mobility
27
performance as well as control over electromagnetic emissions in order to comply with regulatory requirements.
28
The problem associated with traditional mMIMO BF is that its performance is highly dependent on the choice of the BF
29
pattern. Manual configuration is usually based on the empirical knowledge and manual test results of the domain expert(s)
30
and is performed in a semi-static way. That is, (near-)real time contextual, per-site information (such as cell geometry
31
change, user/traffic distribution, mobility patterns, seasonalities etc.) is taken into account in a suboptimal and non-real
32
time way. This may cause one or more of the following problems:
33
1. High inter-cell interference.
34
2. Unbalanced traffic between neighboring cells.
35
3. Low performance at the cell edges or throughout the cell.
36
4. Poor handover performance.
37

metadata.section_title: Problem Statement, Solution and Value Proposition

chunks.section_title: Problem Statement, Solution and Value Proposition
chunks.text:
38
This solution proposes a framework that allows the operator to flexibly configure the mMIMO BF parameters in a cell or
39
in a cluster of cells by means of policies and configuration assisted by machine learning (ML) techniques. The
40
configuration optimization relies on contextual information and patterns such as the user distribution, traffic demand
41
distribution, cell geometries, and mobility.
42

43
