Objectives
O-RAN supports multi-vendor deployments where failures can occur at various levels. This document captures the WG1
Resiliency study outcomes, outlining use cases where the SMO monitors criteria and triggers actions to reconfigure
system components, minimizing the impact of component failures on service availability. It can also consider the
scenarios with both single and multiple component failures, ensuring effective utilization of diverse designs from various
solution providers. This leads to a robust end-to-end resiliency solution covering Fronthaul, RAN OAM, Network
Functions, and O-Cloud infrastructure.

5.1
Resiliency Concepts
It describes the fundamental principles, strategies, and mechanisms designed to ensure system reliability and continuous
service availability, despite failures or adverse conditions.
•
Redundant architectures: Implementing redundant paths and components to provide alternative routes or
backups in case of failure.
•
Fault detection and recovery: Using mechanisms for detecting faults and quickly recovering from failures to
minimize downtime.
•
Load balancing and failover: Distributing traffic and workloads across multiple nodes in NR Cells and optionally
LTE cells prevent overloading any single component, enhancing resiliency by ensuring smooth failover and
continuous service availability when failures occur.
•
Proactive measures: Employing predictive analytics and monitoring tools to identify potential issues before
they cause service interruptions.

5.4
Resiliency for NF failures
5.4.1
Overview
Resiliency for NF failures ensure service availability with minimal disruption by leveraging static or dynamic failover,
session recovery, and robust redundancy mechanisms. An appropriate recovery mechanism can be employed for the
critical interfaces like O1, Fronthaul, E2, and F1-C to ensure service with minimum disruption during link failures. For
example, SCTP based transport redundancy for F1-C [i.4] and cloud-native deployments [i.5 and i.6] can leverage the
various resiliency capabilities (e.g., Kubernetes based) to ensure high availability and implement failover mechanisms for
NF, thereby enhancing the overall resiliency of the O-RAN Network. Multi-layered resiliency spans both physical and
virtual components, supporting high-priority services with active-standby setups and an appropriate recovery action. This
approach integrates cross-domain fault detection and configuration to support efficient service transitions and minimize
service disruptions.
Protocols including for example TNL [i.3 and i.4], and additional appropriate recovery mechanisms, can be utilized to
ensure that O-RAN networks meet robust resiliency objectives, and can be recovered from the diverse failure scenarios
while maintaining service quality.

An O-RU failure can affect the operation of carrier(s), potentially affect cell availability and resulting in service
degradation, such as reduced throughput. This failure affects the data flow between the affected cell of network and end-
users, potentially leading to interruptions in data transmission, reduced throughput, and a decrease in overall network
capacity.  The impact of the failure can extend to multiple users, causing widespread connectivity loss, and degraded
service quality.

5.5
Resiliency for interface failures
5.5.1
Overview
Resiliency for interface failures focuses on maintaining efficient network operations with minimal disruption, even in the
event of physical or virtual interface issues in 5G systems. Key strategies include NIC card failures through physical
and/or virtual NIC failovers, implementing dynamic IP routing with SCTP multihoming, and utilizing TNLA [i.2] to
enhance control plane reliability. These methods leverage heartbeat mechanisms and multiple transport addresses to
facilitate rapid failover and recovery. By adhering to 3GPP standards (e.g., TS 23.501 [i.2], TS 29.244 [i.16]), these
approaches ensure service continuity and effectively minimize disruptions during failures.
5.5.2
Generic aspects
Resiliency for interface failures aims to ensure seamless network operations with minimum disruption, even when
physical or virtual network interfaces experience issues. This requires deploying robust mechanisms to maintain service
availability and reduce downtime.
Strategies for ensuring interface resiliency in 5G RAN systems focus on redundancy and load balancing, for e.g., utilizing
Linux bonding for physical NICs and failover-capable virtual NICs in virtual environments. IP-level routing resilience is
achieved through multiple IP addresses, SCTP multihoming, and dynamic protocols such as IP Fast Reroute. Control
plane protocol stability is reinforced through TNLA, incorporating features like multiple transport addresses and heartbeat
mechanisms. These reliability measures, outlined by 3GPP (for e.g., TS 23.501 [i.2] and TS 23.502 [i.3]) enable quick
recovery from failures while minimizing service disruptions.

5.5.2.1      NIC failure - hardware or virtual interface failure
NIC failures can occur in both physical and virtualized environments due to hardware malfunction, driver issues, or
connectivity disruptions. These failures result in the inability of the system to send or receive network traffic, potentially
leading to service interruptions and degraded performance.
NIC failure mitigation ensures uninterrupted network connectivity in the event of hardware or virtual interface failures.
For physical NICs, solutions such as Linux bonding aggregate multiple NICs into a single logical interface, providing
redundancy and load balancing. In the event of a failure, traffic is automatically redirected to functioning NICs, with
configurations like active-standby for failover or load balancing for enhanced throughput. In virtualized environments,
failover-capable virtual NICs provide redundancy by switching traffic to backup NICs during a failure. The configurations
such as NIC teaming, further ensure smooth failover and high availability. Together, these strategies are to improve the
stability and reduce service disruption caused by NIC failures.
5.5.2.2      IP level routing failure
IP level routing failures occur when the primary network path becomes unavailable due to issues such as link disruption,
node failure, or routing misconfigurations. These failures can lead to packet loss, increased latency, or total service
interruptions, affecting critical network operations.

5.5.2.3      SCTP connection failure
SCTP connection failures can occur when the communication path between two endpoints is disrupted. This can result
from physical link issues, routing failures, or misconfigurations. Such failures impact data transfer, control signalling,
and application performance. SCTP, however, provides mechanisms like multihoming and retransmission strategies to
recover from such failures [i.4].
Application protocol stability is enhanced through mechanisms like 3GPP TNLA, heartbeat monitoring, and redundant
associations [i.4]. TNLA enables multihoming by supporting multiple transport addresses, allowing traffic to reroute
through alternate paths if the primary path fails. Heartbeat mechanisms actively monitor path availability by exchanging
regular signals between endpoints to detect and handle failures quickly. Redundant SCTP associations provide parallel

Service restoration time considerations
Service restoration time is an important factor that plays a critical role in resiliency. There are several critical factors that
affect service restoration time after an O-DU failure:
•
Failover mechanisms: Networks using automatic failover mechanisms with pre-configured backup O-DUs
reduce service restoration times. In contrast, systems with manual or dynamic reconfigurations experience
longer delays.
•
IP switchover and NF coordination: IP switchover and NF coordina

automatic failover mechanisms with pre-configured backup O-DUs
reduce service restoration times. In contrast, systems with manual or dynamic reconfigurations experience
longer delays.
•
IP switchover and NF coordination: IP switchover and NF coordination with the resiliency controller are
essential for re-establishing the service.
•
Backup strategies: 1:1 (one backup per O-DU) offers faster recovery but are more resource-intensive.

This approach facilitates a distributed recovery mechanism to ensure network resiliency against failures. It also ensures

recovery actions. The O-RAN hierarchical deployment offers significant advantages for resiliency from an OAM
perspective. By clearly defining roles and responsibilities, it simplifies management, enhances fault detection and

6.3.1
Backup options
The SMO serves as the resiliency controller, playing a critical role in minimizing service disruptions caused by failures.
It manages the switchover to backup units and resources, ensuring uninterrupted service across the network. To achieve
this, the SMO ensures resiliency by managing resilient instances for network functions such as O-DU and O-CU. This is
accomplished through backup mechanisms like software-based backups and hardware-based backups, to maintain service
continuity.
6.3.1.1
Software-based backup
Involves creating snapshots or backups of the software configurations, which can be utilized to recover the service in case
of failure. For example, NF software images, container images, or application states.
6.3.1.2
Hardware-based backup
Dedicated standby hardware components along with associated software that can take over in case of failure. This is
usually more costly but provides a quicker recovery.
6.3.2  Redundant node options
To ensure the resiliency in an end-to-end O-RAN systems, the redundant or standby node options are necessary to quickly
recover from the failures, but at the associated cost.
The standby node or NF can have the same capabilities as the active NF. The SMO can manage this depending on the
resiliency scenarios and deployments. The above can be quantified in terms of the management of carrier resources,
associated throughput, the number of UEs, and the number of cells/sectors.
In a scenario where a standby O-DU is unavailable, malfunctioning, or experiencing issues such as port failures or M-
plane connectivity problems, it cannot be utilized for recovery. In such cases, the SMO may need to explore alternative
recover

ors.
In a scenario where a standby O-DU is unavailable, malfunctioning, or experiencing issues such as port failures or M-
plane connectivity problems, it cannot be utilized for recovery. In such cases, the SMO may need to explore alternative
recovery strategies like having more than one resilient O-DU instance, but end-to-end service availability might not be
fully restored if no functional back-up O-DU is available. In a scenario with multiple back-up O-DU instances, SMO can
decide which O-DU can take over the O-RU operation based on the traffic requirements and network conditions.
For example, the O-DU resiliency options can consider the following.
•
Active-standby – If the active O-DU fails, the standby O-DU is activated. The M-plane connection with the O-
RU can remain active, enabling the standby O-DU to take over the O-RU services as quickly as possible. In
this scenario, resources can either be pre-allocated or allocated only after a failure occurs depending on the
deployment.
•
The active and standby O-DUs can be connected to the same O-CU (Intra O-CU) or different O-CUs (Inter O-
CU) depending on the deployment.
•
The example standby configuration options include 1+1, N (Active) + K (Standby), and N+1 (All active with 1
hot spare).

Each active node has a dedicated standby node and it is simple but can be resource-intensive and expensive.

One standby node serves multiple active nodes. This is more resource-efficient and cost effective for managing failovers.

within O-RAN system to minimize service disruptions. This includes fault detection, performance monitoring, and
proactive maintenance for critical components such as O-RU, O-DU, and associated network services. It also covers the
cloud infrastructure in the case of CNF deployment, as well as the interfaces like fronthaul and O1. The SMO plays a

cloud infrastructure in the case of CNF deployment, as well as the interfaces like fronthaul and O1. The SMO plays a
critical role in managing these aspects, ensuring service disruptions minimized as much as possible by appropriate
recovery mechanisms.
SMO can leverage the AI/ML capabilities to enhance decision-making during resiliency scenarios. This enables the SMO
to efficiently recover service paths and restore service availability while minimizing disruptions. This approach

Performance monitoring and fault detection: Utilizing supervisory controls to detect failures at multiple elements involved

6.4
Relationships with rolling upgrade
6.4.1
Overview
Ensuring resiliency during rolling upgrades in a 5G network is critical to maintaining uninterrupted service for users while
upgrading network components incrementally. Rolling upgrades in 5G networks involve updating software, hardware, or
configurations in a phased manner to avoid downtime and ensure continuous service availability. Many resiliency
techniques for protecting 5G network against failures are key enablers for resilient rolling upgrade also. Below are the
key resiliency technologies and strategies for rolling upgrades in 5G mobile networks.

________________________________________________________________________________________________
26
6.4.2
Redundant NF architectures
Redundant architecture ensures that multiple instances of critical network components (e.g. O-DU, O-CU-CP) are
available to handle traffic and prevent service down time not only due to unexpected failures but also due to rolling
upgrades. High availability distributing traffic across redundant instances. Service interruption in one instance during the
upgrading will not affect the entire system thus ensure service continuity.
Both active-standby or active-active NF redundancy architecture can be approached. In active-standby configuration, new
NFs take over the UE traffic when a NF fails or being shut down due to upgrading. In active-active configuration, critical
UE traffic is steered to healthy network functions that were serving other users before a failure or upgrading happens to
a NF. The rolling upgrading case, the new NF taking over the traffic can be the newer version of application or equipment
to be upgraded to or the older version to be fallback to. Cross-region redundancy, e.g. deploy active and standby O-CU-
CPs and O-CU-UPs in different regional data, may be also required to prevent single regional failures during upgrading.
Existing redundant and failover features supported in O-RAN and 3GPP, e.g. OFH shared O-RU for redundancy,
F1/X2/Xn/Ng interface multi-TNL associations and failovers, are important techniques to support rolling upgrade also. It
ensures standby NF instances are brought in and connected with other NFs automatically and the service recovers quickly
or is completely uninterrupted during the upgrading.

6.4.3
Resiliency technologies in cloud-native NFs
5G networks increasingly rely on cloud-native principles, such as containerization and microservices, for scalability and
flexibility. Cloud-native architecture enables rolling upgrades of individual microservices without affecting the entire NF.
Automated scaling ensures network capacity is not affected during failures or upgrading. Automated failover mechanisms
ensure existing traffic and context are hand overed to other healthy microservice instances seamlessly with less effort and
service interruption during the upgrading. Load balancers distribute traffic across multiple instances of an application,
traffic is routed away from instances being updated to ensure uninterrupted service.
Rollback mechanisms allow reverting to a previous version of software or configurations if issues are detected during
rolling upgrades. It minimizes downtime and service disruptions in case of failures during the upgrading. For example,
the related cloud technologies include:
•
Kubernetes rollback
•
Version control for network configurations (e.g., GitOps)
•
Other cloud-native rollback tools
6.4.4
Redundant transport paths
Redundant network paths ensure that traffic can be rerouted in case of failures during upgrades. It prevents single points
of failure in the transport network and ensures continuous connectivity during upgrades.
6.4.5
Monitoring and observability
Performance monitoring and fault management data provide insights into the health and performance of the 5G network
during either unexpected failures or rolling upgrades. Detecting and mitigating issues in real-time is important. Automate

servability

Basic objective

another O-DU that has its management plane fully operational and ready to take over.
The actors involved can include the SMO, O-CU, O-DUs, and O-RU, which work together to maintain service continuity
against O-DU failures.

7.3.1 Basic objective
This solution outlines the system behaviour for ensuring resiliency in O-CU-CP failure recovery within O-RAN networks.
It addresses complete loss of management or partial failures causing service interruptions while the O1 interface remains
active. The framework enables operators to detect failures and restore services through appropriate recovery actions. The
focus is on maintaining network resiliency and minimizing disruptions, while root cause analysis is outside the solution's
scope.
The objective is to provide an effective approach for operators to manage and recover from failures, ensuring robust
network operations.
7.3.2 Roles of involved entities
The description below outlines the actors involved:
1)
SMO
a.
SMO assigns initial roles to O-CU-CPs (active, standby) or resiliency pairs based on operator decisions.
b. It facilitates high-level decision-making during failures and resiliency scenarios, including managing
O-CU-CP during partial or complete failures, interface disruptions, and planned maintenance.
c.
SMO enables service recovery by transitioning operations from the active O-CU-CP to a standby O-
CU-CP, minimizing service disruption for end users.
2)
O-CU-CPs
a.

7.4 Solution 3: Enhanced network resiliency through O-RU rehoming,
leveraging the SMO framework's transport resiliency
management capabilities.
7.4.1 Basic objective
This solution describes how the SMO framework monitors FM and PM datas from transport networks and various network
functions (O-RU, O-DU, O-CU-CP, O-CU-UP) to detect failures and facilitate the rehoming of O-RUs from failed O-
DUs to operational ones. The rehoming process involves reconnecting O-RUs with the operational O-DU through either
pre-configured transport paths or those configured by the transport network manager, based on policies provided by the
SMO. Once alternate transport paths are established, O-RUs connect to the new O-DU via M-plane. SMO configures the
necessary transport and cell/carrier resources to restore services.
O-RU rehoming can be initiated proactively, based on failure predictions, performance degradation detection, planned
maintenance (e.g., O-DU software updates), or resource utilization status (for load balancing or capacity optimization).
Alternatively, it can be triggered reactively in response to failures or unexpected events such as disasters. The process is
part of SMO-driven automation to minimize service impact during maintenance or network disruptions.
In case of scenario based on resource utilization, if network function resources (e.g., CPU, memory, I/O) fall below a
defined threshold (e.g., 20%), SMO identifies underutilized O-DUs. For example, during non-peak hours (e.g., 24:00–
05:00) in locations like shopping malls or stadiums, aggregated O-RUs connected to specific O-DUs may experience low
utilization. SMO evaluates the target O-DU's capacity to ensure it can acco

d O-DUs. For example, during non-peak hours (e.g., 24:00–
05:00) in locations like shopping malls or stadiums, aggregated O-RUs connected to specific O-DUs may experience low
utilization. SMO evaluates the target O-DU's capacity to ensure it can accommodate additional O-RUs before rehoming.
This enables the shutdown of underutilized O-DUs, saving energy, especially in cloud-native deployments.
O-RU rehoming can be utilized during planned maintenance, such as O-DU software upgrades, by redirecting O-RUs to
another O-DU.
The transport path resiliency ensures minimal service disruption during maintenance or unexpected failures that occur
with O-DU(s). Overall, the SMO orchestrates these processes to improve network resiliency as shown in Figure 7.4.1-1.

O-Cloud managed by the SMO Framework
7.5.1 Basic objective
To address NF Deployment(s) failure in O-Cloud, this solution ensures rapid redeployment of the affected NF.
Once the SMO framework detects the failure through RAN OAM, FOCOM, and NFO, SMO coordinates with FOCOM
and NFO for an automated recovery process, for e.g., instructing DMS to recreate the NF Deployment(s). This enables
efficient, automated recovery, minimizing service disruption without manual intervention.

Solution 5:  Multi-Domain Recovery Service
7.6.1 Basic objective
The following solution applies to the path failure scenario described in clause 5.6. The details of multi-domain recovery
service procedures are described below.
When a traffic failure is identified, e.g., by the SMO or the network operator, the SMO can trigger a recovery process by
providing the details of the failed path to a recovery service, such as the MDRS, within the SMO. In response, the recovery
service queries the RAN NF OAM and TE&IV services for information pertaining to network topology, alarms/events,
loading, along with operator defined policies.  The recovery service uses this information to identify existing Alternative
Path (AP), e.g. using available backup hardware, and if possible, can generate the new AP(s) information.

________________________________________________________________________________________________
58
AP generation can be the responsibility of a function, alternate path generation function (APGF), within the MDRS. Once
the information AP is determined, the MDRS configures the relevant network domains, e.g. via O1/O2/new interface, to
enable the recovery with the AP.
7.6.2
Roles of involved entities
The description below outlines the actors involved:
Transport network Manager (TN Manager):
Uses SMO policies/configurations to manage transport paths, facilitating updated configuration from SMO to be applied
(directly or indirectly) to the transport network nodes.  Notifies the SMO when a transport node failure occurs, e.g. in the
transport path between O-RU and O-DU.
SMO:
Accountable for delivering data on existing failed paths to the MDRS_API and receiving updates on AP identification
and successful reconfiguration implementation.  Triggers MDRS process when notified by TN Manager when transport
network failures occur.
RAN-NF-OAM:
Collects, aggregates and exposes network-wide events and alarms of network objects (including and not limited to
infrastructure, platform, application and transport).
TE&IV:
Pulls, stores and exposes a detailed (high-level and low level) network information, network objects including utilization
parameters.
MDRS_API:
Queries RAN NF OAM service and TE&IV service to gather data on topology, alarms, and load conditions followed by
identifying or generating optimal AP(s) and sending AP details to relevant network domains.
APGF:
Identifies existing alternative paths (AP) and generates new AP information that can be utilized, assigns weights to each
identified existing AP and new AP information, and selects an AP based on assigned weights.

NTN development status in standard organizations
4.1
3GPP
4.1.1
Overview
Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTN) are a significant focus within the 3GPP standards, particularly for integrating satellite into 5G
and beyond. Here's a summary of the current development status:
1. Release 15 and 16: Study phase on scenarios, use cases, channel models and impact of NTN to the 5G System, as well
as solutions for 5G New Radio (NR) support for Non-Terrestrial Networks.
2. Release 17 and 18: These releases introduced NTN with a transparent (bent-pipe) architecture, where satellites act as
radio repeaters without on-board processing capabilities. This approach was chosen for its simplicity and early
deployment potential. Both NR-NTN and IoT-NTN are supported. Release 18 introduced support for NR NTN above
10 GHz, such as broadband in Ka band.
3. Release 19: This release marks a major milestone with the introduction of a regenerative payload architecture. In this
scenario, a complete gNB (Next Generation Node B) is placed on the satellite, allowing for greater integration and
flexibility, and opening up new constellation topologies and use cases). This architecture supports packet processing
directly on the satellite, enabling features like improved mobility management.
4. Release 20: The next release is currently in the planning phase and a 3GPP RAN workshop in RAN#106 (12/2024)
discussed potential NTN features for Rel-20. The initial work plan for Rel-20 was decided in RAN#108 (06/2025).

Technological Challenges: The development of NTN involves unique challenges such as high Doppler shifts, longer
propagation delays, and larger cell sizes due to the high altitudes of satellites. Enhanced beam management and regulatory
considerations are also crucial. Most of these challenges are already covered by Rel-17 and 18.
Future Prospects: The ongoing work aims to further integrate NTN with terrestrial networks, enhancing global coverage
and resilience. The regenerative payload architecture is expected to support advanced functionalities like "store and
forward," which allows satellites to store data temporarily and forward it when connectivity is restored, and also UE-
satellite-UE communication with reduced latency.
4.1.2

2. Adaptation to physical and access layer aspects, radio access network, system architecture, radio resource
management, and RF requirements.
3. Support for NTN-NR (5G New Radio (NR)) based satellite access in FR1 bands for handheld devices.
4. Support for NTN-IoT (NB-IoT and eMTC) based satellite access for massive IoT and handheld messaging use cases.
Release 18:
1. Enhancements for NR-NTN and IoT-NTN, especially the time and location based conditional handover (CHO) for

38.108 and 38.101-5).

Key NTN use cases analysis in O-RAN enabled by RIC
5.1
Use Case Group 1: TN and NTN interworking and cooperation
5.1.1
Overview
In most cases, these NTN networks and services are not anticipated to be completely standalone offerings, but rather intended
at least in part as a complement to Terrestrial Networks, for example to provide coverage extension in white spots and hard to
reach areas, 3D coverage at altitude, or a layer of resiliency.  In fact, the ability for NTN to eliminate or alleviate coverage gaps
in the Terrestrial Network was one of the key motivations for the introduction of NTN in 3GPP since the beginning.
Based on the current market trends, it appears NTN deployment motivations will in most cases fall into one of the following
categories:
-
Existing Satellite Network Operators (SNOs) who are looking to serve the NTN market in addition to or in evolution
of their existing non-3GPP satellite services.
-
New entrant SNOs who are seeking to uniquely provide NTN services.
-
Mobile Network Operators (MNOs) who are seeking to extend their network via NTN.
-
New entrant MNOs who are seeking provide homogenous TN and NTN coverage
Therefore, it is expected that many MNOs may seek to extend their own Terrestrial Network services via NTN, however the
current market trends indicate that they will likely not seek to deploy and operate their own satellites, but rather form
agreements with one or multiple NTN SNOs, who will provide coverage over areas of interest on behalf of their partner
MNOs.
For this to be achieved, the MNO’s and SNO’s networks will need to interact and coordinate with one another at some level.
The required degree of interaction and information sharing required between the two operator domains will depend on the
requirements of the specific use

he MNO’s and SNO’s networks will need to interact and coordinate with one another at some level.
The required degree of interaction and information sharing required between the two operator domains will depend on the
requirements of the specific use case and on the depth of integration between the two segments.  This interaction is essential in
order to for example make the NTN network aware of where the boundaries of the terrestrial network exist, share handover
preparation information, reselection targets, etc. and conversely make the terrestrial network aware of when an NTN is
available to its users.
The following clauses describe some of the use cases that fall within the category of TN and NTN interworking and
cooperation and that have been grouped under Use Case Group 1 (UCG#1).
5.1.2
Use Case 1-1: TN-NTN Coverage Information Sharing
5.1.2.1
Use Case Description
In order for an MNO and their partner SNO(s) to be able to support efficient complementary coverage via NTN, the TN
network may need to be aware of the available NTN coverage footprint, and vice versa.  This can include current coverage (i.e.
already active) as well as potential coverage (i.e. not yet active, but possible), and will need to include some details of the
coverage to be provided (e.g. applicable NTN cells, their configuration and corresponding serving satellite ephemeris).
Depending on a number of operational factors and system constraints, such as feeder link availability, power and radio
resource availability of the satellites forming the NTN constellation, the active cells, allocated resources (and thus capacity), as
well as the specific coverage areas that an NTN operator chooses to serve or not serve may change over time.  In addition, due
to orbital precession, the specific satellite(s)

stellation, the active cells, allocated resources (and thus capacity), as
well as the specific coverage areas that an NTN operator chooses to serve or not serve may change over time.  In addition, due
to orbital precession, the specific satellite(s) serving a given cell coverage area on the ground at any point of time (e.g. in a
scenario with Earth-fixed or quasi-Earth-fixed Cells) also change over time. Thus there is a need for the NTN segment to be
able to communicate this information to the TN segment, such that the TN segment can be aware of which NTN cells are
available or might become available in the future, as well as update the information being broadcast in SIB19/SIB31 messages
in terrestrial edge cells.
Likewise, in the reverse direction, an NTN operator may normally not be aware of the footprint, topology, configuration or
even presence of terrestrial networks within the coverage of an NTN, unless this information has been separately sourced or
disclosed by the MNO.  Whilst some of this information can be shared at network planning by the TN MNO to the NTN SNO,

the TN MNO network is expected to evolve over time, potentially also dynamically via the introduction of network energy
saving (NES) techniques, and thus may need to be updated at runtime.
In scenarios where the NTN coverage may totally or partially overlap with the TN coverage or its edge, by having awareness
of the TN footprint or of its edge, the NTN operator may be able to selectively deactivate NTN coverage in overlapping areas,
in order to save system power, capacity, or to enable coverage in other locations. In scenarios with no overlap (e.g. due to TN
spectrum reuse in space), the NTN operator may need to adjust the NTN coverage edge to match as closely as possible the TN
coverage edge, at least for certain frequencies.
5.1.2.2
Problem statement and challenges
In order to fulfil the requirements of these scenarios, the TN and NTN segments would need to have a method of exchanging at
least the minimum necessary information on their respective coverage footprints, required to fulfil complementary coverage
functionalities. The current 3GPP- and O-RAN-specified interfaces between operator domains, such as the roaming interfaces
and other interfaces at the Core network and RAN level (e.g. Xn), do not support sharing of this type of information.
Sharing of neighbor cell information, including neighbor relationships, and other coverage related information within a single
network domain (e.g. within a TN or an NTN) is typically expected at least in part to be addressed by interfaces such as
X2/Xn. However, in the interaction between TN and NTN this is either not sufficient (e.g. due to lack of the necessary
primitives), or outright not possible, such as in the scenario where SNO and MNO, with both networks assumed to be aligned
with 3GPP and O-RAN architecture, are two

between TN and NTN this is either not sufficient (e.g. due to lack of the necessary
primitives), or outright not possible, such as in the scenario where SNO and MNO, with both networks assumed to be aligned
with 3GPP and O-RAN architecture, are two distinct operator domains, where inter-operator Xn is currently not contemplated
(or implemented) and presents potential feasibility issues.  In addition, both the TN footprint, topology and configuration, as
well as the NTN footprint, topology and configuration, are expected to be continuously evolving and dynamic in nature,
especially as operators (MNOs and SNOs alike) increasingly target maximization of energy and deployment efficiencies.
Therefore, traditional manual or static mechanisms of sharing this information are not going to be fit for purpose, and there is
instead a need for automated mechanisms that can dynamically provide updates on the changes to the coverage in a timely
manner (order of seconds at least), as soon as they happen. It is also important that this sharing of information is performed
securely and with a fine-grained level of control on the type and amount of information that is respectively shared, at any given
instant of time.
Therefore, there is a gap and an identified need for a secure, programmatic and reactive mechanism for TN and NTN networks
in different operator domains to interface and interact, for the purpose of selectively sharing coverage related information.
5.1.3
Use Case 1-2: TN-NTN Mobility and Service Continuity
5.1.3.1
Use Case Description
This use case covers the support for mobility and service continuity between a terrestrial network (TN) and a Non-Terrestrial
Network (NTN). One of the key value propositions for Non-Terrestrial Networks is to enable complementary coverage for

ption
This use case covers the support for mobility and service continuity between a terrestrial network (TN) and a Non-Terrestrial
Network (NTN). One of the key value propositions for Non-Terrestrial Networks is to enable complementary coverage for
terrestrial networks, and to help MNOs fulfil coverage gaps. As such, enabling or facilitating mobility and service continuity
between the TN and the NTN and vice-versa is a key requirement.
Whilst 3GPP defines the procedures at RAN level for TN-NTN idle and connected mode mobility and stipulates the need for
sharing of coverage and satellite assistance information (e.g. Ephemeris), the 3GPP specifications do not explicitly address
how this information is shared, and further how these procedures are coordinated when the TN and NTN are in different
operator domains. This use case thus describes the requirements, expected procedure and possible solution to address these
remaining aspects in respect to TN-NTN mobility and service continuity.
In order to be able to support TN-NTN mobility, the TN RAN needs to be aware of the NTN coverage footprint, and
specifically which satellite(s) are or will be serving a given coverage area at any point in time, and which are or may be the
applicable neighbor NTN cells, with their respective configurations.  In 3GPP NTN Rel-17+ systems, some of this
information, alongside other details such as Ephemeris of the satellites, is expected as per the 3GPP specifications to be
delivered via SIB19 or SIB31 into the TN cells bordering or overlapping with the NTN coverage area. However, in order for
the information to be delivered to the TN cells, the terrestrial network has to first be aware of the information in the first place.
This information may in many cases need to come from an external source

Problem statement and challenges
Whilst 3GPP specifies mechanisms for TN-NTN mobility and service continuity, many of the capabilities and information
exchanges required to implement said mobility, and to more in general facilitate the seamless interworking between TN and
NTN are currently not addressed by 3GPP specifications, and could on the other hand be effectively addressed by O-RAN.
In order to support mobility from TN to NTN, the TN network must be aware at least of the following information, and their
applicability in time:
●
Satellite assistance information (e.g. Ephemeris) of the target NTN systems, satellites and cells available for handover
or reselection
●
Cell topology and availability of the NTN cells neighboring or overlapping the TN coverage edge, that could be
candidate target cells for measurement, reselection or handover
●
Cell configuration of the NTN cells neighboring or overlapping the TN coverage edge, necessary for measurement
configurations, reselection policy configuration and handover triggering
In addition, the network-initiated Connected Mode handovers must also be explicitly triggered by the network, which must be
able to:
●
Request measurements to the target NTN network, to identify HO cell candidates
●
Request HO triggering to the target gNB
In a terrestrial network scenario or an intra-operator TN-NTN scenario, many of these capabilities are or can be enabled by the
X2/Xn interface. However, X2/Xn may not be feasible in an inter-domain/inter-operator environment.

5.1.4
Use Case 1-3: Request of NTN coverage for Disaster Response
5.1.4.1
Use Case Description
In some cases a Terrestrial MNO might wish to explicitly request NTN coverage in a given area, either to fulfil a coverage gap,
or to respond to a total or partial outage of the terrestrial network, such as in a disaster scenario.  This same capability could
also be used simply to request the NTN to allocate additional capacity in a given area, in order to respond to an expected or
witnessed increase in demand.
Scenario 1) TN MNO1 identifies a coverage gap in its coverage, or is interested in providing additional coverage overlay, and
thus requests NTN coverage to specific target geographical area to NTN SNO1.
Scenario 2) TN MNO1 already has active NTN coverage by NTN SNO1 in a given target geographical area, but identifies a
need to allocate additional capacity (e.g. due to an upcoming event).
Scenario 3) During a disaster scenario (e.g. a hurricane), cell towers of TN MNO1 in a given area are affected by an outage
(e.g. power outage) and are thus unavailable. TN MNO1 requests NTN coverage (in dedicated or shared spectrum) to the
affected target geographical area to NTN SNO1.
The scenarios from 1 to 3 are applicable also when an MNO has a commercial relationship or wishes to establish a commercial
relationship with more than one NTN SNO partner.
In addition to the basic coverage or capacity request, a TN MNO may wish to communicate additional information to their
NTN SNO partner, for example:
•
Expected load or last-known load
•
Required capacity
•
QoS information and/or Slice pol

O partner.
In addition to the basic coverage or capacity request, a TN MNO may wish to communicate additional information to their
NTN SNO partner, for example:
•
Expected load or last-known load
•
Required capacity
•
QoS information and/or Slice policies for specific services that may be required (e.g. public safety, emergency
messaging and/or calling)
•
List of UEs for prioritization/QoS policy
•
Pre-sharing of UE capabilities mapped to explicit list of UEs
•
Interference thresholds and coverage edge contours or other constraints (e.g. to prevent interference, in case of
terrestrial spectrum reuse)
•
Desired cell configuration parameters
•
In case of terrestrial spectrum reuse or other form of spectrum lease, information on the spectrum available for
deployment and any configuration requirements.
5.1.4.1 Problem Statement
Current methods for an MNO to request NTN coverage from an SNO are entirely reliant on traditional office IT
communication (e.g. emails, meetings), and require extensive discussions and pre-agreements not only at the commercial level,
but also at the technical level, as a pre-requisite.
With current methods, derivation of technical parameters for requests of either complementary coverage or capacity rely on
extensive offline simulations performed by both parties respectively. These simulations are usually based on abstracted
knowledge of the network, and relatively limited advance knowledge of the respective systems, also due to confidentiality
constraints.  From these simulations and plans, a notional NTN network plan is usually derived and agreed by both parties, via
extensive discussion.  In some cases, the simulations used to derive the plan may not even be fully reflective of the up-to-date
conditions of the network (mostly because they are gene

N network plan is usually derived and agreed by both parties, via
extensive discussion.  In some cases, the simulations used to derive the plan may not even be fully reflective of the up-to-date
conditions of the network (mostly because they are generated not from the live network, but from offline system-level
simulator toolsets), nor of the real-world practical conditions in which the system will operate.
In addition, any subsequent update usually needs to go through a similar formal cycle of discussions, simulations, agreements
and formal approvals, de-facto preventing the enactment of any reactivity to changing requirements or events in responsive
timeframes.  In some cases, due to the relatively “static” nature of the plan and of the need to pre-plan in advance, often with a
high level of detail, this can also lead to inflexibility in any regulatory filings submitted, where exact static values may be
specified or filed for, and thus require an update to the regulatory filings in case some parameters are altered or optimized.
As a consequence, the resulting plan exhibits a few unfortunate byproducts:

1) Staleness: The NTN network plan derived is relatively static and represents a snapshot of the respective systems at a
given moment of time, which may become stale over time, due to being unable to automatically reflect any
subsequent changes or optimizations in either the MNO terrestrial network coverage, or the SNO’s NTN coverage.
2) Immutability and lack of reactivity: Changes in the NTN network plan are difficult and slow to introduce, and not
only it cannot easily accommodate either changes in the actual respective network topologies, capabilities and plans,
but it is also unable to be adapted in responsive time frames, to react to changing or unforeseen needs by either SNO
or MNO, such as need to provide Disaster Coverage in response to an outage, spikes in demand or other time-
sensitive events.
3) Poor accuracy: Due to the simulation environments used to derive the technical parameters of the plan, and due to
issues with confidentiality, the plan may not reflect the accurate and up-to-date state, capabilities or parameters of the
live network, reducing the accuracy of representation.  Its accuracy also to the physical live environment and its
interaction with terrain, weather and other factors is also very limited.
4) Conservativeness and sub-optimality: Due to the above issues, the plans are usually defined with relatively
(sometimes extremely) conservative margins, in order to avoid, or at least reduce, any risks of disruption to user
experience.  Inevitably, this also results in significant sub-optimality.
These issues could be resolved via a form of automated and programmatic mechanism, enabling the exchange of requests (as
well as advertisements of availability) for coverage and capacity between different entities, such as for example between one
MNO and

MNO and one or more SNOs to provide NTN coverage and capacity in reaction to changing demand or to an unforeseen even,
such as a disaster scenario.
There are currently no existing interfaces, APIs or otherwise programmatic and/or automated mechanisms to support either
static, semi-static or let alone dynamic requests for coverage and/or capacity between different operator entities within either
the 3GPP or the O-RAN specifications. Such requirements and concepts have been raised and discussed from time to time, at
least within 3GPP in the context of NTN, but have never so far been introduced. In particular, there is currently no satisfactory
mechanism to satisfy certain mission-critical use cases for the public good, such as respond to the need to supply Disaster
Coverage via NTN in response to total or partial outages to parts or totality of an MNO’s terrestrial network within
meaningfully responsive timeframes from the occurrence of an event (e.g. seconds or at most minutes).

5.1.5.1
Summary of Gap Analysis
The previous clauses describe a number of use cases that involve interaction between the TN and NTN networks and
summarize the current gaps and required interactions. Due to the commonalities between the different use cases, it was decided
to address possible solutions in a single, common clause. The following clause thus analyzes possible common solutions to
address the aforementioned use cases. From analyzing the different use c

alities between the different use cases, it was decided
to address possible solutions in a single, common clause. The following clause thus analyzes possible common solutions to
address the aforementioned use cases. From analyzing the different use cases in Group 1, we can also summarize a list of
requirements that a possible solution must be able to fulfil.
In all the previously discussed use cases of Group 1, it is assumed that the TN and NTN segments could be either part of the
same operator domain or, more typically, part of two different and independent operator domains.  It is also possible that,
within a single operator domain, the operator may choose to maintain domain separation between the TN and NTN segments.
Any new solution(s) must be capable of addressing all such cases.
In addition, the solution should not be limited to a one-to-one relationship between TN and NTN segments, but should also
enable one-to-many relationships, for example to support the case where an MNO may have multiple SNO partners, and vice-
versa the case where an SNO may have multiple MNO partners/customers, but also the case where multiple separate TN and
NTN segments exist within a single operator, as separate administrative domains.
The key requirements for the solution can thus be summarized as follows:
1) Allow interaction between TN and NTN segments in the same operator, assigned to a single administrative domain
2) Allow interaction between TN and NTN segments in the same operator, assigned to multiple separate administrative
domains
3) Allow interaction between TN and NTN segments in different operators and independent operator administrative
domains

The requirements described above cannot be presently satisfied by any existing interface, architectural element or procedure in
the current 3GPP or O-RAN Architecture, at least for the case where the TN and NTN segment are operated by different
entities (e.g. different operators) or part of different administrative domains.
The O-RAN architecture and RIC/SMO complex, however, do offer a unique framework for management of radio coverage in
an operator domain, to complement the 3GPP specification and address challenges not addressed by 3GPP, and are either
already capable, or are expected to be capable (e.g. in the case of NTN) of accessing the required information in the respective
operator networks.  They therefore offer a unique opportunity to introduce a viable solution for TN-NTN radio network
coverage level inter-working and cooperation, if a suitable mechanism to enable communication between the TN and NTN
domains can be identified.
5.1.5.2
Proposed Solution: New TN-NTN Interface
In order to satisfy the requirements outlined above, for the scenario in which the TN and NTN segments are operated by
different operators, an MNO and an SNO respectively, or under otherwise different administrative domains, a potential
proposed solution is the introduction of a new and novel O-RAN interface or API between the two operator domains that is
suitably designed to cross the inter-operator domain trust boundary.
If we assume that both the TN and NTN are respectively adopting the O-RAN architecture and thus both have their own
respective Near/Non-RT RIC and SMO deployments, the new interface could be designed to

cross the inter-operator domain trust boundary.
If we assume that both the TN and NTN are respectively adopting the O-RAN architecture and thus both have their own
respective Near/Non-RT RIC and SMO deployments, the new interface could be designed to exist between the MNO’s and
SNO’s respective Near/Non-RT RICs or SMOs, facilitating different levels of information sharing.  Such capability and
interface are not currently specified or contemplated by the O-RAN Architecture and Specifications, and therefore it is
identified as a gap.  Overall, this cross-operator mode of operation and interaction was not envisaged by 3GPP or the O-RAN
Alliance previously and would require investigation into how the O-RAN architecture may need to evolve, potentially with the
specification of one or more new interfaces.

After several discussions on at which layer should this new interface exist, and considerations for various candidate options, it
seems  that the most likely suitable approach may be to specify this interface between the Non-RT RICs or SMOs. However,
the possibility of supporting a new interface between the Near-RT RICs could also be considered and should be further studied
if the requirements for use cases demand it.
5.1.5.3
Impact to the O-RAN Architecture
This clause of the Technical Report outlines different architecture options for TN-NTN interworking depending on whether the
two segments are operated by the same or a different operator (or different administrative entities within the same operator),
and considers as a solution the specification of at least a new interface between an NTN Non-RT RIC or SMO and a TN Non-
RT RIC or SMO, at least for the case where TN and NTN segment are operated by different entities.
The impact can thus be summarized as follows:
-
Case 1 (TN and NTN operated by different entities): Introduction of a new East/West API interface or service
between Non-RT RICs or SMOs of the two operators.
-
Case 2 (TN and NTN operated by the same entity): Reuse of the existing A1 interface reference point and
augmentation of the A1 and the RIC/SMO layer with procedures and information relating to TN-NTN information
sharing.
For the scenario in which the TN and NTN segment are operated by different operators, an MNO and an SNO respectively, or
part of different administrative domains, a potential proposed solution is to introduce a new East/West API interface or service
between the SNO’s NTN Non-RT RIC and the MNO’s TN Non-RT RIC. Via such interface, the TN Non-RT RIC and the
NTN Non-RT RIC could exchange information regarding the respective coverage ar

between the SNO’s NTN Non-RT RIC and the MNO’s TN Non-RT RIC. Via such interface, the TN Non-RT RIC and the
NTN Non-RT RIC could exchange information regarding the respective coverage areas as well as other information as
required for mobility and service continuity procedures.

Benefits
There are several benefits to this new proposed interaction, some of which have been captured in the Use Cases of the Use
Case Group 1, and include the enablement of TN to NTN and NTN to TN mobility and service continuity scenarios, such as
reselection and handover between the TN and the NTN and vice-versa, the enablement of the ability to request NTN coverage
in a number of operator scenarios, as well as opportunities for higher levels of optimization, for example in how coverage is
provided between the TN and NTN segment, and in ensuring truly complementary and mutually-beneficial and optimal
coverage between the TN and NTN segments.

3GPP Releases 17, 18 and 19 introduced new procedures specifically to address NR-NTN and IoT NTN mobility management,
that are designed to take into account such NTN-specific impairments and influencing factors.  However, whilst the procedures
are specified in detail in the 3GPP specification, their actual implementation and the full implications from a network architecture
and implementation are not stipulated and are instead left up to operator and/or vendor implementation choice.
This chapter analyses a number of mobility use cases that fall in the categories listed above and that leverage existing 3GPP
procedures as of Release 18, within the context of the O-RAN architecture as a possible implementation, in a bid to efficiently
allocate the limited resources of the NTN system whilst maintaining and maximizing fulfilment of user service requirements.
Lastly, an initial assessment of the possible impact of the introduction of such use cases to the O-RAN architecture and
specifications is made.
5.2.2  Use Case 2-1: Connected mode NTN inter-gNB handover (HO) due to
Satellite mobility
5.2.2.1
Use Case Description
This use case covers the use of an NTN near-RT RIC and xApps to optimize the implementation of inter-satellite inter-gNB
Connected Mode Handover (HO) within an NTN Non-Geostationary Orbit (NGSO) constellation, exemplified by a Low Earth
Orbit (LEO) constellation, driven by satellite mobility. This use case is in principle formulated in a way that is largely agnostic
of the NTN gNB architecture (e.g. Transparent vs Regenerative).  In this scenario, users are assumed to be practically stati

(LEO) constellation, driven by satellite mobility. This use case is in principle formulated in a way that is largely agnostic
of the NTN gNB architecture (e.g. Transparent vs Regenerative).  In this scenario, users are assumed to be practically stationary
or slow moving (e.g. handheld), and the mobility events are driven by satellite motion.  This scenario use case description
assumes Earth-fixed cells (EFC) or quasi-Earth-fixed cells (QEFC), but is applicable also to Earth-moving cells (EMC).
Many upcoming 5G NTN constellations will be deployed in Low Earth Orbit, where a significant number of satellites are needed
in order to achieve ubiquitous global coverage. LEO constellations are highly-mobile and their network configuration is
continuously changing, and as such UEs may experience frequent handovers from one satellite to the next.
In addition, in dense constellations, multiple candidate satellites may be able to serve a given coverage area, introducing the need
for the network to select the appropriate target satellite to serve the incoming users. This could be influenced by a number of
factors, such as feeder link availability, expected satellite visibility period, maximum number of concurrent beams, on-board
power limitations, UE TX power and antenna gain, line of sight, spectrum constraints and more.

dots associated to the green dotted lines) and a single gNB broadcasting a single PCI.  Feeder link mobility is thus not considered
for the sake of simplicity. This allows this use case to focus on user link mobility, and makes the scenario applicable to both
Transparent and Regenerative architectures.
Co-planar satellites are numbered with the same most-significant digit, whereas cross-planar satellites are assigned a different
most-significant digit. The current scenario assumes that the associated satellites project a beam which is fixed to the satellite
and is sweeping the Earth beneath. This eliminates the need for a system to be present which will intelligently control a steerable
beam antenna that would direct energy towards a particular Earth-fixed direction, as well as maintain things like beam hopping
schedules. However, in most future 5G NTN constellations, steerable beam antennas would be a key component, and their
management and scheduling would have to be coordinated with the management of the 5G NTN RAN in order to achieve truly
optimized operations.
At the beginning of the scenario, a UE located in Spain is currently served by satellite 11, which forms the user link to the UE
(in yellow) and is supported by a feeder link (in green) to a ground station in central Italy. As shown by the orbital trajectory, in
some time, satellite 11 will be approaching the end of its viable service time for the target UE (e.g. due to low elevation, scan
angle or link budget). Simultaneously, the remaining three satellites 12, 21 and 31 will approach the UE coverage area and
become eligible to place a beam (and a cell) in the UE’s location, and t

ime for the target UE (e.g. due to low elevation, scan
angle or link budget). Simultaneously, the remaining three satellites 12, 21 and 31 will approach the UE coverage area and
become eligible to place a beam (and a cell) in the UE’s location, and they therefore offer potentially viable candidate handover
opportunities. Figure 5.2.2.1-3 shows the possible candidate satellites and UE service links at the instant in which all satellites
are in principle eligible to serve the coverage area.
An NTN Near-RT RIC and an associated NTN xApp could be tasked with taking all the various factors into account and driving
the decision of which of the 3 available candidate handover satellites should start serving the UE once its currently serving
satellite becomes unsuitable.
In addition, the previously mentioned power and spectrum constraints present a further optimization opportunity to the network
and NTN xApp: for example one of the available satellites could deliver the requested level of service to the UE while
consuming fewer resources than another satellite. Lastly, in a scenario with several UEs in a given coverage area, the NTN
Near-RT RIC and NTN xApp must make a handover decision that accounts for the requirements and conditions of all the users
in the coverage area, which may create the need for trade-off decisions.
5.2.2.2
Problem statement and challenges
The first part of the problem statement is relatively trivial.  In order to support NR NTN scenarios aligned with 3GPP Release
17 and above, the NTN xApp must be able to configure the required NTN-specific measurement configurations, as well as the
necessary handover triggers.
In Release 17, a new SSB Measurement Timing Configuration (SMTC) specific to NR NTN, namely SMTC4 (SSB-MTC4List-
r17), has been introduced.  In

nfigure the required NTN-specific measurement configurations, as well as the
necessary handover triggers.
In Release 17, a new SSB Measurement Timing Configuration (SMTC) specific to NR NTN, namely SMTC4 (SSB-MTC4List-
r17), has been introduced.  In addition, the NTN cells must be able to broadcast Satellite Assistance information, in particular
Satellite Ephemeris, in the form of SIB19, containing serving and neighbor satellite and cell information.  Furthermore, in order
to trigger a HO, the gNB must be able to include specific SIB19 content in the HO triggers.
This implicitly requires the NTN Near-RT RIC and xApp(s) to be aware of the constellation Ephemeris, the serving and target
satellite timing information, as well have the ability to deliver the necessary configurations to the O-CU/DU.
The second aspect of the problem is related to coordination of the HO across multiple satellites (and cells, potentially gNBs), in
order to hand the UE over to the best satellite.
Several criteria and KPIs may be taken into account to select the best target satellite, and, depending on the service requirements
set by the SNO, the NTN RIC may have to either privilege one or more specific KPIs at the expense of others, or to perform a
multi-constraint evaluation by ensuring adequate and balanced satisfaction of several different KPIs at once.
In terrestrial networks, assessment of handover opportunities is almost entirely focused on KPIs affecting the user link, and
would typically be driven by UEs measuring the SSBs of relevant neighbour cells, and then the gNB or Near-RT RIC monitoring
for SMTC-configured measurement events and reports where the quality of a neighbour cell signal would exceed that of the
serving cell signal by some threshold, such as is the case in the A3 event. M

r cells, and then the gNB or Near-RT RIC monitoring
for SMTC-configured measurement events and reports where the quality of a neighbour cell signal would exceed that of the
serving cell signal by some threshold, such as is the case in the A3 event. Measurement reporting, based on SSBs but also CSI-
RS, is also very important for channel estimation in terrestrial networks to aid link adaptation, primarily due to urban deployments
where the various channel state and effects of multi-path propagation are highly and frequently variable and difficult to predict,
except perhaps at the cell edge. In NTN deployments, on the other hand, limited multipath effects due to focus on outdoor
environments, and the predictable movement of the satellite in the sky coupled with accurate weather forecast data make it such
that the user link channel state by itself is much more steady and predictable, driven mostly by satellite motion, and can thus be

quite reliably modelled and estimated. The overall link and HO candidate selection is, however, on the other hand, affected by a
number of other factors, many of which are completely opaque to the gNB and cannot be addressed with measurements.
Some examples include:
●
Ability to sustain the link vector for the duration of the satellite pass (or UE call flow) - influenced by a number of
factors including feeder link availability
●
Available on-board battery power
●
Overall network load balancing goals
●
Cleanest channel, and thus best achievable MCS
●
Feeder link availability - e.g. due to weather or other system constraints such as antenna field of regard and LoS to the
satellite.
●
Line of sight (LoS) on the user link (but not only)
Feeder link availability is a particularly interesting example as it is chiefly important in transparent NTN deployments where,
even in cases where the user link is in FR1, the NR-Uu waveform has to traverse also the feeder link between the satellite and
the ground station, which often utilises higher frequencies (e.g Ku-, Ka-, Q- or V-band) that are notably susceptible to attenuation
due to weather effects, and which makes it such that the feeder link directly impacts the NR-Uu user link radio interface. The
feeder link behavior and impacts are not specified in 3GPP; this effectively makes it opaque to the gNB and its internal processes.
In addition, due to the dynamic nature of the system and of the external effects (e.g. weather) that might intervene, the impact to
the NR-Uu user link introduced by the feeder link might not be completely known in advance by any of the individual gNBs at
the moment of handover, due to the fact that a feeder link might not even have been established yet.
Continuous satellite movement also makes it such tha

ced by the feeder link might not be completely known in advance by any of the individual gNBs at
the moment of handover, due to the fact that a feeder link might not even have been established yet.
Continuous satellite movement also makes it such that the channel quality is, albeit predictably, always continually and steadily
changing, driven effectively by satellite motion, unlike in terrestrial networks. Not only might the different satellites and their
respective feeder and user link vectors, propagating through variable weather and atmospheric conditions, result in varying
channel qualities and therefore attainable MCS regimes, but they can also result in varying viable service times before either the
user link or the service link becomes unsustainable, due to factors such as Line-of-Sight (LoS) or minimum elevation angles due
to field-of-view (FoV) and obstructions.
Thus, serving or neighbour cell signal measurements prior to the handover can by themselves be at least partially misleading in
NTN, since they do not indicate much about either the end-to-end channel quality including the feeder link and the satellite itself
(e.g. on transparent systems), past and future channel state evolution throughout the satellite pass, or future vectors between each
satellite and the UEs being served, or expected to be served in the future (e.g. impacted by LoS effects, such as mountain ranges
which might block LoS from a given area and UEs or feeder links to a given satellite at any future point of the service pass). For
example, for Satellite 31 in Figure 5.2.2.1-1, a feeder link is formed with a ground station in the Azores. As the satellite
propagates due North-East, it may witness its current ground station fall out of the feeder link view before the UE falls out of
the user

Satellite 31 in Figure 5.2.2.1-1, a feeder link is formed with a ground station in the Azores. As the satellite
propagates due North-East, it may witness its current ground station fall out of the feeder link view before the UE falls out of
the user link view, thus requiring a feeder link handover. While feeder link is not a 3GPP-specified element of the network,
mobility procedures associated with it may still require intervention from the RAN, and, depending on network implementation,
may potentially result in an L3 Handover as well for the UE, leading to potential service discontinuity and signaling overhead.
Furthermore, since the NTN link is often more constrained compared to a terrestrial link, an excessive reliance on user link
signalling and UE measurement reports may create significant overhead on the link, negatively affecting user throughput and
system capacity.
This introduces the need for intervention, and opportunity for optimization, from an external control plane that has awareness of
the satellite constellation, its sub-components and its evolution, and is thus capable of predicting the behaviour of both the user
links and their channel state across multiple satellites throughout their motion, as well as the impact of components of the system
that are outside of the scope of any individual gNB, such, in this example, other gNBs, other satellites or NTN service nodes, or
any of the gateway feeder links. In addition, to account for events in the future impacting links that have not come into existence
yet, there might be a need for the NTN control plane to be able to be spatially-aware, in addition to it being temporally-aware,
to propagate predict where the NTN service nodes (e.g. satellites, but not only) might be at any future point in time and which

ere might be a need for the NTN control plane to be able to be spatially-aware, in addition to it being temporally-aware,
to propagate predict where the NTN service nodes (e.g. satellites, but not only) might be at any future point in time and which
links they might be able to form.
5.2.2.3
Proposed Solution
A possible solution could be leveraging the NTN RIC, either as a combination of the Near-RT and the Non-RT RIC, or via the
Near-RT RIC alone, with the introduction of a new control loop provided by one or more NTN xApp(s). Such xApps would
leverage the holistic view of the satellite network provided by the NTN RIC, combined with predictive capabilities, to produce
handover decisions which take into account multiple concurring factors, as well as reducing the reliance on signal measurements
and reporting.

20

The NTN RIC and xApp(s)/rApps are configured with a digital twin of the NTN network, including, not only the 3GPP RAN
segment, but also the NTN ground  and space segments (e.g. the gateways, the feeder links, the satellites, etc) via which the NTN
service is delivered, even though some of these elements are presently not within the scope or control of the existing O-RAN
reference framework.
It is assumed that the NTN RIC may be capable of predicting NTN network node state, motion, trajectory (e.g. orbit) and
behaviour in time and space. It is also assumed that the NTN RIC may be able to ingest external data sources, such as, but not
limited to, weather data, to predict impact of external events on the active or candidate links, in order to aid the control loop
affecting handover decisions.
By knowing the predictable orbital movement of the candidate satellites , their association with ground stations and feeder links,
the relatively static position (compared to the satellites) of UE or groups of UE in a given target coverage area (e.g. cell or cell
portion) and the impact of weather effects, an NTN xApp could drive the decision of which satellite to hand over the UE to by
modelling the candidate link vectors which could be formed and sustained until the need for the next handover, and aiming to
choose the one that satisfies the appropriate combination of constraints. The use of prediction can be considered a supplement
to, not a replacement of the evaluation of UE measurement reports.

5.2.2.4
Benefits
The first and main benefit is the introduction of support of Release 17+ NR NTN network-controlled Handover (HO) from RRC
Connected Mode, including support for NTN-specific satellite assistance information in the HO request/trigger, which is
presently not supported by the O-RAN specifications.
The second benefit, achieved by the introduction of an NTN RIC (Near/Non-RT RIC) that is aware of the dynamic topology,
physics and evolution of the constellation, and is capable of predicting its behaviour, is a potentially significant reduction of
the signalling overhead, as well as a reduction of the potential for handover failures or sub-optimal handovers, leading to an
improved service experience, as well as overall improved efficiency of the network by reduction of the resources consumed to
support a mobility event.
5.2.2.5
Impact on O-RAN WGs
The use case brings an intelligent NTN handover management approach to O-RAN, which also utilizes information that is not
natively exposed by the O-RAN interfaces (information owing to the non-3GPP components of an NTN constellation, and the
constellation’s own dynamic evolution.
There is a need to support the configuration of the previously described new measurement configurations specific to NR NTN
introduced in Release 17, such as the new SSB Measurement Timing Configuration (SMTC) or SMTC4 (SSB-MTC4List-r17).
In addition, the NTN cells must be able to broadcast Satellite Assistance information, in particular Satellite Ephemeris, in the
form of SIB19, containing serving and neighbor satellite and cell information.  Furthermore, in order to trigger a HO, the gNB
must be able to include specific SIB19 content in the HO triggers.
