5.2.3 Use Case 2-2: NTN QoS-based inter-cell traffic steering and load balancing
5.2.3.1  Use Case description
This use case covers the use of an NTN RIC, specifically a Near-RT RIC and xApp(s) to support the implementation of traffic
steering and load balancing for administrative and network optimization reasons in an NTN network supporting NR NTN with
satellite access via Release 17 and above.  This use case is similar to the Traffic Steering Use Case described in the O-RAN
Alliance WG1 Use Cases Analysis Report, however it focuses on Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTN) with satellite access and
includes Load Balancing, as well as explicit awareness of orbits, orbital dynamics, cell load and QoS.
The current O-RAN use case definitions on Traffic Steering and QoS-aware scheduling do not take into account issues specific
to NTN deployments, satellite or otherwise.
This use case’s applicability is not limited to a specific orbit, and is instead applicable to any GSO or NGSO orbit, including but
not limited to GEO, MEO and LEO.  This use case can also apply to multi-orbit scenarios (e.g. GEO + LEO, GEO + MEO, etc),
where different orbit types are specified in 3GPP as different RAT types. The scope of inter-RAT Traffic Steering and Load
Balancing for this use case is presently focused on 5G NR RAT types where the RAT type is used to differentiate the NTN orbit.
5.2.3.2 Problem statement and challenges
It is well understood that in terrestrial cellular networks, imbalances in the traffic load across different cells, or differences in
their available bandwidth and QoS capabilities, can lead to network hotspots, network congestion, suboptimal spectrum
utilization and negative impact on the user experience due to for example increased latency.
It is also understood that networks ma

their available bandwidth and QoS capabilities, can lead to network hotspots, network congestion, suboptimal spectrum
utilization and negative impact on the user experience due to for example increased latency.
It is also understood that networks may provide access to users with diverse profiles, as well as support different types of services
and their associated requirements.
This challenge is tackled in the terrestrial domain by the RICs evaluating the QoS targets of the various DRBs/UEs as well as
the current resource utilization in the network to determine whether there are sufficient resources allocated in the correct locations
to meet the QoS requirements of users.
In NTN deployments, particularly those in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), the inherent movement of satellites means that components
of the RAN, the air interface and even its transport might      no longer traverse deterministic fibre optic connections, but rather
wireless links between various space and ground assets of the NTN network which are likely to have time- and space-variant
properties, such as high mobility, bandwidth constraints, high, variable or diverse delay, as well as potentially low reliability.
Even in 3GPP Release 17/18 specifications, which mostly focus on transparent/bent-pipe architectures, even though the entire
RAN and the interconnections between its associated RAN Network Functions are placed on Earth, the NR Uu air interface has
to traverse at least one transparent satellite hop via a radio feeder and user link, which can induce a series of time-variant
impairments and latencies that impact the network’s (and a RIC’s and xApp’s) ability to appropriately steer and load balance
traffic in sync with the RAN scheduler.
It is also worth noting that traffic steering methodologies have been

of time-variant
impairments and latencies that impact the network’s (and a RIC’s and xApp’s) ability to appropriately steer and load balance
traffic in sync with the RAN scheduler.
It is also worth noting that traffic steering methodologies have been devised to achieve intelligent mapping of UEs to cells with
an assumption that the cells might be at worst macro and micro cells, or more typically closely adjacent and similar tier cells. In
the NTN context, on the other hand, the scenarios might involve networks with multiple orbits, where UEs in a given region
could be split between GSO and NGSO segments, as well as within NGSO networks where different types of UEs in the same
cell could be best served by different NGSO satellites depending on their specific connectivity requirements (e.g. eMBB vs
URLLC) as well as the dynamic state of the network.  This diversity of access layers may create significant differences in the
latency, mobility, capacity, coverage area as well as several other factors.
Lastly, in terrestrial macro mobile networks, UEs with specialized characteristics and vertical-specific QoS requirements might
be a comparatively small minority as opposed to eMBB smartphone users, at least in a given area of the network or band group.
In NTN, on the other hand, this diversity is expected to be quite significant, both in terms of a mix of handheld (e.g. smartphone)
and non-handheld UE (e.g. automotive, CPE, UAV, etc) even within the same cell, frequency band and RAT.
This makes it such that a number of aspects introduced by the nature of NTN systems, and that will be impacting the ability of
the RIC to perform accurate traffic steering and load-balancing, are not yet accounted for in the O-RAN specifications, and thus
require further analysis.

5.2.3.3 Proposed Solution
5G NTN aims to primarily serve UEs in rural outdoors environments where limited LoS obstruction on the ground, limited
multipath effects and the predictable movement of the satellite in the sky coupled with accurate weather forecast data means that
the channel quality can be more reliably modelled and estimated. Such a capability would allow an xApp/rApp solution to not
only rely on instantaneous signal measurements, but also to perform modelling of the user and feeder link channel qualities as
their link vectors change due to the orbital movement of the satellite. Additionally, by having access to information about the
Satellite Transport Network such as the possible or currently employed antenna configurations onboard the satellites and the
scheduled feeder link handovers, an xApp/rApp solution could obtain this cognisance of the downstream impacts of steering
specific types of traffic and services in different ways.
For example, upon handover opportunities for a specific UE which are “forced” such as those that occur because the current
serving satellite is dropping below the horizon, the xApp/rApp could perform channel modelling and predictions on the array of
potential user and feeder link vector pairs which could be employed for that UE during the viable service time of that user-feeder
link pair (i.e. prior to the next necessary user or feeder link handover). From this, it could derive which handover opportunity for
a given UE/group of UEs would result in a service time during which the highest attainable spectral efficiency would be achieved
on the user/feeder link pair, which would be the criterion on the basis of which DRBs and associated UEs with eMBB type of
QoS flow targets would be managed. In parallel, for those UEs which are req

st attainable spectral efficiency would be achieved
on the user/feeder link pair, which would be the criterion on the basis of which DRBs and associated UEs with eMBB type of
QoS flow targets would be managed. In parallel, for those UEs which are requesting a URLLC type of service, the xApp/rApp
would also take into account any associated packet delay budget requirements which would have to be enforced, while also
attempting to evaluate which of the candidate handover opportunities could deliver service the longest before either a user or
feeder link handover would require temporary service disruption.
In cases of significant congestion, the xApp/rApp would prioritise those UEs and QoS targets which are regarded as being of
highest priority, and would use other measures such as those defined in the existing QoS-based resource optimisation use case
in WG3 UCR to find alternate solutions for those UEs whose QoS targets cannot be met in the current network state. To support
the kinds of Conditional Handovers which are crucial for NTN mobility, as was highlighted in Use Case 2-3 in Clause 5.2.4, the
current interface specification(s) would need to be extended. Lastly, if only a subset of potential satellites are relevant handover
candidates for a UE consuming a specific type of service, the xApp/rApp solution would aim to decrease the overall power
consumption and signaling overhead on behalf of the UE and RAN by constraining the SIB19 contents (e.g. ntn-
NeighCellConfigList) and SMTC4 configuration to only produce Measurement Reports for those satellites which are determined

5.2.3.4 Benefits
Employing limited network resources to communicate information is naturally at the centre of mobile networks, and especially
critical for NTNs. By leveraging access to network telemetry as well as employing accurate models of the behaviour of the
system components and channel(s) to produce prediction-based data-driven decisions, the adoption of an O-RAN RIC and xApp-
driven NTN control plane would lead to overall increase in efficiency of the system, lower spectral and power usage in the
network, both from the aspect of achieving higher MCS on link vectors, as well as exhausting fewer resources.
This is expected to also lead to a higher overall rate of satisfied QoS and QoE requirements by increasing the number of fulfilled
service targets with the same amount of resources, in turn improving the overall commercial viability of the SNO’s NTN
operations.
5.2.3.5 Impact on O-RAN WGs
The use case brings forth an NTN-specific angle and approach to Traffic Steering and QoS-based optimization use cases which
were already addressed for terrestrial networks in WG2 and WG3. While the 5G QoS framework has not changed significantly
for NTN, there is a need to support the configuration of NTN-specific network-controlled HO for traffic-steering and load-
balancing purposes. For the SIB19 component, an opportunity exists for an xApp/rApp to update the relevant RAN nodes with
some of the contents of the System Information Block 19 (e.g. Satellite Assistance Information and Ephemeris, neighbor satellite
and cell configurations, k_offset, etc) which it ought to broadcast in the cell or unicast to specific users during HO command.

5.2.4 Use Case 2-3: NTN Time-based and Distance-based Conditional Handover
(CHO)
5.2.4.1 Use Case Description
This use case covers the support of the new Time-based and Distance-based Connected Mode Conditional Handovers (CHO)
introduced in 3GPP for NR NTN since Release 18.
The handover end-to-end call flow requires a sequence of signaling exchanges between the UE, its serving cell and a target
neighboring cell to take place in order for the full procedure to be successful. In an event where the UE loses connectivity to its
serving cell before it has received the required instructions to join the target cell, this could inhibit it from successfully
undergoing a handover in RRC Connected Mode. Such an event is largely avoided in terrestrial networks by tailoring the
signal measurement event on the serving cell to be triggered before its signal becomes too weak, but can become more likely to
occur in 5G NTN constellations where the physical mobility of the satellites could mean that one which is currently delivering
a cell to a specific location on the ground would all of a sudden become unable or ineligible to continue doing so, interrupting
the procedure. This risk is only made higher by the increased control plane latencies witnessed in NTN networks, especially in
transparent NTN systems where the RTT could be quite long, and when coupled with any additional processing time on the UE
and RAN it might leave the UE(s) with insufficient time to receive the command to initiate the Random Access procedure
prior to losing connectivity to the serving cell.
To account for such events, 3GPP has extended the capabilities of the Conditional Handover (CHO) with support for Ti

prior to losing connectivity to the serving cell.
To account for such events, 3GPP has extended the capabilities of the Conditional Handover (CHO) with support for Time-
based and distance-based CHO configurations in the UE, in which its serving cell can preauthorize the UE to initiate the
handover to a neighbor cell under conditions which are precomputed, and which provide the UE(s) with sufficient opportunity
to undergo a successful handover, while not attempting it either before the neighboring cell becomes available or unnecessarily
early, the latter of which would increase the frequency of handovers which are a costly procedure. This functionality is
particularly relevant in NTN because the difference in signal strength owed to the UE being located at the cell center versus the
cell edge is not as pronounced as it would be in terrestrial networks, as discussed in Use Case 2-1 in Clause 5.2.2, and is an
insufficient trigger to determine the necessity for a handover to take place. The Time-based and Distance-based triggers on the
other hand do not account for what could be a potentially ephemeral drop in signal quality of the serving cell as more
traditional signal measurement triggers might, but rather communicate that there is a hard limitation to the currently serving
cell’s ability to sustain service to the UE. By applying this configuration to all UEs in a cell, significant reductions in signaling
overhead can be achieved compared to the regular handover scenario.
The Time-based and Distance-based CHO, introduced in 3GPP Release 17 as condEventT1 and condEventD1 in 3GPP TS
38.331 [1], have their applicability in both Earth-Moving Cell (EMC), and Earth Fixed Cell and quasi-Earth F

5.2.4.3 Problem Statement and challenges
5.2.4.3.1 Time-based CHO
Accounting for Earth-Moving Cell based systems first, NTN constellations in NGSO employing the EMC configuration
include satellites which project beams onto the Earth which are fixed to the body of the satellite itself, and are effectively
sweeping over the Earth underneath. Even though the individual beams can be hundreds of kilometers in diameter, the high
orbital velocity of a satellite that is for instance in LEO would mean that a UE would enter into the coverage of a single beam
and exit it within the order to seconds (depending on factors like satellite elevation angle, angular beam width, satellite
altitude, etc.).
This is exemplified in the Figure 5.2.4.3.1-6 below, showing a simplified representation of UE (orange point) mobility between
cells illuminated by two NTN LEO satellites (blue and green points), applicable to both Transparent and Regenerative
architectures, employing Earth-Moving Cells.

Figure 5.2.4.3.1-1: EMC inter-satellite handover scenario
In the first instance, the handovers occur between cells illuminated by the same satellite, exemplified as the blue satellite in
Figure 5.2.4.3.1-1. In a Regenerative architecture, these would most often involve cells which belong to the same onboard gNB
and would constitute intra-gNB handovers. In Transparent architectures, the same could be the case (successive cells belong to
same gNB on the ground), or the satellite could be connected via multiple feeder links to different gateways and gNBs, in
which case successive beams could carry cells delivered by different gNBs and would therefore constitute an inter-gNB
handover. Nevertheless, eventually the UE would be covered by one of the “outer” beams of a single satellite after which there
is no further beam arriving from the same satellite. In this event, there needs to be another satellite coming either in succession
in the same orbital plane or from another crossing orbital plane (the green satellite in the same Figure) which can resume
service to the UE with a new beam and cell. Again, depending on the architecture employed, this could either lead to an intra-
or inter-gNB handover. As discussed before, signal measurement-based handover mechanisms would be insufficient to drive
this type of mobility. Because of the frequency of handovers and the potential high number of UEs on the ground, significant
signaling overheads would be generated as the UEs are being swept by different beams and cells. Time-based CHO was
introduced in 3GPP to address exactly this.
Even if the satellites in the NTN constellation are capable of beam steering, allowing them to illuminate and track Earth-Fixed
Cells, there is still a fundamental limitation whereby a satellite in LEO would

ntroduced in 3GPP to address exactly this.
Even if the satellites in the NTN constellation are capable of beam steering, allowing them to illuminate and track Earth-Fixed
Cells, there is still a fundamental limitation whereby a satellite in LEO would eventually fall beneath the minimum elevation
angle, causing it to stop illuminating a 5G cell over the EFC, and the EFC would need to be handed over to a 5G cell served
via a subsequent satellite. The two satellites could provide overlapping service with their respective cells for a short period of
time during the handover of the EFC from one to the other, but they need not to, and the coverage can even be discontinuous in
time as long as the associated timers (e.g. T304, T310) do not expire before the UEs in the EFC connect to the subsequent cell,
causing RLF. This type of handover of entire EFCs (and constituent UEs) is applicable to Transparent architectures where
different gNBs on the ground deliver successive cells via different gateways and satellites, where the same gNB delivers
successive cells via different gateways and satellites, as well as in cases where two different gNBs via different gateways form
feeder links with the same Transparent satellite that illuminates both of the successive cells onto the same EFC. It is also
applicable to Regenerative architectures where the gNB is placed onboard the satellite, and the two gNBs/satellites deliver
successive cells to the same EFC.
The Figure 5.2.4.3.1-2 below showcases a simplified view of the above scenarios from the point of view of the satellite user
links (omitting gateways and feeder links), whereby the orange UE is initially served by a cell delivered via the blue satellite
(PCI 3). As the blue satellite is progressing along its orbit due North-East, it is n

point of view of the satellite user
links (omitting gateways and feeder links), whereby the orange UE is initially served by a cell delivered via the blue satellite
(PCI 3). As the blue satellite is progressing along its orbit due North-East, it is nearing the moment where it will no longer be
capable of illuminating and tracking the EFC in which the orange UE is located. At the same time, the red LEO satellite is

29

coming into view, moving due South-East, and can resume the service to the EFC. It would deploy a new cell on top of the
EFC (PCI 13), either with overlapped or discontinuous service.

Figure 5.2.4.3.1-2: EFC inter-satellite handover scenario
Yet again, the need for a handover is not driven by variable signal quality by serving and candidate neighboring cells, but
either by a hard limitation to the serving cell’s ability to sustain service to the EFC in question, or a higher layer decision by an
NTN optimization xApp to redirect the blue satellite’s beam and power resources to provide coverage onto another EFC, even
if the blue satellite could sustain coverage to the original EFC for a longer period of time. While UEs in EFCs would nominally
undergo handovers less frequently compared to UEs in EMCs, risks owing to the reliability of just-in-time control plane
signaling delivery and overall impacts on signaling overhead can be mitigated through the employment of Time-based CHO to
drive handovers, where the exact moment of handover can be precomputed and delivered ahead of time to the NTN gNB, who
would signal it to the UEs in the EFC in question.
5.2.4.3.2 Distance-based CHO
While the ephemeral nature of satellite coverage over a given region defines the time bounds between which UEs in the region
in question can be served, there are also other determinants which might cause a UE to exit coverage of one cell or beam, and
necessitate a handover to another cell or beam, if present. One of these determinants is spatial in nature; namely, a UE’s
physical location with respect to the spatial coverage footprint of a satellite beam via which the serving cell is illuminated will
determine if the UE can continue to be served by that cell. By the same logic, a UE’s physical location with respect to that of a
neighboring beam and cell will determine if the UE can be handed over to that cell.
Focusing on EMC-based systems first, this determinant can be exemplified

be served by that cell. By the same logic, a UE’s physical location with respect to that of a
neighboring beam and cell will determine if the UE can be handed over to that cell.
Focusing on EMC-based systems first, this determinant can be exemplified by reusing Figure 5.2.4.3.1-1. With considerations
on whether the architecture is Transparent or Regenerative being equal to the Time-based CHO EMC case, the coverage beams
of NGSO satellites for which the EMC scenario applies are often approximated using hexagons, but their illumination
footprints are in practice more circular in nature, with overlapping coverage towards the circular beams’ edges. Therefore, the
footprint area can be nominally defined using the circular footprint’s center and radius (this holds true best when satellites are
directly at zenith over a coverage region; at lower elevation angles the beam footprint illuminates the Earth’s surface at an
angle, causing the effective footprint to be more oval). Focusing on Figure 5.2.4.3.1-1, the orange UE is initially inside the
satellite beam and cell with PCI 3. As the blue satellite traverses overhead along its orbital path, at one point the orange UE,
even if stationary, will find itself more than the radius distance away from the moving center of the cell with PCI 3 (implicitly
exiting its coverage), and less than the radius distance away from the moving center of the neighboring cell with PCI 4
(implicitly entering its coverage). With the expected slight overlap of the beams, there is a short period of time during which
the UE can be expected to be in coverage of both cells. As was the case with Time-based CHO, relying on signal
measurements from the serving and neighboring cell(s) to drive such mobility cases is insufficient, and the legacy handover
proced

ng which
the UE can be expected to be in coverage of both cells. As was the case with Time-based CHO, relying on signal
measurements from the serving and neighboring cell(s) to drive such mobility cases is insufficient, and the legacy handover
procedure can be expected to meaningfully contribute to signalling overhead and reduce the robustness of the handover
procedure in an NTN scenario. For this purpose, the Distance-based CHO mechanism was extended in 3GPP Release 18 to
support EMC cases.
The Distance-based CHO mechanism was in fact originally introduced in 3GPP Release 17 in support of EFC-based systems.
In contrast to EMC, satellite beams and cells are fixed to the Earth and so, while their footprints can still be approximated as
circles with a center and radius, the footprints’ centers are stationary. Nevertheless, the UEs themselves could be moving, and
with them their distance from the serving and neighboring cell centers could be changing. At one point, a UE will have moved
outside the effective coverage of its currently serving cell, and into that of another neighboring cell, if present, leading to a
handover event.

30

Taking Figure 5.2.4.3.2-3 as an example scenario, the orange UE is initially located inside the blue cell with PCI 6. After some
time, due to the UE’s mobility, it will have travelled due North and crossed over into the coverage of the blue cell with PCI 3.
At this point, the UE becomes closer to the center of the cell with PCI 3 than to that of the cell with PCI 6. Similar to the
explanation for EFC in Time-based CHO scenarios, the blue satellite could either be Regenerative and the handover between
two blue cells would be an intra-gNB handover, or the blue satellite could be Transparent, potentially forming one or more
feeder links to one or more gNBs, depending on which the handover could be intra- or inter-gNB.

Figure 5.2.4.3.2-3: EFC inter-beam handover scenario
Once in the blue cell with PCI 6, after some time the orange UE might move Eastwards towards the area which is covered by
the green cell with PCI 12, coming from the green satellite. Once more, the overall architecture at play would influence what
type of handover this is. If the blue and green satellites are Regenerative, this would be an inter-gNB handover while if they
are Transparent, the same could be the case or both might even be connected via feeder links to the same gNB, implying an
intra-gNB handover.
The current E2SM-RC [2] specification does not presently support Time-based and Distance-based measurement and
Conditional Handover events (e.g. condEventT1, condEventD1 and condEventD2 in TS 38.331[1]) required for the Near-RT
RIC to implement the new NTN-specific Time-based and Distance-based Conditional Handover (CHO) procedures introduced
by 3GPP in Release 17 and Release 18.
As described previously, this can lead to a high signaling load, especially in Earth-Moving Cells (EMC) systems, whenever the
satellite exits the coverage area and all the UEs within the cell need to be handed over. For high-speed UEs (e.g. aircraft, fast
UAV), due to the signal profile in an NTN cell, this could lead to the call being dropped in case the traditional HO procedure
cannot be sufficiently responsive as the UE reaches the cell edge, causing it to hit Radio Link Failure (RLF).
5.2.4.4 Proposed Solution
5.2.4.4.1 Time-based CHO
Addressing the EMC case first, whether the system is Transparent or Regenerative, 3GPP has not provisioned or accounted for
the NTN gNBs to have the ability to keep track of which satellites, and by proxy which EMC cells, are valid neighboring
candidates for handover in a continuously evolving system

Transparent or Regenerative, 3GPP has not provisioned or accounted for
the NTN gNBs to have the ability to keep track of which satellites, and by proxy which EMC cells, are valid neighboring
candidates for handover in a continuously evolving system such as an NGSO NTN constellation. This is exemplified in the
simplified Figure 5.2.4.3.1-6 but would be even more pronounced in a denser deployment, as it would be in a real
constellation.
The blue satellite in the Figure, orbiting due North-East along its orbit, is the one which is initially serving the orange UE via
the cell with PCI 3. Following 3GPP Release 17, the NTN gNB, as prompted by the NTN xApp via the E2 interface, can
instruct the UE with GNSS capabilities to record coarse location information (with ~2 km accuracy) and report it to the NTN
gNB [1], who subsequently uses the E2 interface to deliver it to the NTN Near-RT RIC and the NTN xApp. By knowing the
coarse coordinates of the UE as well as using the digital twin to derive the coverage footprints of the individual cells/beams
delivered by the blue satellite, the NTN xApp can compute the remaining service time of the cell with PCI 3 after which the
UE needs to be handed over to the cell with PCI 4, and subsequently to the cell with PCI 5. These derived remaining service
times and handover target cells are UE-specific even within the same cell (e.g. PCI 3) as the relative location of different UEs
within the same cell would define their mobility opportunities. For instance, if the UE in Figure 5.2.4.3.1-6 was instead in the
North-West corner of the cell with PCI 3 in the initial view, its target handover cell would instead be the cell with PCI 1, and
the handover would need to occur sooner due to the shape of the beam and cell with PCI 3.

The NTN xApp would instruct the NTN gNB delivering the cell with PCI 3 to configure the orange UE with the T1 CHO
(condEventT1 [1]) conditions that would signal to it the time interval during which it ought to attempt to connect to the cell
that is subsequent to it, the one with PCI 4, as well as with appropriate SIB19 parameters to be broadcast that would contain
the ntn-Config-r17 of all of the neighboring cells, itself containing the epochTime-r17 and ephemerisInfo-r17 of the blue
satellite, among other parameters. Taking the cell with PCI 3 from the above Figure as an example, its neighboring cells would
be cells with PCI 1, PCI 4 and PCI 6.
After some time, the orange UE enters the trailing beam/cell of the blue satellite (PCI 5) after which it needs to be handed over
to a cell illuminated by another satellite, in this instance the green one (first cell being one with PCI 14). The NTN Near-RT
RIC and NTN xApp would yet again combine coarse UE location information and digital twin modelling of the NTN
constellation to produce the T1 CHO (condEventT1) and SIB19 parameters which aid the handover from blue cell with PCI 5
to the green cell with PCI 14. This could be coupled with another condition, such as one that is dependent on the signal quality
of the neighboring cell exceeding some nominal value to ensure that the handover stands a greater chance of success (e.g.
condEventA3, condEventA4, condEventA5) for which the SMTC4 configuration defined for NTN is employed (or otherwise
can be used to pre-synchronize with the neighboring SS/PBCH transmissions). Furthermore, the overlapping coverage from
multiple satellites also necessitates close coordination of which frequencies are employed by which cell in order to avoid
interference, and the question of which are permitt

ghboring SS/PBCH transmissions). Furthermore, the overlapping coverage from
multiple satellites also necessitates close coordination of which frequencies are employed by which cell in order to avoid
interference, and the question of which are permitted to be employed is in many cases dependent on the region of the Earth that
is being illuminated. Therefore, there is a further need for a higher order NTN control function, such as an NTN Near-RT RIC
and constituent NTN xApp(s), to drive this functionality.
As for the EFC case, in good time prior to the scheduled discontinuation of coverage to the EFC by the blue cell with PCI 3,
the NTN Near-RT RIC and NTN xApp would instruct via the E2 interface the NTN gNB to configure the UEs in the cell with
the appropriate T1 CHO (condEventT1) configuration, potentially in conjunction with signal measurement-based CHO
configurations (e.g. condEventA3, condEventA4, condEventA5). As was the case in the EMC instance, the NTN xApp will
infer, if not decide itself, through the NTN digital twin and forward-looking scheduling that it will be the red satellite which
will deploy a particular cell (PCI 13) at a particular moment over that EFC in order to continue providing service, and will
have therefore provisioned the T1 CHO configurations in good time prior to the handover occasion taking place, taking into
account any dependency on signaling delays induced by the RTT influenced by the orbital regime and Transparent vs.
Regenerative nature of the constellation. Likewise, this will need to be accompanied with the updated SIB19 containing the
ntn-Config-r17 which will indicate to the UE crucial information about the cell with PCI 13 and the red satellite, such as its
ephemeris information, enabling the UE to synchronize with it.
In the event

companied with the updated SIB19 containing the
ntn-Config-r17 which will indicate to the UE crucial information about the cell with PCI 13 and the red satellite, such as its
ephemeris information, enabling the UE to synchronize with it.
In the event that there is a significant number of UEs in the blue cell with PCI 3, their handing over to the red cell with PCI 13
during the potential overlap period should be managed carefully in order to reduce the chances of preamble collisions,
contention resolution delays, etc. Since the two satellite beams and cells in question are intended to cover the same EFC, the
relative location of different UEs within the EFC would not play as much of a role as it did in the EMC case, as all of the UEs
would be affected by the withdrawal of the blue cell with PCI 3 and illumination of the red cell with PCI 13 in the same
manner and time (there is an edge case where this need not be true; if the elevation angles of the blue and red satellites cause
their beam footprints and therefore cell coverages on top of the EFC at the moment of handover to be of different shapes,
excluding certain UEs). In this respect, the same T1 CHO parameters could be configured for all of the UEs within the same
cell. Nevertheless, in order to balance the RA load onto the red cell with PCI 13, the NTN Near-RT RIC and NTN xApp(s) can
theoretically alter the duration of any overlap or discontinuity of service to the EFC (T310 timer for RLF in UEs starts as blue
cell shuts off – UEs must perform RA to the red cell prior to expiry to avoid exiting RRC Connected Mode) as well as tune the
per-UE group RACH-Config and T1 CHO parameters to better distribute their RA across the red cell’s RACH occasions.

5.2.4.4.1 Distance-based CHO
Focusing again on the EMC case first, and with respect to the scenario in Figure 5.2.4.3.1-6, the UE is initially served by the
blue satellite via the beam and cell with PCI 3. It requires a mechanism by which to evaluate its distance from the moving
locations which represent its current serving cell and a candidate neighboring cell in an EMC system. In 3GPP Release 18, a
new CHO configuration was introduced, called D2 CHO (condEventD2 [1]), for this purpose. This allows the NTN xApp, by
proxy of the E2 interface to the NTN gNB, to specify two distances, distanceThreshFromReference1-r18 and
distanceThreshFromReference2-r18 alongside a hysteresis distance, to a UE in a cell. The UE is expected to use its GNSS
capabilities to ascertain its location, but it also needs the two moving locations to measure and compare its distance to.
At the same time, the NTN xApp can use the E2 interface to deliver to the NTN gNB the parameters which it is supposed to
broadcast to UEs in cell with PCI 3 as part of SIB19. Other than including crucial parameters such as epochTime-r17 and
ephemerisInfo-r17 which are found in the ntn-Config-r17, starting from 3GPP Release 18 the SIB19 is also supposed to also
include a field called movingReferenceLocation-r18. This is supposed to signal to the UEs a serving cell-specific reference
location which they are supposed to measure their distance to, and compare it to the distanceThreshFromReference1-r17 value

provided via the D2 CHO configuration. Nominally this location can be regarded as representing the moving cell center, but
strictly speaking need not be, and it is up to the NTN xApp to define what this is going to represent. The
movingReferenceLocation-r18 is in its definition a static point on the ground, timestamped to the epochTime-r17 from the ntn-
Config-r17, and the UE is expected to combine this with the ephemerisInfo-r17 to propagate the satellite’s orbital trajectory in
the immediate future and ascertain how the movingReferenceLocation-r18 would move along with the satellite, before it
receives the subsequent SIB19 broadcast with the network-updated movingReferenceLocation-r18.
The other reference location, the distance to which the UE is measuring using its GNSS-derived coordinates and comparing to
the distanceThreshFromReference2-r17 value provided via the D2 CHO configuration, is delivered inside the measObjectNR,
namely in the ntn-NeighbourCellInfo-r18 field, for a specific candidate neighboring cell. Within this field, the neighboring
cell’s epochTime-r17, ephemerisInfo-r17, and referenceLocation-r17 are specified, where the latter is a static location which
indicates the reference location at epochTime-r17, which the UE can use alongside the epehemerisInfo-r17 to propagate the
satellite’s orbital trajectory in the immediate future and ascertain how the referenceLocation-r17 would move along with the
satellite, as was the case with movingReferenceLocation-r18.
Once the distance to the movingReferenceLocation-r18 of the serving cell exceeds the distanceThreshFromReference1-r17,
and simultaneously the distance to the referenceLocation-r17 of a neighboring candidate cell drops below the

5.2.4.5 Benefits
This would enable the new NTN-specific Time-based and Distance-based Conditional Handover (CHO) procedures introduced
by 3GPP in Release 17 and further refined in Release 18. These types of handovers were created specifically for their potential
for reduction of the signaling overhead in a cell, by adding flexibility to when the network can trigger UE handovers, allowing
the control signaling to be spread over time or sent during low-traffic intervals, in turn improving the user experience and
smoothness of mobility. This is especially important for NTN systems with Earth-Moving Cells (EMC) and for fast-moving
UEs.

5.2.6 Use Case 2-5: NTN UE Location-aware Connected Mode Handover and Inter-
cell Traffic Steering and Load-balancing
5.2.6.1 Use Case description
This use case describes leveraging of knowledge of UE location (coarse or fine) by the NTN network to aid mobility (e.g. HOs),
as well as other network control procedures such as inter-cell Traffic Steering and Load Balancing.

5.2.6.2 Problem statement and challenges
Normally, in a mobile network it is assumed that handover decisions are taken without awareness of the UE’s location in the
network. This is typically sufficient in terrestrial networks because the cells, even macro cells, are in general reasonably small
and, in MIMO and other beamforming systems, the spatial granularity of the UE positions within the cell is within the resolution
of a single gNB beam in the beamforming matrix.  As the number of UE per cell densifies, a typical solution is to aim for ever
larger MIMO arrays, thus increasing the spatial resolution (e.g. Massive MIMO).
In addition, heavy multipath environments typical of terrestrial urban networks help the MIMO system by creating very distinct
channel transfer functions between each user and the network.
This however is mostly not true for NTN, where each NTN node (e.g. a satellite) should be seen as a single large multi-beam
MIMO array, and where each NTN beam is expected to cover a very large geographic area (e.g. several km, 10s or even 100s of
km) and thus several UEs or groups of UEs.  This has also the collateral effect of creating very large overlap areas between
beams/cells, which, coupled with a typically “flat” cell signal distribution per-beam, makes it such that the cell boundaries are
more complicated to establish. In addition, the NTN node motion makes it such that, as the NTN node, such as a satellite, flies
over the service area, the signal level and quality will naturally vary quite significantly even as seen by a stationary UE.
This creates a number of gaps and problems, such as:
1. Inability of the network to precisely assess when a UE is approaching edge of cell (e.g. due to satellite mobility in EMC
scenarios, or UE mobility in all other cases)

s seen by a stationary UE.
This creates a number of gaps and problems, such as:
1. Inability of the network to precisely assess when a UE is approaching edge of cell (e.g. due to satellite mobility in EMC
scenarios, or UE mobility in all other cases), which can make it difficult to assess whether a UE is about to require
handover to an adjacent beam/cell.
2. Ambiguity in assessing the UE mobility and the signal reporting state across multiple beams/cells, as a UE may report
a signal drop even when stationary, due to satellite movement, which can lead to ping-pong effects by making the
network wrongly think that a UE is approaching the threshold at which it can be better served by an adjacent cell, beam
or NTN node.
3. Inability of the network of discerning in which portions of the NTN beam (and thus potentially cell) UE are located or
clustered, which may force a worst-case resource assignment, and may make it impossible (or very difficult) for the
network to assess whether some UE could be offloaded to an adjacent cell/beam or NTN mode (e.g. satellite) to smooth
cell load.
All of the above knowledge gaps can create problems and inefficiencies with both mobility, as well as resource assignment and
traffic load-balancing at the network level.  In all such cases, knowledge of UE locations or clustering, at least at coarse-grained
level, by the NTN network, can significantly improve mobility reliability and resource management decisions.
Whilst some of the procedures are technically available since at least Release 16, new NTN-specific procedures have been
introduced in Rel-18, and moreover there may be gaps in the O-RAN specifications to prevent full leveraging of existing
solutions. Therefore the exact O-RAN specification gaps need to be further investigated.

5.2.6.3 Proposed Solution
Several mechanisms are available for the network to become aware of UE locations, at either coarse- or fine-grained degree.
For example, once the UE is in RRC_CONNECTED mode and AS security has been established, the network can request the
UE to report its GNSS-derived location information, either coarse or fine-grained, through location management procedures
either directly to the gNB, or via the Core Network (e.g. LMF).

4.1
Current challenges for spectrum aggregation in multi-

Spectrum aggregation across different bands plays an essential role for user experience and efficient use of frequency
resources. As MNOs get access to new NR spectrum, they usually desire to aggregate the capacity across the different
bands to improve the user experience. The coverage areas of different frequency bands can be very different. There has
been interest from several companies for spectrum aggregation over multi-vendor RAN deployment, where different
bands may have different component suppliers. In addition to a greenfield multi-vendor RAN deployment, how
spectrum can be aggregated when a new band with a new supplier(s) is introduced in an existing network is an area of
potential interest.

Scenarios and considerations
5.1
Overview
In its most general form, deployed RAN network functions in an MNO's network can be sourced from a single-vendor
or multiple vendors.  The connectivity between the RAN logical functions may need to consider ideal and non-ideal
transport scenarios. RAN deployments can also be mixed involving a combination of D-RAN, C-RAN and vRAN

5.3.2
Spectrum considerations
5.3.2.1
Overview
Most commercial RAN deployments involve multiple frequency bands. Spectrum aggregation across different bands
should consider frequency band characteristics (coverage, supported SCS, duplexing).
The following clauses cover use cases, such as (i) intra-band contiguous and non-contiguous in FR1/FR2, (ii) inter-band
within and across FR1/FR2, and (iii) considerations for DL-UL link balance in high-frequency bands and different
duplexing schemes (FDD/TDD).
5.3.2.2
Duplexing (FDD/TDD)
Spectrum usage is regulated into FDD and TDD domains. While FDD uses separate frequencies for the uplink and the
downlink, TDD uses a single frequency for both uplink and downlink.
Generally, the unpaired spectrum for TDD is allocated in higher frequencies than FDD. The low-band FDD, due to
physical propagation characteristics, offers a wider coverage area than the higher-frequency TDD spectrum. Typically,
the low-band FDD is limited in capacity. Mid-band TDD has a higher bandwidth and capacity compared to the low-
band FDD. However, mid-band TDD uplink coverage is more limited than the low-band FDD. Spectrum aggregation
across FDD and TDD carriers can improve TDD cell coverage and deliver higher throughput than a TDD-only solution.
Figure 5.3.2.2-1 illustrates a possible way to aggregate the low-band FDD carrier (primary cell) and mid-band TDD
carrier (secondary cell). By using the low-band FDD as the primary cell (PCell), the coverage-limiting UL data and
control channels of the mid-band TDD carrier can be moved to the low-band FDD. This increases the overall mid-band
cell coverage, which means that now the mid-band spectrum can be accessed by more

imary cell (PCell), the coverage-limiting UL data and
control channels of the mid-band TDD carrier can be moved to the low-band FDD. This increases the overall mid-band
cell coverage, which means that now the mid-band spectrum can be accessed by more users in the network. By using
the mid-band TDD as secondary cell (SCell), the downlink throughput can be significantly improved. This use case
provides the unique capability of aggregating low-band FDD and mid-band TDD for higher peak rates and increased
cell coverage.

bands. To increase bandwidth and bitrate aggregation, MNOs need to consider spectrum aggregation from same or

5.3.3
Synchronization considerations
Spectrum aggregation often requires deploying multiple nodes to serve a single UE. Such nodes run their own clocks
which may or may not be synched with GPS clock. Thus, it cannot be assumed that synchronization required by 3GPP
for spectrum aggregation is always possible (as defined in TS 38.133 [i.6], for intra-FR1, maximum received timing
difference cannot be bigger than 33 µs). While considering techniques for spectrum aggregation, it should be made sure
that the requirements for time synchronization between aggregated cells should be as flexible as possible to enable
deployments also where the above requirements for time synchronization cannot be achieved.

5.3.6
Considerations for solution evaluation
When evaluating different solutions and techniques for spectrum aggregation with multi-vendor deployments, the
following criteria is proposed:
1)
Minimize complexity: Solution complexity in terms of network deployment is an important evaluation
criterion. The bandwidth and latency requirements on the underlying transport are to be considered. A multi-
vendor interface is designed to be well-defined with clear functional split.
2)
Minimize impact to inter-operability testing and standardization effort: Efforts needed in the standardization
process and inter-operability testing are important criteria in the evaluation of the solutions. In addition,
standardizing multiple solution options addressing the same problem is not desirable.
3)
Increase performance and lower latency: The solution(s) can be evaluated for maximizing utilization of
available system capacity (e.g., maximize average and 5th percentile user throughput) and lowering
experienced latency to end users.
4)
Minimize impact on O-RAN architecture: Impact on O-RAN architecture is considered in the evaluation of the
solution. There is a benefit in reusing existing interfaces as well as minimizing the impacts to existing O-RAN
functions.

6.2
Solution 1: Intra O-DU Carrier Aggregation
6.2.1
Solution description
6.2.1.1
Intra O-DU multi O-RU carrier aggregation
In carrier aggregation, spectrum aggregation is achieved at O-DU level. Each O-DU can support multiple cells possibly
through multiple O-RUs. The cell where UE is attached is called the Primary Cell (PCell) for that UE while other cells
used for carrier aggregation are called Secondary Cells (SCells).
In DL CA, the primary O-DU receives data from O-CU-UP and schedules the data between the PCell and SCells to
transmit to the UE. The UE maintains multiple downlink links as per the number of component carriers (CCs)
configured to receive data from gNB. Data received from SCells as well as from PCell is aggregated at MAC level in
the UE and forwarded to higher layer. There is a single instance of PDCP, RLC, and other higher layers in the UE,
when carrier aggregation is activated.
In UL CA, SCells and PCell receive UL data (PUSCH) separately from the UE. Data is then aggregated in the PCell
and forwarded to the O-CU-UP. The UCI (PUCCH) can be transmitted on the component carriers configured for UL.
Both SCells and PCell are processed in a single O-DU which is connected with multiple O-RUs using the Open
Fronthaul interface. The Open Fronthaul (and F1) interface enables multiple vendor options for an MNO to decide for
deployment considerations as shown in Figure 6.2.1-1. Figure 6.2.1-1 shows the intra O-DU DL CA scenario, where the
PCell is configured on a carrier served by O-RU1 and DL only SCell(s) are served by O-RUn. In this scenario, PUCCH
is carried by the PCell.  The UE transmits the PUCCH for PCell PDSCH as well as for SCell PDSCHs on PCell
resourc

6.2.3
Impact analysis on specifications
Carrier aggregation for NR is defined in 3GPP specification [i.4]. In Intra O-DU carrier aggregation, the scheduler is
residing in the single vendor O-DU and the vendor can implement proprietry algorithms to coordinate DL and UL
resources and manage data transfer between PCell and SCells. There is no impact on any specification, as both the cells
are running in the same O-DU and O-FH is a well-defined interface in O-RAN for O-DU and O-RU interoperability.

specifications [i.14], [i.15] might be needed to enable an O-RU to connect with two O-DUs and for the O-RU to share
its resources (carriers) dynamically between the two O-DUs for single MNO use case with carrier sharing. This
resource partitioning (static or dynamic) use case of sharing carriers is described in clause 4.20.1.2, clause 4.20.2.2 and

6.3
Solution 2: Inter O-DU Carrier Aggregation
6.3.1
Solution description
In case the product/server realizing the O-DU is not capable of being upgraded to support new band or capability either
because of software or hardware limitations, carrier aggregation still can be achieved by installing a new O-DU with the
required capability or to increase the capacity. Newly installed O-DU can be provided by the same vendor or different
vendors. For supporting CA, O-DUs can be connected with a newly proposed O-RAN interface inter-connecting the
two MAC layers. Details on how this solution can potentially be implemented is described below.
For supporting carrier aggregation across multi-vendor O-DUs which are running in different servers, existing
interfaces Xn (at O-CU-CP/O-CU-UP level), F1 (between O-CU-CP/O-CU-UP and O-DU) and Open Fronthaul
(between O-DU and multiple O-RU) cannot be used as none of the interfaces support connection between O-DUs.
Hence, support for newly proposed interface between O-DUs is required in this scenario. If existing O-DUs already
support the interface or it can be supported by a software upgrade, carrier aggregation across O-DUs can be achieved.
By supporting an inter O-DU interface for CA, MNO can benefit from all the benefits of spectrum aggregation through
CA.
A Service Management & Orchestrator (SMO) configures O-DUs using O1 interface as shown in Figure 6.3.1-1. O-
DUs and O-RUs need to be compatible from Management plane perspective. This is the requirement for interworking
of newly installed O-DU with existing/new O-RU irrespective of inter O-DU CA. The O1 interface can be updated to
bring additional information such as IP address of the O-DUs, C-RNTIs, or PCIs, that is needed for the functioning of
inter O-DU interface. The inter O-DU int

DU with existing/new O-RU irrespective of inter O-DU CA. The O1 interface can be updated to
bring additional information such as IP address of the O-DUs, C-RNTIs, or PCIs, that is needed for the functioning of
inter O-DU interface. The inter O-DU interface can also be configured automatically based on self-detection of O-DUs
supporting cells that can be aggregated.

Figure 6.3.1-1: O-DU configuration by SMO (modified from [i.17] to show the new interface).
In Figure 6.3.1-2 O-DU1 is hosting primary cells while O-DU2… O-DUn are hosting SCells. The dotted colored
interface is indicating the DL CA across O-DUs using the new interface (D2-C and D2-U). O-DU1 receives data from
O-CU-UP and schedules DL Data with O-DU2 … O-DUn to transmit on SCells. If there is no UL CA supported,
PUCCH for SCells and PCells shall be received by O-DU1 as shown in Figure 6.3.1-2. O-DU1 shall extract the relevant
part of the PUCCH information such as CQI, HARQ feedback and forward it to SCells.
NOTE:

inter-connected O-DUs for a given deployment that are used for CA across relevant SCells.

Figure 6.3.1-2: Inter O-DU DL Carrier Aggregation without UL CA.
At power up, each O-DU connects to its peer O-DUs based on the configuration received via O1 interface. SCells from
peer O-DUs can be added only if link establishment between the O-DUs is successful. Once a O-DU triggers the link
establishment request towards another O-DU, it may accept or reject the request. If the request is rejected, pair of O-
DUs can not be used for CA. On SCell addition from O-CU-CP, primary O-DU shares the SCell information such as
CRNTI, Cell ID of SCell, QoS, RLC configuration etc with secondary O-DUs supporting SCells. After successful
addition of SCells from other O-DUs, SCells can be activated for the UE. At SCell activation, the primary O-DU,
informs secondary O-DUs about CA activation so that data exchange can take place.

________________________________________________________________________________________________
24
If UL CA is also enabled along-with DL CA, UE maintains multiple links for uplink data. UE transmits data on the
respective SCells, which can belong to different O-DUs, depending on the scheduling of PUSCH in SCells. Data is then
transferred from secondary O-DUs to the primary O-DU for aggregation. The primary O-DU sends the aggregated data
to O-CU-UP. In this case UCI for both PCell and SCell can also come multiplexed with PUSCH data on SCell
depending on scheduling in the SCell.
As showing in Figure 6.3.1-3 & Figure 6.3.1-4, UE is connected to PCell running in the O-DU1 while SCells are
running in the O-DU2 and the O-DUn. UE transmits the data on the cell(s) as scheduled by the PDCCH. SCell(s)
receive PUSCH containing user data and control (UCI) information. Secondary O-DU (O-DUn) then forwards the user
data and UCI information (for example HARQ feebdback, CQI) for PCell and SCells to the Primary O-DU (O-DU1).
Primary O-DU shares the UCI information with other secondary O-DUs (O-DU2). In Figure 6.3.1-3, UCI bits are
scheduled on the primary O-DU (O-DU1). O-DU1 receives UCI information related to SCells.  O-DU1 then parses and
sends UCI information to O-DU2 and O-DUn if present. In Figure 6.3.1-4,, UCI is scheduled on secondary O-DUn
multiplexed with PUSCH. The O-DUn receives the UL data along with the UCI information and shares UL Data and
UCI information with the O-DU1. The O-DU1 forwards UCI information to secondary O-DU2, if present.

Figure 6.3.1-4: Inter O-DU UL CA, PUCCH on SCell.

In the case of intra gNB, inter O-DU CA, MLB can be achieved through F1 interface. For MLB, one or more UEs can
be handed over to other O-DUs. Handover can be done to both co-located and non-co-located O-DUs. Inter O-DU
handover using F1 interface is defined in 3GPP specifications. Additionally, the new interface between O-DUs, if
defined, also can be used to share the resource status information between the O-DUs so that the PCell can avoid
activating SCells on the O-DU facing loading condition as shown in Figure 6.3.1-5 below.

Figure 6.3.1-5: Mobility load balancing with intra gNB, inter O-Dus CA.
In the case of inter gNB, inter O-DU CA, MLB can be achieved via F1 and X2/Xn interface [i.12] [i.13]. On a condition
triggering MLB, one or more UEs can be handed over to other O-DU. On detecting any MLB condition, O-DU can
inform O-CU-CP about the resource status on F1 interface. Based on these reports, O-CU-CP can trigger X2/Xn
handover towards another O-DU. All these procedures are defined in 3GPP specifications. Additionally, if secondary
O-DU is loaded, interface between O-DUs can be used to report the resource condition to primary O-DU as shown in
Figure 6.3.1-6 below. Primary O-DU can avoid SCell activation towards this O-DU to avoid loading with exchanging
resource information such as “Radio Resource Status” IE defined in 3GPP TS 38.423 [i.13].

Figure 6.3.1-6: Mobility load balancing with inter gNB, inter O-DUs CA.

DU is common for both primary and secondary O-DU for a particular UE while MAC layer can be present in both
primary and secondary O-DUs for a UE.

Figure 6.3.1-7: Protocol stack in O-DUs for Inter O-DU CA.
There are two parts of the inter O-DU interface referred to as D2 here.

D2-C: Exchange of Control information. SCTP can be used as transport protocol.

D2-U: Exchange of user data and PUCCH information. GTP-U is used for transport mechanisms.
D2 Control Interface (D2-C):
D2-C functionality involves the establishment and management of the link between O-DUs. SCTP is used as
transport protocol. Link establishment between O-DUs takes place before any UE is connected to the O-DU. Main
functionality of D2-C includes:

Establish connection between O-DUs.

Connection establishment can happen as soon as the O-DU comes up.

SCell Addition/Deletion/Modification. It can be triggered on SCell addition/deletion/modification for a
particular UE.
Figure 6.3.1-8 indicates the sample message sequence for D2 link establishment. Figure 6.3.1-8 indicates the procedure
and not the actual interface name or parameters.

Figure 6.3.1-8: D2 link establishment.

________________________________________________________________________________________________
27
D2 User Interface (D2-U):
The D2-U part of the interface is responsible for user data and PUCCH/UCI information exchange between O-DUs.
GTP-U is used as the transport protocol for this interface. Main functionality of D2-U includes:

Data exchange between primary and secondary O-DU.

For DL-CA, primary O-DU receives data from O-CU-UP. The PDCCH is scheduled on both the O-DUs
independently, similar to Intra O-DU CA case.

For DL CA, PUCCH resource allocation is done by primary O-DU. PUCCH related information (e.g. PUCCH
Resource Indicator etc), required to be encoded in PDCCH, is shared between the primary and secondary O-
DUs. UCI information on PUCCH for all the O-DUs is received by primary O-DU. It then forwards the
information related to an SCell to the respective secondary O-DU.

For UL CA, both PCell on primary O-DU and SCells on secondary O-DUs receive data from UE. After MAC
layer processing, secondary O-DU sends UE UL data to the primary O-DU, which then forwards it to the RLC
layer residing in the primary O-DU.
Figure 6.3.1-9 indicates the information exchange on D2-U interface.

Figure 6.3.1-9: D2-U usage.
For D2 interface configuration and management, existing O1 interface that brings O-DU configuration from SMO can
be enhanced. The D2 interface can be defined in a manner similar to the 3GPP defined F1 interface: a control part D2-C
to carry control related information and a user plane part D2-U carrying user data as described above. Existing security
mechanism defined in WG11 e.g., IPSec or any other mechanism can be utilized for protecting D2 interface as well.
Brief outlines of control and data plane procedures expected from D2 interface are also described in Figure 6.3.1-8 and
Figure 6.3.1-9.  An example of protocol stack split for supporting inter O-DU CA is also captured in Annex B.
As the interface between the O-DUs is kept at MAC sub-layer for user plane, this tends to reduce the bandwidth
requirement. Bandwidth requirements for inter O-DU CA can be the same or lower then F1 bandwidth requirement. The
D2 interface can be designed to accommodate the latency class High75, High100 & High200 as described in Table A-1.
The total round trip transmission and processing delay is bounded by 500 μs. Coverage of mid/high band carrier can be
improved if inter O-DU CA is supported between O-DUs with PCell on low band FDD carrier and SCell on mid/high
band TDD carrier. This coverage improvement, due to PUCCH for mid/high band SCells being received on low band
PCell, can be similar to the intra O-DU CA solution.
6.3.2
Mapping to deployment scenarios and other consideration
This solution can cover all the deployment scenarios mentioned in clause 5.2.1.2 and clause 5.2.2 if the latency
requirement between O-DUs is maintained as mentioned in clause 6.3.1. Spectrum aggregation across multiple multi-
vendor O-DUs, either in co-located or non-co-located sc

deployment scenarios mentioned in clause 5.2.1.2 and clause 5.2.2 if the latency
requirement between O-DUs is maintained as mentioned in clause 6.3.1. Spectrum aggregation across multiple multi-
vendor O-DUs, either in co-located or non-co-located scenarios, can be achieved with this solution. Band combinations
for NR CA are defined in Table 6.2.2-1 in clause 6.2.2. Energy consumption at UE is similar to intra O-DU CA solution

________________________________________________________________________________________________
28
as defined in clause 6.2.2, but at the network side, energy consumption can be higher due to message exchange between
O-DUs. SDL bands are low bands that can be used to increase the coverage and throughput. If an SDL band is allocated
to the MNO and it is supported in a different O-DU, it can be used for CA using this interface. On allocation of SUL
band, if support of the SUL band cannot be extended in existing O-DU(s), another O-DU supporting SUL carrier can be
used to provide the switching between the carriers for better coverage and performance. The proposed interface can be
used to support this switching.

6.4.1

Dual Connectivity (DC) is a well defined spectrum aggregation technique specified by 3GPP in TS 38.331 [i.9] and TS

to provide connectivity to the UE using Xn or F1 interface as shown in Figure 6.4.1-1 which results in better
throughput. Data exchange takes place at PDCP PDU level in DC. O-DU is transparent for data transfer in DC
technique. For O-DUs, there are two separate links established in downlink and uplink direction for a particular UE for
data and control (UCI) information exchange. Figure 6.4.1-1 indicates the DC between multiple O-CU-CPs/O-CU-UPs.

Figure 6.4.1-2.  O-DU and O-RU can also be provided by the same vendor or different vendors.

7.1
Summary of evaluation
In the present document different deployment scenarios are described which are relevant to spectrum aggregation. For a
multi-vendor network deployment, the following spectrum aggregation solutions are documented.

Intra O-DU CA

Inter O-DU CA

Dual connectivity
Figure 7.1-1 summarizes the key properties of the three spectrum aggregation solutions. Intra O-DU CA relies on Open
FH interface (PHY layer) which enables multi vendor O-RUs. Inter O-DU CA using the D2 interface interconnects the
two MAC layers in separate O-DUs. Dual connectivity makes use of PDCP aggregation at the O-CU-UP level.
Depening on deployment scenario, one of the three solutions or a combination thereof can be used for spectrum
aggregation. A decision tree to help arrive at a solution, considering different deployment scenarios, is described in
Annex C.

As shown in Table 7.1-1, Table 7.1-2 and Table 7.1-3, for supporting spectrum aggregation across non-co-located nodes
with non-ideal backhaul, DC is a preferred option. DC can support spectrum aggregation in non-synchronized
components. It is a well defined solution in 3GPP and O-RAN. DC is the preferred option for spectrum aggregation
between FR1 and FR2.

________________________________________________________________________________________________
36
Table 7.1-2 indicates that CA has more band combinations (also see Table 6.2.2-1) defined in 3GPP specifications.
Spectrum aggregation across intra band carriers cannot be achieved by NR DC. CA provides better coverage and
capacity compared to DC for mid/high band aggregated with low band cells. If multiple cells are supported in single O-
DU, intra O-DU CA with/without Shared O-RU solution can be utilized for spectrum aggregation across different bands
to achieve the best coverage and capacity results with least energy consumption.
In a deployment scenario, where different frequency bands are supported in different O-DUs or if an O-DU instance
cannot host further cells due to its processing limits, inter O-DU CA (assuming legacy O-DU can be upgraded to
support new interface) can be used for achieving the benefits of carrier aggregation. This will be beneficial for both co-
located and non-co-located deployments. The new interface between O-DUs can be specified within the transport
latency requirements as described in clasue 6.3.1. Coverage and capacity (in terms of users) improvement can be similar
to the intra O-DU CA solution. The new interface between O-DUs can provide further flexibility to the MNOs to install
RAN NFs as per their need and from different vendors.
7.2
Impact on standardization
For intra O-DU CA multi-O-RU scenario and dual connectivity, there is no impact on any WG as it is specified in
3GPP and O-RAN specifications. For intra O-DU CA with shared O-RU, WG4 enhancements may be needed to
support dynamic carrier sharing.
There is no direct standardized inter O-DU interface defined in 3GPP or in O-RAN. For supporting inter O-DU carrier
aggregation, a new

support dynamic carrier sharing.
There is no direct standardized inter O-DU interface defined in 3GPP or in O-RAN. For supporting inter O-DU carrier
aggregation, a new inter O-DU interface, referred to as D2, needs to be defined. Table 6.3.3-1 details the WGs and the
specifications impact of standardizing the proposed interface.
Based on the prior Open FH experience, the development timeline of D2 interface is expected to be about 2 years from
the start of the work item until the specification can be considered robust enough for the implementation.
7.3
Recommendations
The objective of this study is to evaluate spectrum aggregation techniques (carrier aggregation and dual connectivity) in
both co-located and non-co-located scenarios utilizing specific assessment criteria. As shown in Table 7.1-1, Table 7.1-
2 and Table 7.1-3, dual connectivity is appropriate when a user equipment (UE) connects to two separate cells
concurrently, typically with different frequencies (e.g., FR1 and FR2) over non-ideal backhaul links.
In intra O-DU CA (shared O-RU or multi-O-RU) O-DUs, O-RUs can be provided by different vendors.  Intra O-DU
CA provides the best coverage and capacity improvement in spectrum aggregation. It can be used in co-located
scenarios or deployments where single O-DU will be supporting multiple cells connected to different O-RUs. For non-
co-located deployment use cases of clause 5.2.2, this solution can cover all scenarios if the fronthaul connecting the O-
RU and O-DU has latency within the latency classes of High25, High75 of Table A-1. The High100 and High200
latency classes can also be supported depending on implementation and performance trade-offs.
Multi-vendor dual connectivity a

onnecting the O-
RU and O-DU has latency within the latency classes of High25, High75 of Table A-1. The High100 and High200
latency classes can also be supported depending on implementation and performance trade-offs.
Multi-vendor dual connectivity and intra O-DU CA are well-defined in 3GPP specifications and are supported by O-
RAN.
For catering to deployment scenarios where different frequency bands are supported in different O-DUs or if an O-DU
instance cannot host further cells due to its processing limits, multi-vendor inter O-DU CA can be used for achieving
the benefits of spectrum aggregation. This will be beneficial for both co-located and non-co-located deployments. This
assumes that legacy O-DUs are upgradable to support the new inter O-DU interface.

SMO Intent driven management concepts
4.1
Overview
An intent specifies the expectations including requirements, goals, and constraints, without specifying how the expectations
should be fulfilled. In short, an intent is a statement or specification on the desired state of the system. Following are some
general concepts for intent:
o
An intent is understandable by both humans as well as the machines without any ambiguity.
o
An intent specifies “what” needs to be achieved without specifying “how” it can be done.
The expectations expressed by an intent is agnostic to the underlying system implementation, technology, and infrastructure.
Intents are a means to allow consumers of SMO Services to express their end goals, requirements and constraints, and then
allows the SMO Service Producers, nonRT-RIC, and relevant rApps to figure out how to execute the realization of that intent.
Advanced options can also be available, such as consumer making feasibility inquiries using various sets/subsets of its
requirements or to obtain the possible available options for certain requirements.
In O-RAN SMO, intents can have a wide range

In O-RAN SMO, intents can have a wide range of applicability including the various interactions within SMO management
loops (closed, open), serving as a simplified method for management exposure of RAN services both externally and internally
to other management or business systems. The external exposure allows external management and business entities to interact
with the SMO by expressing their requirements and goals for RAN instances in a simplified manner, without needing to be
aware of all the details of the RAN models and the various types of management and orchestration interfaces design. An
example of such external management service can be an E2E Service Management (E2E SM) system that is tasked to create
and maintain a 5G service which includes all the access/RAN, core, transport and cloud services needed. Internally, different
SMOS producers and rApps can use intents to interact with each other for different RAN management related tasks. Using
intents would simplify the interactions and minimize dependencies between the consuming and producing entity of the
management service, e.g., E2E SM entity, or a BSS, and the O-RAN SMO.
A simplified approach of the SMO NBI, SMOS exposure, and R1 using intent-based management is beneficial, for the
following reasons:

(a) Separation of concerns, between SMO and other management entities in OSS or BSS, which do not need to have a detailed
knowledge of the O-RAN information models and data models to be able to request an O-RAN service.
(b) Ability for SMOS producers to produce and/or consumer intent based services (be it SMO framework services or SMOS
realized via rApps).
(c) Enable an evolution path of the SMO towards knowledge-driven management systems, where machine reasoning
capabilities can process received O-RAN intents, perform data inference when needed and are easily extensible.
(d) Establish a common intent management framework in the SMO that can handle the O-RAN service level management
via intents, which can be reused and extended as necessary. The extensions to add further scoping of O-RAN intents can be
done by simply defining their intent models (since the interface definition and intent management framework are reusable
throughout the SMO).
(e) Leverage existing standardization work on intents management, specifically intent interfaces, models, and management
aspects such as intent capabilities tracking (registration, discovery), such as TM Forum´s TR290X, TR291X, TR292X,
TR293, TMF921A and GB921, 3GPP TS 28.312, 3GPP TR 28.912, ETSI GR ZSM011 and ETSI GS ZSM016, etc.

Intent negotiation procedures help the RMIO (an authorized consumer of the SMO services) to find the best possible way to
fulfil an intent. These procedures are important since they help the RMIO and RMIH engage with each other in a collaborative
way that is beneficial for both. When an intent is provided to the RMIH, it can go either of the two ways:

way that is beneficial for both. When an intent is provided to the RMIH, it can go either of the two ways:

Pre-evaluation/Exploration: if the intent is provided to RMIH for pre-evaluation/exploration, nothing in the network
or the system (including SMO) changes. Intent negotiation in this phase includes:
o

o

The attribute corresponding to intent reporting in the intent model can be configured to choose from these options. This will be
discussed further in detail during the intent modelling in the subsequent normative work.

Fulfilment: if the intent is provided to the RMIH for fulfilment, it means that RMIH starts taking necessary actions
(e.g., allocating resources) and actual changes in the network and/or the system can be observed.

The ANP develops specifications for various aspects of autonomous networks including its generic architecture, the definition,
and assessment of levels of autonomy and closed loop management. Intent is a particular focus with specifications about:

The definition of intent

The architecture of intent-based networks with intent management functions

The scope of the work is not limited to a single operational domain. It rather introduces concepts that would be applicable
vertically in multiple operational layers as well as horizontally across multiple domains. The API as well as the model for
intent expressions are designed to adapt to domain specific use cases while maintaining a generic core model.
Although the models are different, the proposed O-RAN intent definitions in this study are similar and compatible to other
SDOs, such as TMForum and 3GPP.
Intents are declarative. They specify “what” is reached, but not “how” to reach it leaving the intent handlers with full
autonomy to handle them. Therefore, any explicit instructions of what to execute is excluded from being specified within intent
or by the intent API. Both are rather concerned with the definition, distribution, and management of requirements enabling
subsystems to make suitable decisions and find solutions on their own rather than being instructed what actions to take. This
way of interaction between subsystems enhances separation of concerns which is advantageous for AI-native implementations.
4.2.1.1
Intent modeling
Intent is a knowledge object expressing requirements. Sending an intent therefore means informing the receiving system about
a set of requirements it needs to comply to. When the requirements in the intent are not needed anymore then they are
removed. This means intent objects are actively lifecycle managed and need to be fulfilled, as long as the requirements they
relayed are needed. The TM Forum intent API TMF921 [i.9] is therefore primarily concerned with executing the lifecycle
management of intent knowledge objects.
The TM Forum intent ontology (TIO) is the model for intent expression. It is based on the Resource Descriptor Frame

TM Forum intent API TMF921 [i.9] is therefore primarily concerned with executing the lifecycle
management of intent knowledge objects.
The TM Forum intent ontology (TIO) is the model for intent expression. It is based on the Resource Descriptor Framework
(RDF) standard by W3C. It was chosen due to its capabilities and track record for knowledge modeling applications, since
RDF is used in native machine reasoning implementations provided by different opensource solutions. Intent instances are a
subgraph within the ontology and therefore anchored with full semantical context. Logical reasoning about the requirements is
directly supported by this approach.
The intent ontology model proposed by TM Forum is highly modular. The ontology used for intent expression within a domain
is a federation of a common generic model referred to as intent common model and domain-specific additions referred to as
intent extension models. The intent common model is specified in TM Forum (TR290) [i.8], with a simple common structure
that defines the internal structure of intent objects and provides general purpose vocabulary for expression of requirements.
Other SDOs are invited to leverage the common intent model and then develop their own intent extension models for their
scope of expertise (e.g., specific extensions to RAN management intents in O-RAN). No central or formal governance is
required for intent extension models. The goal of the model federation is to keep intent expressions consistent across domains
(business, management, traffic, etc.), while still being able to easily adapt it to new domain specific needs.
