449
accuracy. This information is required for the NTN xApp(s) to have cognizance of which satellites are available over
which area of the Earth, enabling them to drive NTN connected mode mobility, but also for the NTN xApp(s) to provide
the ephemeris information to the E2 node for the latter to include in its scheduling, for instance for the purposes of System
Information Block (SIB) 19 broadcast.
The satellite ephemeris information is itself typically updated and generated on a periodic basis by the Satellite Control
Center (SCC), which is a system that is most often proprietary to the satellite constellation and operator. In an O-RAN
architecture, this information could enter the system as external information, packaged as a data type for which the SCC
is an external data producer. The mechanism through which this ingestion occurs is left to implementation.
Once the data is ingested into the SMO and Non-RT RIC, it would be delivered to the Near-RT RIC as A1 enrichment
information, via the A1 interface. Once the information is available to the NTN xApp(s), the use case can proceed.
4.30.3.2 Time-based CHO
Addressing the EMC case first, whether the system is Transparent or Regenerative, 3GPP has not provisioned or accounted
for the NTN gNBs to have the ability to keep track of which satellites, and by proxy which EMC cells, are valid
neighboring candidates for handover in a continuously evolving system such as an NGSO NTN constellation. This is
exemplified in the simplified figure 4.30.1.2-1 but would be even more pronounced in a denser deployment, as it would
be in a real constellation.
The blue satellite in the figure, orbiting due North-East along its orbit, is the one w

exemplified in the simplified figure 4.30.1.2-1 but would be even more pronounced in a denser deployment, as it would
be in a real constellation.
The blue satellite in the figure, orbiting due North-East along its orbit, is the one which is initially serving the orange UE
via the cell with PCI 3. Following 3GPP Release 17, the NTN gNB, as prompted by the NTN xApp via the E2 interface,
can instruct the UE with GNSS capabilities to record coarse location information (with ~2 km accuracy) and report it to
the NTN gNB [53], who subsequently uses the E2 interface to deliver it to the Near-RT RIC and the NTN xApp. By
knowing the coarse coordinates of the UE as well as using the digital twin to derive the coverage footprints of the
individual cells/beams delivered by the blue satellite, the NTN xApp can compute the remaining service time of the cell
with PCI 3 after which the UE needs to be handed over to the cell with PCI 4, and subsequently to the cell with PCI 5.
These derived remaining service times and handover target cells are UE-specific even within the same cell (e.g., PCI 3)
as the relative location of different UEs within the same cell would define their mobility opportunities. For instance, if
the UE in figure 4.30.1.2-1 was instead in the North-West corner of the cell with PCI 3 in the initial view, its target
handover cell would instead be the cell with PCI 1, and the handover would need to occur sooner due to the shape of the
beam and cell with PCI 3.
The NTN xApp would instruct the NTN gNB delivering the cell with PCI 3 to configure the orange UE with the T1 CHO
(condEventT1 [53]) conditions that would signal to it the time interval during which it ought to attempt to connect to the
cell that is subsequent to it, the one with PCI 4, as well as w

(condEventT1 [53]) conditions that would signal to it the time interval during which it ought to attempt to connect to the
cell that is subsequent to it, the one with PCI 4, as well as with appropriate SIB19 parameters to be broadcast that would
contain the ntn-Config-r17 of all of the neighboring cells, itself containing the epochTime-r17 and ephemerisInfo-r17 of
the blue satellite, among other parameters. Taking the cell with PCI 3 from the above figure as an example, its neighboring
cells would be cells with PCI 1, PCI 4 and PCI 6.
After some time, the orange UE enters the trailing beam/cell of the blue satellite (PCI 5) after which it needs to be handed
over to a cell illuminated by another satellite, in this instance the green one (first cell being one with PCI 14). The Near-
RT RIC and NTN xApp would yet again combine coarse UE location information and digital twin modelling of the NTN
constellation to produce the T1 CHO (condEventT1) and SIB19 parameters which aid the handover from blue cell with
PCI 5 to the green cell with PCI 14. This could be coupled with another condition, such as one that is dependent on the
signal quality of the neighboring cell exceeding some nominal value to ensure that the handover stands a greater chance
of success (e.g., condEventA3, condEventA4, condEventA5) for which the SMTC4 configuration defined for NTN is
employed (or otherwise can be used to pre-synchronize with the neighboring SS/PBCH transmissions). Furthermore, the
overlapping coverage from multiple satellites also necessitates close coordination of which frequencies are employed by
which cell in order to avoid interference, and the question of which are permitted to be employed is in many cases
dependent on the

verlapping coverage from multiple satellites also necessitates close coordination of which frequencies are employed by
which cell in order to avoid interference, and the question of which are permitted to be employed is in many cases
dependent on the region of the Earth that is being illuminated. Therefore, there is a further need for a higher order NTN
control function, such as a Near-RT RIC and constituent NTN xApp(s), to drive this functionality.
As for the EFC case, in good time prior to the scheduled discontinuation of coverage to the EFC by the blue cell with PCI
3, the Near-RT RIC and NTN xApp would instruct via the E2 interface the NTN gNB to configure the UEs in the cell
with the appropriate T1 CHO (condEventT1) configuration, potentially in conjunction with signal measurement-based
CHO configurations (e.g., condEventA3, condEventA4, condEventA5). As was the case in the EMC instance, the NTN

xApp will infer, if not decide itself, through the NTN digital twin and forward-looking scheduling that it will be the red
satellite which will deploy a particular cell (PCI 13) at a particular moment over that EFC in order to continue providing
service, and will have therefore provisioned the T1 CHO configurations in good time prior to the handover occasion
taking place, taking into account any dependency on signaling delays induced by the RTT influenced by the orbital regime
and Transparent vs. Regenerative nature of the constellation. Likewise, this will need to be accompanied with the updated
SIB19 containing the ntn-Config-r17 which will indicate to the UE crucial information about the cell with PCI 13 and the
red satellite, such as its ephemeris information, enabling the UE to synchronize with it.
In the event that there is a significant number of UEs in the blue cell with PCI 3, their handing over to the red cell with
PCI 13 during the potential overlap period should be managed carefully in order to reduce the chances of preamble
collisions, contention resolution delays, etc. Since the two satellite beams and cells in question are intended to cover the
same EFC, the relative location of different UEs within the EFC would not play as much of a role as it did in the EMC
case, as all of the UEs would be affected by the withdrawal of the blue cell with PCI 3 and illumination of the red cell
with PCI 13 in the same manner and time (there is an edge case where this need not be true; if the elevation angles of the
blue and red satellites cause their beam footprints and therefore cell coverages on top of the EFC at the moment of
handover to be of different shapes, excludi

nd time (there is an edge case where this need not be true; if the elevation angles of the
blue and red satellites cause their beam footprints and therefore cell coverages on top of the EFC at the moment of
handover to be of different shapes, excluding certain UEs). In this respect, the same T1 CHO parameters could be
configured for all of the UEs within the same cell. Nevertheless, in order to balance the RA load onto the red cell with
PCI 13, the Near-RT RIC and NTN xApp(s) can theoretically alter the duration of any overlap or discontinuity of service
to the EFC (T310 timer for RLF in UEs starts as blue cell shuts off – UEs must perform RA to the red cell prior to expiry
to avoid exiting RRC connected mode) as well as tune the per-UE group RACH-Config and T1 CHO parameters to better
distribute their RA across the red cell’s RACH occasions.

4.30.3.3 Distance-based CHO
Focusing again on the EMC case first, and with respect to the scenario in figure 4.30.1.2-1, the UE is initially served by
the blue satellite via the beam and cell with PCI 3. It requires a mechanism by which to evaluate its distance from the
moving locations which represent its current serving cell and a candidate neighboring cell in an EMC system. In 3GPP
Release 18, a new CHO configuration was introduced, called D2 CHO (condEventD2 [53]), for this purpose. This allows
the NTN xApp, by proxy of the E2 interface to the NTN gNB, to specify two distances, distanceThreshFromReference1-
r18 and distanceThreshFromReference2-r18 alongside a hysteresis distance, to a UE in a cell. The UE is expected to use
its GNSS capabilities to ascertain its location, but it also needs the two moving locations to measure and compare its
distance to.
At the same time, the NTN xApp can use the E2 interface to deliver to the NTN gNB the parameters which it is supposed
to broadcast to UEs in cell with PCI 3 as part of SIB19. Other than including crucial parameters such as epochTime-r17
and ephemerisInfo-r17 which are found in the ntn-Config-r17, starting from 3GPP Release 18 the SIB19 is also supposed
to also include a field called movingReferenceLocation-r18. This is supposed to signal to the UEs a serving cell-specific
reference location which they are supposed to measure their distance to and compare it to the
distanceThreshFromReference1-r17 value provided via the D2 CHO configuration. Nominally this location can be
regarded as representing the moving cell center, but strictly speaking need not be, and it is up to the NTN xApp to define
what this is going to represent. The movingReferenceLocation-r18

via the D2 CHO configuration. Nominally this location can be
regarded as representing the moving cell center, but strictly speaking need not be, and it is up to the NTN xApp to define
what this is going to represent. The movingReferenceLocation-r18 is in its definition a static point on the ground,
timestamped to the epochTime-r17 from the ntn-Config-r17, and the UE is expected to combine this with the
ephemerisInfo-r17 to propagate the satellite’s orbital trajectory in the immediate future and ascertain how the
movingReferenceLocation-r18 would move along with the satellite, before it receives the subsequent SIB19 broadcast
with the network-updated movingReferenceLocation-r18.
The other reference location, the distance to which the UE is measuring using its GNSS-derived coordinates and
comparing to the distanceThreshFromReference2-r17 value provided via the D2 CHO configuration, is delivered inside
the measObjectNR, namely in the ntn-NeighbourCellInfo-r18 field, for a specific candidate neighboring cell. Within this
field, the neighboring cell’s epochTime-r17, ephemerisInfo-r17, and referenceLocation-r17 are specified, where the latter
is a static location which indicates the reference location at epochTime-r17, which the UE can use alongside the
epehemerisInfo-r17 to propagate the satellite’s orbital trajectory in the immediate future and ascertain how the
referenceLocation-r17 would move along with the satellite, as was the case with movingReferenceLocation-r18.
Once the distance to the movingReferenceLocation-r18 of the serving cell exceeds the distanceThreshFromReference1-
r17, and simultaneously the distance to the referenceLocation-r17 of a neighboring candidate cell drops below the
distanceThreshFromReference2-r17 (taking into account hysteresis in both cases),

serving cell exceeds the distanceThreshFromReference1-

distanceThreshFromReference2-r17 (taking into account hysteresis in both cases), the UE regards itself as having satisfied

the conditions for the D2 CHO, and attempts to join the neighboring cell. Nominally, the NTN xApp does not need to
know the coarse location of the UEs in a cell to supply them with the D2 CHO parameters, making the D2 CHO
configuration common to all UEs in the cell. Referring to the scenario in figure 4.30.1.2-1, if the UE were to be initially
located inside the blue cell with PCI 4, it would be supplied with D2 CHO configurations only for the neighboring blue
cells which could at some point in the future (no farther than the TimeToTrigger in the D2 CHO config) illuminate the
current footprint of the cell with PCI 4. These would be the cells with PCIs 2, 5 and 7, but not the ones with PCIs 1, 3 and
6, since those wouldn’t be valid handover candidates due to the movement of the blue satellite. Then, if the serving and
various neighboring cell reference locations were tied to the cell centers, the distances supplied in the D2 CHO config
would relate to the serving and neighboring cells’ radii.
Moving on to EFC-based systems next and taking the scenario from figure 4.30.1.3-1 as reference, the orange UE is
initially located within the blue cell with PCI 6. The NTN xApp is aware of the overall EFC topology of the network and
can infer the cells which are neighbors to the cell with PCI 6. In the simplified example in the figure, these are the blue
cells with PCIs 3, 4, 7 and the green cell with PCI 12. In this instance, the cell centers are not influenced by the movement
of the blue and green satellites, but are instead fixed on the ground. For supporting mobility cases where the UE’s relative
proximity to these reference locations is driven by the mobility of the UE itself,

enters are not influenced by the movement
of the blue and green satellites, but are instead fixed on the ground. For supporting mobility cases where the UE’s relative
proximity to these reference locations is driven by the mobility of the UE itself, 3GPP introduced in Release 17 support
for D1 CHO (condEventD1 [53]). Within it, the two reference locations (referenceLocation1-r17 and referenceLocation2-
r17) and the distance thresholds to the two reference locations (distanceThreshFromReference1-r17 and
distanceThreshFromReference2-r17) are defined right in the D1 CHO configuration and are common for all UEs in the
cell. Referring again to the starting position of the orange UE, it receives a D1 CHO configuration for each of the
neighboring cells. After some time, the UE moves due North sufficiently such that its distance from the center of the
serving cell with PCI 6 (referenceLocation1-r17) exceeds the configured distanceThreshFromReference1-r17, while its
proximity to the center of the neighboring cell with PCI 3 (referenceLocation2-r17) drops below the configured
distanceThreshFromReference2-r17, taking into account hysteresis for both distances. At that point, the D1 CHO
configuration for cell with PCI 3 is triggered, and the orange UE attempts to join it, where upon success it becomes
configured with the D1 CHO configurations for the new set of neighboring cells (blue cells with PCIs 1,4 and 6 and green
cells with PCIs 9 and 12). The triggering condition could again be coupled with another condition, such as one that is
dependent on the signal quality of the neighboring cell exceeding some nominal value to ensure that the handover stands
a greater chance of success (e.g. condEventA3, condEventA4, condEventA5) for which the SMTC4 configuration defined
for NTN is emp

dependent on the signal quality of the neighboring cell exceeding some nominal value to ensure that the handover stands
a greater chance of success (e.g. condEventA3, condEventA4, condEventA5) for which the SMTC4 configuration defined
for NTN is employed (or otherwise can be used to pre-synchronize with the neighboring SS/PBCH transmissions). Yet
again, after some time, the orange UE moves, this time Eastwards into the coverage footprint of the green cell with PCI
12. Here, the same conditional measurement procedure takes place, and the orange UE eventually joins the cell with PCI
12.
The solution to the distance-based CHO driven mobility is described in table 4.30.3.3-1 and is covered in [i.17], clause
5.2.4.

Annex A (informative):
Additional information
A.1
Traffic steering use case A1 interface usage example
NOTE: Please refer to WG2 Use Cases and Requirements Specification for more details and up to date definitions of this
use case A1 interface usage examples.
An example scenario is here used to describe the use of A1 for traffic steering, implying the Non-RT RIC sending policies
for allocation of the control plane (RRC) and the user plane for different services, identified by their 5QI.
In the scenario a UE with UEid=1, belonging to a subnet slice identified by S-NSSAI=1, having a voice (5QI=1) and an
MBB (5QI=9) connection established, enters an area covered by four frequency bands. The Non-RT RIC understands the
requirements and characteristics of the services and decides to let the voice and RRC connection reside on the low band
(here covered by a macro cell B becoming the PCell), while the MBB connection should preferably use the higher band
(here provided by a smaller cell C and D becoming the SCells) and avoid the low band if possible. Cell A is used for MBB
if required for coverage reasons.
Policies are sent to any cell of concern, e.g. where the UE resides and can move.
The desired use of the cells is shown in figure A.1-1.

Figure A.1-1: Desired use of the cells
Two policies over A1 are needed to accomplish the desired behavior, described in JSON format below. Note that as part
of the scope, the cell_id is optional, and if omitted it is up to the Near-RT RIC to locate the UE and there enforce the
policy.

4
Analysis of Data Format
4.1
Background
4.1.1
MnS Component Type B
A Management Service Component Type B is defined in clause 4.2.3.1 of 3GPP TS 28.533 [i.4] as referring to
management information represented by information models representing the managed entities. The definition goes on
to state that the terminology “MnS component type B” is interchangeable with the term “Network Resource Model
(NRM)”. Two examples of NRMs are given, one being the generic NRM 3GPP TS 28.622 [i.6] and one being the 5G
NRM 3GPP TS 28.541 [i.5].
3GPP TS 32.156 [i.8] defines a model repertoire for building abstract information models of network resources. It
outlines a subset of the Unified Modeling Language (UML) to be used in model development. It defines the stereotype
Information Object Class (IOC) as a key building block for information models. To define a new IOC, a modeler gives
it a class name and an associated table of attributes, each of which can take on a range of usually primitive or simple
compound values according to its data type. The repertoire also defines the <<names>> stereotype association which
allows one class to name-contain other classes. The name-containment relationship can be single (represented with
[ParentIOC] 1 <<names>> 0..1 [Child IOC] in the UML diagram) or multiple (represented with [ParentIOC] 1
<<names>> * [ChildIOC] in the UML diagram). Typically, when a 3GPP document defines a collection of IOCs, the

Extensibility
O1 specifications refer to 3GPP models for the modelling of the logical RAN entities. 3GPP NRM models are defined
in 3GPP TS 28.621[i.16] and 28.622[i.6], related YANG solution set is defined in TS 28.623 while YANG mapping
rules and vendor extension mechanisms are defined in TS 32.160 [i.9].
Each 3GPP solution set has defined its own set of mapping rules and vendor extension mechanisms to provide a
consistent set of models.
Extensibility mechanisms can be used to add non-standardized contents through vendor specific entities in addition to
the standardized ones.
In general, the 3GPP Vendor specific extensibility mechanisms can be used by a vendor or by an SDO. In the context of
O-RAN Alliance, the O-RAN Alliance community can use vendor specific extensibility mechanisms and define a new
standardized data model as O-RAN YANG modu

nd OpenAPI constructs when specifying data models. This arises because of the separation of the
attributes of an IOC from the name-contained relationships to other IOCs, and the enforcement of this separation with
conventions such as declaring an “attributes” container for each MOC and expressing name-containment with property
names (in the case of OpenAPI/YAML) or the “augments” construct (in the case of YANG). (The current O1
specification mandates the use of the YANG Stage 3 solution set rather than the OpenAPI/YAML Stage 3 solution set
and so we restrict our discussion to the YANG Stage 3 solution set in what follows).
Non-3GPP SDOs do not necessarily follow the 3GPP methodology of separately modeling the information to be
managed at an abstract level and then mapping these models into solution sets. Indeed, many extant YANG
specifications from the IETF community are written and edited directly in YANG and make use of the full power of that
notation to define data models that, for instance, do not place attributes into a container named “attributes” and which
don’t enforce name-containment conventions. The O-RAN Alliance WG4 has developed such a model for the OpenFH
M-plane. Finally, vendor-specific YANG models also exist for which no prior information model was developed.
It is not immediately obvious that non-3GPP data models need to be managed via the O1 interface. Perhaps, these
models can always be relegated to being managed over other interfaces. For example, the OpenFH M-plane is depicted

5.2.1
Declarative vs. Imperative Pattern
5.2.1.1
Introduction
Declarative and Imperative patterns are different paradigms that describe whether or not to describe the
“how”. In operations applying an imperative pattern, the “how” is described explicitly by step-by-step
instructions; in operations applying a declarative pattern, the desired state is managed, without explicitly
describing about “how” to achieve it.
In the context of this specification, the declarative pattern provides the abstraction to get the element to the
desired state. For example, declarative pattern for configuration management involves specifying the desired
configuration state rather than explicitly detailing the steps needed to achieve that state.

Declarative Patterns to achieve those O1 Specified operations. This benefits the consumers to prepare the data and not

Configuration Repository as Source of Truth
5.3.1.1
Overview
A logically centralized entity or repository hosting the desired configurations for O-RAN NFs intended to be further
synchronized to a target NF residing in an O-Cloud environment based on a declarative description. It is referred as
logically centralized because the realization of the repository for configuration can be multiple and distributed.
Configuration repository is referred as a source of truth in the context of configuration data of NFs and configuration
data related to O-Cloud.
Such configuration repository enables access to the configuration data to consumer of configuration data. In the context
of provisioning of configuration data, the producer of provisioning management services uses the configuration
repository to store the configuration data.
The configuration repository
enables storing the configuration data from the source of configuration changes [consumer of provisioning MnS],
hosts the artifacts of configuration (e.g. day 1, day 2, etc.),
enables delivery of configuration data to the target NFs, based on declarative approach, and
exposes operations to support create / update / read / delete configuration data.
The consumer of provisioning management services can use methods to push data of desired configuration to the
configuration repository. The desired configuration created / modified on the configuration repository, can then be
synchronized to the target O-RAN NF(s).

5.3.2
Configuration Data Changes and Consumers
5.3.2.1
Overview
In the O-RAN system, MOIs are representing the management aspects of an O-RAN NF instance. Changes in the MOIs
of O-RAN NFs may occur for reasons including, but not limited to, the following:
1)Software Updates and Upgrades: O-RAN NFs and rAPPs/xAPPs update and upgrade may result in MOIs value
and status change.
2)RAN Scaling: New O-RAN NF deployment, scaling, migration or other LCM operations in response to the
capacity optimization requirement, the O-RAN NF LCM may trigger configuration changes reflected in the
O-RAN NF MOI, e,g., vnfParametersList modifications as defined in [i.6].
3)Fault Recovery: In the event of a NF fault, configuration changes may be needed to isolate problematic NFs, or
enable fault recovery.
4)Security Updates: The encryption settings as one kind of configuration data will be updated with the
development of new integrity and encyption algorithms.
5)Integration of New Technologies/Features: The integration of new technologies, such as the introduction of new
spectrum bands, Carrier Aggregation (CA), sidelink, network slice, etc., usually requires configuration
changes to the corresponding features.
6)Automated RAN Management: With the introduction of AI/ML in RAN, networks are progressively becoming
automated. In O-RAN, configuration changes can be triggered by CI/CD pipelines, Non-RT RIC for RAN
data collection, automated configuration/optimization (e.g., C-SON, D-SON), as well as triggered by the
deployment and removal of xAPPs.

service as defined in 3GPP TS 28.532 [i.3] in clause “12.1.1 RESTful HTTP-based solution set”.

Background
6.1.1
MnS Component Type C
MnS component type C, as defined in 3GPP TS 28.533, represents the performance and fault information of managed
entities. It provides essential data for monitoring and maintaining the operational health of network elements,
facilitating effective performance management and fault detection. MnS component type C exposes management data to
RAN NF OAM SMOS. Performance information, fault information are network management data collected from the
network (including e.g. service, slicing and/or network functions related data). RAN analytics SMOs can consume RAN
NF OAM SMOs to utilize the network management data and make the corresponding analytics based on the collected
information. The performance information provided by RAN NF MnS producer can be used to optimize network
performance, and the fault information provided by RAN NF MnS producer can be used to

and make the corresponding analytics based on the collected
information. The performance information provided by RAN NF MnS producer can be used to optimize network
performance, and the fault information provided by RAN NF MnS producer can be used to predict and prevent failures
of the network.
Mobile networks have the capability to support a wide variety of services and requirements. This, along with increasing
flexibility of the network may present management and operational challenges and complexities. The management
system can therefore benefit from management data analytics services for improving networks performance and
efficiency to accommodate and support the diversity of services and requirements.
MnS component type C consists of below primary elements:
Performance Data is defined in[i.28], 3GPP TS 28.552 and TS 28.554.
Alarm Information is described in 3GPP TS 28.532 and TS 28.111.
NOTE: The alarm information also includes alarms defined in O-RAN WG10 WI O-RAN-WG10.O1.Alarms,
which will be referenced here once the O-RAN-WG10.O1.Alarms specifications are published.
Traces information as defined in TS 32.421 and TS 32.423.
Trace information is diverse, and it mainly supports troubleshooting and validation testing. The Trace records should
contain Information Elements or signaling messages from control signaling and/or the characteristics of the user data.
Together with MnS component type A and MnS component type B, MnS component type C forms a comprehensive
management service that supports the configuration, monitoring, and optimization of network resources.
In the O-RAN architecture, MnS component type C can be accessed through the O1 interface. The SMO utilizes the O1
interface to collect and process MnS component type C information, enabling the monitoring

oring, and optimization of network resources.
In the O-RAN architecture, MnS component type C can be accessed through the O1 interface. The SMO utilizes the O1
interface to collect and process MnS component type C information, enabling the monitoring and management of the
performance and fault status of O-RAN NFs. MnS component type C can also be provided to the Non-Real-Time RIC
through the RAN NF OAM SMOS producer in the SMO, enabling intelligent network performance optimization, fault
detection, and recovery.
6.1.2
Performance Metrics
3GPP TS 32.401 defines the concept of Performance Management activity as one to collect data, which can be used to
verify the physical, virtual, and logical configuration of the network and to locate potential problems as early as
possible. The type of data to be collected is defined by the equivalent measurements (e.g., as specified in 3GPP TS 32.

________________________________________________________________________________________________
21
425 for E-UTRAN related performance measurements, and 3GPP TS 28.552 for NR related performance
measurements). O-RAN O1 Interface Specification refers to 3GPP 28.622 for the performance management job
operation, based on the PerfMetricJob IOC, where a MnS consumer lists the performance measurements to be produced
(performance metrics are identified by name). All object instances below and including the instance name-containing
the PerfMetricJob are scoped for performance metric production.
In measurement data reporting, according to 3GPP 32.404, a performance measurement includes the measurement
object class, describing the measured object class level where the measurement has been collected (e.g. NRCellCU,
NRCellRelation).
Performance measurements, which are a permanent source of information, provide values aggregated on an observation
period.
6.1.3
Events and Alarms
Event is defined as network occurrences which have significance for the management of an NE (Network Element) in
clause 3.1 Terms of 3GPP TS 28.111 [i.21], for example a configuration change, a threshold crossing, a transition to an
error state or a transition to a failure state. Events do not have state.
3GPP TS 28.111 [i.21] defines in clause 3.1 Terms, an alarm as a representation of an error or failure that requires
attention or reaction by an operator or some machine. Alarms have state.
6.1.4
Traces
Introduction of 3GPP TS 32.421 [i.19] cites that Subscriber and equipment trace provide very detailed information at
call level on one or more specific mobile(s). Such data is an additional source of information to Performance
Measurements and allows going further in monitoring and optimization operations. S

and equipment trace provide very detailed information at
call level on one or more specific mobile(s). Such data is an additional source of information to Performance
Measurements and allows going further in monitoring and optimization operations. Subscriber and Equipment (UE)
Trace give instantaneous values for a specific event (e.g. call, location update, etc.). Subscriber tracing includes tracing
of IMSI or Public User Identity, and equipment (UE) tracing includes tracing of IMEI or IMEISV. Trace is the easy way
to go deeper into investigation and network optimization.
The use cases for Trace can be divided into two basic categories:
Troubleshooting use cases cover situations where the operator is solving an existing problem in the operator
network.
Validation testing use cases cover situations where the operator is not solving a known problem but merely
analyzing, fine-tuning or optimizing the network.
Subscriber and UE Trace are commonly used for the purposes (to list a few) such as:
Checking radio coverage in certain areas, testing radio coverage on a particular geographical area following
network extension for instance (e.g. new site installation) by collecting RLF reports,
Fine-tuning and optimization of algorithms/procedures; Trace data are used to get feedback on the network
quality and capacity after optimization operations like parameter fine-tuning, for instance, by using
measurement data (Measurement Report).
Periodic sampling of network performance.

7.2
Performance Metric Transport
7.2.1
Overview
The transport of performance metric specified in O1 specifications is file-based (bulk) and/or streaming (real time).
For file-based (bulk) performance data reporting, PM data pull-based file reporting method and/or the PM data push-
based file reporting method is supported. Asynchronous notifyFileReady notification event is supported when PM File(s)
is ready for retrieval or asynchronous notifyFilePreparationError notification event is supported when there is any error
while preparing the file(s), which is optional for push-based file reporting. When transferring files, a secure connection
is established from or to the File Management MnS Producer (SFTP, FTPeS or HTTPs) as defined in clause 7.1.3 of
3GPP TS 28.537 [i.29].
Performance data file content and file naming is as specified in clause 11.3.2.1 of 3GPP TS 28.532 [i.3].
Performance data file XML Format is as specified in clause 12.3.2 of 3GPP TS 28.532 [i.3] and/or in clause 4.1 of
3GPP TS 32.432 [i.30].
For performance data streaming, A secure WebSocket connection is established between the Performance Assurance
MnS Producer and the Performance Assurance MnS Consumer. The description of performance data streaming is in
clause 7.1.2 Transport of Performance Metrics in Current SBMA Solution Sets of the present document.

WebSocket is point-to-point persistent connection. To maintain it, streaming data reporting MnS producer and consumer
need keep alive messages, that costs extra resource.
WebSocket is stateful connection in nature. Streaming data reporting MnS producer and consumer need to maintain
state or consider stateless solution in cloud-native deployments, which introduces architectural and operational
complexities.
WebSocket doesn’t support auto-reconnect by default. WebSocket reconnection time mainly depends on failure
detection time and reconnection strategy according to configuration. WebSocket reconnection interrupt time may impact
PM data streaming transmission.
WebSocket doesn’t support message queueing. To ensure delivery guarantees, Streaming data reporting MnS producer
and consumer need additional processing.
7.2.3
Potential solution
Compared with WebSocket, Kafka is a message bus (not point-to-point) and stateless, so MnS producer and consumer
don’t need to maintain peer state. Other issues described in clause 7.2.2 are also handled by Kafka which is described in
clause 7.3.3.

The issues described in clause 7.3.2 are handled by Kafka as below:
1. In-sequence-delivery is guaranteed in each partition based on in sequence storage.
2. Kafka provides a low protocol header overhead ( multiple messages in one batch and share a common message
header). Kafka is still based on TCP, but TCP head-of-line blocking issue is resolved by multiple partitions
and sending messages in batch.
3. Kafka protocol includes group id which guarantees multiple consumers in one group have load balancing and
fail-over capability. In addition, Kafka heart-beat interval is short (second level), so failure detection is soon.
4. Kafka is not only a protocol, but also a product which handles all aspects of load balance, fault-tolerance and
data integrity. It enables application layer to push these features to transport layer.
Based on the above advantages, Kafka could be considered as a potential solution. In case Kafka is introduced as

7.4
Trace Transport
7.4.1
Overview
The transport of trace specified in O1 specifications is file-based (bulk) and/or streaming (real time).
File-based trace collects trace records in files that are available to the consumer with a time delay. The producer
optionally sends the file directly to the consumer or sends the location of the file to the consumer.
Procedures for naming the trace data file are described in 3GPP TS 32.423[i.27] clause B. File Naming Convention is
described in 3GPP TS 32.423[i.27] clause B.1. Trace files are produced in XML format. The XML format is described
in 3GPP TS 32.423[i.27] clause A2.2. Example XML files are provided in 3GPP TS 32.423[i.27] Annex D.
In the case of streaming trace, the data is sent in bursts across a WebSocket connection to the consumer, maintaining the
relevance of the data while minimizing transport overhead.
Definitions of trace record content for all trace types, XML trace file format, and streaming trace GPB record definition
are found in 3GPP TS 32.423[i.27]. definitions for streaming data reporting are specified in 3GPP TS 28.532[i.3].
For trace data streaming, A secure WebSocket connection is established between the Trace MnS Producer and the Trace
MnS Consumer. The description of trace data streaming is in clause 7.1.3 Transport of Traces in Current SBMA
Solution Sets of the present document.

Scope
The present document provides an overview of Filtered Measurements, as well as their use cases and requirements in line with
WG1 Filtered Measurements TR [i.2]. In addition, it elaborates what is expected to be collected by the RAN and in particular
from the UEs. Furthermore, it explores potential OAM solutions to meet these requirements, including impact analysis, to
identify the necessary enhancements to relevant interfaces (e.g., enhancements to management services, modeling for the O1
interface, etc.). It also identifies the impact on WG10 technical specifications. In addition, it may identify impacts on relevant
WG1 technical specifications if needed.

4
Objectives
In the WG1 Filtered Measurements TR [i.2], the status and limitations of existing measurement data, as well as the definition,
use cases, and requirements of Filtered Measurements, have been studied. However, these use cases and requirements need more
detailed analysis from a specialized OAM perspective in order to identify potential solutions for Filtered Measurements. The
objectives of this report are to conduct a detailed analysis of the use cases, identify OAM requirements, and study potential OAM
solutions, taking feasibility into consideration, before proceeding to normative work. Additionally, the report assesses the impact
on WG10 specifications.
5
Filtered Measurements
5.1
Overview
Filtered Measurements refer to measurements associated with UEs that have been determined by a network function (e.g., O-
DU, O-CU) to satisfy specific filtering conditions. Instead of collecting measurements indiscriminately from all UEs in the
network, this concept enables the retrieval of measurements only from those UEs that are contextually relevant—such as UEs
near the cell edge or experiencing high mobility—thereby improving the specificity and relevance of the measurements. The
types of measurements to be retrieved (target metrics) and the filtering conditions need to be explicitly configured by the SMO
via O1 interface, while the filtering conditions are evaluated by the NF using its internal information to determine the set of
satisfying UEs.
Filtered Measurements can be applied in various ways depending on the granularity and volume of data required. As illustrated
in Figure 5.1-1, the existing measurement collection mechanisms, PM and trace, have their inherent limitations; PM with low
data gra

Measurements can be applied in various ways depending on the granularity and volume of data required. As illustrated
in Figure 5.1-1, the existing measurement collection mechanisms, PM and trace, have their inherent limitations; PM with low
data granularity and trace with heavy data volume. With retrieval of measurements only from those UEs that are contextually
relevant, Filtered Measurements enable PM to provide more relevant measurements that is not contaminated by the noise of the
entire UE population. Also, Filtered Measurements enable trace to reduce overall data volume and avoids overwhelming the
interface or storage.
By enabling the selective retrieval of only the most relevant measurements, Filtered Measurements offer several benefits to O-
RAN architecture. They allow the SMO to obtain relevant measurements tailored to specific use cases without overwhelming
the interface or storage. The retrieved measurements can then be used by rApps for their inputs and performance monitoring.
Also, the measurements can be exploited to OSS so that the human network engineers are able to carefully evaluate network
changes set by rApps or xApps. In other words, Filtered Measurements provides higher measurement accuracy and better
resource efficiency for both automated and human-in-the-loop network optimization.

6
OAM Use Case Analysis
6.1
Analysis of Massive MIMO use case
6.1.1
Background
In the AI/ML-assisted non-GoB optimization use case [i.5], it is assumed that the SMO/Non-RT RIC is responsible for obtaining
the beamforming configuration information from the gNB (O-DU/O-CU), training the AI model to decide the best beamforming
mode based on the collected measurements over O1 interface, and transferring the model to the Near-RT RIC. Among the
required measurements, ‘Average DL/UL UE throughput in gNB’, are proposed to be obtained with certain filtering conditions
like following:
mMIMO Mode Index: Considering multiple factors such as radio conditions, availability of reference signals and overall cell
load, the gNB (O-DU/O-CU) dynamically selects the beamforming mode applied to each UE. As a result, the achieved UE
throughput varies according to the configured beamforming mode. To enable effective optimization of beamforming mode
selection, it is essential that the gNB (O-DU/O-CU) collect throughput measurements that are explicitly correlated with the
respective beamforming mode applied during transmission.
DL/UL UE data volume: Small traffic UEs, characterized by low data volumes, introduce noise into throughput statistics. These
low-traffic UEs, whose behavior is not strongly correlated to beamforming modes, often dominate the dataset, skewing the
distribution toward low

: Small traffic UEs, characterized by low data volumes, introduce noise into throughput statistics. These
low-traffic UEs, whose behavior is not strongly correlated to beamforming modes, often dominate the dataset, skewing the
distribution toward low-throughput values and obscuring meaningful distinctions between beamforming modes. This noise
reduces the sensitivity of comparisons, as it fails to reflect the true performance variations between different configurations.
High-traffic UEs, by contrast, provide data that better represents a more accurate assessment of beamforming performance.

6.1.2
Description
As pre-conditions, it is assumed that the SMO/Non-RT RIC and gNB (O-DU/O-CU) are deployed and operational as well as
that the connectivity between the SMO/Non-RT RIC and the gNB (O-DU/O-CU) is established for management and
measurements collection. The SMO/Non-RT RIC first requests a report of supported beamforming configurations from the gNB
(O-DU/O-CU). Subsequently, the process enters the data collection phase, during which the SMO/Non-RT RIC requests
measurements collection from the gNB (O-DU/O-CU) via O1 through RAN NF OAM service. The target metrics and filtering
conditions corresponding to certain target metrics are configured by SMO/Non-RT RIC. The target metrics applicable to this use
case are ‘Average DL/UL UE throughput in gNB’, SS-RSRP, SS-RSRQ, SS-SINR and SRS RSRP [i.5]. Also, the filtering
conditions for ‘Average DL/UL UE throughput in gNB’ are ‘mMIMO mode index’ and ‘DL/UL UE data volume’.
Thereafter, the gNB (O-DU/O-CU) responds with the measurements derived from the UEs that meet the criteria of the filtering
conditions. For example, when the filtering condition is ‘DL data volume’, the UEs whose accumulated volume of data burst(s),
ThpVolDl, during the granularity period is larger than a certain threshold value should be selected to derive ‘Average DL UE
throughput in gNB’. Based on the collected measurements, the SMO/Non-RT RIC trains AI/ML model(s) that predict the relative
performance between the N beamforming modes and deploys the trained models (or simply inform the best mode) to the Near-
RT RIC.

6.2
Analysis of Interference detection and optimization use case
6.2.1
Background
The objectives of interference detection and optimization use case [i.3][i.4] are to detect inter-cell interference and to dynamically
manage radio resources for a specific UE, UE group, or slice, thus further improving the efficiency of radio resource utilization.
Such interference detection and optimization should be performed based on interference-related data focusing on a specific UE
group, e.g., a cell-edge UE group or a slice, which is the primary target of improvement. Otherwise, irrelevant data could cause
inappropriate optimization or evaluation errors. However, the following types of data available in the SMO/Non-RT RIC present
several challenges [i.2]:
•
Performance measurements such as SINR are defined per cell [i.14] and are not appropriate for optimizing interference
and evaluating its effectiveness for the specific UE group.
•
MDT data [i.18] or UE level measurements [i.15] are defined per-UE, but random selection of the traced UEs makes it
hard to track all UEs within a target group, leading to collection of insufficient or irrelevant data for interference
optimization and evaluation. On the other hand, tracing all UEs in the cell can be resource-intensive.
•
UE log data from drive tests is time-consuming to collect and provides too few samples for reliable statistical evaluation.
Filtered Measurements are effective in addressing the above challenges by allowing the SMO to collect per-UE interference-
related data (e.g., DL SS-SINR, UL MCS) along with throughput from a specific UE group. The UE group can be identified by
identifiers such as Slice IDs, received signal power, data volume, and so on. Importantly, Filtered Measurements are in reducing
the volume of data collec

SINR, UL MCS) along with throughput from a specific UE group. The UE group can be identified by
identifiers such as Slice IDs, received signal power, data volume, and so on. Importantly, Filtered Measurements are in reducing
the volume of data collected over the interface, which has been a major challenge with existing per-UE data collection.
6.2.2
Description
As preconditions, it is assumed that the SMO and O-CU/O-DU are deployed and operational, and the connectivity between them
is established for management and measurement collection. The SMO requests measurements collection from the O-DU/O-CU
via O1 interface. The target metrics and filtering conditions corresponding to certain target metrics are configured by SMO.
Based on the configuration, the filtering conditions are evaluated, and the selected UEs for data collection are determined.
Subsequently, the measurements associated with the selected UEs are collected in SMO. These measurements are used for
optimization and/or evaluation of interference.

6.3
Analysis of QoE optimization use case
6.3.1
Background
Highly demanding 5G native applications such as cloud VR and connected vehicles are both bandwidth consuming and latency
sensitive. However, they are currently often handled in a best effort manner with little or no application-specific optimization,
which does not efficiently satisfy diverse QoE requirements. These traffic-intensive and highly interactive applications are not
well served by the current semi-static QoS framework, which struggles to cope with performance fluctuations and dynamic
application requirements. Therefore, an application-specific QoE estimation/prediction approach is needed to enhance radio
resource efficiency and improve user experience.
In [i.3], the main objective of QoE optimization use case is to support QoE optimization within the O-RAN architecture and its
open interfaces by enabling slice or 5QI-based optimization of RAN configurations according to application requirements or
other inputs. To achieve this, a QoE optimization approach utilizing the SMO, Non-RT RIC, and Near-RT RIC has been proposed.
The SMO/Non-RT RIC collects O1 PM data to build and train relevant AI/ML models, while the Near-RT RIC optimizes QoE
operations by leveraging policy inputs and E2SM-KPM data.
However, the SMO/Non-RT RIC faces an OAM challenge in filtering and collecting measurements associated with a specific
UE group within a cell via O1 PM. Although UEs can be classified by 5QI or Slice ID, this approach cannot fully account for
the diverse conditions of UEs within the cell. For example, when monitoring a group of UEs using a specific service, different
QoE optimization actions may be required based on varying radio conditions (e.g. RSRP) and velocity, even among UEs running
the same application. The

UEs within the cell. For example, when monitoring a group of UEs using a specific service, different
QoE optimization actions may be required based on varying radio conditions (e.g. RSRP) and velocity, even among UEs running
the same application. These limitations could lead to biased evaluations, consequently making it difficult to generate optimized
policies. Therefore, to achieve effective QoE optimization, it is essential to classify and monitor UEs based on these contextual
differences.
6.3.2
Description
As pre-conditions, it is assumed that the SMO/Non-RT RIC and O-DU are deployed and operational as well as that the
connectivity between the SMO/Non-RT RIC and the O-DU is established for management and measurements collection. The
SMO/Non-RT RIC first requests the O-DU to collect measurements via O1 through RAN NF OAM service. The filtering
conditions and required measurements are configured by SMO/Non-RT RIC. The filtering conditions can be associated ‘Slice
ID’, ‘5QI’ and ‘DL SS-RSRP’ to classify UE groups for QoE optimization. And, ‘Mobility state of a UE’ may optionally be
used as one of filtering condition. For the required measurements perspective, O-DU can respond with the measurements such
as ‘Average DL/UL UE throughput in gNB’, ‘Total number of TBs’, ‘Total error number of TBs’, ‘Total PRB Usage’ and ‘delay’.
Based on the collected measurements, the SMO/Non-RT RIC trains or deploys the AI/ML model(s) for QoE optimization.

6.4
Analysis of MU-MIMO use case
6.4.1
Background
MU-MIMO is one of the key technologies available for increasing UE and cell capacities using existing time/frequency resources.
The use of multiple antennas enables the pointing of beams to multiple UEs with each beam spatially avoiding the interference
from the other beams. However, in commercial deployments, some subscribers can be stationary, some can be moving at
pedestrian speeds, and others at high speeds. Due to the high sensitivity of trad

s with each beam spatially avoiding the interference
from the other beams. However, in commercial deployments, some subscribers can be stationary, some can be moving at
pedestrian speeds, and others at high speeds. Due to the high sensitivity of traditional MU-MIMO solutions to subscriber mobility,
the capacity gains achieved with multiple antennas are limited. To address this limitation, AI/ML-assisted MU-MIMO
optimizations are emerging to support MU-MIMO. These solutions are applicable to both downlink and uplink data channels
and to TDD as well as FDD and can provide high user and cell performance for subscribers moving within a wide range of
speeds. Also, to verify the effectiveness of MU-MIMO, the SMO/Non-RT RIC could collect and monitor statistics such as RSRP,
SINR, DL/UL throughput, and HARQ information from the O-DU via the O1 interface, while training AI/ML models for
optimization.
However, there is the OAM challenge in filtering and collecting measurements associated with MU-MIMO UEs. Although
required measurements such as “Average DL UE throughput in gNB with associated non-GoB BF mode and MIMO mode” are
defined in [i.5], it is noteworthy that they require the introduction of new reporting mechanism that incorporates the associated
non-GoB mMIMO mode index in order to focus on the performance of MU-MIMO UEs.

6.5
Analysis of UE capability based measurements use case
6.5.1
Background
In mobile networks, there are different types of the UEs with different UE capabilities.  Some UEs support carrier aggregation
(CA) (e.g., FDD+TDD CA, TDD+TDD CA), while other low-end UEs do not support CA. Similarly, various UE capabilities
are possible, such as high power UEs, number of MIMO layers, modulation order (e.g., QPSK, 16QAM, 64QAM, 256QAM).
As the characteristics of a UE differ depending on its capabilities, UEs should be treated differently in terms of configuration of
base stations to optimize their performance. However, configurations are typically set to the same value for the entire cell. As a
result, a configuration value may be suitable for one group of UEs in the cell but may not be suitable for another group. For
example, the RSRP values in mobility thresholds (A1, A2, A3, A5, etc.) [i.22] are typically optimized by

e entire cell. As a
result, a configuration value may be suitable for one group of UEs in the cell but may not be suitable for another group. For
example, the RSRP values in mobility thresholds (A1, A2, A3, A5, etc.) [i.22] are typically optimized by the SMO based on
performance measurements [i.14] or field trials of UEs. As a result, these thresholds also tend to be set to common values for
CA-capable UEs and non-CA-capable UEs.
In this use case, the SMO collects aggregated data only from UEs that support specific capabilities, enabling the operator to
analyse and configure optimal parameters for each UE‑capability group [i.2]. Figure 6.5.1-1 shows an example of handover
triggers based on different mobility thresholds for CA-capable UEs and non-CA-capable UEs. In this example, CA (FDD+TDD)
UEs are moved to low-band FDD from mid-band earlier than non-CA UEs, to fully benefit from CA-enabled coverage extension
(UL on FDD and DL on TDD). This helps the CA UEs to maintain their performance near the cell edge. Specifically, CA UEs
are handed over from TDD band to low-band FDD band at higher RSRP values (not waiting till cell-edge), whereas non-CA
UEs would continue further being on TDD until the cell edge. This can be achieved by setting the mobility RSRP thresholds
(from TDD to FDD) differently for CA and non-CA UEs.

6.6
Analysis of filtering condition evaluation methods
This clause provides a detailed analysis of how filtering conditions are evaluated to determine the subset of UEs for the requested
measurements. The evaluation mechanism differs depending on whether the target metrics are aggregated performance
measurements or per-UE data (e.g., Trace/MDT).
6.6.1
Evaluation for aggregated target metrics
To derive the aggregated target metrics, the filtering conditions (e.g., DL data volume, mMIMO mode index) need to be evaluated
to determine which UEs should be included in the measurement derivation. The granularity period refers to the period during
which the measurements derivation is performed. The filtering condition evaluation can be performed either during the
measurement derivation process (Approaches 1-4) or as a pre-selection step prior to the measurement derivation (Approach 5).
The following alternative approaches can be considered for this evaluation:
Approach 1: Continuous satisfaction
In this approach, UEs are included in the measurement derivation only if the filtering condition is continuously satisfied
throughout the entire granularity period. For example, when the filtering condition is 'mMIMO mode index = PMI', only UEs
that are configured with PMI mode for the entire duration of the granularity period are selected.
This approach ensures that the derived measurements strictly reflect the behavior of UEs under the specified condition without
any contamination from other states. However, it may result in a reduced number of selected UEs, particularly when the filtering
conditions frequently change during the granularity period.
Approach 2: Any-time satisfaction
In this approach, UEs are included in the measurement derivation if the filtering condition is satisfied

r of selected UEs, particularly when the filtering
conditions frequently change during the granularity period.
Approach 2: Any-time satisfaction
In this approach, UEs are included in the measurement derivation if the filtering condition is satisfied at any point during the
granularity period. For example, when the filtering condition is 'mMIMO mode index = PMI', only UEs that are configured with
PMI mode at least one time during the granularity period are selected.
This approach maximizes the number of selected UEs and ensures sufficient samples for statistical reliability. However, the
derived measurements may include contributions from UEs that only briefly satisfied the filtering condition, potentially
introducing noise into the measurement results.
Approach 3: Dominant satisfaction
In this approach, UEs are included in the measurement derivation if the filtering condition is satisfied for a dominant portion of
the granularity period, where "dominant" can be defined as exceeding a configurable threshold (e.g., more than 50% or 70% of
the time). For example, when the filtering condition is 'mMIMO mode index = Zero-forcing', only UEs that are configured with
Zero-forcing mode for the majority of the granularity period are selected.
This approach provides a balanced trade-off between the strictness of Approach 1 and the inclusiveness of Approach 2. It ensures
that the derived measurements primarily reflect the behavior under the specified condition while maintaining a reasonable sample
size. If the threshold for determining "dominant" satisfaction can be configurable, this approach can incorporate Approach 1 as
well as Approach 2.
Approach 4: Sample-based satisfaction
In this approach, filtering conditions are evaluated at each individual sample or event occurrence, rat

"dominant" satisfaction can be configurable, this approach can incorporate Approach 1 as
well as Approach 2.
Approach 4: Sample-based satisfaction
In this approach, filtering conditions are evaluated at each individual sample or event occurrence, rather than at the granularity
period level. UE data is included in the measurement derivation only for those specific samples or events where the filtering
condition is satisfied at the moment of measurement. For example, when the filtering condition is 'MIMO (SU/MU) = MU', each
sample is evaluated independently for its MIMO mode at that instant and only samples where MU-MIMO is active at the
sampling time are included. The same UE may contribute to some samples but not others within the same granularity period,
depending on its instantaneous MIMO configuration.
This approach provides accurate measurements by considering only the samples within the granularity period that satisfy the
filtering condition. However, if a sufficient number of samples is not collected, the reliability of the measurements may be
reduced. In addition, by collecting only the samples that satisfy the filtering condition to calculate the measurements, the
computational load can be increased.
Approach 5: Prior-window satisfaction
In this approach, the filtering conditions are evaluated during a prior time window before the measurement derivation begins,
rather than during the granularity period itself. The selected UEs based on the prior window evaluation are then used for
measurement derivation in the subsequent granularity period(s). For example, the filtering conditions can be evaluated over the

preceding granularity period (e.g., granularity period N-1), and the UEs that satisfy the conditions during that window (using
continuous, any-time, or dominant satisfaction criteria) are selected for measurement derivation in the current granularity period
(e.g., granularity period N).
This approach separates the UE selection logic from the measurement derivation process, enabling more stable UE selection and
reducing computational overhead during measurement collection. However, it may not capture dynamic changes in UE behavior
that occur after the pre-selection phase.
6.1.2
Evaluation for per-UE target metrics
For per-UE data collection such as MDT measurements (e.g., SINRs, UL MCS), the filtering conditions (e.g., List of UE IDs,
DL SS-RSRP, DL PDCP SDU Data Volume) need to be evaluated to determine which UEs should be selected for trace activation.
Two alternative approaches can be considered for this evaluation:
Approach 1: Window-based selection
In this approach, the filtering conditions are evaluated at a certain period of time before the trace activation to determine the set
of selected UEs for trace activation. For example, when the filtering condition is 'DL SS-RSRP < threshold', it is necessary to
evaluate the average value of DL SS-RSRP with respect to each UEs during the period of certain window and activates trace
only for those UEs whose SS-RSRP falls below the threshold.
This approach provides a deterministic set of selected UEs based on its average values of filtering conditions during the window.
It is suitable for use cases where the target UE group is relatively stable and does not require frequent re-evaluation. However, it
may not capture UEs that enter the target condition after the initial evaluation, and it may continue tracing UEs that no long

table for use cases where the target UE group is relatively stable and does not require frequent re-evaluation. However, it
may not capture UEs that enter the target condition after the initial evaluation, and it may continue tracing UEs that no longer
satisfy the condition.
Approach 2: Continuous monitoring-based selection
In this approach, the filtering conditions are continuously evaluated throughout the trace session, and the set of selected UEs is
dynamically updated based on the current state. For example, when the filtering condition is 'DL SS-RSRP < threshold', it is
necessary to continuously monitor the DL SS-RSRP of all active UEs and automatically activates trace for UEs whose SS-RSRP
falls below the threshold and deactivates trace for UEs whose SS-RSRP rises above the threshold.
This approach ensures that the collected per-UE data accurately reflects the target UE group at all times, adapting to changes in
network conditions and UE mobility. It is particularly suitable for use cases involving dynamic filtering conditions such as RSRP
ranges or data volume thresholds. However, it requires more complex implementation in the network function to continuously
monitor and update the selected UE set, and may result in varying trace durations for different UEs.
7
Potential OAM Requirements
This clause defines the potential OAM requirements for Filtered Measurements, derived from the OAM use case analyses in
Clause 6. These requirements serve as a justification for investigating the potential OAM solutions for Filtered Measurements
detailed in the subsequent clause.
The O-RAN OAM architecture should support the capability to provide Filtered Measurements, which enables the collection of
target metrics derived from the specific UEs that match the filtering conditions.

The O-RAN OAM architecture should support the capability to provide Filtered Measurements, which enables the collection of
target metrics derived from the specific UEs that match the filtering conditions.
The example target metrics and filtering conditions are described in Clause 6. Specifically, the use cases in Clauses 6.1, 6.3, 6.4
and 6.5 require the aggregated data derived from specific UEs, whereas the use case in Clause 6.2 requires the per-UE data
collected from specific traced UEs.
Furthermore, the O-RAN OAM architecture should support the capability to evaluate the filtering conditions. The mechanism
for evaluating these conditions may differ between aggregated data scenarios and per-UE data scenarios. A detailed analysis of
how the OAM architecture evaluates filtering conditions to select UEs in each case is a subject for further study.

8.1
Enhanced PM via O1 interface
8.1.1
Description
This solution aims to enhance the existing Performance Assurance Management Service [i.10] by modifying the PM job to
support the retrieval of Filtered Measurements. This enhancement will serve as the solution for the use cases in clauses 6.1, 6.3,
6.4 and 6.5, since most of the required data identified in these use cases have been defined in TS 28.552 [i.14], although
extensions are needed to support the filtering conditions. While the original metrics defined in TS 28.552 are aggregated across
all the UEs in a measurement object (e.g., NRCellDU, NRCellCU), Filtered Measurements are aggregated only across UEs in
the measurement object that satisfy the filtering conditions. In this solution, while leveraging the configuration mechanisms of
the existing PM job, the job is extended to support the configuration of the filtering conditions.
There are several options for extending the PM job:
l
Extending measurement name: The configuration of filtering conditions is supported by appending sub‑counters to the
measurement name, using the format “family.measurementName.filter” [i.14], which is consistent with the existing

variations. For example, the existing filters include 5QI, S-NSSAI, PLMN ID, and active BWP, but they do not support
configuring filters based on value ranges such as Threshold_1 < DL_Data_Volume < Threshold_2. In addition, while
specifying multiple filters with logical AND operators is supported, specifying them with logical OR operators is not
supported.

8.1.3
Impacts on interfaces and entities
O1 interface:
-
Extensions for MnS for Filtered Measurements might need to be defined in the O1 interface TS [i.10].
-
A new IOC for Filtered Measurements needs to be defined in the O1 NRM TS [i.11]. The new IOC inherits from the
PerfMetricJob IOC and supports the configurability of target metrics and reporting method by utilizing the
performanceMetrics and reportingCtrl attributes, respectively. In addition, the configurability of the filtering
conditions identified is supported by new attributes of the IOC.
-
Alternatively, in order to preserve 3GPP consistency it is possible to evaluate the extension of the 3GPP
PerfMetricJob IOC to allocate the necessary attributes required to define specific filtering conditions.
O-CU/O-DU:
-
The O-CU/O-DU/O-eNB needs to support the role as the MnS producer. This requires the O-CU/O-DU/O-eNB to
support the capability to process the target metrics along with the filtering conditions in order to generate Filtered
Measurements.
-
As a result of this solution, O-CU/O-DU/O-eNB might need to satisfy different use cases where different consumers
might request filtered and unfiltered measurements from the same cell or set of UEs. This approach implies the
collection and filtering of same measurement data multiple times, increasing the NF processing load and storage,
reducing the speed of data processing and forwarding to SMO.

8.2
Enhanced MDT via O1 interface
8.2.1
Description
The previous solution, Enhanced PM via O1 interface, provides Filtered Measurements aggregated across UEs that satisfy the
filtering conditions. However, in certain use cases, there is a need to retrieve per-UE measurements, for example when the
analysis requires UE-specific contexts for precise operation. To be specific, Clause 6.2 investigated the list of required per-UE
measurements (e.g., DL SS-SINR, Average DL/UL UE throughput in gNB) defined in [i.18][i.15]. In this respect, MDT is a
suitable approach, as MDT trace records are UE-specific and even further include location information (e.g., GNSS) of UEs,
enabling the analysis to correlate UE performance with geographical information [i.17].
Therefore, another solution - Enhanced MDT via the O1 interface - is proposed for Filtered Measurements. In particular, this
solution targets management-based MDT. This is because management-based MDT produces UE-specific measurements,
whereas other job types such as Cell Traffic Trace are not UE-specific. Furthermore, signalling-based MDT is excluded as it
already identifies the UEs explicitly through IMSI, IMEI, or SUPI, making additional filtering unnecessary. Also, 5GC UE level
measurements [i.15], where the measurements originate in the core network, are outside the present scope, since the focus of this
work is on enhancing radio access network measurements that can be configured and controlled via the O1 Trace Management
Service.
However, it is noticeable that the applicability of the existing management-based MDT is limited to the selection of UEs based
only on the area information (e.g., list of cells or tracking areas) [i.17]. This implies that the traced UEs are selected
indiscriminately within the area when the exi

ity of the existing management-based MDT is limited to the selection of UEs based
only on the area information (e.g., list of cells or tracking areas) [i.17]. This implies that the traced UEs are selected
indiscriminately within the area when the existing management-based MDT is activated, which does not meet the requirement
for Filtered Measurements studied in Clause 7.
To address this limitation, this solution aims to introduce a new MnS by enhancing the Trace job, defined the existing Trace
Management Service [i.10], to configure and collect Filtered Measurements. While leveraging the configuration mechanisms of
the existing Trace job, it is extended to support the configuration of the filtering conditions. Specifically, a new IOC for the
retrieval of Filtered Measurements needs to be introduced, which inherits from the TraceJob IOC (clause 4.3.30 of [i.16]). This
IOC needs to incorporate additional attributes corresponding to the configuration of the filtering conditions.

8.2.3
Impacts on interfaces and entities
O1 interface:
-
Extensions for Management Service [i.10] might need to be introduced to support the configuration of the MDT-based
Filtered Measurements. While referencing the Trace Management MnS (clause 6.4 of [i.10]), extensions might be
required to allow the consumer to specify filtering conditions as part of the trace job provisioning.
-
A new IOC needs to be introduced to support Filtered Measurements. While referencing the TraceJob IOC (clause
4.3.30 of [i.16]), new attributes are required to define the specific filtering conditions for UE selection in management-
based MDT. These attributes allow the OAM system to instruct the RAN nodes to collect measurements only from the
subset of UEs matching the criteria.
-
Alternatively, in order to preserve 3GPP consistency it is possible to evaluate the extension of the 3GPP TraceJob IOC
to allocate the necessary attributes required to define specific filtering conditions.

O-CU/O-DU/O-eNB:

-
O-CU/O-DU/O-eNB need to support the capability to evaluate the filtering conditions during the MDT UE selection
process. The NF must be able to evaluate whether a specific UE matches the configured filtering criteria before
initiating the trace recording or when reporting the measurements.
-
As a result of this solution, O-CU/O-DU/O-eNB might need to satisfy different use cases where different consumers
might request filtered and unfiltered measurements from the same cell or set of UEs. This approach implies the
collection of same measurement data multiple times, potentially reducing success in the objective of avoiding the
overwhelm in the interface or storage.
8.3.
Filtered Measurements via O1 interface data collection and
SMO based filtering
8.3.1
Description
This proposal suggests that all the call trace, as described in O1-Interface [i.10], and MDT data are collected by SMO to make
it accessible to any internal and external O-RAN SMO consumer, enabling the filtering mechanism to be done in SMO (by
RAN NF OAM SMOS producer, rApps or other SMOS producers) or in external SMO consumers. This allows to address
current standard use cases and new filtered measurements use cases while balancing the use of resources.
Different solutions are possible in SMO. For example, a final consumer can perform its own filtering process or a dedicated
rApp(s) can perform the filtering task for a specific NF or for a RAN. It is also possible that the RAN NF OAM SMOS
provides this additional capability. This approach offers advantages in terms of NF processing load reduction, data speed
processing and forwarding to SMO. First, when multiple consumers target the same cell/set of UEs with different filtering
criteria, the NF is relieved from executing redundant per-use case filtering oper

ms of NF processing load reduction, data speed
processing and forwarding to SMO. First, when multiple consumers target the same cell/set of UEs with different filtering
criteria, the NF is relieved from executing redundant per-use case filtering operations, as the raw measurement data is not
processed in NF. Second, since the full unfiltered dataset is already available within the SMO, both filtered and unfiltered
measurement requirements from different consumers can be served from a single data collection instance, avoiding duplicated
data collection requests toward the NF. In addition, when many Filtered Measurements use cases target the same cell/set of
UEs, the NF may be required to expose the measurement data for all or most of the UEs in the cell, which could potentially
make the volume of data transmitted in O1 comparable in both scenarios, filtered and unfiltered measurement data collection.
As an example of this approach, in the use case for interference detection and optimization, described in clause 6.2,:
-
the filters, DL SS-RSRP and UL SS-RSRP are available as trace record data in MDT M1, DL PDCP volume and UL
PDCP volume are available in MDT M4 and as UE level measurements.
-
the measurements, Average DL UE throughput in gNB and Average UL UE throughput in gNB are available as trace
record data in MDT M5 or as UE level measurements with S-NSSAI filter already defined. SINR is available as trace
record data in MDT M1, and UL MCS would need to be reported.
By combining the different trace records for the same UE and DRB, information can be filtered freely, applying any threshold
and creating any counter definition in the management layer of SMO. In this layer, it could be easier to create user-friendly
interfaces for configuration and subscription. This enab

and DRB, information can be filtered freely, applying any threshold
and creating any counter definition in the management layer of SMO. In this layer, it could be easier to create user-friendly
interfaces for configuration and subscription. This enables more flexible configuration so that different filters can be applied to
different measurements as required.
8.3.2
Procedure
The procedure summarizing the solution is presented in Table 8.3.2-1 and illustrated by Figure 8.3.2-1. As example in the
procedure, rApp is described as the filtering entity, but any designated O-RAN SMOS producer can perform that role. In
addition, it could be also possible that external SMO consumer plays the role.
