9.3.7           Solution #7: Resolution of authorization decision between authorization server and
resource server
9.3.7.1          Background

In typical operator deployments, RBAC requires that administration and execution of roles (coarse-
grained authorization) and permissions (fine-grained authorization) are distributed between the
authorization server and resource servers.

Considering the size of a token and that various APIs have different levels of authorization, the
permissions are part of the resource server and not part of the confidential client request.

The authorization servers are typically centralized overseeing the administration and validation decision
of coarse-grained authorization related roles which are part of the confidential client request. The
examples of roles could be considered from Appendix I related to the function set group in [i.24].

The resource servers are typically distributed overseeing the roles to permission mapping administration
and validation decision of fine-grained authorization.

Permissions are considered to be the operation (usually CRUD) on a particular object in the resource
server as in [i.19] clause 7.

In the solution below we consider examples of roles as rol1, rol2, rol3, etc. to be mapped to permissions
per1, per2, per3, etc. for ease of understanding.

NOTE 1:  The above discussion related to coarse-grained authorization and fine-grained authorization
which is mentioned in the 9.3.7 needs further study.
NOTE 2:  The above discussion related to roles in [i.24] which is mentioned in the 9.3.7.1 and 9.3.7.3
needs further study.

Figure 9.3.7-1 - Validation decision of roles and permissions

2.2 General principles
3
Principle 1: In O-RAN we will always have some offline learning as a proposed best practice (even for reinforcement learning
4
type of scenarios). In the current document, offline training means a model is first trained with offline data, and trained model
5
is deployed in the network for inference. Online training refers to scenarios such as reinforcement learning, where the model
6
‘learns’ as it is executing in the network. However, even in the latter scenario, it is possible that some offline training may
7
happen.
8
Principle 2: A model needs to be trained and tested before deploying in the network. A completely untrained model will not
9
be deployed in the network.
10
Principle 3: As a best practice, it would be useful if ML Applications are designed in a modular manner that are decoupled
11
from one another.  This includes their ability to share data without knowing each other’s data needs.  It also implies that they
12
need not understand the location or nature of a data source.  For example, an ML Application that is consuming RAN data
13
need not know whether that data is being provided directly via E2, or by some other ML Application on the same Inference
14
Host that is consuming and re-publishing that RAN data.  Sections 4.2 and 4.3 describe this in more detail.
15
Principle 4: Given that the criteria for determining the deployment scenario for a given ML Application may differ between
16
service providers, as a best practice, it should be possible for a Service Provider to decide whether an ML Application should
17

14

be deployed to a Non-RT RIC or a Near-RT RIC as its Inference Host.  See Section 5.2 for a discussion on the types of criteria
1
that may be weighed differently by different providers.
2
Principle 5: As a best practice, to improve the execution efficiency and inference performance in the inference host, the ML
3
model for inference should be optimized and compiled with the consideration of the inference host hardware capability. A
4
trade off between efficiency and inference accuracy need to be taken into consideration. Therefore, the optimization should
5
take acceptable accuracy loss as one of the goals, and optimization parameters should be obtained based on this threshold.

and the compiled/optimized model in different inference framework.

Today, AI systems have been able to accomplish certain tasks with a level of accuracy surpassing that of humans.  These

3.1 Supervised learning
6
Input data is called training data and has a known label or result. Supervised learning is a machine learning task that aims to
7

3.2 Unsupervised learning
22
Input data is not labeled and does not have a known result. Unsupervised learning is a machine learning task that aims to learn
23

24
and principal component analysis (PCA).

3.3 Reinforcement learning
5
A goal-oriented learning based on interaction with environment. In reinforcement learning (RL), the agent aims to optimize
6
a long-term objective by interacting with the environment based on a trial and error process. The most typical RL framework
7
is based on Markov Decision Process (MDP), which is defined by a 4-tuple (S, A, R, T), where:
8

S is the state space of an environment
9

A is the set of actions an agent can select from
10

R is the reward function
11

T is the transition probability function
12
There are multiple ways to categorize RL algorithms, and one widely used classification is: model-based RL vs. model-free
13
RL. In wireless network, it might be beneficial to rely on a model for predicting future behavior of the environment. In model
14
based RL algorithms, reward and transition probability is based on a predictive model of the environment. The agent uses the
15
model to find out what will happen if an action is taken. On the other hand, the model of the environment might not be of
16
interest or hard to obtain for some use cases. Model-free algorithms forgo any explicit knowledge of the dynamics of the
17
environment and evaluate how good actions are through exploration and exploitation. RL algorithms can also be categorized
18

3.4 Mapping AI/ML functionalities into O-RAN control loops
9
There are three types of control loops defined in O-RAN. ML assisted solutions fall into the three control loops.  Time scale
10
of O-RAN control loops depend on what is being controlled, e.g., system parameters, resources or radio resource management
11
(RRM) algorithm parameters. For example, if O-RAN control loop adapts the parameters of RRM algorithms, its time scale
12
is slower than that of the RRM algorithm which directly controls resource.
13
Loop 1 deals with per TTI msec level scheduling and operates at a time scale of the TTI or above. Loop 2 operates in the near
14
RT RIC operating within the range of 10-1000 msec. Loop 3 operates in the Non-RT RIC at greater than 1000 msec (policies,
15
orchestration). It is not expected that these loops are hierarchical but can instead run in parallel.

1
Figure 3-4 - Control loops in O-RAN
2
Figure 3-4 shows the three control loops in O-RAN architecture. AI/ML related functionalities can be mapped into the three
3
loops. The location of the ML model training and the ML model inference for a use case depends on the computation
4
complexity, on the availability and the quantity of data to be exchanged, on the response time requirements and on the type
5
of ML model. For example, online ML model for configuring RRM algorithms operating at the TTI time scale could run in
6
O-DU, while the configuration of system parameters such as beamforming configurations requiring a large amount of data
7
with no response time constraints can be performed using the combination of Non-RT RIC and SMO where intensive
8
computation means can be made available.
9
In the first phase of O-RAN, ML model training will be considered mainly in the Non-RT RIC and ML model inference will
10
be considered in loops 2 and 3. For loop2, the ML inference is typically running in Near-RT RIC. For Loop 1, the ML model
11
inference is typically running in an O-DU. ML workflow on loop 1 is not covered by this version of the technical report.
12
While ML model implementation in O-RU could be envisaged, it is presently not supported in O-RAN.
13
3.5 Federated learning
14
Federated learning is a well-known distributed learning methodology where multiple AI/ML entities collaboratively train an
15
AI/ML model. Instead of gathering training data into a central server, federated learning keeps the training data
16
decentralized to mitigate privacy risks. AI/ML models are trained locally in distributed entities, and the local models are
17
aggregated by a central server. The central server orchestrates the federated learning.
18
In O-RAN architecture, since both Non

tralized to mitigate privacy risks. AI/ML models are trained locally in distributed entities, and the local models are
17
aggregated by a central server. The central server orchestrates the federated learning.
18
In O-RAN architecture, since both Non-RT RIC and Near-RT RIC are capable of AI/ML training, the Non-RT RIC can
19
serve as the central server in the federated learning, and its connected Near-RT RICs can serve as distributed AI/ML entities
20
as illustrated in Figure 3-5.
21

19

Note: Other federated learning deployment scenarios are FFS.
1

2

3

4
Figure 3-6: Procedure of federated learning among Non-RT RIC and Near-RT RICs
5
The procedure of federated learning among Non-RT RIC and Near-RT RICs can be summarized into following steps:
6

Step 1: The Non-RT RIC distributes the AI/ML model to its connected Near-RT RICs.
7

Step 2: The ML training host in the Near-RT RIC trains local model using training data collected locally. Note that
8
training data collected locally are not required to be transferred to the Non-RT RIC.
9

Step 3: Local model weights or gradients are uploaded to the Non-RT RIC.
10

Step 4: The training host in the Non-RT RIC update the AI/ML model (e.g., using FedSGD, FedAvg, etc.).
11

Step 5: The updated model is downloaded to the Near-RT RICs.
12

Step 6: If the model training converges, then the model is deployed for inference in the Near-RT RIC.
13
A1-ML (model management) service can be used to manage model downloading/distribution and uploading/aggregation in
14
federated learning. For example,
15

The Non-RT RIC can subscribe/request model uploading from its connected Near-RT RICs.
16

The Non-RT RIC can notify its connected Near-RT RIC to download a model.
17

20

ML model download and upload between Non-RT RIC and Near-RT RICs over O1 or A1 interface is FFS.

5
Based on the framework, some key phases of machine learning are expected to be applied to any ML-assisted solution planned
6
in O-RAN architecture. Any use case defined for ML-assisted solution shall have one or more phases (as applicable) and the
7
phases are defined below:
8
1. ML model and inference host capability query/discovery
9
This procedure shall be executed whenever AI/ML model is to be used for ML-assisted solution. This procedure can be
10
executed at start-up or run-time (when a new ML model is to be executed or existing ML model is to be updated). The
11
SMO/Non-RT RIC will discover various capabilities and properties of the ML inference host, and the ML-assisted solution
12
such as:
13
a) Processing capability of the inference host (for example: dedicated resources  such as CPU/GPU, memory etc.  for ML
14
model inference).
15
b) Requirements on the ML assisted solutions such as execution time cap, delay sensitivity
16
c) Properties such as supported ML model formats and ML engines (for example: Protobuf, JSON, or any ONAP specific
17
VES data formats).
18
d) NFVI based architecture support in MF to run ML model(s)
19
e) Data-sources available to run ML-pipeline (for example: support for data streams, data lake, or any specific database
20
access)
21
This discovery of the capabilities and properties shall be used to check:
22
a)  if an ML model can be executed in the target ML inference host (MF),
23

b) which ML models can be executed in the MF.
1
Note: Exact mechanism and contents of capabilities discovery is FFS.
2
2. ML model Training and Generation
3
This procedure corresponds to design time selection and training of a ML model in relation with a specific ML-assisted
4
solution (use case) to be executed. The ML designer or the SMO/Non-RT RIC will select and onboard the ML model and
5
relevant meta data into the ML training host. Utilizing on the ML training data collection, the ML training host will initiate
6
the model training. Once the model is trained and validated, it is published back in the SMO/Non-RT RIC catalogue. In
7
addition, new trained ML models for a given ML-assisted solution can be generated also by modification techniques such as
8
compression, truncation etc., or training on different training data sets. These ML models are also published in the SMO/Non-
9
RT RIC catalogue.
10
3. ML model Selection
11
The ML designer can check whether a trained ML model from the SMO/Non-RT RIC catalogue can be deployed in the ML
12
inference host for the given ML-assisted solution, by mapping the ML model and ML assisted solution requirements to
13
performance capabilities  discovered from Step 1. Upon successful validation, ML designer will inform the SMO/Non-RT
14
RIC to initiate model deployment.
15
4.  ML model Deployment and Inference
16
The AI/ML model that is selected for the ML use case can be deployed via containerized image to MF where ML model shall
17
be running. The container image also includes the necessary configuration of ML inference host with the AI/ML model
18
description file.
19
Note: The O1 interface mechanism for ML model deployment is being specified by WG1.
20
Once the ML model is deployed and activated, ML online data shall be used f

cessary configuration of ML inference host with the AI/ML model
18
description file.
19
Note: The O1 interface mechanism for ML model deployment is being specified by WG1.
20
Once the ML model is deployed and activated, ML online data shall be used for inference in ML-assisted solutions, which
21
includes:
22
a) 3GPP specific events/counters (across all different Managed Elements) over O1/E2 interface
23
a.
Events: 3GPP 32.423
24
b. Counters: 3GPP 32.425
25
b) Non-3GPP specific events/counters (across all different Managed Elements) over O1/E2 interface (to be defined in O-
26
RAN WGs)
27
c) Enrichment information from Non-RT RIC over A1 interface (to be defined in O-RAN WGs)
28
Based on the output of the ML model, the ML-assisted solution will inform the Actor to take the necessary actions towards
29
the Subject. These could include CM changes over O1 interface, policy management over A1 interface, or control actions or
30
policies over E2 interface, depending on the location of ML inference host and Actor.
31
5.  ML model performance monitoring
32
The ML inference host and actors are expected to feedback or report the performance of the ML model to the SMO/Non-RT
33
RIC so that the SMO/Non-RT RIC can monitor the performance (e.g., accuracy, running time, network KPIs) of the ML
34

model and potentially update the model or reselect the model to be executed. Based on the use-case, specific set of data as
1
applicable for use-case shall be used for ML model re-training. Based on the performance evaluation, either some guidance
2
can be provided to use a different model in the ML inference host, or a notification can be sent indicating the need for retraining
3
the model.
4
Note: Feedback mechanism and how the ML model switching can occur at runtime is FFS.
5
6.  ML model retraining update
6
Based on the feedback and data received from various MFs and actors, the SMO/Non-RT RIC can inform the ML designer
7
that an update is required to the current model. The ML designer will initiate the model selection and training step, but with
8
the existing trained model. Once the model has been retrained, it will be deployed as described in Step 3, and the updated
9
model will be used for ML inference.
10
7. ML model reselection
11
Based on the feedback and data received from various MFs and actors, the SMO/Non-RT RIC can inform the ML designer
12
or the the respective module that the running ML model does not comply with the requirements (e.g., because the HW
13
capabilities of the ML inference host or the execution time/delay constraints have changed) and thus a different ML model is
14
necessary to drive the ML application. The SMO/Non-RT RIC or the ML designer selects a suitable ML model from the ML
15
model catalogue and deploys it in the ML inference host as in Step 4.
16
8. ML model termination
17
In certain scenarios involving severe degradation in the ML model performance, a simple model update and redeployment
18
may not be the suitable option. To avoid large impact on network, malfunctioning ML models (or models that are
19
degrading) need to be term

scenarios involving severe degradation in the ML model performance, a simple model update and redeployment
18
may not be the suitable option. To avoid large impact on network, malfunctioning ML models (or models that are
19
degrading) need to be terminated. Non-RT RIC needs to have access to ML model’s termination conditions to determine
20
whether a ML model is working properly or not. Termination conditions are regarded as ML model attributes.
21
For example, if a ML model is used to predict QoE, then one termination condition for this ML model could be “when the
22
prediction accuracy is below a certain threshold”. Typically, the statistical properties of a target variable, which the model is
23
trying to predict, changes over time (i.e., drift) in unforeseen ways. This causes problems because the prediction become
24
less accurate as time passes. In another example, if a ML model is used to optimize handover sequences, then one possible
25
termination condition could be “when the generated neighbor relation table leads to an increase in number of handover ping
26
pongs or handover failures above a certain threshold”. Network KPI monitoring can be used as general termination
27
conditions for an AI/ML model to detect anomaly, i.e., when the performance of a model does not meet its baseline.
28
For AI/ML-assisted solutions, there are at least following scenarios:
29
1. A single ML model (for one application/use case) impacts the monitored network KPIs
30
2. Multiple ML models are chained together in one application/use case, and these models collectively contribute to
31
the monitored network KPIs
32
3. Multiple ML models for different applications/use cases contribute to the monitored network KPIs
33
Mechanism to identify malfunctioning ML model varies for the above

e, and these models collectively contribute to
31
the monitored network KPIs
32
3. Multiple ML models for different applications/use cases contribute to the monitored network KPIs
33
Mechanism to identify malfunctioning ML model varies for the above scenarios. For scenario 1, network KPI degradation
34
would serve as a good indicator for ML model performance degradation. However, for scenario 2 and 3, it might be hard to
35
pin-point the degraded model(s) only based on the network KPI monitoring. Different approaches can be used to address
36
scenario 2 and 3. For example, Non-RT RIC could first identify candidate models that may be causing the network KPI
37

26

degradation, and then Non-RT RIC could terminate these suspect models one by one until the RAN performance gets back
1
to normal. Another approach could be that Non-RT RIC decides to terminate all relevant AI/ML models at the same time.
2

3
Figure 4-2. ML model termination based on performance monitoring at Non-RT RIC
4
As illustrated in Figure 4-2, AI/ML model performance monitoring is assumed to be placed in the Non-RT RIC. Based on
5
the model performance monitoring, the Non-RT RIC can calculate performance metrics and compare them against
6
termination conditions of a model. If the termination conditions are met, the model termination procedure should be
7
triggered.
8
In the ML model termination procedure, ML inference host, which can be in Non-RT RIC or Near-RT RIC based on
9
deployment scenarios, would receive termination commands requesting to stop the ML inference. A backup solution, which
10
can be another well trained and tested ML model, a slightly modified version of the given ML model (e.g., compressed or
11
less compressed versions, truncated or less truncated versions etc.), or, more conservatively, a non-AI-based algorithm,
12
needs to be provided to ML inference host. After terminating the model and activating the backup solution, the ML
13
inference host should send out messages to acknowledge the commands. The above discussion is summarized in Figure 4-3.
14

15
Figure 4-3. ML model termination procedure
16
For deployment scenario 1.1, where Non-RT RIC acts as inference host, termination/backup activation commands and
17
acknowledgements would be communicated via SMO internal interface. On the other hand, for deployment scenario 1.2, in
18
which AI/ML model is deployed in the Near-RT RIC, whether the termination command and acknowledgement should be
19

27

carried over O1 or A1 is left for further study. Moreover, how SMO/Non-RT RIC could delegate model performance
1
monitoring and the decision making on ML model termination to the Near-RT RIC is also left for further study. Other
2
deployment scenarios, e.g., in which inference host could be in O-CU/O-DU, are FFS.
3

4
4.2 Model Design and Composition
5
ML model design is the first step to conceiving the initial model. This requires connecting to data sources, parsing messages
6
and tokenizing to create and select features. This activity is offline and requires data exploration mechanisms to help the
7
model designer.
8
One question to address for complex problem spaces is whether to design the solution as a single model with many inputs, or
9
as a chain of modular models.  These two approaches can be seen in the figures below.
10
A chain of models provides a more modular solution that can facilitate reusability.  For example, another model X may be
11
shown to produce a better prediction A-out by considering an additional input m.  In such a case, model A can be replaced
12
with model X without the need for retraining or otherwise modifying models B or C.
13
On the other hand, in a chaining approach any errors in the prediction A-out will be propagated to model C, perhaps resulting
14
in a less accurate prediction C-out than produced by the Single model approach shown below.
15

16
Figure 4-4 - Chained modular models
17
A single model allows machine learning to have access to all inputs, which can detect unexpected data relationships and
18
perhaps lead to a more accurate overall model.
19

20
Figure 4-5 - Single model with many inputs
21

28

Note that the predicted values A-out and B-out are not directly available to the single model C’ whereas they are available to
1
the chained model C.  However, the model C’ could be designed to derive these in the same way models A and B did in the
2
chained approach.
3
Note also that inputs a, b, c, d, e and f are not directly available to as inputs to model C, only the predicted values A-out and
4
B-out.  If they are not needed, then the chained approach may work well and achieve the desired modularity.  In this case on
5
would expect models C and C’ to produce equivalent “C-out” predictions.  If, however, it turns out that the raw variables c
6
and d are also useful for a good prediction by model C, then the chained approach may not yield as good a prediction as the
7
single model C’ approach might which has access to those inputs.  Of course such a problem could be mitigated by also
8
providing input values c and d to model C as shown below.
9

10
Figure 4-6 - Chained modular models with common inputs
11
As an example of a chained model, consider a business problem that attempts to predict when a UE’s serving cell QoE will
12
deteriorate to an unacceptable level, and also predicts when each of the neighbor cell’s QoE reaches an acceptable level.  Such
13
a prediction would be used it to determine when to trigger a handover, as well as to select among the various handover cell
14
options.
15
One way to design such a solution would be as follows:
16

A: RF signal strength predictor – Predicts RF signal KPIs a UE would experience with a neighbor cell at the current
17
time “x”, as well as predict the signal strength that same UE would experience with both its current serving cell and
18
its neighbor cells at time “x+Δ”.
19

B: Cell utilization predictor – Predicts the cell utilization KPIs for both the serving and neighbor cells above at time
20
“x+Δ”.
21

C: QoE predictor – Predicts the QoE KPIs that a UE would experience at time “x+Δ” for both its current serving and
22
neighbor cells.
23

24
Such a modular approach could be desirable in that other uses for RF signal strength prediction and cell utilization prediction
25
might be envisioned other than to predict UE future QoE.  Also, a modular approach would allow each of the prediction
26
models to evolve separately.  For example, cell utilization predictor “B” might be improved by including as input trending
27

29

information or venue schedule information among its inputs without having to retrain a single model “C’”.  Or an RF signal
1
prediction model might be improved based on inputs capturing the UEs predicted travel path based on commute patterns.
2
However, in order for such a chained approach to work, the variables available to the QoE predictor must be carefully
3
considered.  Whether a chained or a single model approach would be better for solving such a business problem would require
4
analysis that is beyond the intended scope of this paper and will be left as an exercise for the reader.
5

6
4.3 Model Runtime Access to Data
7
In the prior section we noted that the value of chaining models is the modularity which can be realized.  In Figure 4-4 for
8
example, the models A, B, and C could be improved upon and replaced independent of each other.  Such modularity could
9
facilitate a marketplace whereby different vendors produce different modular solutions in the predictive space, allowing
10
service providers to select from among the various models with the best predictive abilities for their specific environment.
11
Because such marketplace vendors would want to provide complete solutions and not simply ML models, we will extend the
12
concepts in the last section to apply also to applications.  We will thus in this section re-interpret figures Figure 4-4, Figure
13
4-5, Figure 4-6 as representing applications A, B, C and C’ which contain the models in question.
14
Extending the discussion of the prior section, there can be scenarios in which two separate applications require access to the
15
same data.  This was seen in Figure 4-6 with applications A and C sharing input c and B and C sharing input d.  Because such
16
sharing of inputs may be common it would be wise to avoid an approach in which applications are seen as “owning” data.  In
17
addition, independence of the applications is impacted if one is aware of the inputs required of the other.  For example, in
18
Figure 4-6 as drawn, application A can be seen as knowing that application C requires Predication A-out as input.  If
19
application C was changed to no longer require Prediction A-out as input, then application A would need to be appropriately
20
modified.  Such coupling of applications negatively impacts overall solution modularity.
21
Rather, a better paradigm might be one in which data is c

to no longer require Prediction A-out as input, then application A would need to be appropriately
20
modified.  Such coupling of applications negatively impacts overall solution modularity.
21
Rather, a better paradigm might be one in which data is commonly held by all applications, those applications being granted
22
access to the data that they require.  This common repository for the data along with the mechanism for making that data
23
accessible to each application through some mechanism can be thought of as being the “platform” that underlies the
24
“applications.”
25
Figure 4-7 illustrates a re-imaging of Figure 4-6 with such an approach in mind
26

1
Figure 4-7 - Chained modular models with common inputs
2
With such an approach, applications can be created independently with their own independent descriptors.  When an
3
application is loaded, it could “register” with the Platform to declare what types of data it consumes and what types of data it
4
produces.
5
For example, when application A is loaded, its descriptor would be used to declare that it consumes as input variables a, b
6
and c and that it writes Prediction A-out.  If the consumed variables are standard attributes that the Platform knows how to
7
obtain (e.g., E2 data), it could respond that those input variables are available through the Platform.  Later application A could
8
send a formal “subscription” request with more information (such as the specific geographic “scope” from which to collect
9
that input) to have the Platform actually start providing those values.   Regarding the produced variables (e.g., A-out), the
10
Platform could assign some space in the common data repository for that output to be written.  The Platform might also
11
perform some added value validations to ensure that no other registered application also produces/writes that same variable,
12
or if it does to ensure that the two application instances work within different “scopes” (e.g., geography).
13
Extending our example, when application C is loaded its descriptor would be used to declare that it reads as input variables g,
14
Prediction A-out and Prediction B-out.  Variable g, being standard in our example, would be treated as described above.   The
15
Platform could also respond that input variable Prediction A-out is also available through the Platform.  However, if
16
application B had not yet been loaded and registered, the Platform would respond that no source for

as described above.   The
15
Platform could also respond that input variable Prediction A-out is also available through the Platform.  However, if
16
application B had not yet been loaded and registered, the Platform would respond that no source for Prediction B-out can be
17
found.  Perhaps application C has been written such that Prediction B-out is optional input.  In this case application C would
18
respond as such and processing would proceed.  When application B was later loaded and registered, the Platform could notify
19
all applications of new functionality being available.  At that point application C could decide to re-register, again asking for
20
a source for Prediction B-out, this time with favorable results.
21
Thus, the Platform could provide some added value services to ensure that applications are loaded and registered in the proper
22
order.
23
The above described Platform responsibilities with respect to application registration.  Now we can address data subscription.
24

chunks.text:
Let’s return to our example in the prior section whereby application A is an RF signal predictor, application B a cell utilization
1
predictor and application C a UE QoE predictor.  Perhaps the service provider considers cell utilization prediction to be a
2
fundamental need that should be always “on” for all cells.  The service provider would thus configure application B or provide
3
it some policy (e.g., received across an A1-P interface) to generate these predictions, specifying the prediction interval.
4
Application B would then send a “subscribe” request to the Platform asking for variables d, e and f including the desired
5
measurement interval.  As part of this “subscription” request Application B would also indicate that it will begin writing
6
Prediction B-out with a certain measurement interval.  The Platform would determine if these variables are already in the
7
common data repository or not, and if not the Platform would go about securing them (e.g., by sending an E2 SUBSCRIBE
8
request to the appropriate RAN network functions).  The Platform would forward to application B the data content found in
9
the data respository that matches that application’s subscription request.  Upon having secured its input data, application B
10
would continuously be writing Prediction B-out to the common data repository.
11
For applications A and C, however, perhaps the service provider only wants prediction for a certain set of UEs.  One way to
12
accomplish this is for service provider to configure application C or provide it some policy describing the UE set of interest
13
as well as the prediction interval.  Application C subscription of its input variable g would proceed with the Platform in the
14
same way as was described above for Application B.  Application C would

metadata.section_title: Data, Model Training and Model Evaluation pipeline

chunks.text:
ome policy describing the UE set of interest
13
as well as the prediction interval.  Application C subscription of its input variable g would proceed with the Platform in the
14
same way as was described above for Application B.  Application C would also subscribe to input variables Prediction A-out
15
and Prediction B-out with a certain measurement interval, the former including a descriptor of the UE set of interest.  For
16
Prediction B-out, the Platform would determine that those values are already in the common data repository with the desired
17
measurement interval and forward that content to application C.
18
For Prediction A-out, however, the Platform would determine that there is no data in the common data repository, nor is there
19
any application that has subscribed to write it.  The Platform would then identify the application that has registered for writing
20
this data type, in this case application A, and forward to it the subscription request information to that application A.  (Note
21
that this is the local equivalent functionality of the Platform sending the E2 SUBSCRIBE request to the RAN for the
22
application B subscription request.)
23
Application A would receive the Prediction A-out subscription request, including the measurement interval and UE set of
24
interest, and determine what the implications are for its own data needs.  It would then send to the Platform a subscription
25
request asking for variables a, b and c along with the measurement interval and UEs of interest.  It would also declare its
26
intention to begin writing Prediction A-out with a certain measurement interval.  Assuming that the Platform does not find
27
this data already in the common data repository, it would go about securing it (e.g., via an E2 SUBSCRIBE request),
2

chunks.text:
its
26
intention to begin writing Prediction A-out with a certain measurement interval.  Assuming that the Platform does not find
27
this data already in the common data repository, it would go about securing it (e.g., via an E2 SUBSCRIBE request),
28
forwarding the resultant data values to application A.  At that point application A would begin writing Prediction A-out to the
29
common data repository, which the Platform would in turn begin forwarding to application C.

4.4 Data, Model Training and Model Evaluation pipeline
31
This section describes the data, model training and evaluation pipelines.
32

metadata.section_title: Data, Model Training and Model Evaluation pipeline

chunks.text:
32

1
Figure 4-8 - Data pipeline
2
Figure 4-8 defines the data pipelines. The “extract-transform-load” (ETL) process describes how data can be extracted from
3
storage, transformed and loaded into training and testing sets. Additional data quality and validation stages can be inserted
4
into the ETL pipeline. Data cleaning can also be part of the Transform block. This is outside the scope of WG2.
5

6
Figure 4-9 - Model training and evaluation pipelines
7
Figure 4-9 shows the model training and evaluation pipelines. Model training pipeline may change with model types. Model
8
evaluation pipeline, however, is a more generic process. Model evaluation can be used to evaluate a single model or extended
9
to select the best model from a range of models.
10
The end-to-end training process includes the following
11
•
Fulfills the data requirements of the model (format, sample distribution, extent)
12
•
Connects with requisite data via Data Pipeline (simplest ex: a data broker)
13
•
Partitions data into appropriate sets (training, validation, testing, sample)
14
•
Keeps Training data cached for error recovery and subsequent usage
15
•
Manages model training though all phases
16

33

•
Implements training by invoking a Model Training Pipeline
1
•
Training Client tunes model parameters during training phases
2
•
Scoring client monitors performance in order to declare training phase complete
3
•
Communicates with license manager for usage and versioning
4
4.5 ML Model Lifecycle Implementation Example
5
The section provides an example (see Figure 4-10) of ML model lifecycle implementation example and key phases involved
6
in the design and deployment in O-RAN architecture.
7

8
Figure 4-10 - ML model lifecycle (an implementation example)
9
Note: ML Model capability query and discovery can occur in ML designer and Non-RT RIC.
10
The typical steps involved in AL/ML based use-case application in O-RAN architecture is shown in Figure 4-10 considering

5.2 Criteria for Determining Deployment Scenario (Options)
1
This section discusses some criteria that can be used to decide whether an ML Application should execute in a Non-RT RIC
2
or Near-RT RIC Inference Host.  It also discusses some criteria for whether an ML Model within such an ML Application
3
should be initially trained (offline learning) in a Non-RT RIC as its Training Host, or in a more centralized or remote location.
4
(Note that subsequent online learning would be expected to occur in the execution environment.)  Considerations for these
5
decisions relate to the amount of data that is required by the ML Model both in training as well as in execution, as well as
6
latency considerations in execution.  It is assumed in this section that the type of data that an ML Model requires at runtime
7
will also be required, perhaps in aggregated form, during training.
8
It is assumed that the Near-RT RIC would not be a suitable candidate for offline Training Host.  Initial training would typically
9
require a large pool of compute and storage resources.  The very nature of the Near-RT RIC as a Network Function is geared
10
towards high performance runtime processing with a small footprint.  It is unlikely to have sufficient compute and storage
11
resources to also handle initial offline learning.  In addition, offline learning at the Near-RT RIC would also introduce
12
complexity into its design to provide the assurances that ML training would not affect its runtime network function processing.
13
The Non-RT RIC functionality of the SMO, a management (as opposed to a network) function, seems better suited to host
14
initial training.
15
Regarding the Inference Host decision, criteria include:
16
1. The availability of data across a given interface.  For example, if t

lity of the SMO, a management (as opposed to a network) function, seems better suited to host
14
initial training.
15
Regarding the Inference Host decision, criteria include:
16
1. The availability of data across a given interface.  For example, if the data needed at execution time is available only
17
across the E2 interface, then either the ML Application that includes this ML Model must either consider the Near-
18
RT RIC as its Inference Host, or a Near-RT RIC function must be employed to forward across the O1 interface that
19
E2 data to the Non-RT RIC as Inference Host.  If the data needed at execution time is available only across the O1
20
interface, then the ML Application would need to consider the Non-RT RIC as its Inference Host, or a Non-RT RIC
21
function must be employed to forward that O1 data to the Near-RT RIC with its own O1 interface.  Clearly some of
22
these options are very inefficient and likely undesirable.
23
2. The cost of data movement.  Obviously the data movement costs of the various choices described in #1 above differ
24
from one another.  Ideally, if an ML Model requires E2 data, the Inference Host of its associated ML Application
25
would be the Near-RT RIC.  Similarly, if an ML Model requires O1 data, the Inference Host of its associated ML
26
Application would be the Non-RT RIC.  If an ML Model requires E2 data but considers the Non-RT RIC to be its
27
Inference Host, then some function within the Near-RT RIC would need to be used as a vehicle to forward that E2
28
data to the Non-RT RIC.  This would obviously be inefficient and costly.  However, if the Non-RT RIC is also the
29
Training Host for ongoing learning of that ML Model, then perhaps this inefficiency and cost would be warranted.
30
Less understandable would be using the Non

This would obviously be inefficient and costly.  However, if the Non-RT RIC is also the
29
Training Host for ongoing learning of that ML Model, then perhaps this inefficiency and cost would be warranted.
30
Less understandable would be using the Non-RT RIC as a vehicle to forward O1 data to the Near-RT RIC acting as
31
Inference Host.
32
3. Latency considerations.  The data latency associated with the various choices described in #1 above differ from one
33
another, and the Loop 2 versus Loop 3 considerations will factor heavily into whether a ML Model consider its
34
Inference Host to be a Near-RT RIC or a Non-RT RIC.
35
4. Compute resource availability considerations.  The Near-RT RIC may run in an “edge” location where compute
36
resources are very limited and hence expensive.  The Non-RT RIC may more likely run in a location with more ready
37
access to compute resources, such as a data center.
38
Regarding the initial Training Host decision, criteria include:
39

40

1. The local versus general significance of the data.  A data lake will be required in order to train an ML Model.
1
Assuming that a typical Service Provider will have more than one Non-RT RIC instance, if that training data lake
2
coincides with the Non-RT RIC then the data lake will contain data of only local significance.  Only by merging this
3
“local data” from many locales into a “central data lake” could future ML applications perhaps find unexpected
4
correlations within data that was incorrectly assumed to be of only local significance.
5
2. The cost of data movement.  While the previous item discussed the benefits of a “central data lake”, transporting
6
“local data” to such a central location is not without its costs.
7

8
Thus the decision as to whether to use a “local” Non-RT RIC as an initial (offline) Training Host or not in large part depends
9
on the service provider’s assessment of the value of that training data for more general purposes.  The results of such an
10
assessment can clearly differ from one service provider to another.
11
Looking at the criteria above, one can see how the decision as to whether the appropriate Inference Host for an ML model is
12
a Non-RT RIC or a Near-RT RIC can reasonably differ between Service Providers.  For example, consider two service
13
providers below in their assessment of how to deploy a ML Application “X” that takes large volumes of E2 data to calculate
14
some “enrichment information” regarding UEs (e.g., the UE’s predicted QoE on various cells measured on the order of
15
seconds), which can be used by a different “traffic steering” application (perhaps not ML-enabled) to appropriately drive
16
handovers of those UEs.  Assume that the “traffic steering” application would run at the Near-RT RIC using E2 mechanisms
17
to drive handovers.  Service Provider A and Service Provider B may come to quite different conclusions of how to deploy
18
such an ML Application “X”:

7.2 AI/ML Model Deployment
4
In deployment scenario 1.2, Non-RT RIC acts as the ML model training host and near-RT RIC acts as the ML model inference
5
host. ML/AI model can be deployed and enabled in Near-RT RIC in different options:
6
1. Image based deployment: The AI/ML model will be deployed as a xAPP or within a xAPP instance, and also can be updated
7
via the xAPP software update. In this case, the ML inference runtime is self-contained in the image, which simplifies the
8
deployment. This is a generic deployment of ML xAPP – in the sense that ML xAPP is treated no differently from other types
9
of xAPP.
10
2. File based deployment: The AI/ML model can be deployed based on the AI/ML model file, which is generally decoupled
11
with the xAPP software version, and can be enabled and updated via the xAPP file configuration. For this scenario, a ML
12
model catalog and an inference platform/engine are usually required for the ML model inference host (i.e., Near-RT RIC).
13
The Near-RT RIC may have an unified inference platform/engine, which can help to accelerate the inference efficiency
14
(exploiting native ML capabilities of the platform) and enable greater customization but which requires the ML model file
15
format to be supported by the inference platform.
16

2 Overview of Non-RT RIC
27
2.1 Non-RT RIC in O-RAN Overall Architecture
28
In the O-RAN Logical Architecture, as seen in Figure 2.1-1 below, the Non-RT RIC is portrayed as a function that resides
29
within the Service Management and Orchestration Framework and which has a direct association with the A1 interface.
30
The Non-RT RIC’s position internal to, as opposed to interfacing with, the SMO is intended to communicate that the
31
Non-RT RIC is comprised of a subset of functionality of the SMO itself.
32
The direct association with the A1 interface is intended to convey that the functionality of the Non-RT RIC is directly
33
responsible for driving that which is sent and received across the A1 interface. The O1 and O2 interfaces are shown as
34
being directly associated with the SMO Framework itself, that which is not specific to the Non-RT RIC. This
35
representation is intended to communicate that the SMO Framework functionality, but not the Non-RT RIC functionality
36
therein, is directly responsible for driving that which is carried across these interfaces.
37

10
The representation of the Non-RT RIC in the center (as opposed to the bordering the bottom edge) of the SMO Framework
1
visibly indicates that the Non-RT RIC can access SMO Framework functionality, including influencing that which is
2
carried over the O1 interface. While it is not prohibited from accessing any SMO Framework functionality, the Non-RT
3
RIC’s role of RAN resource optimization per current O-RAN definition implies that the Non-RT RIC would only access
4
SMO Framework functionality for that purpose. Thus, the Non-RT RIC would influence that which is carried across the
5
O2 interface only to the extent that the O-Cloud is considered a RAN resource.
6

7
Figure 2.1-1: Logical Architecture of O-RAN
8
Similar to the Near-RT RIC, there is business value in visualizing the Non-RT RIC as being modularly extensible, that
9
functional extensibility being accomplished through modular applications that can be understood as running within the
10
Non-RT RIC function itself. Such applications have different lifecycles from the “framework” in which they run. For
11
convenience we will use the term “rApp” to refer to such applications.
12
Because rApps are associated with the Non-RT RIC, any framework services exposed to the rApps can be considered as
13
being exposed by the Non-RT RIC. Some of these framework services, for example access to O1, are not specific to the
14
Non-RT RIC, whereas others, such as access to A1, are specific to the Non-RT RIC.
15
There is a clear business benefit to allow “porting” of a Non-RT RIC application from one SMO Framework
16
implementation to another. Hence it would be useful for the O-RAN Alliance to define an open and standard interface
17
through which the Non-RT RIC exposes SMO Framework functionalities to “rApps” via the R1 Services exposure
18
functionality. We will refer to this as the “R1” interface.
19
With the above understandings, the Non-RT RIC itself can now be described as follows:
20

Non-RT RIC – That functionality that drives the content carried across the A1 interface to the RAN. It can also
21
access other SMO Framework functionality, for example influencing that which is carried across the O1-CM
22
interface. It is comprised of two sub-functions:
23
o
Non-RT RIC Framework – That functionality internal to the SMO Framework itself that:
24

Logically terminates the A1 interface to the Near-RT RIC.
25

________________________________________________________________________________________________
11

Exposes to rApps, via its R1 interface, the set of internal SMO Framework services needed for
1
their runtime processing.
2
o
Non-RT RIC Applications (rApps) – Modular applications that leverage the functionality exposed by
3
the Non-RT RIC Framework to provide added value services relative to RAN operation.  Examples of
4
such added value services include:
5

Driving content (Policy or Enrichment Information) across the A1 interface.
6

Recommending content for the O1 interface.
7

Generating “enrichment information” for the use of other rApps.
8
Figure 2.1-2 graphically illustrates these definitions.
9
As observed above, rApps will require services from the R1 interface that are not necessarily associated with the Non-RT
10
RIC Framework, such as access to O1, data sharing services, and access to RAN inventory. The Non-RT RIC Framework,
11
via its R1 Services exposure functionality, would be responsible for exposing all of these services to the rApps,
12
irrespective of the location within the SMO Framework of the provider of those services.
13
A declared business need to “port” a Non-RT RIC Framework from one SMO Framework implementation to another
14
would drive the need for a formal interface within the SMO Framework between the Non-RT RIC Framework and the
15
rest of the SMO Framework. Absent this, different implementations of SMO Framework could make different design
16
choices as to how to manifest the boundary between the Non-RT RIC Framework and the rest of the SMO Framework,
17
or even to choose not to implement a clear boundary at all.
18
The lack of a clear boundary between the Non-RT RIC and the rest of the SMO Framework need not negatively impact
19
th

tween the Non-RT RIC Framework and the rest of the SMO Framework,
17
or even to choose not to implement a clear boundary at all.
18
The lack of a clear boundary between the Non-RT RIC and the rest of the SMO Framework need not negatively impact
19
the ability to proceed with a formal definition of the R1 interface nor impact definition of the R1 Services exposure
20
functionality needed to support this interface. Rather, such definitions can proceed, agnostic to the source of the SMO
21
Framework services being exposed. However, it may be useful to define some terms that we can use to help us in
22
discussion of these topics.
23
Particularly it would be useful to have terms to distinguish between:
24

An indication that a particular R1-exposed functionality is sourced from the Non-RT RIC Framework. This
25
functionality would be considered “inherent” to the Non-RT RIC Framework.
26

An indication that it is left as an SMO Framework implementation decision whether a particular R1-exposed
27
functionality is sourced from the Non-RT RIC Framework or not.
28

An indication that a particular R1-exposed functionality is not sourced from the Non-RT RIC Framework. This
29
functionality would be considered “inherent” to the SMO Framework itself, but not the Non-RT RIC Framework.
30
The functionality that is inherent to the Non-RT RIC Framework is that functionality related to the two interfaces that the
31
Non-RT RIC “owns”, specifically that functionality needed to drive the A1 and R1 interfaces. The O1 and O2 interfaces
32
are clear examples of functionality of the third bullet.
33
The term “Implementation Variable Functionality” is descriptive of that functionality described in the second bullet.
34
Examples might include functionalities such as “Data Sharing”, “Analytic S

lear examples of functionality of the third bullet.
33
The term “Implementation Variable Functionality” is descriptive of that functionality described in the second bullet.
34
Examples might include functionalities such as “Data Sharing”, “Analytic Services”, “Policy”, “RAN Inventory”,
35
“General ML/AI Model LCM/Catalog”, RAN Mediation/Control”, “RAN Configuration Database”, “PM Short Term
36
Data Repository”, “Operations Intent Interface” and “External Interfaces”.
37
These terms and the relationships between the functions they describe can be seen in Figure 2.1-2 below.
38

1
Figure 2.1-2: Exposure of SMO Framework Services to rApps
2
The “Internal” arrows in the diagram represent that it is within the scope of the Non-RT RIC Framework’s R1 Services
3
exposure functionality to expose all required services of the SMO Framework, even those that are not or may not be
4
associated with the Non-RT RIC Framework itself. It is outside of O-RAN’s scope to define the “Internal” mechanism
5
through which these services are exposed to specific SMO Framework implementations.
6
Note that each of the endpoint functional blocks of the SMO Framework’s external interfaces have interface termination
7
functions and functionalities associated with them to drive that respective interface. Thus, the Non-RT RIC Framework
8
has associated with it the “A1 Functionalities”, i.e., A1 Policy, A1 EI and A1 ML, required to drive the A1 interface, as
9
well as the A1 interface logical termination functions. Examples of R1 Services exposure functionality would include
10
what is needed to manage the runtime interactions of individual rApps with the Non-RT RIC Framework itself.
11
The Non-RT RIC architecture lends itself to be described by using two views, based on different approaches: a functional
12
approach and a service-based approach. In the functional approach, the architectural view focuses on “packaging”
13
functionalities into functions, i.e., logical entities with well-defined behaviour, connected by interfaces. In a service-based
14
approach, the architectural view focuses on describing the functionalities as capabilities offered through services by
15
service producer entities to service consumer entities, inspired by the service-based design principles defined in ETSI
16
ZSM [12]. Service consumer and service producer entities are interconnected by means of

bilities offered through services by
15
service producer entities to service consumer entities, inspired by the service-based design principles defined in ETSI
16
ZSM [12]. Service consumer and service producer entities are interconnected by means of communication support that
17
enable adequate communication patterns e.g. 1-1, 1-many, pub-sub, routed etc. In general, a functional architectural view
18
can be regarded as a deployment option, or specific realization, allowed by the service-based architectural view, and both
19
provide the same functionalities. As described in the following, this principle is valid also for the Non-RT RIC case.
20
Following the principles above, Section 2.2 provides the functional view of the Non-RT RIC architecture, whereas Section
21
2.2a shows the service-based view. The functional decomposition of the Non-RT RIC shown in Section 2.2 facilitates
22
analysis and description of the required functionality of the combination of Non-RT RIC and SMO framework. Based on
23
that analysis, the service-based view of the Non-RT RIC architecture focuses on interoperability aspects – namely the
24
interfaces with other O-RAN components and the R1 services that allow interworking between the Non-RT RIC and the
25
rApps as the main multivendor integration point. To facilitate flexibility of deployment, the service-based architectural
26
view defines SMO and Non-RT RIC capabilities, but abstracts from a detailed representation of functional blocks that
27
realize the capabilities and produce or consume the R1 services. This architectural approach allows multiple different
28
instantiations; the detailed functional view presented in Section 2.2 being one of these possible instantiations. All such
29
instantiations will all be interoperable towards rApps

R1 services. This architectural approach allows multiple different
28
instantiations; the detailed functional view presented in Section 2.2 being one of these possible instantiations. All such
29
instantiations will all be interoperable towards rApps as long as they support the R1 services, and towards other O-RAN
30
system components as long as they support the interfaces defined towards these.

2.2a Non-RT RIC Architecture Service-based View
21
The service-based architectural approach is today widely adopted by telco industry. Service-based principles allow to
22
describe an architecture not based on fixed functional components and interfaces between them but based on the definition
23
of services as the central point of architecture consideration. Though there’s no formal definition available, a service-
24
based architecture follows principles of which some are listed below:
25

Modularity: The functionality is modularized into a set of services at the appropriate granularity level.
26

Extensibility: The architecture allows simple extensibility by adding new services and making them
27
discoverable.
28

Functional abstraction: Service-based architecture abstracts from the complexity and details of the underlying
29
functions that produce the services.
30

Discoverability: Services are searchable for their availability.
31

Composability: Services can be composed, forming new services.
32

Reusability: Since services ar

lexity and details of the underlying
29
functions that produce the services.
30

Discoverability: Services are searchable for their availability.
31

Composability: Services can be composed, forming new services.
32

Reusability: Since services are modularized, they can be re-used and can be invoked at multiple stages of the
33
business process.
34

Loose coupling: Services are loosely coupled and independent from one-another.
35
Designing an architecture in a service-based fashion allows a great degree of deployment flexibility and future-
36
proofedness, as it leaves the choice of components that produce and/or consume certain services to the deployment, yet
37
facilitating multi-vendor interoperability through the definition of standardized services respectively standardized service
38
interfaces. Services are produced by service producers and consumed by service consumers through service endpoints.
39
Service-based architecture allows modularization of the services rather than the components of a deployment. Service
40
consumers need to be authenticated and authorized to access services at runtime by policies, rather than pre-assigning
41
fixed consumer-producer relationships at the time the standard is developed. Produced services are registered in a registry
42
from which service consumers can discover the available services, and the technical parameters how to consume them,
43

________________________________________________________________________________________________
15
such as the service endpoint, the data format and access protocol. For the service communication, different possibilities
1
exist. Service consumers can access the service endpoints directly in a point-to-point fashion, after discovering them.
2
Alternatively, service-related communication can be facilitated using an overarching communication framework such as
3
a message bus or service mesh. Using a service-based design for the functionalities that are consumed and/or produced
4
by rApps, these apps can run in any deployment that offers these services, without the need to document implementation
5
variability. Also, future evolution of rApps into more generic smart network management apps is enabled, as such evolved
6
apps would simply be able to discover and use more services.
7

The diagram in Figure 2.2a-1 shows the decomposition of the Non-RT RIC into Non-RT RIC Framework and rApps,
9
interacting with each other through the R1 services, described in Section 3.4.
10
A service is a set of capabilities offered by a service producer to service consumers for consumption through defined
11
endpoints. The purpose of a service is to access, use and control a certain functionality (set of capabilities) available in
12
the system. Production and consumption of services, which are specified, are roles of (software) entities in deployments,
13
however, the exact software entities are not called out in the specification. A service may be standardized by O-RAN
14
Alliance, by another organization, or be proprietary, but it can be made available in the system if it implements a common
15
and standard way to register, to be

ties are not called out in the specification. A service may be standardized by O-RAN
14
Alliance, by another organization, or be proprietary, but it can be made available in the system if it implements a common
15
and standard way to register, to be accessed and controlled.
16
According to the above, the architecture in Figure 2.2a-1 depicts the R1 services and the related capabilities which are
17
part of the SMO and Non-RT Framework. Such capabilities also include communication support to enable adequate
18
communication patterns for the service requirements, e.g., 1-1, 1-many, pub-sub, routed etc., inspired by the service-
19
based design principles defined in [12]. Furthermore, the diagram shows that the service-based approach describes
20
consistently how services provide access to Non-RT RIC inherent functionalities, SMO inherent functionalities,
21
implementation variable functionalities and also capabilities external to the SMO.
22
The Non-RT RIC service-based architectural view caters for different deployment options, including the one illustrated
23
in Figure 2.2-1, by applying an appropriate configuration of the authorized producers-consumer pairs.
24

3.4.2 General Principles
3
As described in section 5.2 of [11], at least some ML applications may profitably be deployed either to the Non-RT RIC,
4
to the Near-RT RIC, or to both. This is certainly not true for all ML applications, as the same interfaces are not available
5
in both platforms (e.g., E2, A1 downstream) nor do each have the same real-time requirements. However, for the types
6
of interactions needed by the application types for which such portability would be beneficial, the design choices of the
7
R1 interface should not unnecessarily become an obstacle for such portability.
8

Leverage Existing Work: Because rApps will share some common functionality with xApps (startup, messaging,
9
data sharing, etc.), the prior work done for xApps should be analyzed for applicability to the R1 use cases and
10
leveraged where appropriate.
11

Aligned integration services: Because integration or enablement services (such as registration, discovery,
12
authorization, authentication, etc.) are needed to integrate rApps with the Non-RT RIC as well as to integrate
13
xApps with the Near-RT RIC, the work done for xApp integration/enablement should be analyzed for
14
applicability to rApp integration/enablement and leveraged where appropriate.
15

Behavioral Alignment Where Practical: Because at least some ML applications will be deployable to the Non-
16
RT RIC, Near-RT RIC, or both, the design choices made for R1 interactions should strive to minimize the
17
refactoring needed of an rApp to enable deployment into a Near-RT RIC environment.
18

Decoupled Interface: Although rApps will share some common functionality with xApps, they will also have
19
many unique functi

ns should strive to minimize the
17
refactoring needed of an rApp to enable deployment into a Near-RT RIC environment.
18

Decoupled Interface: Although rApps will share some common functionality with xApps, they will also have
19
many unique functionalities and needs that are not applicable to the Near-RT RIC.  Therefore, the analysis and
20
design choices made for the R1 interface should be done in parallel and not considered dependent on that of
21
xApps.
22

The R1 interface is the sole interface between an rApp and the functionality of the Non-RT RIC and SMO.
23
Therefore, the R1 interface should be defined to meet all functional needs of rApps, with appropriate interface
24
extensibility capabilities as needed.
25
The R1 interface will provide a level of abstraction between rApps that are consumers of data and their data sources:

versus an entity external to the Non-RT RIC or SMO).


The R1 interface will provide functionality such that an rApp that is a consumer of data will not need to know

involves only data types and their periodicity, whereas “data subscription” involves specific sets of data within a given
26
“scope”.1 Thus, the purpose of “data registration” interactions is to enable the Non-RT RIC Framework to facilitate data
27
type level value-added services, such as:
28

Authorizing an rApp to produce data of a certain data type. For example, a service provider may want to enforce
29
a policy that two separate rApp instances should not produce the same data type within the same Non-RT RIC
30
Framework instance.
31

Authorizing an rApp to consume data of a certain data type. For example, a service provider may want to restrict
32
the availability of certain data types, such as data types that relate to sensitive data.
33

Accounting for the number of rApp consumers that exist for a given data type. For example, licensing of certain
34
data-producing rApps may be sensitive to the number of consumer instanc

a types, such as data types that relate to sensitive data.
33

Accounting for the number of rApp consumers that exist for a given data type. For example, licensing of certain
34
data-producing rApps may be sensitive to the number of consumer instances of that data type.
35
As part of registration processing, the Non-RT RIC Framework will match the needs of data type consumers against the
36
capabilities of data type producers. A valid data type producer for matching purposes would include previously registered

A1 policy enforcement
4.1
Introduction
4.1.1
A1 specifications
A1 policy management is defined in the A1 specifications:

General aspects and principles, including lifecycle management aspects, are described in A1GAP [i.1];

Use cases and procedures are described in A1UCR [i.2];

Application protocol based on REST methodology, including service operations, resource definitions and Open API,
are defined in A1AP [i.3];

Type definitions, including policy types, policy representations, status and feedback content, is defined in A1TD [i.4].
The A1 policy management service is referred to as A1-P. A1GAP [i.1] and A1UCR [i.2] corresponds to the stage 2
description while A1AP [i.3] and A1TD [i.4] corresponds to the stage 3 description of this service.
4.1.2
A1 policy management
A1GAP [i.1], clause 4.1.3.1, describes the A1 policy management service (A1-P) and the purpose of A1 polices as:
“... the Non-RT RIC can define policies that are provided to the Near-RT RIC over the A1 interface. The purpose of the A1
policies is to guide the RAN performance towards the overall goal expressed in RAN intent. The A1 policies are
declarative policies that contain statements on policy objectives and policy resources applicable to e.g. UEs and cells.
The Non-RT RIC can manage the A1 policies based on A1 policy status and feedback information provided by the Near-
RT RIC, and on the network status provided over O1. The Non-RT RIC can use the O1 observables to continuously
evaluate the impact of the A1 policies towards fulfilment of the RAN intent and based on internal conditions it can decide
to issue/update the goals expressed in the A1 policies.
The Near-RT RIC functions based on its internal functions or applications, the configuration received

When Near-RT RIC receives an A1 policy from Non-RT RIC, it uses its internal functions and configuration to determine
appropriate actions towards the E2 nodes which it controls. The activity that Near-RT RIC performs based on an A1 policy is

observes the impact on the E2 nodes via the O1 interface.

4.2.2
State machine
As described in A1GAP [i.1], clause 5.1.3:

An A1 policy exists in the Near-RT RIC after Non-RT RIC has sent a Create policy request that was accepted by the
Near RT RIC. When the A1 policy has been created, the Non-RT RIC can assume that its enforcement status is
ENFORCED. If Near-RT RIC cannot enforce the A1 policy, it will reject the Create policy request.

The enforcement status of the A1 policy is determined by the Near-RT RIC and reflects the status of the policy
enforcement activity in the Near-RT RIC. When enforcement status changes between ENFORCED and
NOT_ENFORCED, Near-RT RIC sends a Notify policy status message (given that Non-RT RIC has subscribed to
status notifications).

An A1 policy can be updated by Non-RT RIC and Near-RT RIC will accept the Update policy request only if the
enforcement status can be ENFORCED after the update.

After the Non-RT RIC has sent a Delete policy request, policy enforcement is stopped, and the policy no longer exist.
