7 Conclusions and recommendations
7.1 General
Updating the A1 interface specification for support of partiality aspects would imply update of several clauses in several of the
specifications, and an update of the A1 policy management service (A1-P) may imply a non-backward compatible change.
Clause 7.2 provides a summary of major findings of the study in the present document that could be considered for inclusion in
an updated A1 interface specification. Clause 7.3 then provides further details on inclusion of partiality

mpatible change.
Clause 7.2 provides a summary of major findings of the study in the present document that could be considered for inclusion in
an updated A1 interface specification. Clause 7.3 then provides further details on inclusion of partiality in the definition and
interpretation of policy enforcement status.
Clause 7.4 summarizes identified issues and items that were not further considered in the present study.
Clause 7.5 provides the high-level recommendations from the study.
7.2 Common aspects
7.2.1 Terms
7.2.1.1 General
The partiality discussion in the present document relies on fundamental definitions related to A1 policy enforcement
capabilities and to how (the scope, objectives, and resources of) an A1 policy is considered as applicable and enforceable. The
reasoning of how partiality can be considered during policy creation and enforcement introduced refined terms for referring to
an A1 policy and enforcement as an activity.
The following clause summarizes where the definitions are made.
7.2.1.2 Capabilities
The configured A1 policy enforcement capabilities and the available A1 policy enforcement capabilities defined as in clause
5.3.2 and 6.2.2.
The required A1 policy enforcement capabilities and the available A1 policy enforcement capabilities as discussed in clause
6.1.

7.2.1.3 Abilities
Scope applicability as defined in 6.2.2.
Objectives applicability as defined in 5.3.4 and 6.2.1.
Resources applicability as defined in clause 5.3.5.
Policy applicability and enforceability as defined in clauses 5.4.3 and 6.2.
7.2.1.4 Scopes and policies
Requested/Valid/Accepted/Rejected/Existing A1 policy, and Requested/Applicable/Enforceable scope, as summarized  in
clause 6.5.
7.2.1.5 Enforcement
Enforcement as described in clause 5.4.1 and partial enforcement as defined in clause 6.1.
7.2.2 Constraints and status
7.2.2.1 General
The definition of policy type constraints and policy type status in clause 6.3.2 would provide detailed information for Non-RT
RIC related to what it could expect if a requested A1 policy was formulated in certain ways and in certain contexts so that

if Non-RT RIC was aware of the policy type specific constraints containing configured A1 policy enforcement
capabilities, it would be able to formulate a requested A1 policy with an applicable scope;

if Non-RT RIC was aware of the policy type specific supported attributes and value ranges, it would be able to
formulate a requested A1 policy with applicable objectives;

if Non-RT RIC was aware of the policy type specific constraints containing available A1 policy enforcement
capabilities, it would be able to formulate a requested A1 policy with enforceable scope; and

if Non-RT RIC was aware of the policy type status, it would be able to realize when the constraints change and reflect
status that provides guidance regarding if partial enforcement could be expected for A1 policies.
7.2.2.2 Procedures
Policy type constraints can be provided in the response of a Query policy type constraints operations, or in the response to the
Query policy type operation, as discussed in cla

artial enforcement could be expected for A1 policies.
7.2.2.2 Procedures
Policy type constraints can be provided in the response of a Query policy type constraints operations, or in the response to the
Query policy type operation, as discussed in clause 6.3.2.2.
Policy type status can be provided in the response of a Query policy type status operation, or by a Notify policy type status
operation, as discussed in clause 6.3.2.5.
7.2.2.3 Schema
Constraints schema and policy type status schema would be part of policy type definitions (together with policy schema and
status schema), see clause 6.3.2.
7.2.3 Creation/update requests
7.2.3.1 General
The design patterns for how A1 policies can be created and updated using HTTP PUT operations, and the HTTP status codes
related to evaluations of policy creation requests, can be applied to support partiality aspects. In addition, the message content
could include detailed information that could correspond to information provided in other operations.

7.2.3.2 Create/update policy operations
The Create single policy operations and Update single policy operations are based on HTTP PUT where the requested A1
policy is provided in the message content.
If the requested A1 policy is not considered as applicable, the PUT request could be rejected with a 501 error, and if the
requested A1 policy is not considered as enforceable, the PUT request could be rejected with a 503 error, as discussed in clause
5.5.4.2.
NOTE:
The usage of the error codes 501 and 503 is already allowed, see A1AP [i.3], clause 6.2.7.3, although their
relation to A1 policy enforcement capabilities is not covered by the current A1 specification.
The reject message could contain any detailed information on the reject reasons but need not if the corresponding information
is provided as policy type constraints and/or status.
7.2.3.3 Design patterns
Evaluation of policy creation requests can be based on only evaluation of applicability/enforceability but can also be based on
the status after start of enforcement (when actions are taken for the parts of the policy) as described in clauses 5.5.2 and 5.5.3.
Clause 5.5.5 provides potential clarifications to the current A1 specification related to this while clause 6.3.4 elaborates further
on how policy creation transactions could be impacted by partiality (depending on cases as described in clause 7.3).
7.2.3.4 Assumptions and expectations
Non-RT RIC can assume that an A1 policy is enforced until policy status is queried or a change in enforcement status is
notified while Near-RT RIC can assign any value of enforceStatus when creating the A1 policy before enforcement activity
starts and the actual status may be notified. To avoid risk for situations where the assumptions may leave Non-RT RIC
unaware of the actua

while Near-RT RIC can assign any value of enforceStatus when creating the A1 policy before enforcement activity
starts and the actual status may be notified. To avoid risk for situations where the assumptions may leave Non-RT RIC
unaware of the actual status of the enforcement activity, the proposed clarification (see clause 5.5.5) is that the Non-RT RIC
should query the policy status after receiving the 201 Created as that enables understanding of the policy status in both cases
when a policy status notification is either received or not.
7.2.4 Status and notifications
The change reason attributes values in the policy status notifications can reflect partiality information. In addition, the message
content could include detailed status information that could correspond to information provided in other operations.
Potential updates of enforceReason attributes values are discussed in clause 6.2.4 and detailed policy status information in
clause 6.2.5. Clause 5.5.5 provides potential clarifications to the current A1 specification related to this while clause 6.3.5
elaborates further on how policy creation transactions could be impacted by partiality (depending on cases as described in
clause 7.3).
7.3 Defining and interpreting enforceStatus
7.3.1 General

7.3.2 Lifecycle management
The current description of A1 policy lifecycle management in A1GAP [i.1], clause 5.1.3, would be impacted by

NOTE:
The present document does not consider any changes to the principle that Non-RT RIC is the lifecycle
management owner of A1 polices while Near-RT RIC determines the status of the A1 policy enforcement

7.3.3 Reinterpreting the current case
Case 0 introduced in clause 6.2.3 corresponds to the current A1 specification. By introducing supporting information as per

if requested A1 policy is not applicable (i.e. it is not "fully applicable"), the policy creation request can be rejected
using the 501 error code;

if requested A1 policy is not enforceable (i.e. it is "fully enforceable" or "partly enforceable"), the policy creation
request can be rejected using the 503 error code;

if the requested A1 policy is accepted using the 201 response code, Non-RT RIC can assume Near-RT RIC considers
it as enforceable and will start an enforcement activity.

can be expected, and if to consider keeping/updating/deleting the A1 policy. The enforceReason attribute values, and any
detailed policy status information, would enable Near-RT RIC to express detailed partiality information. Policy status
notifications could indicate changes in the detailed policy status information as well as changes in enforceStatus attribute
value.
The policy type constraints and status would provide guidance to Non-RT RIC regarding what can be an expected outcome of
a policy creation transaction. The policy type status would indicate if full or partial enforcement could be expected based on
configu

olicy type constraints and status would provide guidance to Non-RT RIC regarding what can be an expected outcome of

NOTE:
Even if the same attributes (providing information on availability of A1 policy enforcement capabilities) are used
to indicate status of policy types as to indicate status of an individual policy, the policy type status does not

7.3.4.1 Case 1
Case 1 introduced in clause 6.2.3 implies stricter expectations, compared to case 0 described in clause 7.3.2, regarding Near-

7.5.2 Specific

The A1 specification should define terms related to applicability, enforceability, and A1 policy enforcement capabilities to

See further clauses 7.2.1.2 and 7.2.1.3.
7.5.2.2 Rejection of not applicable policy
The A1 specification should define usage of the 501 Not Implemented error code for the case when a policy creation request is

4
Impact analysis of Decoupled SMO
4.1
WG2 specifications impact analysis
4.1.1
Non-RT RIC architecture related aspects
4.1.1.1
Overview and highlights
The architecture defined in Non-RT RIC Architecture specification [i.3] provide a functional description of Non-RT RIC and
SMO, where reference to SMO functions is given in support of the services exposed over the two open interfaces, i.e. R1 and
A1.
4.1.1.2
Impact analysis
4.1.1.2.1
Introduction
In the Decoupled SMO FWID, the standardization of a Service Based Architecture for SMO, as defined in OAD [i.2] aims at
ensuring the interoperability between components based on the definition of services instead of functions and interfaces. The
new approach, however, does neither change the role of the Non-RT RIC nor introduce non-backward compatibility issues
over R1 and A1, being the functions defined in the current Non-RT RIC Architecture specification [i.3] are one-to-one related
to the corresponding services, which can now be referred to a SMOS in OAD [i.2].

Both Decoupled SMO Architecture TR [i.1] and OAD [i.2] state that grouping of SMOS producers in one SMOF is not subject
to specification.
Moreover, current Non-RT RIC architecture, shows O1, O2 and Open FH M-Plane interface terminations as distinct functions
from the functions providing services to Non-RT RIC. With the introduction Decoupled SMO architecture, as described in
OAD [i.2] the O1/Open FH M-Plane and O2 interface terminate to RAN NF OAM and NFO/FOCOM SMOS producers,
respectively. Hence, Figure 6.1-1 and the definitions of interface terminations should be revised accordingly.
4.1.1.2.1a Requirements
The Non-RT RIC Architecture specification [i.3], clause 5.1 defines the requirements for the Non-RT RIC framework. Some
of these requirements are defined considering the functional architecture of SMO. The introduction of a service-based
architecture for SMO, implies that SMOS related requirements should be analysed and aligned to the decoupled SMO
Architectural principles. For example, the requirement REQ-NRTFWK-FUN2 is defined as,
The Non-RT RIC framework shall support functionality to allow Service Consumers to discover services.
This requirement can be seen as consisting of two sub requirements.
1. The service management and exposure (SME) services shall support functionality to allow Service Consumers to
discover services.
2. For the R1 interface, the R1 interface termination shall enable the SME Service Producers and the SME Service
Consumers to exchange messages related to the SME service capabilities that are accessible via the R1 interface.

6

In the decoupled SMO context, the 1st sub requirement should be a requirement towards SME SMOS and should be specified
in the SME SMOS UCR TS. The 2nd sub requirement is relevant to be specified in the Non-RT RIC Architecture specification
[i.3], clause 5.1.
The 2nd sub requirement could be generalized as below,
For the R1 interface, the R1 interface termination shall enable the Service Producers and the Service Consumers to exchange
messages related to the service capabilities that are accessible via the R1 interface.
4.1.1.2.2
Conclusions
Based on the above analysis, the following can be concluded:

•
Non-RT RIC architecture remains consistent with the overarching Decoupled SMO architecture, improving
interoperability and enabling a modular approach to service management.
•
SMOS (SMO Services) concept should be integrated into the Non-RT RIC Architecture specification [i.3] to ensure it
aligns with the Service-Based Architecture (SBA) principles of the Decoupled SMO framework.
•
Description of O1/Open FH M-Plane and O2 interfaces and the related services should be adapted to the align with the
Decoupled SMO architecture and principles, e.g. by removing the interface termination boxes and refer to the
corresponding SMOS producers (RAN NF OAM and NFO/FOCOM).
•
The requirements in the Non-RT RIC Architecture specification [i.3], clause 5.1 which are relevant for a SMOS need
to be specified in the corresponding SMOS specific UCR TS.
•
The requirements relevant for the Non-RT RIC need to be specified in the Non-RT RIC Architecture specification [i.3],
clause 5.1.

4.1.2
A1 related aspects
4.1.2.1
Overview and highlights
In the Non-RT RIC Architecture specification [i.3], A1 termination function which is anchored function in the Non-RT RIC
reference architecture is defined as,
A1 termination: It enables the Non-RT RIC framework and the Near-RT RIC to exchange messages over the A1 interface.
However, In the Decoupled SMO Architecture TR [i.1] A1 termination function is neither mentioned nor shown in Fig 6.2.1-1.
It's not clear then whether it is consistent with the Non-RT RIC Architecture.
4.1.2.2
Impact analysis
4.1.2.2.1
Introduction
A1 Policy, A1 Enrichment Information and A1-ML Model management (A1-P, A1-EI, A1-ML) services are critical for
facilitating interaction between the SMO/Non-RT RIC framework and Near-RT RIC through the A1 interface. The
management of policies, enrichment information and ML model ensures that near real-time decisions made at the Near-RT
RIC are guided or assisted by the management and orchestration services in the SMO/Non-RT RIC.
However, there is currently ambiguity about whether producers of these services should be anchored within the Non-RT RIC
or be non-anchored (i.e. flexibly deployable as part of the SMO framework or the NonRT RIC framework).

The introduction of A1 related SMOSs with the exposure of services offered by a function consuming A1 interface services,
i.e. A1-P, A1-EI and A1-ML in A1GAP [i.4], does not conflict with the A1 interface specifications and with the role of Non-
RT RIC, there is however an inconsistency related to the concept of “A1 termination" anchoring, introduced in Non-RT RIC
Architecture specification [i.3].
As for SMOS related to other external SMO interfaces, i.e. O1 and O2, it would be straightforward to assume that the A1-
related SMOS producer and the termination of A1 interface are tightly coupled.

7

The alternative, i.e. introducing a functional separation between the A1 related SMOS producer and the A1 interface
termination, would require the definition of an additional interface or reference point between these to ensure interoperability
between the two functions.
Before the introduction of SMOS concept, the only consumers of A1 related services were the rApps. With the introduction of
other SMOS, e.g. Service Assurance SMOS, also other SMOS producer may consume A1 related services SMOS to e.g.
provide policies to Near RT RIC. For this reason, it seems appropriate to expose A1 related services as individual SMOS, as
defined in OAD [i.2]
Following the analysis given above, in order to confirm the assumption that A1 related functions are not anchored to the Non-
RT RIC, it is necessary to revise the concept of A1 termination, possibly aligning to other SMO interfaces like O1 and O2, for
example avoiding the term “A1 termination function” and use “A1 interface" or “A1 services consumer/producer” instead.
4.1.2.2.2
Conclusions
Based on the above analysis, the following can be concluded:

•
Update the descriptions of “A1 termination” in Non-RT RIC Architecture specification [i.3], remove the box “A1
termination" from the Non-RT RIC architecture and terminate the A1 interface into the “A1 related functions”. Remove
the reference to "A1 termination" from clause 8.1 and replace the remaining two occurrences of "A1 termination" with
"A1 interface. This will ensure consistency between the concepts “A1 related SMOS” given in OAD and the “A1 related
functions” described in Non-RT RIC Architecture TS.

4.1.3
R1 related aspects
4.1.3.1
Overview and highlights
The standardization of a Service Based Architecture for SMO, as defined in OAD [i.2] aims at ensuring the interoperability
between components based on the definition of services.

Several SMOS were introduced in OAD [i.2] clause 5.3.1.2.1 to support a service-based architecture in SMO.

In particular, the scope of SME and DME SMOS have been defined to support service and data exposure to both internal and
external SMOS consumers:

SME SMOS supports the exposure of other SMOSs, to both internal and external SMOS consumers.
DME SMOS supports the exposure of data produced by SMOS Producers, to both internal and external SMOS consumers.

The R1 interface related specifications refer to the services exposed as “R1 services”, since the scope is the service exposure
over R1 interface.

The relationship between R1 services, SMOS and R1 interface has been provided in OAD [i.2]:

R1 Services: The SMOS capabilities available for consumption by rApps, and the capabilities produced by rApps,
that are accessible via the R1 interface

8

4.1.3.2
Impact Analysis
4.1.3.2.1
R1 Interface
The following paragraphs describe the R1 interface (Non-RT RIC Architecture specification [i.3] clause 6.2):

The R1 interface is a service-based interface via which the R1 services can be consumed and produced.
The R1 termination enables the R1 Service Producers and R1 Service Consumers to exchange messages via the R1
interface.
The R1 termination enables the SMO/Non-RT RIC framework and the rApps to exchange messages via the R1 interface,
assuming that the R1 service APIs and the rApps are registered with the R1 service management and exposure functions.

The R1 interface is clearly identified between SMO/Non-RT RIC Framework and the rApps. This is not changed by the
Decoupled SMO Architecture.

4.1.3.2.2
R1 services
The following paragraphs describe “R1 services” concepts.

From Non-RT RIC Architecture specification [i.3] clause 6.2:
The R1 services are a collection of services produced and consumed by logical functions in the SMO/Non-RT RIC
framework or by rApps.
The invoker of an R1 service is referred to as R1 Service Consumer and the provider of an R1 service is referred to as R1
Service Producer. R1 Service Consumers can be rApps and/or SMO/Non-RT RIC framework functions. Further, R1
Service Producers can be rApps and/or SMO/Non-RT RIC framework functions.
An rApp as well as a SMO/Non-RT RIC framework function can produce zero or more R1 Services, likewise an rApp as
well as a SMO/Non-RT RIC framework function can consume zero or more R1 Services.

From Non-RT RIC Architecture specification [i.3] clause 7.1:

The set of R1 services which can be accessed via the R1 interface includes (but is not limited to):
•
Service management and exposure services, which include service registration and service discovery services,
authentication services, authorization services and communication support services. The service management
and exposure services support extensibility of the set of R1 services.
•
Data management and exposure services, which deliver data created or collected by Data Producers to Data
Consumers according to their needs.
•
A1-related services, which provide access to functionality related to A1.
•
AI/ML workflow services, which provide access to AI and ML workflow.
•
RAN OAM-related services, which provide access to RAN OAM functionality related to the O1 and open
fronthaul M-plane interfaces, and to the OAM functionality related to RAN-specific network slicing in the
SMO framework.
•
O2-related services, which provide access to functionality related to O2.
•
rApp management services, which provide functionality for managing rApps.
•
TE&IV-related services, which provide access to topology and inventory data.

9

4.1.3.2.3
Conclusions

From the above, the following considerations can be derived:
•
R1 services and SMOSs listed in OAD [i.2] clause 5.3.1.2.1 and in Non-RT RIC Architecture specification
[i.3] clause 7.1 are based on the same SMO capabilities
•
SMOSs capabilities can be consumed/produced by rApps via R1 interface
•
the introduction of Decoupled SMO architecture does not conflict with the R1 interface principles listed in
R1GAP [i.5] clause 4.2
•
The R1AP [i.6] defines a service-based interface. The procedures can be extended to align with the Decoupled
SMO principles without major changes to the APIs.

4.1.4
Use cases and requirement related aspects
4.1.4.1
Overview and highlights
WG2 Use cases and requirements so far assume a functional architecture for SMO.
The Decoupled SMO feature relies on a Service Based Architecture for SMO and introduces the concepts of SMOS
producers/consumers.
4.1.4.2
Impact analysis
4.1.4.2.1
Use cases
Some of the use cases in UCR [i.8] describe the procedures involving SMO components as considering the functional
architecture of SMO. The introduction of a service-based architecture for SMO, implies that the SMO functional entities, and
the related blocks in the diagrams, should be analysed and aligned to the corresponding SMO service producers/consumers (as
an example, ‘RAN NF OAM SMOS producer’ instead of ‘Collection & Control’ in Fig. 4.1.3.1-1).
4.1.4.2.2
Requirements
Clause 5 of UCR [i.8] specify Non-RT RIC, A1 and R1 functional and non-functional requirements. Terminology may need a
revision to align to Decoupled SMO architectural principles and definitions.
4.1.4.2.3
Conclusions
UCR [i.8] should be analysed and aligned to comply with Decoupled SMO Architectural principles.

4.2
Recommendations
The following actions are recommended to ensure alignment of WG2 specifications for the introduction of the Decoupled
SMO Architecture:

-
Introduce SMOS (SMO Services) concept into the Non-RT RIC Architecture specification [i.3] to ensure it aligns with
the Service-Based Architecture (SBA) principles of the Decoupled SMO framework and the definition of R1 services.
-
Analyze and align description of O1/Open FH M-Plane and O2 interfaces and the related services in Non-RT RIC
Architecture specification [i.3] to comply with Decoupled SMO Architectural principles, e.g. by removing the interface
termination boxes and refer to the corresponding SMOS producers (RAN NF OAM and NFO/FOCOM).
-
Remove the box “A1 termination" from the Non-RT RIC architecture and terminate the A1 interface into the “A1 related
functions”.
-
Remove the reference to "A1 termination" from clause 8.1 of Non-RT RIC Architecture specification [i.3] and replace
the remaining two occurrences of "A1 termination" with "A1 interface.

10

-
Analyse and align UCR [i.8] to comply with Decoupled SMO Architectural principles.
-
Analyse and align Non-RT RIC Architecture specification [i.3], clause 5.1 to comply with Decoupled SMO
Architectural principles.

4
Overview
4.1
Background
Within O-RAN, A1 Policies and E2SMs [i.10] IE/Objects enable the intelligent guidance of the RAN towards better
fulfilment of the RAN Intent. Non-RT RIC and Near-RT RIC, each has its own context that needs to be broken down
into more detailed ones and to be passed to next lower layer as shown in Figure 4.1-1.
NOTE:
The RAN intent is outside the scope of the A1 interface.

Figure 4.1- 1: Context for each layer
The purpose of the A1 policies is to guide the RAN towards the overall goal expressed in RAN intent in A1GAP [i.6].
As the service consumer of A1 policy management services, rApps can send A1 policies based on their own business
purpose, and A1 policy conflict may happen there. Non-RT-RIC-ARCH [i.7] has defined conflict mitigation for A1
policies as follows: If more than one policy generation rApps set contradicting A1 policy statements to the same or
overlapping policy scope identifiers, A1 policy function decides to reject the creation/modification request of one or
more A1 policies or to temporarily suspend the enforcement of one or more A1 policies.
4.2
Concept
4.2.1
A1 policy conflict
4.2.1.1
Definition
A1 policy conflict: A situation where it is not feasible for a Near-RT RIC function, and hence the RAN to apply the
guidance provided by a set of two or more A1 policies to concurrently achieve the policy objectives and/or to satisfy the
conditions for policy resource usage.

________________________________________________________________________________________________
7
4.2.1.2
General description
A1 policy conflict would be generally recognized in two ways; “actual conflict” and “potential conflict”. The actual A1
policy conflict would be detected and handled for created A1 policies at a Near-RT RIC while the potential A1 policy
conflict would be predicted and mitigated for requested A1 policies over R1 interface at the Non-RT RIC before a new
A1 policy is requested to be created or an existing policy at a Near-RT RIC is requested to be updated over A1 interface.
The potential A1 policy conflict would be predicted by analysing contents of a requested policy and existing policies to
be concurrently enforced at a Near-RT RIC, and mitigated to avoid the policy conflict with possible approaches of
resolutions.
This TR will study and describe ways to predict and mitigate potential A1 policy conflicts in Non-RT RIC, and this
involves further study of A1 policy conflict mitigation functionality of A1 policy functions as specified in Non-RT-RIC-
ARCH [i.7], clause 8.4.1.
NOTE:
The potential A1 policy conflict is referred to as the A1 policy conflict or just the policy conflict, and the
usage of term “predict” for policy conflict does not preclude the usage of term “detect” for policy conflict
if not necessary to distinguish between them in the Technical Report.

Use cases
5.1
Use case #1 “reserve policy” vs. “release policy”
5.1.1
Description
Policies of different A1 policy types currently defined in A1TD [i.9], clause 7.2 could be conflicting with policy
objectives and policy resources. Policies of different types with policy objectives (possibly with policy resources) such
as QoS/QoE target, QoS/QoE optimization with resource directive, UE le

n A1TD [i.9], clause 7.2 could be conflicting with policy
objectives and policy resources. Policies of different types with policy objectives (possibly with policy resources) such
as QoS/QoE target, QoS/QoE optimization with resource directive, UE level target, Slice SLA target, Load balancing,
Energy savings could be conflicting to achieve their objectives concurrently. Policies of the TSP type with policy
resources such as Traffic steering preferences could be conflicting to satisfy the conditions for resource usage for the
policy concurrently.
It is assumed that one of ways to categorize policy types is into mutually exclusive groups in terms of effect on RAN
resource: “reserve policy” group and “release policy” group. The “reserve policy” group is for guaranteeing the service
quality possibly by reserving resources, and the “release policy” group is for offloading cells and hence releasing the
reserved resources. A general grouping of A1 policy types with clause numbers of A1TD [i.9], clause 7 into these
groups is illustrated in Figure 5.1.1-1.

Figure 5.1.1- 1: Grouping of A1 policy types into “reserve policy” group and “release policy”
group.

________________________________________________________________________________________________
8
NOTE 1: A Traffic steering preferences policy is allowed to have both a cell list of SHALL/PREFER preference
and a cell list of AVOID/FORBID preference. In this case the policy would have both characteristics of
reserve policy and release policy groups with each specified scope.
NOTE 2: A Load balancing policy would have characteristic of reserve policy with traffic increase effect on
specified cells and of release policy with traffic decrease effect on other specified cells in the middle of
fulfilling the policy. At the stable condition brought by the LB policy there remains characteristic of
reserve policy for both specified cells.
NOTE 3: An Energy savings policy would imply the coordination with appropriate traffic steering not to impair the
user experience, and a policy without esObjectives would not be conflicting with reserve policy group
resulting in best effort behaviour for energy savings. With esResource statement along with
AVOID/FORBID, the possible energy saving schemes would be more strictly limited for specified cells,
but it leaves to the Near-RT RIC whether it can perform the energy saving scheme (e.g. ASM) so as not to
give impact on traffic or cell coverage as described in AITD [i.9] clause 6.3.4.5.
Co-existence of these different groups of A1 policies in a Near-RT RIC would have a conflicting situation for
achieving their objectives.
5.1.2
Some representative scenarios
1.
Service-guaranteed vs. Network energy saving without EsResource.
Service-guaranteed policies (QoS/QoE/UE-level/Slice_SLA) guide to reserve RAN resources while NES without
EsResource policies to release the same reserved RAN resources to expand its potential power-off duration.
2.
Load

gy saving without EsResource.
Service-guaranteed policies (QoS/QoE/UE-level/Slice_SLA) guide to reserve RAN resources while NES without
EsResource policies to release the same reserved RAN resources to expand its potential power-off duration.
2.
Load balancing vs. Traffic steering preference with AVOID/FORBID
LB policies guide to reserve RAN resources at the target cells listed in the LbResources for distributing traffic
load while TS preference policies to release the same reserved RAN resources at the target cells listed in the
TspResources with AVOID/FORBID.
3.
Traffic steering preference with SHALL/PREFER vs. Network energy saving without EsResource.
TS preference policies guide to reserve RAN resources at the target cells listed in the TspResources with
SHALL/PREFER while NES without EsResource policies to release the same reserved RAN resources.

Detection of A1 policy conflict
6.1
General
The detection of A1 policy conflict would be performed when a new policy is requested to be created against a set of
existing policies, or an existing policy is requested to be updated within a set of existing policies. The decision to regard
a set of policies as a set of conflicting policies would be performed based on the following aspects:
1.
to detect if there are overlapping scopes with their policy scopes or overlapping resources in their policy
resources, and
2.
to detect if A1 policies in each overlapping scope have potential conflict.

6.2.1
A1 policy applicable entity type
The ScopeIdentifier in an A1 policy contains the attributes (ueId, groupId, sliceId, qosId, cellId, cellIdList and talList)
defined in A1TD [i.9], clause 6.3.1.1, and also the policy statement contains the policy resources (TspResources,
SliceSlaResources, LbResources, EsResource) defined in A1TD [i.9], clause 6.3.4 which include identification of policy
resources with the attributes commonly used by the ScopeIdentifier (e.g., cellIdList in TspResource, cellIdList/taIList in
SliceSlaResources, cellIdList in LbResources, cellIdList in EsResource).
Applicable entity is an entity which is derived explicitly or implicitly by policy scope, relevant granularity level of O1
observables corresponding to the policy objectives, and possibly by policy resources in a policy for identifying
overlapping scope or overlapping resource between policies. An A1 policy would have at least one applicable entity
type by policy scope and another applicable entity type possibly by policy resource. Based on the A1TD [i.9], clause
7.2, there are several types of A1 policy applicable entity to be derived from allowed combinations of attributes in
ScopeIdentifier for policy types: explicit UE, implicit UE(s), explicit Slice and explicit Cell as shown in Table 6.2.1-1.
As for A1 policy applicable entity derived by policy resource, there is only one type of explicit Cell.

6.3
Detection of conflicting situations
The detection of conflicting situations starts with finding a set of overlapping pairs of policies. Policy scope and/or
policy resource of a requested policy is analysed with policy scope and/or policy resource of an existing policy to detect
an overlapping pair of requested policy and existing policy. This overlap detection process is repeated over all the pairs
of requested and existing policies to arrive at a set of overlapping pairs of policies. According to figure 6.1-1, once
overlaps with policy scope and/or policy resource are detected among A1 policies, it would be evaluated per overlap if
there are any conflicting situations with policy objectives and/or policy resources to finally recognize a set of
overlapping policies as conflicting policies.
6.3.1
Evaluation of conflicting situation for collection of overlaps
As explained in clause 6.2, detection of overlap would be performed on a cell-by-cell basis for simplicity acro

ally recognize a set of
overlapping policies as conflicting policies.
6.3.1
Evaluation of conflicting situation for collection of overlaps
As explained in clause 6.2, detection of overlap would be performed on a cell-by-cell basis for simplicity across all cells
which a Near-RT RIC controls. And the evaluation of conflicting situation would be performed for collection of
detected overlaps.
Given that multiple Near-RT RICs are connected with an SMO/Non-RT RIC, there would be groups of overlaps per
Near-RT RIC which would be divided into groups per cell. An example of grouping of detected overlaps is illustrated in
Figure 6.3.1-1 in which detected overlaps are indexed by p-q-r where p is the index of Near-RT RIC, q the index of cell
and r the index of detected overlap uniquely for that cell, along with corresponding sets of overlapping policies.

Figure 6.3.1- 1: An example of grouping of detected overlaps.
It is noted that there would be cases that the same A1 policy belongs to different detected overlaps concurrently.
Considering the flexibility of related functional placement in the SMO/Non-RT RIC, the uniqueness of complete
information regarding detected conflicts in the SMO/Non-RT RIC would be necessary. For example, in a case where
SMO/Non-RT RIC FW is the producer of A1 policy conflict detection service and an rApp is the consumer of the A1
policy conflict detection service to perform conflict avoidance, information related to a detected conflict needs to be
uniquely conveyed over the R1.
6.3.2
Approach to evaluate conflicting situation.
Possible conflicting situations have been studied in clause 5 Use cases with representative scenarios. There would be
possibly various approaches to evaluate conflicting situation with use of such as the AI/ML or Digital twin, and related
discussion regarding those detailed algorithm would be left for further investigation, however, here it is suggested that
basic approach to evaluate conflicting situation is to check if pairs of policy scope and/or policy resource with overlap
between two policies would meet those A1 policy conflict use cases; UC#1 “reserve” vs “release” policy, UC#2
objectives not uniquely identified, and UC#3 conditions not uniquely identified.
Possible A1 policy conflict use cases could be related into pairs of policy scopes and/or policy resources with a detected
overlap as shown in Figure 6.3.2-1. There would possibly be four pairs of policy scopes and/or policy resources having
an overlap between a requested policy and one of existing policies, and for each of detected overlaps between two
policies, it would be checked if corresponding A1 policy co

would possibly be four pairs of policy scopes and/or policy resources having
an overlap between a requested policy and one of existing policies, and for each of detected overlaps between two
policies, it would be checked if corresponding A1 policy conflict use cases would meet or not. If a requested policy has
at least one conflicting situation to meet those A1 policy conflict use cases for detected overlaps, a set of detected
overlapping policies would be regarded as a set of conflicting policies and the requested policy would be a member of
conflicting policies.

6.4
A1 policy conflict detection service
A1 policy conflict detection service optionally takes A1 policies, for which conflicts need to be detected, as input and
provides overlap information (clause 6.2.4) and information of conflicting situation (clause 6.3.3) for detected sets of

the SMO/Non-RT RIC FW or an rApp.

7 A1 policy conflict avoidance
7.1
General
A1 policy conflict avoidance in SMO/Non-RT RIC aims to prevent the detected conflicts before the A1 policies that
introduce conflicts with one or more existing policies are sent to Near-RT RIC. A potential A1 policy conflict can be
detected by an rApp prior to sending a create or update A1 policy request or by the producer of the A1 policy
management service as part of processing the create or update A1 policy request. An rApp or the producer of A1 policy
management service can detect potential A1 policy conflicts by themselves or by consuming the SMO service/R1
service that has the capability to detect potential A1 policy conflicts. Once a potential conflict detected, rApp or any
other consumer of the A1 policy management services or the producer of the A1 policy management services can
proceed with conflict avoidance by relying on conflict arbitration service.
The conflict arbitration service consumer consumes conflict arbitration service to determine the execution preference
among a set of conflicting policies. Based on this, SMO/Non-RT RIC can further implement conflict avoidance
procedures to prevent the conflicts.
One of the conflict avoidance strategies, among others, could be to reject a request for the creation or update of an A1
policy. Information regarding the conflicts details and the proposals for alternative A1 policies can be conveyed in reject
message. As a follow-up action to the earlier conflict avoidance actions, an rApp can be notified to retry the creation of
the previously rejected policy once the existing A1 policies causing the conflicts are deleted.

7.2
A1 policy conflict arbitration service
A1 policy conflict arbitration service provides A1 policy conflict arbitration rules as set by the operator or outside
customer which then can be used by the consumer of the A1 policy conflict arbitration service to decide among two or
more conflict avoidance actions when there is a potential A1 policy conflict. Similarly, A1 policy conflict arbitration
service can also provide A1 policy conflict arbitration rules as set by the operator or outside customer which then can be
used by the consumer of the A1 policy conflict arbitration service to decide among two or more conflict resolution or
mitigation actions when there is an actual A1 policy conflict. A1 policy conflict arbitration rules help the consumer of
the A1 policy conflict arbitration service to know the execution preference among the conflicting A1 policies. Conflict
arbitration service producer can provide priorities for a set of conflicting policies, the A1 policies with priorities will be
provided as follows:

7.2.2
A1 policy conflict arbitration - Option #2. Priority, Preemption
protection
In Option#2, these A1 Policy conflict arbitration rules indicate the priority, preemption flags, and preemption protection
flags of different policies to the consumer of A1 policy conflict arbitration service. Preemption Flag and Preemption
Protection effectively address the needs of services that require immediate execution or cannot be interrupted once
execution has begun.
Some guidelines for the arbitration rules regarding priority, the preemption flag, and the preemption protection flag are
listed below:
•
Preemption Flag indicate that, when a set of A1 policies conflict is detected, one of an A1 policy with this flag
can pre-empt the execution of another A1 policy.
•
Preempt Protection Flag indicates that when conflict is detected among a set of A1 policies, if one of the A1
policies with this flag is already being enforced, the execution of this A1 policy cannot be pre-empted by
another A1 policy.
•
Priority indicates the execution preference among a set of conflict A1 policies.
Some corner cases may also need to be considered in implementation. For example, both preemption flag and priority
are present. Another example is a conflict is detected when two A1 policies share the same priority.

7.3
Procedures
7.3.1
General
There are different approaches for conflict avoidance.
Approach #1 is that the A1 policy function enforces A1 policies based on arbitration results by requesting rApps to
delete, reject, or update an A1 policy. The A1 policy function implements conflict avoidance actions, such as rejecting a
new create request from an rApp, request the rApp to delete an A1 policy or notifying rApps to update the A1 policy
with proposed alternative A1 policies and conflict details information. In this approach, rApp serves as the lifecycle
management (LCM) owner of A1 policies, while the A1 policy function can propose alternative A1 policies to avoid the
conflicts.
Approach #2 is that send A1 policies with the information of A1 policy priorities and pre-emption information to Near-
RT RIC.
Approach #3 is that SMO/Non-RT RIC provides an alternative set of conflict-free policies based on conflict detection
information and conflict arbitration result.
An example of approaches for policy conflict avoidance in subset/superset overlapping scope is illustrated in Figure
7.3.1-1. In the referred figure, there are two policies (P1, P2) having subset/superset overlapping scope and conflicting
situation. With case.1 as shown in the leftmost of the referred figure, approach1 is applied, exclusively one of the two
policies would be selected to avoid policy conflict based on the arbitration result. In this approach, entities d and e in
case.1-1 of the referred figure would not have applicable policy due to selection of the policy P1 with smaller policy
scope while there are no such entities without applicable policy in case.1-2 of the referred figure with selection of the
policy P2 with bigger policy scope. Wit

7.3.2.2   Notify an rApp to retry
After a former A1 policy creation has been rejected due to conflict or an A1 policy previously causing conflict has been
deleted or updated, and an URI for retry notification had been provided in the A1 policy creation message, the related
rApp can be notified to retry the previously rejected or deleted A1 policy once the existing A1 policies that are causing

do not send an A1 policy at all. In extreme scenarios, there may be more than one previous rejected or deleted A1
policies, rApp can process all these A1 policies after receiving one A1 policy retry notification message.

Recommendations for A1 policy conflict related services
[REC-A1PCRS1]

Recommendations for A1 policy management services
[REC-R1-A1P-FUN1]

an update A1 policy request if the requested policy has a conflict with any of

8.3
Note for recommendations in terms of formulation for A1
policy conflict-related services
Through the A1 policy conflict mitigation SI, we propose to support two A1 policy conflict-related services in the TR
below:
•
A1 policy conflict detection service
•
A1 policy conflict arbitration service

These are surely the A1-related services but not obvious if they should be regarded as part of the A1 policy management
service(s) as defined in Non-RT-RIC-ARCH [i.7], clause 7.4.1 because the A1 policy conflict-related services have
totally new and possibly independent functions from such fundamental ones as the A1 policy management service.
There would be options to formulate the A1 policy conflict-related services:
•
Option.1 A1 policy conflict-related capabilities as part of A1 policy management services
•
Option.2 A1 policy conflict-related service separate from A1 policy management services
•
Option.3 Individual A1 policy conflict detection and A1 policy conflict arbitration services

The formulation of the A1 policy conflict-related services would be an item for further investigation to align with
existing services and other related items like the R1 Services-Related Conflict Mitigation WI.

Annex A:
Compatibility of A1 policy conflict with R1 Service-related
conflict
A.1
General
The A1 policy conflict mitigation TR which has been studied according to WG2 A1 specifications would have
compatible aspects with the R1 Service-related conflict study in case that a set of CM Write(s) over O1 and/or OFH M-
plane interfaces are performed for fulfillment of RAN’s KPI targets. This means there are CM Writes (ex. start-up
configuration, PM collection configuration) not related to configuration changes for any fulfillment of RAN’s KPI
targets and those CM Writes are out of focus in terms of A1 policy conflict compatibility.
As for A1 policy specification, there are explicit RAN’s KPI target definition as policy objectives (as specified in A1TD
[i.9], clause 6.3.3) and policy resources (as specified in A1TD [i.9], clause 6.3.4), and those are based on 3GPP defined
network entities (as specified with ueId, groupId, sliceId, qosId, cellId, cellIdList and talList in A1TD [i.9], clause
6.3.1.1). And an A1 policy is a declarative approach which leaves its implementation to Near-RT RIC.
As for CM Write(s) along with intention of fulfillment of RAN’s KPI targets, it is beneficial to add generalized
objectives which are comparable with A1 policy objectives. And a set of those CM Write(s) is an explicit control
approach which leaves its implementation to rApps.

4 Overview
4.1 Background

The R1 interface is defined between the rApps and the Non-RT RIC framework, as specified in R1GAP [i.6] clause 3
and clause 4 and the R1 interface requirements are specified in R1UCR [i.2] clause 5. R1 Services specified in R1GAP
[i.6] such as SME services, DME services, RAN OAM-related services, AI/ML workflow services, and A1-related
services.
Multiple rApps may be onboarded as specified in Onboarding GAP [i.4] and rApp instances are instantiated on the Non-
RT-RIC. These rApp instances may avail different R1 services as specified in R1GAP[i.6]. As per behavior of an rApp,
multiple rApps can consume RAN OAM-related services to write network function configurations resulting in network
conflicts.
4.2 Concepts
4.2.1 Network Conflict
4.2.1.0 General
A network conflict occurs when two or more R1 service consumers independently invoke R1 services intending to
change one or more network configurations which, if applied, can result in behavior that contradicts the intended
outcome of another service consumer’s request. Such outcome(s) are typically reflected as deviation from the expected
targets such as policy objectives or KPI goals, etc. which the participating R1 service consumer(s) intended to achieve
by proposing their respective configuration changes.
The overall impact on the network behavior can show up as, but not limited to:
•
Coverage holes
•
Capacity issues
•
Overloaded cells
•
Compromised cell-edge performance
•
HO failure/ping-pongs

4.2.1.1 Types of network conflicts
Network conflicts can be broadly classified into the following three categories:
1. Direct conflict: These conflicts can be identified directly by comparing two or more R1 Write configuration
changes requests. When two or more Write configuration changes requests are intended to change the same
attribute of the network configuration; they are considered to be in a direct conflict. These conflicts can be
detected pre-action i.e. before applying the proposed changes to the network.
2. Indirect conflict: These conflicts cannot be identified directly by comparing two or more R1 Write
configuration changes requests. However, there is known dependency between the attributes intended to be
changed using the R1 Write configuration changes requests. A known dependency here refers to an inferable
relationship between the network configuration attributes and the system impact it causes in terms of network
resource(s) or KPI(s) which can be used to detect the conflict. E.g. as per the rApps’ objectives, two rApps can
change different attributes of a given cell to optimize the same KPI. Based on the pre-existing knowledge of
the dependency, these conflicts can be detected pre-action i.e. before applying the proposed changes to the
network or and sometimes post-action i.e. after applying the proposed changes to the network.
3. Implicit conflict: These conflicts cannot be identified directly by comparing two or more R1 Write
configuration changes requests and there is no known dependency between the network configuration
attributes intended to be changed using these requests. Nonetheless, after applying the configurations to the
network, a network behavior can be observed that contradicts with the intended outcome of each of the R1
service consumer’s

network, a network behavior can be observed that contradicts with the intended outcome of each of the R1
service consumer’s request. Therefore, these types of conflicts can mostly be detected post-action. Sometimes,
these conflicts can be detected pre-action by use of simulation such as digital twin, AI based predictions, etc.
4.2.2 Conflict management
To avoid different types of network conflicts, conflict management capabilities need to be defined. A comprehensive
approach to conflict management consists of the basic functionalities of conflict detection, conflict arbitration and conflict
mitigation.
The role of conflict detection functionality is to detect network conflicts between multiple R1 Write configuration changes
requests received from one or more R1 service consumers. Based on the conflict detection logic, it may result in either –
“no conflict” or “conflict”. In case conflict(s) is detected, it is fed as an input to the conflict mitigation functionality.
The role of conflict mitigation is to prevent a detected pre-action conflicts from getting applied in the network. In case of
post-action conflict, the conflict mitigation may provide a guidance back to the R1 service consumer or act on the detected
conflict to revert conflicting configuration and hence nullify the conflict. Conflict mitigation may also provide guidance
to the R1 service consumers which it can use to avoid any future conflicts. These are achieved based on the service
provided by the conflict mitigation functionality.
Conflict arbitration helps in arbitrating the detected conflicts by applying the arbitration rules. The conflict arbitration
rules can be pre-defined b

provided by the conflict mitigation functionality.
Conflict arbitration helps in arbitrating the detected conflicts by applying the arbitration rules. The conflict arbitration
rules can be pre-defined by the operator.
The following primary inputs are required to carry out these functionalities:
1. Records of R1 Write configuration changes requests: R1 Write configuration changes requests containing the
network configuration details (w.r.t MoI instance, attribute(s), value(s)) are the most basic inputs to decide
whether they are in conflict with each other or not.
2. Current network configurations: This is needed so that the baseline network information is available to the
conflict management.

3. Performance management (PM) data from the network: Continuous monitoring of the KPIs and other PM data
is critical for the functioning to the conflict management. This is needed to monitor the effect on the KPIs of
the changes executed in the network by the R1 service consumer.
4. Arbitration rules: Once the conflict(s) is detected, information is required based on which, detected conflicts
may be arbitrated. This information, defined as arbitration rules, is used to indicate which of the Write
configuration changes requests should be further passed on to the network, and which of these requests should
be rejected.
This list is expanded in subsequent section to include some more inputs which are required for the comprehensive
conflict detection, arbitration and mitigation functionalities. However, given the complexity of the network and multiple
factors impacting the network behaviour, there is always a possibility that some network conflicts may not be detected
by the Conflict mitigation.
The potential primary outcomes include:
1. Conflict-resolved R1 Write configuration changes request(s): This is the primary goal of the conflict mitigation
i.e. to select which of the conflicted R1 Write configuration changes requests are executed and which ones are
rejected.
2. Guidance information as feedback to R1 service consumer: One of the secondary goals of the conflict
mitigation is to provide assistance-information to the R1 service consumers, which might help avoid future
conflicts.
3. Bookkeeping information regarding the conflicts: From an operator’s point of view, records of the detected
conflicts and the associated details are valuable to obtain insight into the co-existential behavior of the R1
service consumers. It also sheds light on how a change in an attribute mi

conflicts and the associated details are valuable to obtain insight into the co-existential behavior of the R1
service consumers. It also sheds light on how a change in an attribute might impact certain KPI(s).
4.2.3 Conflict Detection
4.2.3.0 General
Conflict detection functionality provides the service of detecting network conflicts between multiple R1 Write
configuration changes requests received from two or more R1 service consumers. For network conflicts to be detected,
certain minimum conditions need to be satisfied. These are captured in terms of Impact time, Impact map and Impact
scope.
In the following sections, each of these concepts are explained in detail.
4.2.3.1 Impact time
4.2.3.1.0
General
When a configuration change is applied in the network, the effects are not always immediately noticeable. Often the
impact of the changes such as variations in monitored KPIs, metrics or other network state indicator(s) (referred to here
as the observables) take time to become available to Non-RT RIC/SMO framework and finally to the rApps. If a rApp
proposes network configuration using a R1 Write configuration changes request based on previous state of the network
i.e. before these observables are available for it to take into consideration and propose the changes in network
configuration; it may unintentionally create a network conflict. Impact time, therefore, is defined as the minimum time
required for the network changes to have an impact on the network observables.

configurations. Using this as one of the inputs, rApp1 proposes changes to the network configuration at time T1. And

4.2.3.1.1 Determination of the Impact time
This impact time is a crucial input for conflict detection to detect possible network conflicts. The value of impact time
need not be uniform across attributes or across different R1 service types. Therefore, it need not be statically configured.
It can be pre-configured by operators and/or configured dynamically which then can be used for conflict detection. The
following section mentions factors which may be taken into consideration to determine the impact-time. However, it is
up to the implementation on how this value is decided or generated.
The impact time may be determined based on, but not limited to, the following parameters:
•
Time taken by an attribute to impact the network KPI(s): Different attributes may have different time of impact
on different KPIs. Some changes like altering transmission power may have an immediate effect while the
changes like the handover threshold may take more time to change the observables. E.g. impact of attribute-A
on KPI-1 may be immediate whereas impact of attribute-B on the same KPI may be observed only after some
time e.g. 30 mins etc.
•
KPI availability granularity: Once the impacts of the changes on the KPIs or other observables are there, next
dependency is on the frequency at which these updated KPIs or other observables are available to the Non-RT
RIC/SMO framework.  E.g. if the KPI data is collected every 5 minutes, any impact due to the changes
performed may become available only after the 5-minute cycle.
•
An input from the operator or RAN vendor based on the network knowledge: In some cases, based on the
network insights, an operator or RAN vendor may provide thresholds indicating the time duration for specific
configu

only after the 5-minute cycle.
•
An input from the operator or RAN vendor based on the network knowledge: In some cases, based on the
network insights, an operator or RAN vendor may provide thresholds indicating the time duration for specific
configuration(s) changes typically takes to influence the network behaviour.
•
A digital twin simulation: Simulation provided by digital twin of a network can provide the estimated value
based on which impact time may be derived.
•
AI/ML based outcome based on the historical records: ML models can be trained on historical data to predict
the expected latency between configuration changes and the effects on the observables. These models can
dynamically adjust the impact time estimates based on the type of attributes, cell condition etc.
4.2.3.2 Impact Map
4.2.3.2.0
General
Any change in a network configuration can cause a system impact, which can be observed either as a variation in the
network resource utilization and/or in the KPIs. Hence, there exists a relationship between the network attributes and

________________________________________________________________________________________________
13

the corresponding system impact(s) that they can produce. This dependency information, which can be captured in the
form of an Impact Map, can be one of the inputs to detect network conflict(s) between R1 Write configuration changes
requests.

Figure 4.2.3.2.0-4: Attribute A impacting KPI X
Since, there is a wide range of system impacts in terms of network resources or KPIs, it is important to group these in
well-defined categories. E.g. one rApp changes the CIO (Cell Individual offset) value between a cell pair, and another
rApp changes the measurement threshold for the same cells. In such a case, it is critical to identify that both these
attributes change the mobility behaviour in these cells reflected in same or different KPIs related to Mobility. Therefore,
these system impacts could be combined and classified as e.g. Mobility system impact. It is to be noted that, system
impact can also be classified based on which aspects of the network behaviour e.g. cell capacity, cell coverage,
mobility, QoS/QoE etc. are affected when network configuration is applied.  Such inter-related network resources and
inter-related KPIs can be grouped as system impact group. Moreover, each of the individual attribute can map to one or
more system impact from multiple categories of system impact. For example, change in Antenna Tilt attribute can map
to system impact related to Mobility and to the cell coverage.

In summary, the Impact Map consists of mapping of the relationship between the attributes intended to be changed by
R1 service consumer and the various system impact group. This mapping and the usage of it could be implementation
specific and can evolve over time as more observability analysis and operational insights become available to the entity
generating the Impact Map.

For two or more R1 Write configuration changes requests intending to execute changes in the network configurations,
one of the conditions for network conflict to be detected can be that the attributes being modified by multiple R1 Write
configuration changes requests map to at least one common system impact group. If the targeted attributes do not map
to a common system impact group, then the likelihood of a conflict is significantly reduced. The figure below illustrates
a change in attributes driven by two different rApps mapping to the same system impact group.

4.2.3.2.1 Determination of the Impact Map
The initial mapping between the network attributes and the system impact groups can be pre-configured by operator. It
can then be dynamically updated which then can be used for the conflict detection. This information can be derived
using established RAN domain knowledge. For example, changes in cell-individual offset impacting mobility behaviour
or scheduling configurations impacting throughput are well-understood relationships in the RAN domain.
An implementation to prepare an Impact Map can use different inputs listed below:
1. Input from the operators or RAN vendor: RAN vendor or operators can provide the mapping based on the
network knowledge and network behaviours of the impacted KPIs derived from operational experience, field
data, trace data etc.
2. Simulators (e.g. Digital twin): Simulation of the network can provide outputs based on which the system
Impact Mapping can be dynamically adjusted. The simulations can also be used to identify the significance of
the impact.
3. AI/ML model-based prediction: ML models can be trained on historical data to predict the impact on the KPIs
or network resources based on the changes in network configuration. These models can dynamically adjust the
system Impact Map estimates based on based on cell conditions and traffic behavior etc. and predict the level
of impact.
4. KPI monitoring: Continuous monitoring of KPI trends can help to detect emerging relationships between the
attributes changes and system impacts, especially for non-obvious impacts.

4.2.3.3 Impact Scope
4.2.3.3.0
General
A system-impact caused by the changes in network configuration is not limited to a single cell. Based on the attribute
being changed, the end nodes they affect can vary. An attribute being changed can potentially have a system impact on,
but not limited to:
•
the serving cell whose configuration parameter has changed
•
a specific neighbour of the cell whose configuration parameter has changed
•
neighbours with an overlapping coverage with the cell whose configuration parameter has changed
•
the cells in a cell- cluster

3. AI/ML model-based prediction: ML models can be trained on historical data to predict the Impact Scope.
These models can dynamically adjust the Impact Scope estimates based on based on cell conditions and
traffic behavior etc. and predict the level of impact.
4. KPI monitoring: Continuous monitoring of KPI trends can help to update attribute to scope relationships.
4.2.3.4
Network KPIs
4.2.3.4.0
General
In the context of network conflict detection, all the conflicts may not be detectable by applying the concepts of
overlapping Impact Map and Impact Scope. Implicit conflicts, as defined in clause 4.2.1, can arise when changes made
by different R1 service consumers create a network conflic

ction, all the conflicts may not be detectable by applying the concepts of
overlapping Impact Map and Impact Scope. Implicit conflicts, as defined in clause 4.2.1, can arise when changes made
by different R1 service consumers create a network conflict even if the changed attribute(s) do not map to a common
system impact in an Impact Map and a Impact Scope. These changes, when applied to the network, can result in
unintended degradation in the network performance which might contradict the objective of R1 service consumer(s),

________________________________________________________________________________________________
19

thereby resulting in an implicit network conflict. Therefore, some additional information, other than Impact Time,
Impact Map and Impact Scope, is required for the detection of implicit conflicts.
KPI trends and analysis can fill this gap and facilitate the detection of implicit conflicts. While both the direct and the
indirect conflicts can be detected based on overlapping Impact Map and Impact Scope, implicit conflicts can be inferred
by observing the actual and/or the simulated variations in the KPIs over a period of time.
Consider an example with two rApps, rApp1 and rApp2 which propose changes in attributes A and B to improve the
KPIs KPI-1 and KPI-2 at time T1 and T2 respectively. Attributes A and B do not map to any common system Impact
Map and Impact Scope and therefore, no pre-action conflict (direct or indirect conflict) is detected.  Hence both the
changes are applied to the network, as shown in the figure below. However, after certain configurable duration,
consistent degradation is observed in KPI-1. Using this information, implicit conflict can possibly be detected between
changes performed by rApp1 and rApp2.

Figure 4.2.3.4.0-10: Usage of KPIs in post-action implicit conflict detection
However, since the detection of implicit conflicts is complex in nature and dependent on post-action KPI analysis,
further studies are required to define appropriate thresholds, durations, and validation criteria for the KPIs. It must be
noted that the KPI analysis and trends are subject to the fluctuating network conditions, and therefore, the detection
based on a single instance of aberrant KPI behavior is not sufficient for accurate detection.

4.2.3.4.1
Determination of Network KPIs
The way in which the KPI information is used to detect the implicit conflicts can be implementation specific. However,
the analysis and trends based on KPIs can be derived based on, but not limited to, the following:
1. KPIs indicated by R1 service consumer: This includes the relevant KPIs which are sensitive to the changes
performed by the rApps. In essence, these KPIs reflect the objectives of the rApps.
2. Critical system performance KPI list: This includes a list of KPIs which are indicative of baseline system
performance indicators. For e.g. cell availability, number of RRC Connected UEs, Handover KPIs, DL/UL
PRB Utilization etc.
3. KPI observation duration: The observation duration to indicate how long the KPI data should be collected for
to decide if there is a degradation.

________________________________________________________________________________________________
20

4. Deviation thresholds: Defines the thresholds for the various KPIs, above/below which, the trend of the
monitored KPI can be considered to be aberrant. These thresholds can be configured statically or dynamically.
Moreover, the thresholds can be derived based on AIML model output.

4.2.3.4.2
Additional outcome of KPI analysis
As a result of the KPI analysis, previously unknown dependencies might come to light. Therefore, KPI trend can play a
role in continuously improving the accuracy of the Impact Map and Impact Scope. Using this information, new conflicts
can be detected in the future by applying the criteria of overlapping Impact Time, Impact Map and Impact Scope.
Considering the above example, when degradation in a KPI1 (e.g., a 10% drop sustained over time) is observed
following the change in the configuration of attribute B, then this could indicate a relationship between the KPI1 and
the attribute B, even if this relationship is not captured in the existing Impact Map. If this behaviour is observed to be
consistent, then the Impact Map can be revised to reflect this newly observed relationship. However, such enhancements
must be carefully analysed to avoid reacting to transient anomalies.
Moreover, in the case of indirect conflicts, it is possible that an existing dependency is preventing rApps from reaching
certain KPI targets. And on examining the KPI trends, it can be chosen to fine tune/remove an earlier captured
dependency in the Impact Map or Impact Scope. Therefore, the output from KPI analysis can be used both for adding to
or removing relationships from the existing Impact Map and/or Impact Scope.
4.2.3.5
Other inputs
4.2.3.5.0
General
In addition to already introduced inputs in the previous clauses such as the Impact Parameters (refer to clause 4.2.3.1-
4.2.3.3) and Network KPIs (refer to clause 4.2.3.4), further input(s) may be required by the Conflict detection functionality.
Some of them are outlined below.
4.2.3.5.1
Network information
To ensure that the Impact parameters reflect the current network conditions, additional info

to clause 4.2.3.4), further input(s) may be required by the Conflict detection functionality.
Some of them are outlined below.
4.2.3.5.1
Network information
To ensure that the Impact parameters reflect the current network conditions, additional information may be needed. For
example, to identify the overlap of impact scope, Conflict detection needs to be aware of the current network layout. To
illustrate this further, consider that an rApp performs changes in Tx-power in Cell-A. For the attribute Tx-power, as

network KPIs (refer to clause 4.2.3). This network information can be provided as an input or can be derived using the
neighbour relationship table information or can be implementation specific.

5 Use Cases
5.1 Overview
There could be multiple sources of network conflicts arising due to the R1 service invocation performed by R1 service
consumers. There are several sources of conflicts including, but not limited to:
•
One or more R1 service consumers may propose conflicting RAN OAM CM Write configuration changes
•
One or more R1 service consumers may propose conflicting A1 policy related operations
•
One or more R1 service consumers may propose a RAN OAM CM Write configuration change which conflicts
with a proposed A1 policy related operation.

As part of this TR, conflicts arising due to one or more R1 service consumers proposing conflicting Write configuration
changes request is covered.
5.2 Use case #1: Conflicts between Write configuration changes
requests
5.2.1 Overview
The R1 service consumers can send Write configuration changes requests over the R1 interface. These configuration
changes are applied to the nodes terminating the O1 interface or Open Front Haul M-Plane interface.

The configuration changes requested by the R1 service consumers may result in a conflict with changes with previously
applied by another R1 service consumer.

Network conflicts for this use case can be broadly divided into three types – Direct conflicts, Indirect conflicts, and
Implicit conflicts. Based on the types of conflicts that may arise from the proposed changes with Write configuration
changes requests, different types of solutions may be required to address these conflicts.

To handle the detected conflicts, one possible approach is to use operator configured rules to arbitrate conflicting Write
configuration requests as mentioned in clause 4.2.2. Another solution can be the rApp checks for conflicts even before
sending Write configuration request(s) towards SMO/Non-RT RIC framework. Moreover, rApp(s) can also use the
conflicts information detected in the network and utilize the conflict related information.

5.2.2 Direct Conflicts
5.2.2.1 Description
Direct conflicts can be observed directly by comparing the parameters in a Write configuration changes request. It could
result when two or more R1 service consumers request different settings for the very same configuration of one or more
attributes.
It could also occur when a new Write configuration changes request from an R1 service consumer conflicts with the
current configuration resulting from a previous request of another or the same R1 service consumer. These conflicts can
be detected before applying the changes i.e. at pre-action stage.

5.2.2.2 Some representative scenarios
One rApp for Mobility Load Balancing (MLB) rApp and another rApp for Mobility Robustness Optimization (MRO)
rApp both recommend changes to the CM Write Configuration parameter of Cell Individual Offset (CIO) between the
same pair of O1 terminating nodes.
5.2.3 Indirect Conflicts
5.2.3.1 Description
These conflicts cannot be observed directly, nevertheless, some dependence among the parameters and resources that
the R1 service consumers target can be observed. For instance, different R1 service consumers target different attributes
to optimize the same metric according to their objectives. One example of such indirect conflicts can occur when the
changes required by one R1 service consumer create a system impact which conflicts with that of another parameter
change targeted by another R1 service consumer. These conflicts can be detected before applying the changes i.e. pre-
action stage e.g. by analyzing the parameters in the change request with dependent parameters.
NOTE: It is for further study how to identify the "dependent parameters", current usage of this term is only to
identify different use cases (in this case indirect conflict) relevant for R1 service-related conflict
detection.
5.2.3.2 Some representative scenarios
One rApp changing the antenna tilts and another rApp which changing the measurement offsets affects different CM
Write Configuration parameters, but they both end up impacting the handover boundary.
5.2.4 Implicit Conflicts
5.2.4.1 Description
These conflicts cannot be observed directly as the dependency between the parameters changed by R1 service
consumers is not obvious. For instance, different R1 service consumers may optimize different metrics and
(re-)configure different attributes. Nonetheless, optimizing

be observed directly as the dependency between the parameters changed by R1 service
consumers is not obvious. For instance, different R1 service consumers may optimize different metrics and
(re-)configure different attributes. Nonetheless, optimizing one metric may have implicit, unwanted, and maybe
adversary side effects on one of the metrics optimized by another R1 service consumer. These conflicts can only be
detected after the changes are applied i.e. post-action based on, but not limited to, performance monitoring etc.
Implicit conflict detection requires consideration of multiple factors such as the number of occurrences, correlation of
parameter changes along with detailed analysis of impacted KPIs as mentioned in clause 4.2.3.4. When such impacts
are observed repeatedly and coincide with changes made by two or more R1 service consumers, an implicit conflict can
be inferred. Moreover, repeated classification of such cases contributes to improving the mapping of impact parameters
thereby enabling the conflict detection algorithm to detect such conflict prior to applying the network configuration
changes in the network.
5.2.4.2  Some representative scenarios
One rApp may recommend changes to protect the throughput metrics of GBR users, and it may end up causing conflicts
which may unintentionally degrade non-GBR metrics or even cell throughput.
5.3
Key issues
Following are some key issues related to Conflict detection which have been identified and should be addressed to
fulfill the use-case defined in clause 5.2.

•
KeyIssue1: Detection of network conflict before applying the Write configuration changes requests in the
network.
•
KeyIssue2: Detection of network conflict after applying Write configuration changes requests in the network.
•
KeyIssue3: An authorized consumer (including rApps) requesting detection of possible conflicts for a Write
configuration changes request before sending the Write configuration changes request SMO/Non-RT RIC
FWK.
•
KeyIssue4: An authorized consumer (including rApps) can obtain the information about already detected
network conflicts.
Following are some key issues related to handling of the detected conflicts to fulfil the use-case defined in clause 5.2.
•
KeyIssue5: Avoidance of detected direct or indirect network conflicts when none of the received Write
configuration changes requests have been applied in the network.
•
KeyIssue6: Avoidance of detected direct and indirect network conflicts when one or more Write configuration
changes requests have already been applied in the network.
•
KeyIssue7: Handling of the detected implicit network conflict when all the Write configuration changes
requests have already been applied in the network.

5.4.2
Potential solutions for KeyIssue2
5.4.2.1
Overview
KeyIssue2 addresses the detection of implicit conflict which may arise after two or more requested configuration
changes have been applied to the network. To detect such conflicts after the changes have been applied to the network,
information is needed about their resultant impact. One possible way to identify the impact is by monitoring the
Network KPIs periodically and analysing the trend. The configured Network KPIs are considered to be within an
acceptable range, if the KPIs remain within the configured thresholds during a specified observation duration (refer
clause 4.2.3.4 KPI observation duration).
If the KPIs degradation is observed within this observation window and if more than one R1 service consumers have
applied Write configuration change requests within this same observation window, such instance can be flagged for
further analysis. Repeated occurrence of such flagged behaviour can be considered as an implicit conflict; however, the
number of occurrences required to confirm an implicit conflict can be implementation specific.
Once conflict is detected, conflict details can be notified back to R1 service consumers subscribing to the detected
implicit conflicts. Conflict details can contain attributes, time of change and network element being modified by the
conflicting Write config change requests. If monitoring the Network KPIs is used to detect the implicit conflict, details
about KPIs degraded can be part of the conflict details.
There can be different approaches to realize this solution.
