7
TOSCA data model of the ASD
7.1
General concept of using TOSCA to model the ASD
The ASD shall be written as a TOSCA YAML service template using the grammar specified in TOSCA Simple Profile in
YAML v1.3 [4].
However, only a limited set of the TOSCA modelling entities and grammar features specified in [4] are supported in an O-
RAN compliant ASD. Clause 7.2 lists entities and features excluded from the ASD.
Clauses 7.3, 7.4 and 7.5 specifies O-RAN data types, artifact types and node types to be used in an ASD. These clauses also
list the keynames that shall, may or shall not be included in the vendor specific node template and artifact definitions.
Definition of additional, vendor specific, types, is not supported.
Annex A contains the formal, machine readable, YAML definitions of the data types, artifact types and node types specified in
clauses 7.3, 7.4 and 7.5. The Annex A is considered the source of truth. Thus, in case of any discrepancy between the
definitions in clauses 7.3-7.5 and the YAML definitions in the annex A, the latter ones take precedence.
Clause 7.6 specifies the structure of the TOSCA ASD service template, detailing which elements it consists of and whether
they are mandatory or optional.

7.2
Restrictions in the use of TOSCA for the ASD model
The file with the TOSCA specification of the ASD is called a service template. The service template is the
DeploymentDescriptor in figure 6.1-2.  It contains a “topology template” as its main component. As described in [4] the
topology template is a TOSCA construct that represents a graph of the node templates modeling the components a workload is
made up of and the relationships between them.
The ASD topology template consists of one single node template that contains one or several artifacts. The artifacts are the
DeploymentItem and the ExecutableImageItem in figure 6.1-2. The structure of the topology template and the complete service
template is described in clause 7.6. All other entities and features available in the TOSCA language are not supported in the
ASD. In particular, the following features are excluded:
•
Requirements, capabilities and relationships
•
Groups
•
Policies (events, triggers, conditions, actions, etc)
•
Interfaces (operations, notifications, scripts, etc.)
•
Workflows
•
Template substitution (substitution mappings)
•
Functions
•
Inputs/Outputs
•
dsl_definitions (definition of reusable macros for use throughout the service template)
•
Attributes
•
Node filter

The above list is not intended to be exhaustive. Clause 7.6 determines what TOSCA elements are used.

7.6
ASD TOSCA service template

The ASD of a specific application is written in a YAML file which is called TOSCA service template in TOSCA terminology.
The service template shall contain the following elements in this order:
1. A ‘tosca_definitions_version’ key-value pair indicating the applicable version of the TOSCA specification, which is
tosca_simple_yaml_1_3 in this version of the ASD specification.

tosca_definitions_version: tosca_simple_yaml_1_3

27

2. Optionally a description of the content of the service template as a key-value pair, i.e. the key ‘description’ followed
by colon and a string of text:

description: This ASD is …

3. An import statement referencing the TOSCA type definitions file containing the standard O-RAN ASD type
definitions specified in Annex A.

imports:
- oran_asd_types_v02.00.00

The file containing the standard O-RAN ASD type definitions shall not be included in the package delivered by the
solution provider. If it is included it shall be ignored. This is in order to avoid intended or unintended modifications in
the standard types. The file with the standard type definitions is assumed to be well known and its location accessible
to the entity processing the ASD service template.
4. A topology template
In turn, the topology template shall consist of:
4.1
The key ‘topology_template’ followed by colon
4.2
Optionally a description as a key-value pair , i.e. the key ‘description’ followed by colon and a string of text
4.3
The key ‘node_templates’ followed by colon
Both the ‘description’ key, if present’, and the ‘node_templates’ key shall be indented with respect to the
‘topology_template’ key.  It is recommended to use two-space indentation.
4.4
A node template definition of type tosca.nodes.asd.Asd
The node template definition shall be indented with respect to the ‘node_templates’ key.

The node template definition shall include at least one artifact definition of type
tosca.artifacts.asd.DeploymentItem and may contain one or more artifact definitions of type
tosca.artifacts.asd.ExecutableImageItem.

4.2 Degree of Openness

In theory, every architecture component could be open in every sense imaginable, but in practice it is likely that different
479
components will have varying degrees of openness due to economic and other implementation considerations.  Some

might not be viable in an outdoor deployment.
482
Increasing degrees of openness for an O-RAN Physical Network Function or O-RAN Cloudified Network Function(s)
483
are:
484
A. Interfaces among Network Functions are open, e.g., E2, F1, and Open Fronthaul are used. Therefore, Network
485
Functions in different O-RAN Physical NFs/clouds from different vendors can interconnect.
486
B. In addition to having open connections as described above, the chassis of servers in a cloud are open and can
487
accept blades/sleds from multiple vendors.  However, the blades/sleds have RAN software that is not decoupled
488
from the hardware.
489
C. In addition to having open connections and an open chassis, a specific blade/sled uses software that is decoupled
490
from the hardware.  In this scenario, the software could be from one supplier, the blade/sled could be from another,
491
and the chassis could be from another.
492
Categories A and B have O-RAN Physical NFs/clouds, while Category C is an open solution that we are calling an O-

Cloud and is subject to the cloudification discussion and requirements.

4.4 O-Cloud Multi-Site Networking
722

For disaggregated O-RAN deployments, the Network Functions (VNFs/ CNFS) may be deployed in multiple O-
723
Clouds or O-Cloud sites. These sites or O-Clouds are generally interconnected via Transport Networks.
724

O-RAN.WG6.CADS-v08.01 TR

21

725
For these disaggregated NFs to communicate with each other, end-to-end connectivity needs to be established, which
726
includes networking within O-Cloud site and as well Transport Network as shown in the figure below.
727
Figure 4.4-1: Logical view of multi-site connectivity through Transport Network
728
O-Cloud Site Network connects the NFs to the O-Cloud Gateway. If an O-Cloud site has a site fabric, this connectivity
729
is achieved through the fabric. This connectivity is local within O-Cloud site. However, the connectivity between the O-
730
Cloud Gateway and Transport Network Element (TNE) (a.k.a. Transport Endpoint) needs to be established to achieve
731
end-to-end connectivity.
732
O-Cloud and Transport Network Shared Connectivity Information
733
O-Cloud and Transport Networks generally belong to different administrative domains and are orchestrated
734
independently; hence a mechanism is needed to orchestrate the connectivity between the O-Cloud Gateway and the
735
Transport Network Element.
736

737
The subnet between the O-Cloud gateway and the TNE needs to be configured with appropriate Identifiers (such as VLAN
738
ID, subnet CIDR, Getaway IP). These identifiers must match on both sides of the administrative domains to achieve
739
successful configuration of the subnet. Hence, an appropriate mechanism is needed so that these identifiers can be
740
exchanged to allow each side independently to configure their side of the subnet.
741

742
Depending upon the deployment scenarios, the operators may make the choice as to which domain will manage the
743
selection and allocation of these identifiers. For instance, if O-Cloud is the manager for the allocation of these identifiers,
744
it will first configure the O-Cloud gateway port connecting to the TNE. These identifiers are then passed to the Transport
745
Network domain to configure the TNE port that connects to the O-Cloud gateway.
746
Conversely, if Transport Network Domain is the manager for allocation of these identifiers, the TNE is configured first
747
and then the identifiers are passed to the O-Cloud.
748
5 Deployment Scenarios:  Common Considerations
749
In any implementation of logical network functionality, decisions need to be made regarding which logical functions are
750
mapped to which Cloud Platforms, and therefore which functions are to be co-located with other logical functions.  In
751
this document we do not prescribe one specific implementation, but we do understand that in order to establish agreements
752
and requirements, the manner in which the Network Functions are mapped to the same or different Cloud Platforms must
753
be considered.
754
We refer to each specific mapping as a “deployment scenario”.  In this section, we examine the deployment scenarios that
755
are receiving the most consideration.  Then we will select the one or ones that should be the focus of initial scenario
756
reference design efforts.

5.1 Mapping Logical Functionality to Physical Implementations
758
There are many aspects that need to be considered when deciding to implement logical functions in distinct O-Clouds.
759
Some aspects have to do with fundamental technical constraints and economic considerations, while others have to do
760
with the nature of the services that are being offered.
761
Technical Constraints that Affect Hardware Implementations
762
Below are some factors that will affect the cost of implementations and can drive a carrier to require separation of or
763
combining of different logical functions.
764
•
Environment:  Equipment may be deployed in indoor controlled environments (e.g., Central Offices), semi-
765
controlled environments (e.g., cabinets with fans and heaters), and exposed environments (e.g., Radio Units on
766
a tower).  In general, the less controlled the environment, the more difficult and expensive the equipment will
767
be.  The required temperature range is a key design factor and can drive higher power requirements.
768
•
Dimensions:  The physical dimensions can also drive deployment constraints – e.g., the need to fit into a tight
769
cabinet, or to be placed safely on a tower or pole.
770
•
Transport technology:  The transport technology used for Fronthaul, Midhaul, and Backhaul is often fiber,
771
which has an extremely low and acceptable loss rate.  However, there are options other than fiber, in particular
772
wireless/ microwave, where the potential for data loss must be considered.  This will be discussed further in the
773
next section.
774
•
Acceleration Hardware:  The need for acceleration hardware can be driven by the need to meet basic
775
performance requirements but can also be tied to some of the above considerations.  For example, a hardware
77

chunks.text:
rther in the
773
next section.
774
•
Acceleration Hardware:  The need for acceleration hardware can be driven by the need to meet basic
775
performance requirements but can also be tied to some of the above considerations.  For example, a hardware
776
acceleration chip (COTS or proprietary) can result in lower power use, less generated heat, and smaller physical
777
dimensions than if acceleration is not used.  On the other hand, some types of hardware acceleration chips might
778
not be “hardened” (i.e., they might only operate properly in a restricted environment) and could require a more
779
controlled environment such as in a central office.
780
The acceleration hardware most often referred to includes:
781
•
Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs)
782
•
Graphical Processing Units (GPUs)
783
•
System on Chip (SoC)
784
•
Standardized Hardware:  Use of standardized hardware designs and standardized form factors can have
785
advantages such as helping to reduce operations complexity, e.g., when an operator makes periodic technology
786
upgrades of selected components.  An example would be to use an Open Compute Project (OCP) or Open
787
Telecom IT Infrastructure (OTII) –based design.
788
Service Requirements that Affect Implementation Design
789
RANs can serve a wide range of services and customer requirements, and each market can drive some unique
790
requirements.  Some examples are below.
791
•
Indoor or outdoor deployment:  Indoor deployments (e.g., in a public venue like a sports stadium, train station,
792
shopping mall, etc.) often enjoy a controlled environment for all elements, including the Radio Units.  This can
793
improve the economics of some indoor deployment scenarios.  The distance between Network Functions tends
794
to be much lower, and the devices th

chunks.text:
l, etc.) often enjoy a controlled environment for all elements, including the Radio Units.  This can
793
improve the economics of some indoor deployment scenarios.  The distance between Network Functions tends
794
to be much lower, and the devices that support O-RU functionality may be much easier and cheaper to install
795
and maintain. This can affect the density of certain deployments, and the frequency that certain scenarios are
796
deployed.
797
•
Bands supported, and Macro cell vs. Small cell:  The choice of bands (e.g., Sub-6 GHz vs. mmWave) might
798
be driven by whether the target customers are mobile vs. fixed, and whether a clear line of sight to the customer
799
is available or is needed. The bands to be supported will of course affect O-RU design.  In addition, because
800
mmWave carriers can support much higher channel width (e.g., 400 MHz vs. 20 MHz), mmWave deployments
801
can require a great deal more O-DU and O-CU processing power.  And of course, the operations costs of
802
deploying Macro cells vs. Small cells differ in other ways.
803
•
Performance requirements of the Application / Network Slice:  Ultimately, user applications drive
804
performance requirements, and RANs are expected to support a very wide range of applications.  For example,
805
the delay requirements to support a Connected Car application using Ultra Reliable Low Latency
806

O-RAN.WG6.CADS-v08.01 TR

23

Communications (URLLC) will be more demanding than the delay requirements for other types of applications.
807
In our discussion of 5G, we can start by considering requirements separately for URLLC, enhanced Mobile
808
Broadband (eMBB), and massive Machine Type Communications (mMTC).
809
The consideration of performance requirements is a primary one and is the subject of Section 5.2.
810
Rationalization of Centralizing O-DU Functionality
811
Almost all Scenarios to be discussed in this document involve a degree of centralization of O-DU.  In this section it is
812
assumed that O-DU resources for a set of O-RUs are centralized at the same location.
813
Editor’s Note:  While most Scenarios also centralize O-CU-CP, O-CU-UP, and near-RT RIC in one form or
814
another, the benefits of centralizing them are not discussed in this section.
815
Managing O-DU in equipment at individual cell sites (via on-site BBUs today) has multiple challenges, including:
816
•
If changes are needed at a site (e.g., adding radio carriers), then adding equipment is a coarse-grained activity –
817
i.e., one cannot generally just add “another 1/5 of a box”, if that is all that is needed.  Adding the minimum
818
increment of additional capacity might result in poor utilization and thereby prevent expansion at that site.
819
•
Cell sites are in many separate locations, and each requires establishment and maintenance of an acceptable
820
environment for the equipment.  In turn this requires separate visits for any physical operations.
821
•
Micro sites tend to have much lower average utilization than macro sites, but each can experience considerable
822
peaks.
823
•
“Planned obsolescence” occurs, due to ongoing evolution of smartphone capabilities and throughput
824
improvements, as well as introducti

d to have much lower average utilization than macro sites, but each can experience considerable
822
peaks.
823
•
“Planned obsolescence” occurs, due to ongoing evolution of smartphone capabilities and throughput
824
improvements, as well as introduction of new features and services.  It is common practice today to upgrade
825
(“forklift replace”) BBUs every 36-60 months.
826
These factors motivate the centralization of resources where possible.  For the O-DU function, we can think of two types
827
of centralization: simple centralization and pooled centralization.
828
If the equipment uses O-DU centralization in an Edge Cloud, at any given hour an O-RU will be using a single specific
829
O-DU resource that is assigned to it (e.g., via Kubernetes).  On a broad time scale, traffic from any cell site can be
830
rehomed, without any physical work, to use other/additional resources that are available at that Edge Cloud location.  This
831
would likely be done infrequently, e.g., about as often as cell sites are expanded.
832
Centralization can have some additional benefits, such as only having to maintain a single large controlled environment
833
for many cell sites rather than creating and maintaining many distributed locations that might be less controlled (e.g.,
834
outside cabinets or huts).  Capacity can be added at the central site and assigned to cell sites as needed.  Note that simple
835
centralization still assigns each O-RU to a single O-DU resource1, as shown below, and that traffic from one O-RU is not
836
split into subsets that could be assigned to different O-DUs.  Also note that a Fronthaul Gateway (FHGW)/Fronthaul
837
Multiplexer (FHM) may exist between the cell site and the centralized resources, not only to improve economics but also
838
to enable traffic

subsets that could be assigned to different O-DUs.  Also note that a Fronthaul Gateway (FHGW)/Fronthaul
837
Multiplexer (FHM) may exist between the cell site and the centralized resources, not only to improve economics but also
838
to enable traffic re-routing when desired.
839

840
Figure 12:  Simple Centralization of O-DU Resources
841

1 In this figure, each O-DU block can be thought of as a unit of server resources that includes a hardware accelerator, a GPP, memory and any other
associated hardware.

O-RAN.WG6.CADS-v08.01 TR

24

By comparison, with pooled centralization, traffic from an O-RU (or subsets of the O-RU’s traffic) can be assigned more
842
dynamically to any of several shared O-DU resources.  So, if one cell site is mostly idle and another experiences high
843
traffic demand, the traffic can be routed to the appropriate O-DU resources in the shared pool.  The total resources of this
844
shared pool can be smaller than resources of distributed locations, because the peak of the sum of the traffic will be
845
markedly lower than the sum of the individual cell site traffic peaks.
846

847
Figure 13:  Pooling of Centralized O-DU Resources
848
We note that being able to share/ O-DU resources somewhat dynamically is expected to be a solvable problem, although
849
we understand that it is by no means a trivial problem.  There are management considerations, among others.  There may
850
be incremental steps toward true shared pooling, where rehoming of O-RUs to different O-DUs can be performed more
851
dynamically, based on traffic conditions.
852
It is noted that O-DU centralization benefits the densest networks where several cell sites are within the O-RU to O-DU
853
latency limits.  Sparsely populated areas most probably will be addressed by vO-CU centralization only.
854
Figure 14 shows the results of an analysis of a simulated greenfield deployment as an attempt to visualize the relative
855
merit of simple centralization of O-DU (“oDU”) vs. pooled centralization of O-DU (“poDU”) vs. legacy DU (“BBU”),
856
plotted against the realizable Cell Site pool size.
857

858
Figure 14:  Comparison of Merit of Centralization Options vs. Number of Cell Sites in a Pool

An often-used measure is related to the power required to support a given number of carrier MHz.  The lower the power

As stated in Section 4.3.2, an O-Cloud Node is a collection of CPUs, Memory, Storage, NICs, BIOSes, BMCs, etc., and

1005

1006

1007

Accelerator Deployment Model
1022
Figure 16 above presents two common hardware accelerator deployment models as examples: an abstracted
1023
implementation utilizing a vhost_user and virtIO type deployment, and a pass-through model using SR-IOV. While the
1024
abstracted model allows a full decoupling of the Network Function (NF) from the hardware accelerator, this model may

1028
To allow multiple NF vendors to utilize a given accelerator through its Acceleration Abstraction Layer (AAL) interface,
1029
the accelerators must provide an open-sourced API. Likewise, this API shall allow NFs applications to discover,
1030
configure, select and use (one or more) acceleration functions provided by a given accelerator on the cloud platform.
1031
Moreover, this API shall also support different offload architectures including look aside, inline and any combination of
1032
both. Examples of open APIs include DPDK’s CryptoDev, EthDev, EventDev, and Base Band Device (BBDEV).

When delivering an NF to an Operator, it is assumed that the supplier of that Network Function will provide not only the

5.6 Operations and Maintenance Considerations
1444
Management of cloudified RAN Network Functions introduces some new management considerations, because the
1445
mapping between Network Functionality and physical hardware can be done in multiple ways, depending on the Scenario
1446
that is chosen.  Thus, management of aspects that are related to physical aspects rather than logical aspects need to be
1447
designed with flexibility in mind from the start.  For example, logging of physical functions, scale out actions, and
1448
survivability considerations are affected.
1449
The O-RAN Alliance has defined key fundamentals of the OAM framework (see [8] and [9], and refer to Figure 1). Given
1450
the number of deployment scenario options and possible variations of O-RAN Managed Functions (MFs) being mapped
1451
into Managed Elements (MEs) in different ways, it is important for all MEs to support a consistent level of visibility and
1452
control of their contained Managed Functions to the Service Management & Orchestration Framework.  This consistency
1453
will be enabled by support of the common OAM Interface Specification [9] for Fault Configuration Accounting
1454
Performance Security (FCAPS) and Life Cycle Management (LCM) functionality, and a common Information Modelling
1455
Framework that will provide underlying information models used for the MEs and MFs in a particular deployment.
1456
The O1 Interface
1457
As described in [8], the O1 is an interface between management entities in Service Management and Orchestration
1458
Framework and O-RAN managed elements, for operation and management, by which FCAPS management, Software
1459
management, File management shall be achieved.
1460

1464
deploying and managing cloud infrastructure.

1466

316
As Figure 2-1 shows, deployment of a cloud platform occurs in two locations: regional and edge clouds. The physical
317
environment of a regional cloud is typically a modern data center, hosting standard server racks with a 19-inch wide rack
318
enclosure, 42U height, and external depth between 1 and 1.2 meters. In this environment, the cloud platform hardware
319
can use standard rack-mount servers and switches, and does not impose special requirements on the hardware form factors.

321
floor loading, and so forth. The limitations can impose special requirements on the cloud platform hardware that may
322
require telecommunications standard certifications, such as the Network Equipment Building System (NEBS)
323
requirements found in GR-63-CORE [3] and GR-1089-CORE [4]. For example, the Open Telecom IT Infrastructure
324
(OTII) Project specifies a 2U rack server with depth less than 450 mm [5][3]. In addition, the Open Compute Project
325
(OCP) operates an openEDGE project [6], which specifies a compact cloud platform that has the extended environmental
326
requirements often needed in edge deployments.

Hardware Acceleration Abstraction Layer Requirements
503
The Acceleration Abstraction Layer (AAL) provides a set of APIs to VNF/CNF software for offloading certain functions
504
that, for instance, are compute- and power-intensive, to hardware accelerators supported on the O-Cloud platform. The
505
objective of the AAL is to hide the different implementations of hardware accelerators and present APIs to VNF/CNF
506
applications to enable portability and software-and-hardware decoupling. Full listing of the functions that can be offloaded
507
through the AAL is outside the scope of this document.
508
Generic Requirements
509
Extensibility
510
O-RAN has defined the functions that can be accelerated by the cloud platform based on 3GPP specifications and O-RAN
511
deployment scenarios. However, the AAL API should not limit innovation of future implementations and should evolve
512
as the specification requires. In this way, the API shall be extensible to accommodate future revisions of the specification.

Look-aside Acceleration Model
531
The API shall support look-aside acceleration model where the host CPU invokes an accelerator for data processing and
532
receives the result after processing is complete. A look-aside architecture, illustrated in Figure 4-7, allows the application
533
to offload work to a hardware accelerator and continue to perform other work in parallel—this could be to continue to
534
execute other software tasks in parallel or to sleep and wait for the accelerator hardware to complete. This model requires
535
the API to support two operations, one for initiating the offload and another for retrieving the operation once complete.

Inline Acceleration Model
539
The API shall support inline acceleration model where acceleration by function and I/O-based acceleration are performed
540
on the physical interface as the packet ingresses/egresses the platform. Figure 4-8 shows one possible implementation of
541
an inline acceleration model.
542

543
Figure 4-8. AAL inline acceleration model.
544
In Figure 4-8, a “Func” block refers to some algorithmic function that is accelerated in the device before the data egresses
545
or ingresses from the acceleration device. “Tx” refers to the transmission of the data from the acceleration device to an
546
Ethernet interface, while ‘Rx’ refers to the reception of data from the Ethernet interface to the acceleration device.
547
While the look-aside architecture shall support dataflow from the CPU to the accelerator and back to the CPU before
548
being sent to the front-haul interface, the inline architecture shall support data flow from the CPU to the accelerator and
549
directly from the accelerator to the front-haul interface, instead of being sent back to the CPU. The typical data flows for
550
accelerating the O-DU high-PHY functions for the look-aside and inline architectures are as follows.
551
Look-aside architecture dataflow
552
CPU ↔ accelerator ↔ CPU ↔ front-haul: for a set of consecutive PHY functions offload (e.g., FEC)
553
CPU ↔ accelerator ↔ CPU ↔ accelerator ↔…↔ CPU ↔ front-haul: for a set of non-consecutive PHY functions offload
554
Inline architecture dataflow
555
CPU ↔ accelerator ↔ front-haul: for a set of consecutive PHY functions offload (up to the end of the PHY pipeline)
556
Figure 4-9 illustrates one possible implementation of the look-aside and inline architectures. While a set of PHY-layer
557
functions are offloaded to the accelerator hardware for look-aside acceleration, the entire end-to-end high PHY pipeline
558
is offloaded to the accelerator for inline acceleration.

Cloud Platform Software Reference Design
639
This section shows an example reference design for the regional and edge cloud platform software. A single installable
640
package supporting various profiles of the platform software runs in both the regional and edge clouds, and can adjust to
641
the different physical environments and scale requirements. As mentioned in Chapter 2, this document focuses on a
642
container-based cloud platform design and will address VM-based designs in a future release.
643
Kubernetes is a common implementation for container orchestration and management. Platform infrastructure
644
management and additional components, such as Kubernetes plugins, must be added for hosting accelerated O-DU and
645
O-CU network functions.
646
The regional and edge cloud platform requirements also differ based on the network functions they host. Generally, the
647
edge cloud platform requirements are a superset of the functional requirements of the regional cloud platform. The primary
648
differences relate to hardware acceleration features, real-time Linux, precision time protocol and server node scalability
649
down to a single node for cell-site deployments.

Time Synchronization Reference Design
677
Figure 5-7 illustrates an example of the redundant synchronization network for an edge site aligned with the requirements.
678
The O-RUs are expected to be connected to the same leaf-spine fabric, and as such the O-Cloud network is considered to
679
also be part of the fronthaul network.
680

681
Figure 5-7. Key synchronization chain elements in an example implementation in O-Cloud for LLS-C3.
682

683
The salient features of this design example are:
684

The synchronization reference sources (PRTC/T-GM) are redundant and located in the edge cloud. In this
685
example, the references are derived from the GNSS system, but any other implementation compliant with the
686
CUS specification [2] requirements (and references therein), which acts as G.8275.1 T-GM, is acceptable.
687

The synchronization reference sources are connected to the leaf-spine fabric with redundant Ethernet
688
interconnects. Specifically, each grandmaster connects to at least two leaf switches.
689

For larger site configurations (i.e. in which the switch capacity and port count requirements exceed the capabilities
690
of the single physical switch), the structure is expanded in a “leaf-spine” fabric configuration, as illustrated in [2].
691
For most edge site configurations, it is expected that a two-tier structure is sufficient, which implies that the
692
maximum length of any active synchronization transfer path from co-located sources is three boundary clocks
693
between the grandmaster and any node in the edge cloud. Therefore, the synchronization path “length” in terms
694
of number of boundary clocks that needs to be supportable in this configuration is typically from one to three.
695
Capability to support more nodes in the path is desirable to allow for configurations where the grandmasters are
696
not co-located at the edge cloud.
697

________________________________________________________________________________________________
Your use is subject to the terms of the O-RAN Adopter License Agreement in the Annex ZZZ.

39
O-RAN.WG6.CLOUD-REF-v02.00 TS

All edge O-Cloud nodes are attached to at least two physically separated, independent leaf switches to provide
698
network redundancy and tolerance against a single point of failure that can affect more than one node (i.e. switch
699
failures). In addition to normal network fault tolerance, this is also useful for maintaining the synchronization
700
network fault tolerance.
701

702
Many alternative variations and physical realizations of the above design are possible (e.g. PRTCs/GMs can be combined
703
with switches or routers, leaf-spine structure can be integrated onto physical box, sizes of elements can vary, etc.), but
704
functionally with respect to the synchronization transfer chain, all of the entities are expected to be present (i.e. PRTC/T-
705
GMs, Telecom Boundary Clock nodes, as well Telecom subordinate Clock nodes).
706
For this design example, the O-DU synchronization performance requirements as specified in the CUS specification [2]
707
for the O-DU LLS-C3 configuration expected to be met with the following set of elements in the synchronization transfer
708
path:
709

T-GM A and T-GM B clocks with performance class ITU-T G.8272 PRTC/T-GM type PRTC-B serving as
710
grandmasters for O-DUs as well as O-RUs (O-DUs require PRTC-A or better while O-RUs require PRTC-B)
711

The Fronthaul Leafs acting as T-BCs in both the O-RU and O-DU synchronization path, with support for a
712
minimum performance class ITU-T G.8273.2 T-BC Class B (Class C is recommended);
713

The Spine and O-Cloud Leaf switches acting as T-BCs in the O-DU synchronization path only, with the least
714
demanding T-BC performance class ITU-T G.8273.2 T-BC Class A or better;
715

T-TSC implementation on the O-Cloud nodes with the least demanding performance class ITU-T G.8273.2,
716
Annex C, T-TSC Class A or better.
717

718

Chapter 2 Introduction
87
This document describes a REST API that allows Event Consumers (EC) such as a vO-DU or CNF to subscribe to
88
events/status from the O-Cloud.  The cloud infrastructure will provide Event Producers (EP) to enable cloud workloads
89
to receive events/status that might be known only to the infrastructure.
90
An EC will use the REST API to subscribe to specific event types or categories of events by specifying the event /
91
status producer address.   The addressing scheme is covered in Resource Addressing.  An EC will be able to
92
unsubscribe from receiving events and status by deleting the subscription through the REST API.  The REST API is an
93
integration point to an event and status framework that is running in the underlying O-Cloud (IMS and/or DMS).
94
The REST API and associated event framework implementation is intended to be used in situations where the path from
95
event detection to event consumption must have the lowest possible latency.  Intra-node delivery of events is a primary
96
focus with inter-node delivery also supported.
97
The event framework described here is not intended to be an island of communication and should interact with north-
98
bound interfaces such as O2 through the IMS. Hence, this Event Consumers API is not intended to replace O2ims
99
notifications (including PTP loss of sync), but rather to complement it. Please see the CAD [6] for more information.
100
Interfacing with external entities is necessary for communication with orchestrating entities and for permanent storage
101
of event information for root-cause analysis.  Communication with external entities is intended to be in one direction
102
with events flowing from this framework outward.  The flow of events from this framework to external entities m

ent storage
101
of event information for root-cause analysis.  Communication with external entities is intended to be in one direction
102
with events flowing from this framework outward.  The flow of events from this framework to external entities must not
103
affect the latency performance of the framework for intra-node or inter-node delivery.
104
Please note that while this API document describes an interface to general events and status provided by the cloud
105
infrastructure, the discussions and examples in this document will focus on events and status related to PTP /
106
Synchronization as it this is the first defined use case that affects the vO-DU per the CUSP [5] requirements.
107
“If an O-DU transits to the FREERUN state, the O-DU shall disable RF transmission on all connected O-RUs, and
108
keep it turned off until synchronization is reacquired.”
109
“Whether in ‘synchronized’ or ‘Holdover’ state, it is expected that O-DU monitors the ‘SYNCED/HOLDOVER’ status
110
of the O-RUs under its management.”
111
Please note that the timing requirements for notification regarding FREERUN should follow WG4 guidelines when
112
available in the CUSP document. These guidelines may influence the future evolution and design of this API. Please see
113
the CUSP [5] for more information.
114

115
Subscription/Publication use case:
116
-
Subscription by the Event Consumer (e.g. vO-DU or other CNF) triggers the readiness of the Event Consumer
117
to receive the notifications.
118
-
The REST API handler implementation, provided by the Cloud infrastructure, resides in the application
119
(workload) and is an application appropriate implementation of a REST API handler.
120
-
Upon subscription, the EC will receive an initial notification of the EP resource status. For example, the
121
current synchronization status of the PTP system will be sent to the EC when subscribing to the sync-status
122
address. Or as another example, the current interface carrier status will be sent to the EC when subscribing to
123
the interface-status address.  This initial notification allows the joining application to synchronize to the current
124
status of the system being observed.
125
-
Event Consumers will be able to subscribe to resource status notifications offered by the cloud.
126
-
Multiple Event Consumers in the same container, Pod, or VM can subscribe to events and status as the REST
127
API allows multiple receive endpoint URI.
128
-
If the eventing framework cannot provide the requested subscription the eventing framework will deny the
129
subscription request and Event Consumer (vO-DU, vO-CU etc) will be able to make a decision if to proceed
130
with its operation

4.2
Test method
4.2.1 Objective
O-Cloud IOT test focus on verifying the functional correctness between device peers. Performance test and security test
are not in the scope.
To validate the functionality of production grade DUTs, it is important that the DUTs are not negatively impacted with
the utilization of internal functions, so the Device in production environment should not be used for test.
The DUTs are used as black boxes for positive testing, negative testing, abnormal testing, etc.

4.2.2 Testing Tools and set-up
Interoperability tests are performed with a set of testing tools which are used to both apply active stimulus and as well as
monitoring and measurements of the DUTs. Non-DUT devices or corresponding emulation tools can be used as active
stimulus during the test. Passive monitoring and measurement tools can be used to watch the status of DUTs, collect the
information exchanges, and capture the logs during the test.
There is no constrain on the number of DUTs, but there shall be at least one for each DUT. DUTs shall be connected by
corresponding interface before the test.
For each test is differ from others, the suggested tools and the set-up are be detailed in the corresponding configuration
section of each test.

4.2.3
Testing procedure
In adherence to the specifications, the System Under Test (SUT) and the test tool are meticulously configured and
connected to the device, strictly following the predefined conditions for each test case.
The test steps outlined in the test case are executed sequentially.
The tester is responsible for diligently documenting crucial test information during and after the testing process, enabling

________________________________________________________________________________________________
11
detailed comparisons and analyses against the expected outcomes.
It is crucial to note that each test case remains independent of one another.

4.2.4
Statistics and analysis of key indicators
The test execution adheres to the predefined conditions and procedures specified in the test case.
During the testing process, the tester may capture and record test result, including success or failure, along with
corresponding metric data, such as throughput, latency, and device volume.
The expected test results serve as the benchmark for evaluating the test success. If the actual test results align with the
expected outcomes, the test is considered successful.

5
Notification API IOT
5.1
General
The main objective is to test the interoperability of different vendors' O-CU/O-DU with O-Cloud using notification-
related APIs. This includes both push and pull modes for event notifications.
As stated in Section 4.1, the SUT (System Under Test) for the Notification IOT test includes components such as O-Cloud
and O-CU/O-DU/SMO.
Each IOT test case offers a test purpose, test entrance criteria, initialization conditions, test procedure, and expected
results.
The main test scenarios covered are as follows:
1) Functional test of O-Cloud and O-CU/O-DU using notification subscription, query, deletion and event notification
API.
2) Functional test of O-Cloud and O-CU/O-DU using notification pull API.

5.2
Test Configuration
5.2.1
System Under Test requirements
As shown in 5.2-1, the System Under Test (SUT) for the O-Cloud Notification IOT test consists of individual O-CU or
O-DU components, along with the O-Cloud, which provides the notification framework. The notification framework
includes an API producer; O-CU/O-DU act as consumers. O-Cloud, serving as an event generator, provides APIs to
consumers for utilizing these events. These APIs can be used for subscribing to events, unsubscribing, querying
subscriptions, and communicating with consumers using pull/push modes.
At least one O-CU/O-DU and one O-Cloud is required for this test. O-CU/O-DU and O-Cloud are connected through
network, and O-CU/O-DU is configured with the endpoint of notification API for the communication.
Additionally, O-Cloud may need to support traffic mirroring for Protocol Analyzer to capture the requests and responses
for analysing.

5.3
Test Cases
5.3.1
Push mode event notification
5.3.1.1
Test Purpose
The purpose of this test case is to confirm that O-CU/O-DU, irrespective of the vendor, can manage the subscription
resource and receive event notifications from O-Cloud.
This test is conditional mandatory; for push mode, this case applies.
5.3.1.2
Test Entrance Criteria
1)
DUTs: O-CU/O-DU and O-Cloud.
2)
CU/O-DU supports push mode Event Notification.
3)
O-Cloud supports push mode Event Notification.

5.3.1.3
Initial conditions
1)
Protocol Analyzer has started.
2)
Configure the O-Cloud or the network between the O-CU/O-DU and O-Cloud so that Protocol Analyzer can capture
the messages between DUTs, as needed.
3)
Activate the Protocol Analyzer to capture and decode Notification API message flows between the DUTs.

5.3.1.4
Procedure
Step 1. Initiate a subscription procedure of the event notifications from O-CU/O-DU.
Step 2. Initiate a query procedure from O-CU/O-DU, to get the list of subscription resources, check the output.

________________________________________________________________________________________________
13
Step 3. Initiate a query procedure from O-CU/O-DU, to get a specific subscription resource, check the output.
Step 4. Trigger a subscribed event.
Step 5. Initiate a delete procedure from O-CU/O-DU, to delete a specific subscription resource, check the output.
Step 6. Check the message flow recorded by Protocol Analyzer for interoperability verification.

Example of how those procedures can be performed (or triggered) are listed below. The exact method to perform (or
trigger) this procedure is out of scope of this specification and is left up to the implementation of the DUTs:
a.
O&M command in O-CU/O-DU to enable the subscription, query and deletion, for Step 1, 2, 3, 5, or to trig an
event for Step 4.
b. Reboot/restart O-CU/O-DU if O-CU/O-DU subscribes the notification automatically, for Step 1.
c.
Change the Synchronization status of the compute node if O-CU/O-DU subscribes the Synchronization Event,
for Step 4.

5.3.1.5
Expected Results
Successful completion of the test steps with interoperable communication between O-CU/O-DU and O-Cloud with the
output as expected.
Examine the message flow specified in O-RAN.O-Cloud Notification API [3] Section 4 and 5:
In Step 1, a POST request from O-CU/O-DU to O-Cloud and a response from O-Cloud to O-CU/O-DU shall be present
and be followed with a sanity check of the notification endpoint if communication to the notification endpoint is
successful.
In Step 2, 3 and 5, a Get request and a response shall be present.
In Step 4, a notification of the event to O-CU/O-DU from O-Cloud shall be present.

Chapter 2. General Aspects
1
2.1 Introduction to O2
2
The O2 interface is an open logical interface within O-RAN architecture providing secured communication between the
3
SMO and O-Cloud. It enables the management of O-Cloud infrastructures and the deployment life cycle management of
4
O-RAN cloudified NFs that run on O-Cloud. The O2 interface is defined in an extensible way that enables new
5
information or functions to be added without necessarily needing to change the protocol or the procedures. This interface
6
enables a multi-vendor environment and is independent of specific implementations of the SMO and O-Cloud.
7
2.2 Alignment with O-RAN Architecture
8
This section provides any added detail not found in the high-level O-RAN architecture documents which define and
9
describe the O2 interface. The intent is to extend knowledge and not to redefine existing information. Therefore, if a
10
conflict exists between this document and the O-RAN Architecture Description [2] or the O-RAN OAM Architecture [3]
11
the information presented will not supersede those documents.
12
2.2.1 Alignment with Overall Architecture
13
This document adopts the architecture as described in the O-RAN Architecture Description [2]. The O2 is described as
14
the interface between the SMO and the O-Cloud to provide platform resources and workload management.
15
The O-Cloud needs to be created before the SMO can interface with it.
16
O-Cloud can consist of multiple Deployment Management Services. Each DMS can manage leased resources from
17
multiple resource pools and span multiple locations. There is a single IMS for O-Cloud that manages all resources of
18
DMSes as well as resources that are not allocated to any DMS in the O-Cloud. Diagram below depicts relations

DMSes as well as resources that are not allocated to any DMS in the O-Cloud. Diagram below depicts relationship
19
between SMO and components of O-Cloud.
20

21

23

24

Chapter 3. O2 Interface General Principles
1
This section describes the general approach to solving common problems with managing a cloud and the deployments
2
which execute on it.
3
3.1 O-Clouds
4
O-RAN clouds are described in [5] as a distributed cloud composed of O-Cloud [Resource] Pools (as shown as white
5
clouds in the diagram below) where each pool is a collection of O-Cloud Nodes at a specific location. An O-Cloud Node
6
is the basic computational resource designator and can be commonly thought of as a server. An Operator may have several
7
O-Clouds from different vendors but will manage them as a single entity. These O-Clouds are viewed by the Service
8
Management and Orchestration (SMO) Framework as a Federated O-Cloud.
9
O-Cloud Nodes are provisioned into resources which are assigned for a specific use by the O-Cloud Management
10
Software according to a blueprint. As a general concept the cloud is divided into three planes, however the control and
11
management plane described below may be merged or use common tools and therefore may act as or be one plane.
12
•
Management Plane: O-Cloud Nodes in this plane host the software which is responsible for managing the O-
13
Cloud
14
•
Control Plane: O-Cloud Nodes in this plane are responsible for hosting the software which manages the resources
15
assigned in the deployment plane to specific deployment instances
16
•
Deployment Plane: O-Cloud Nodes in this plane are used to host "Service Model" Deployments
17

18
Figure 3.1-1 O-Cloud Planes
19

O-RAN.WG6.O2-GA&P-v01.02 TS
3.2 O-Cloud Inventory
1
From the perspective of the SMO, O-Cloud Inventory consists of the physical infrastructure used to create the O-Cloud,
2
the logical clouds which it provides as interfaces for deployments, and the inventory of deployments using the logical
3
cloud. The SMO is responsible for financial accounting of physical inventory. The SMO inquires about the mapping of
4
resources to their use. The O-Cloud is responsible for the assignment of resources to their use.
5
3.2.1 Infrastructure Inventory
6
Infrastructure inventory is passed between the SMO and the O-Cloud over the O2ims. An O-Cloud Node Identifier is
7
used to correlate the inventory. This identifier needs to be discoverable by the O-Cloud and would likely be on an invoice
8
for the O-Cloud purchase order. The O-Cloud Node Identifier must be immutable.
9
The IMS will add O-Cloud Nodes to the relevant O-Cloud Resource Pools when they are powered on and ready to be
10
provisioned as a resource. The IMS then allocates them to a plane according to its policies and sends the O-Cloud Node
11
characteristics to the SMO.
12
The SMO receives O-Cloud Node startup events and updates its inventory accordingly. The O-Cloud Node Identifier is
13
matched with invoice data in order to provide financial asset tracking requirements. The location and use identifiers are
14
used to track inventory which will be monitored as part of cloud service assurance assurance.
15

16
Figure 3.2-1 O-Cloud Infrastructure Inventory
17
3.2.2 Logical Inventory
18
The SMO will need to know the composition of an ME in terms of its MFs as described in the O-RAN OAM Architecture
19
[3]. This cannot be derived from the deployments and therefore is not addressed by the O2 interface. This data should be
20
contained in the ME configuration and should be collected over the O1 interface [4].
21
The O-Cloud itself must have one or more DMS available within its distributed footprint. These could be based on virtual
22
technologies (Kubernetes/Docker, Open Stack, etc.) used, and/or O-Cloud pool locations. Each DMS endpoint provides
23
an O2dms interface and is inventoried by the SMO as a logical cloud. The logical cloud is used by the SMO in order to
24
select the O-Cloud to be used for a deployment during the cloud selection process.
25

3.2.3 Deployment Inventory
3
Although the cloud could support IaaS and PaaS deployments, most O-RAN MEs are composed of SaaS deployments as
4
defined by NIST [9].  The Deployment Descriptor is a set of metadata contained in a datatype matching a capability
5
advertised by the O-Cloud. Logical Cloud selection in the NFO will match the descriptor type with the capability type to
6
enable deployment. The Deployment Descriptor will cause one or more cloud resources to be allocated (VMs, Pods,
7
Containers, Networks) but will return a single correlation ID, referred to here as the Deployment ID. The O-Cloud will
8
provide, over the O2dms, the ability to fetch the details of these objects from their Deployment ID.
9
3.3 O-Cloud Monitoring Service
10
When the O-Cloud Infrastructure or the ORAN cloudified NFs fails, it needs to be fixed immediately, and preferably
11
automatically, to prevent end users from experiencing service disruptions. To avoid this service disruption Network
12
Operations must consider the telemetry information of O-Cloud deployments in the network. The telemetry information
13
serves as a vital resource for analysing the O-Cloud’s state and health, and for delivering on service monitoring goals.
14
The O-Cloud Monitoring Service uses telemetry data to provide monitoring of O-Cloud infrastructures. The telemetry
15
data is provided by Deployments and Infrastructure and is correlated to reduce duplication of effort in determining the
16
root cause in the network.
17
There are different types of telemetry, Managed Element Telemetry, Deployment Telemetry, and Infrastructure
18
Telemetry.
19
1. For Managed Element Telemetry, the objective is to monitor the application behaviour. This will be addressed
20
in the O1 Specification

ferent types of telemetry, Managed Element Telemetry, Deployment Telemetry, and Infrastructure
18
Telemetry.
19
1. For Managed Element Telemetry, the objective is to monitor the application behaviour. This will be addressed
20
in the O1 Specification [4].
21
2. For Deployment Telemetry, the objective is to monitor the number of deployment instances an O-Cloud has at
22
that moment and how many were expected, how the on-progress deployment is going, and health checks.
23
Additional Deployment Telemetry metrics like CPU, network, and memory usage can also be collected. This
24
will be addressed in the O2 Specification.
25
3. For Infrastructure Telemetry, the objective is to monitor the health of the O-Cloud Infrastructure components.
26
Network Operations are interested in discovering if all the components in the O-Cloud Infrastructure are working
27
properly and at what capacity, how many deployments are running on each node, and the resource utilization of
28
the O-Cloud Infrastructure. This will be addressed in the O2 Specification.
29

3.4.1 Affinity, Anti-Affinity, Quorum Diversity Rules
22
An Affinity rule specifies that deployments with the same rule applied must be collocated within the same scope. This
23
can be applied to a single server or a server group. Anti-Affinity is the opposite of the Affinity Rule in that deployments
24
with the same rule applied cannot be collocated within the same scope. Affinity and Anti-Affinity rules can be applicable
25
to entities outside of the current deployment such as Tenant or Namespace.
26
A Quorum diversity rule stipulates that deployments with this rule can be collocated if less than 50% of th

ame scope. Affinity and Anti-Affinity rules can be applicable
25
to entities outside of the current deployment such as Tenant or Namespace.
26
A Quorum diversity rule stipulates that deployments with this rule can be collocated if less than 50% of the deployments
27
exist within the same scope. This rule can only be enforced when there is a minimum of 3 deployments. In which it will
28
be the same deployment assignment as Anti-Affinity. In scenarios with more than 3 deployments a minimum of 3 different
29
resource assignments at the specified scope (Server or Server Group) will be used. More can be used at the discretion of
30
the O-Cloud Resource Scheduler.

34

The following basic concepts are considered for IMS & DMS fault management:

3.5.2.1
Fault Information Model
1
A fault information model is expected to be developed in the O2ims information model. As a general concept, an
2

3
group of actors. It facilitates communications between groups and aligns their contributions. The fault information
4

3.5.2.2
Subscription
6
It is expected that there will be a subscription mechanism between a client and an agent. The client would pass an
7

8

9

10
For example, the concept of a subscription allows a client, such as the SMO, to register for call-backs to the O-Cloud to
11
receive fault notifications.
12
3.5.2.3
Notifications
13
Fault notifications originate from the O-cloud infrastructure. There is a relationship between the subscription and
14
notification. When a condition occurs within the IMS that warrants a fault notification an event is issued towards clients
15
that have subscribed to receive such a type of notification or event.
16
For example, a user could receive alerts on a fault dashboard GUI based on cloud IMS fault notifications.
17
3.5.2.4
Parallel Reporting
18
A fault occurrence on an O-Cloud resource should be reported through IMS. DMS resource faults are associated with a
19
workload. It is possible that multiple resources can associate with a workload, whereby one fault might trigger a fault
20
notificat

fault occurrence on an O-Cloud resource should be reported through IMS. DMS resource faults are associated with a
19
workload. It is possible that multiple resources can associate with a workload, whereby one fault might trigger a fault
20
notification on IMS, DMS and O1. Due to the nature of the subscribe/notify mechanism for fault reporting, it is possible
21
to: (1) have multiple publishers sending to a single consumer and (2) conversely a single publisher that can send to
22
multiple consumers. The interfaces for subscription & notification of fault reporting are: O2ims, O2dms, O1.
23
For example, it is conceivable that a vDU application might report a fault on O1, and a related physical server allocated
24
to a workload of a vDU would raise a DMS fault which might also have an infrastructure fault raised on IMS.
25
3.5.2.5
Simple Devices
26
Collectively, in the O-Cloud it is conceivable that many devices are simple devices that do not have a full suite of OAM
27
S/W.
28
For example, suppose a network interface card (NIC) is a resource that is a simple device, and if that NIC encounters a
29
fault it might not be able to register, store, or log faults. It is expected that O-Cloud infrastructure could manage  these
30
kinds of simple devices to be able to fulfill some of the other basic fault concepts described in this section. The O-Cloud
31
infrastructure works with the IMS to report these faults.

3.5.2.6
Source of Truth
33
In an O-Cloud IMS context, it is expected that the “source of truth” will be the resources of the O-Cloud itself. When a
34
fault which has been reported to a client, such as the SMO, the fault data is replicated within the fault notification to
35
provide details and information of the fault. Thus, the fault information now exists in multip

the O-Cloud itself. When a
34
fault which has been reported to a client, such as the SMO, the fault data is replicated within the fault notification to
35
provide details and information of the fault. Thus, the fault information now exists in multiple places both in the IMS
36
and the entity receiving the fault notification. Which element then has the “true” information should the network or
37
elements be disconnected or faulty? After connectivity returns, how would the SMO reconcile its view of the existing
38
fault against the current faults on the O-Cloud resource? The answer is to query the source of truth (O-Cloud resource)
39
for the most current faults.
40
For example, if a resource in the O-Cloud goes out of service, and it had previously sent a fault notification, and then
41
later returns to service, potentially the information at the client and the O-Cloud resource may have different fault
42
information. But the O-Cloud resource is the source of truth and it is expected that client (IMS) would query the O-

1
A fault dictionary is a reference that can be provided by an O-Cloud vendor which details the faults that can be emitted
2
from O-Cloud resources. The fault dictionary defines conditions that could be reported by the O-Cloud so that the SMO
3

4

5
For example, the fault dictionary could be used for a variety of purposes. It might help a user decode the meaning of a
6

7
which may constitute a condition which requires a coordinated response.

3.5.2.8
Queries
9
In the IMS case, the SMO (client) can issue a specific fault query towards to IMS (publisher) related to the O-Cloud
10
resources and resource pool. In the SMO to DMS case, the SMO (client) can issue a specific query related to xApp/NF
11
deployments (e.g. workloads) from the DMS (publisher). In the IMS case, a fault query is a message which is expecting
12
a response message from the IMSwhich matches the selection criteria. In the DMS case, the fault query is expecting a
13
response from the DMS.
14
For example, the client may request status of a specific type of fault, or new active alarms conditions. The O-Cloud
15
resource would reply to the query by responding with databased on the parameters of the query (e.g. IDs or severity).

3.5.2.9
Filtering
17
It is expected that the client, such as the SMO, can query for specific kinds of faults or groups of faults through a filter.
18
In addition, filtering can also beapplied to subscriptions to determine if notifications should be set

Filtering
17
It is expected that the client, such as the SMO, can query for specific kinds of faults or groups of faults through a filter.
18
In addition, filtering can also beapplied to subscriptions to determine if notifications should be set.
19
For example, it might request from the O-Cloud all the major severity alarms from a particular O-Cloud resource. The
20
O-Cloud would select records based on the query pattern and send the details according to the notifications. This
21
concept will guide the IMS information model development of procedures that can support filtering.

3.5.2.10 Fault Logging
23
Fault logging may be part of the general event logging and is a concept where faults are stored at the O-Cloud resource
24
(the source of truth) for a configured amount of time. IMS provisioning should be able to configure the amount of time
25
that logs stored for. The concept of fault logging and storing faults allows a client, algorithm, or user to query for the
26
fault log and analyze those faults. The faults should be timestamped with a common time format and clock source.
27
Faults that are intermittent, repetitive, or transient can be identified this way. For example, Debug traces used by some
28
O-cloud providers might be a way to facilitate fault logging meaning that certain condition can trigger writing to the
29
fault log.
30
For example, fault from an O-Cloud resource could be stored in a log for 1 week.
31
3.5.2.11 Alarm Synchronization
32
There are many potential situations where a client and source of truth might become disconnected or disrupted. In this
33
case, the client will need to synchronize with the source of truth after it is able to reconnect.
34
For example, network fault might prevent communication between the SMO (client) and IMS res

truth might become disconnected or disrupted. In this
33
case, the client will need to synchronize with the source of truth after it is able to reconnect.
34
For example, network fault might prevent communication between the SMO (client) and IMS resources in the O-Cloud.
35
By the time connectivity has been restored, many new alarm conditions might have arisen and logged. This would
36
motivate the SMO to resynchronize to get the current alarms again. A variety of mechanisms might be used to trigger
37
alarm resynchronization. It might also trigger an upload of the most recent fault logs.
38
3.5.2.12 Alarm Correlation
39
In Concept #4 with Parallel Reporting, it might be possible that a fault condition might result in a variety of different
40
conditions or be reported in any combination of IMS, DMS and O1 fault notifications. It is not the job of the O-Cloud
41
IMS fault management to correlate faults between the application/NF and O-Cloud resources. Thus, it would be up to
42
higher layers of fault management to correlate disparate fault events to identify common root causes.

3.5.2.13 Escalation Strategy
6
Fault conditions in an IMS resource may trigger an escalation strategy. An escalation strategy is a mechanism to
7
increase visibility to a condition of duress which is typically a precursor to a more severe situation.
8
For example, recurring alarms, fault signatures and severity levels may have an escalation strategy to raise higher
9
severity alarms for higher tier recovery actions. As another example, a minor alarm in an O-Cloud resource with a
10
certain occurrence rate within a time window might trigger an escalation strategy to raise a major alarm.
11
3.5.2.14 Fault Domains
12
A fault domain is a “unit of failure”. A fault domain associates a collection of IMS O-Cloud resources together. We
13
expect a fault domain to be within a Data Center Zone (see the provisioning chapter basic concepts for more detail).
14
Faults could be associated with a fault domain. In the context of IMS fault area, fault domains are an attribute that could
15
be correlative but do not have intrinsic fault operations, they are not a manageable entity.
16
This would allow operators to design systems that are fault tolerant across fault domains. This might also guide
17
placement strategies, and update cycles to improve reliability and availability.
18
For example, a network cloud can host some number of servers per rack (e.g. 40 servers) with a number of racks of
19
equipment (e.g. 10 racks) in a single deployment (totaling 400 servers). A fault domain might be defined to be rack. If a
20
fault occurred, this concept would allow an operator trying to isolate the problem down to a rack (the fault domain). It
21
would also allow a user to correlate a problem if multiple racks served by a common infrastruc

be defined to be rack. If a
20
fault occurred, this concept would allow an operator trying to isolate the problem down to a rack (the fault domain). It
21
would also allow a user to correlate a problem if multiple racks served by a common infrastructure resource.

3.5.2.15 Fault Tolerance
3
A fault tolerant system is one that is designed to withstand failures and continue to be able to provide service. Based on
4
observations, some actions can be taken to insure reliability. Fault tolerant solutions & strategies will vary between O-
5
Cloud providers and network function providers.
6
An example of a fault tolerant strategy is the use of geo-redundancy and Data Center Zones. Geographically separating
7
Data Center Zones allows service to continue should a physical natural disaster strike one data center. An action might
8
be to migrate traffic from one zone to another.
9
3.5.2.16 Metrics
10
Metrics allow users to define thresholds to monitor and manage IMS O-Cloud resources. From these metrics, a
11
user/system could take action based on threshold crossings and/or chart the metrics over time. Also, to achieve fault
12
tolerance, there could be a mechanism for alerting, monitoring & auditing as a health check.
13
For example, in the basic fault concept of Escalation Strategies, we might need metrics of how often a fault occurs
14
within a certain period of time. These metrics might be used as a threshold in an escalation strategy for better reliability.
15
If the fault occurred 100 times in an hour action might be taken.

3.5.3 O-Cloud Performance Basic Concepts
17
The following section describes basic concepts for O2 Performance Concepts.
18
In general, the purpose of performance is to report operational information related to O-cloud resources. Typically,
19
performance information allows an operator or administrator of the O-cloud a sense of how well the system is
20
operating. It is distinct from faults in that it is not about failures in the system but about how well the overall syst

es. Typically,
19
performance information allows an operator or administrator of the O-cloud a sense of how well the system is
20
operating. It is distinct from faults in that it is not about failures in the system but about how well the overall system is
21
performing. Though, faults or alarms may negatively impact performance of the O-Cloud which might be observable in
22
performance measurements.
23
Performance measurements are typically captured periodically through time. They are collected and stored at regular
24
intervals by the system in order to gauge the performance of a system over a period of time. This allows for analytical
25
operations to be performed on the collected data and statistics to be built over time. This can tell an operator or system

modeling.

3.5.3.1
O-Cloud Performance Measurements
7
Measurements are defined as the act of quantitatively checking the O-Cloud resources for defined gauges of operation.
8
A measurement is an individual quantitative gauge of a quality.
9
For example, the O-Cloud might measure the computational performance of an O-Cloud compute resource in terms of
10
CPU utilization.
11
3.5.3.2
Performance Indicators
12
Performance indicators take execution measurements and use them in a way that can give a meaningful notion of how a
13
system is utilizing its resources and/or how well a system is operating. Indicators might be local in the sense of a
14
function or more broader in scope for a group of functions. Performance indicators are typically a formula-driven
15
application usage of performance measurements. Thus, the indicators are amenable to statistical analysis. The indicator
16
formula needs to be exposed so that users can understand the meaning of the indicator. Indicators use a measurement, or
17
gauge, to show an aspect of a thing. Key Performance Indicators (KPI) are performance indicators that are typically
18
used to detect and report overall network health.
19
For example, the CPU utilization might be a performance measurement. A performance indicator might be the fraction
20
of time that a system is over a threshold, such as 80% CPU utilization. This would be a simple ratio calculation that
21
could give a sense of how close to being overloaded a system is.
22
3.5.3.3
Performance Metric
23
A performance metric represents standards of measurements. Metrics might be pre-defined, or they might define
24
performance threshold targets to try to achieve. Metrics may utilize measurements and indicators. Performance metrics
25
could b

Performance Reports
3
Performance reports are a collection of measurements. Usually, they are gathered in a file; however, they may also be
4
sent as a data stream. Typically, reports are created at regular (configurable) intervals or triggered by thresholds. The

creation of performance reports may also be manually invoked.

For example, The O-Cloud might compose a performance report which is comprised of several performance

Performance Management (PM) Job
9
A performance management job is a task whose purpose is to collect measurements, creating a measurement file, and
10
get a performance report according to criteria set by the user. The criteria could be used to specify measurements to
11
collect. Note: 3GPP standards also discuss measurement jobs see references, 3GPP TS28.550, TS28.531. ETSI
12
SOL003.
13
For example, a PM job might be scheduled to run at 11 PM with the criteria to retrieve CPU measurements for O-Cloud
14
resources and compose them into a measurement report.

3.5.3.6
Source of Truth
16
The source of truth is the arbiter of discrepancies in metrics. In an O-Cloud IMS Performance context, it is expected
17
that the “source of truth” will be the O-Cloud (IMS + O-Cloud infrastructure resources). The PM job manages the
18
transformation of data into a performance report. The PM job requests data from the O-Cloud (the Source of Truth) to
19
build the performance report.
20
For example, suppose there is a metric from the source of tru

sources). The PM job manages the
18
transformation of data into a performance report. The PM job requests data from the O-Cloud (the Source of Truth) to
19
build the performance report.
20
For example, suppose there is a metric from the source of truth with a reported value of 50, and the performance report
21
has a value of 20. That value of 20 might have been a result of corruption in sending, composition, or a software bug. In
22
order to obtain the proper value, the source of truth can be consulted.
23
3.5.3.7
Performace Threshold
24
A performance threshold is a level or value which is used to check if a measurement exceeds or stays within. Typically,
25
thresholds are used to trigger behavior or policies in a system.
26
For example, a user might set a CPU utilization threshold of 80%.
27
3.5.3.8
Performance Dictionary
28
A performance dictionary is a reference that is provided by a resource type vendor. A PM dictionary provides
29
information on performance metrics or KPIs that are relevant to that resource type. The Performance (PM) Dictionary
30
would be onboarded when a new resource type is added; and that resource type would come with an associated a PM
31
dictionary.  The PM dictionary for a resource type includes all measurements supported by the resource type including
32
ones defined by standards and the reference to the standard.
33
For example, there will likely be some standardized measurements. For a CPU, that might be CPU utilization measured
34
in percentage. However, there could also be a vendor’s CPU that might have additional features such as pinning or huge
35
page functionality. The PM dictionary for a resource type it might have all measurements that it supports including
36
standardized measurements.

Study of O2-IMS K8s interface
4.1
Context
The background for this study arises from the increasing adoption of cloud-native network
functions and their impact on infrastructure management systems. Cloud-native principles
advocate for declarative-based management for network functions, wherein the desired end state
is described, rather than specifying the sequence of steps to achieve that state. The shift towards
declarative models has not been fully explored for infrastructure management services within the
context of the O2 interface.
As of specification v04.00, O2-IMS interfaces follow an imperative model approach for
infrastructure management. This approach does not enable direct cloud native integration with
Kubernetes which is a prominent container orchestrator widely used in the industry.
The study’s findings are expected to provide insights into the feasibility and benefits of adopting a
declarative K8s API approach for the O2-IMS interface. This analysis will assist WG6 in making
informed choices regarding the evolution of O2-IMS ecosystem. By understanding the impact and
potential modifications, the study aims to accelerate the adoption of O2-IMS and leverage industry
best practices.
4.2   Objectives
The main objective of the present Technical Report is to conduct a comprehensive analysis of the
O2-IMS interface with a focus on exploring the feasibility, drawback and benefits of adopting a
declarative K8s API approach.
To achieve this goal, the study is structured around the following specific objects:
• Declarative K8s API approach
• O2-IMS services analysis
• Proposal for O2-IMS K8s interface support
• Impact on WG6 Specifications and Use Cases
4.3   Declarati

• Declarative K8s API approach
• O2-IMS services analysis
• Proposal for O2-IMS K8s interface support

4.3   Declarative K8s API approach
4.3.1   Kubernetes Object Management techniques
As defined in the Kubernetes Object Management [2] documentation, three management
techniques exist:
• Imperative commands

________________________________________________________________________________________________
7
o “A user operates directly on live objects in a cluster. The user provides operations to
the kubectl command as arguments or flags.”
o “This is the recommended way to run a one-off task in a cluster; it operates directly
on live objects and provides no history of previous configurations.”
• Imperative object configuration
o “The kubectl command specifies the operation (create, replace, etc.), optional flags,
and at least one file name. The file specified contains a full definition of the object in
YAML or JSON format.”
• Declarative object configuration
o “A user operates on object configuration files stored locally; however, the user does
not define the operations to be taken on the files. Create, update, and delete operations
are automatically detected per object by kubectl. This enables working on directories,
where different operations might be needed for different objects.”
The Kubernetes documentation exemplifies and defines advantage and disadvantage for each of
these techniques.
4.3.2   Declarative object management benefits
Declarative Kubernetes (K8s) API is one of the fundamental concepts that Kubernetes is built upon.
As depicted in the previous section, it refers to the practice of defining the desired state of
applications in a declarative manner, rather than imperatively specifying the steps to achieve that
state. There are several benefits to using a declarative approach with the Kubernetes API:
• Desired State Management: Declarative APIs enable specifying what the system is
expected to look like (the desired state) rather than how to get there (the imperative
steps). Kubernetes controllers continuously work to reconcile the current state with the
desired

Management: Declarative APIs enable specifying what the system is
expected to look like (the desired state) rather than how to get there (the imperative
steps). Kubernetes controllers continuously work to reconcile the current state with the
desired state, automatically making adjustments as needed. This simplifies operations of
keeping resources in sync with the intention and reduces the risk of configuration drift.
• Resilient: Declarative object configuration enables Kubernetes to automatically detect and
recover from failures. If a pod or other resource goes down or becomes unhealthy,
Kubernetes will automatically create a new instance to maintain the desired state.
• Idempotence: In a declarative API, applying the same configuration multiple times have the
same result as applying it once. This idempotence property reduces the risk of unexpected
changes or side effects when managing resources.
• Scalability: Objects created declaratively are often easier to scale because multiple
instances of the same resource using the same configuration template can be defined.
Kubernetes can then create and manage these instances as needed.

________________________________________________________________________________________________
8
• Version Control and Auditing: Declarative configurations can be stored in version control
systems like Git [11], allowing for versioning, history tracking, and easy collaboration. This
helps with auditing and troubleshooting as the evolution of the configuration is visible over
time.
• Predictable Rollouts and Rollbacks: With declarative APIs, a new desired state can be
specified, and Kubernetes will manage the rollout and rollback of resources to achieve that
state. This makes it easier to perform updates and handle failures gracefully.
• Portability: Declarative configurations are often agnostic to the underlying infrastructure,
making it easier to move workloads between different Kubernetes clusters or cloud
providers. If the declarative configurations embed some details that are specific to some
environments, then the portability becomes limited to these environments.
• Automation and Tooling: Declarative APIs are well-suited for automation because
configuration is defined as code enabling the use of tools like Helm [10], Kustomize [12], or
operators to manage complex applications and resources.
• Human-Readable: Declarative configurations are often more human-readable and
maintainable compared to imperative scripts or instructions, which can be error-prone and
hard to understand.
In summary, the declarative nature of the Kubernetes API simplifies resource management,
enhances automation, increase reliability, and makes it easier to work with complex infrastructure
and applications in a dynamic environment like Kubernetes.
NOTE:
The present document only assesses Kubernetes technology; it can be possible to
realize these benefits with other technologies as well.
