Chapter 2
Hardware Reference Design 1
1
This chapter describes a white box hardware reference design example for indoor Picocell deployment scenario.  It
2
includes O-CU, O-DU7-2 and FHM7-2/FHGW7-2→8 for IPC deployment scenario.
3
2.1 O-CU Hardware Reference Design
4
The O-CU white box hardware is the platform that perform the O-CU function of upper L2 and L3. The hardware
5
systems specified in this document meet the computing, power and environmental requirements of use cases
6
configurations and feature sets of RAN physical node. These requirements are described in the early hardware
7
requirement specification as well as in the use cases document. The O-CU hardware includes the chassis platform,
8
mother board, peripheral devices and cooling devices. The mother board contains processing unit, memory, the internal
9
I/O interfaces, and external connection ports. The midhaul (MH) and backhaul (BH) interface are used to carry the
10
traffic between O-CU and O-DU7-2 as well as O-CU and core network. The other hardware functional components
11
include: the storage for software, hardware and system debugging interfaces, board management controller, just to name
12
a few; the O-CU designer will make decision based on the specific needs of the implementation.
13
The HW reference design of O-CU is the same as O-DU7-2 except for the need of HW accelerator, thus detail design
14
will be described in O-DU7-2 section 2.2.
15
2.2 O-DU7-2 Hardware Reference Design
16
The O-DU7-2 white box hardware is the platform that performs the O- DU7-2 functions such as upper L1 and lower L2
17
functions. The hardware systems specified in this document meet the computing, power and environmental
18

ardware Reference Design
16
The O-DU7-2 white box hardware is the platform that performs the O- DU7-2 functions such as upper L1 and lower L2
17
functions. The hardware systems specified in this document meet the computing, power and environmental
18
requirements of use case’s configurations and feature sets of RAN physical node. These requirements are described in
19
the early hardware requirement specification as well as in the use cases document. The O-DU7-2 hardware includes the
20
chassis platform, mother board, peripheral devices and cooling devices. The mother board contains processing unit,
21
memory, the internal I/O interfaces, and external connection ports. The fronthaul and backhaul interface are used to
22
carry the traffic between O-RU7-2/FHM7-2/FHGW7-2→8 and O-DU7-2 as well as O-CU and O-DU7-2. The O-DU7-2 design
23
may also provide an interface for hardware accelerator if that option is preferred. The other hardware functional
24
components include: the storage for software, hardware and system debugging interfaces, board management controller,
25
just to name a few; the O-DU7-2 designer will make decision based on the specific needs of the implementation.
26
Note that the O-DU7-2 HW reference design is also feasible for O-CU and integrated O-CU/ O-DU7-2.
27
2.2.1 O-DU7-2 High-Level Functional Block Diagram
28
Figure 2-1 shows the major functional blocks of O-DU7-2. The digital processing unit handles the baseband processing
29
workload. To make the processing more efficient, an accelerator can be used to assist with the baseband workload
30

Functional offload requirements:
5
One of the candidate functions for offloading is the LDPC encoder and decoder, which typically consists of
6

Item Name
Description
High Speed Data

High speed data represents the baseband information being transmitted or received.
Depending on the configuration of the ORAN device, various bandwidths may be
supported leading to a range of payload rates.  Options for data include parallel data paths,
JESD204B and JESD204C.  Up to 8 lanes in each direction may be supported although
fewer is preferred.  Options such as DPD and numeric precision will impact the payload
rate.  Several options are shown in the following table.  All data represents IQ 16-bit
(N=16) precision.  Some devices support IQ 12 bit (N’=12) which may reduce the required
data rates accordingly.  The tables below assume 1 ORx for 2 TRx.  From Table 2-14 and
Table 2-15, the number of lanes required may be determined by dividing the total bit rates
shown by the capacity of a lane, typically 12.5 GBPS for JESD204B and 25 GBPS for
JESD204C.
Reference Clock
(Device Clock)

The transceiver should receive a reference for internal clock and LO synthesis needs.  This
reference clock can function as the JESD204 Device Clock where the interface is by
SERDES.  The specific clock frequency is determined by the operation mode of the
transceiver and may range from 1Hz upward.
SYSREF

If the transceiver supports SERDES, then it should accept a SYSREF signal from the clock
or data source as appropriate.  The number and configuration for the SYSREF is
dependent on the operating mode of the transceiver.

________________________________________________________________________________________________
SYNCB

If the transceiver supports SERDES, then it should also support a SYNCB for each link as
appropriate.
Control

Control of the transceiver is by way of 3 or 4 wire SPI or IIC functioning as a slave.
Support for 1.8V control is required and tolerance of 3.3V is preferred.  The transceiver
may optionally include a separate SPI master for control of peripheral devices as required.
GPIO

The transceiver may optionally include GPIO for controlling peripherals including but not
limited to PAs, LNAs and other devices.  These GPIOs should at a minimum support 1.8V
outputs but the specifics will be determined by the connected devices.  The GPIO should
also support input from peripheral devices.  Input should at a minimum support 1.8V logic
with tolerance of 3.3V preferred.
Tx Enable

The transceiver should provide an output to support enabling and disabling the external
devices in the transmit chain such as a TxVGA (optional) and PA.

Rx Enable
The transceiver should provide an output to support enabling and disabling the external
devices in the transmit chain such as a RF Front End Module or LNA.
LNA Bypass
The transceiver should provide an output to support bypassing the LNA appropriately in
the condition of a large blocker if so required.
RF Outputs
RF outputs including the main Tx signal should support 50 ohm or 100 ohms signalling.
These outputs can be either single ended or differential.
RF Inputs
RF inputs including the main Rx and the Observation Rx (ORx) (for DPD) should support
50 ohm or 100 ohms signalling.  These inputs can be either single ended or differential.
The device should support at least 1 ORx.

the uplink IQ bit stream of the time domain the carrier from O-RU7-2. If the uplink IQ stream is compressed, then it

together. Then capture the IQ streams in the eCPRI frame and transmitted by eCPRI interface to the O-DU7-2.

27
difference is that the downlink signal is duplicated with 8 copies and sends to different O-RU7-2.

A4.8.3.1 Topology Discovery
11
O-DU can obtain the O-RU8 topological relation (adjacency relation) of a shared cell. The shared cell topology
12
discovery procedure is filled in to the ethernet forwarding Information Base (FIB) using the LBM/LBR connection
13
check procedure running at the Ethernet layer as defined in Section 3.3.1.5 Connectivity Detection, and FIB is obtained
14
based on O-DU. The difference is that, since the FHGW7-2→8 southward is based on CPRI IQ link, only the Ethernet
15
network-based M-Plane has MAC address, therefore, the LBM/LBR procedure in the 3.3.1.5 Connectivity detection
16

________________________________________________________________________________________________
section, the FHGW7-2→8 southward is based on M-Plane. Transparent bridge functionality is used for O-RU8 with
1
shared cell functionality running in FHGW7-2→8 and/or cascading mode.
2
O-DU determines the topology by the following two-step procedure：
3
1)
In the first phase, the procedure of using the 3.3.1.5 connectivity detection section is used to execute the
4
Ethernet connection monitoring for all the discovered O-RU8 MAC addresses. The echo of the Ethernet
5
loopback from the found MAC address should ensure that the transparent bridge in the FHGW7-2→8 and
6
the cascading mode is automatically learning to pass the MAC addresses of these devices
7
Note: In addition to Ethernet connection monitoring, DHCP discovery, Call Home and M-Plane connection
8
establishment can also be used to fill in information in FIB, so maybe O-RU8 has a northward port to do the above.
9
2)
In the second phase, O-DU uses the o-ran-ethernet-forwarding.yang model to discovery which MAC
10
addresses have been learned by the ethernet bridge function. O-DU uses each Ethernet forwarding entry
11
to determine adjacency relationships
12

This document specifies the requirements, conditions, configurations, profiles, and sequences for
interoperability testing of O-RAN O-CU and O-DU deployment scenarios with other O-RAN components
in standalone (SA) mode.
This document complies with ORAN Testing and Integration Focus Group (TIFG) recommendation on a
uniform documentation approach for interface testing specifications across all ORAN Working Groups
(WGs).
The following interfaces (logical or physical) are covered in IOT test cases.



1.1 High Level Scenarios
Scenarios included in Release 3 of the IOT specification are aligned with ORAN-WG8.AAD [1]. In this
release, the focus is on functional behavior and limited performance of O-CU/O-DU under different
traffic scenario.

Cell Setup and activation.

SystemInformation (MIB, SIB1, SIB2 and SIB3).

RACH (with PRACH Format 0).

Registration and De-Registration procedure.

PDU session establishment and modification.

Idle mode Paging.

UDP data transfer (DL/UL).

O1 and E2 interface

Beam Management
The following are the performance scenarios:

Throughput under load condition in UL and DL.

Static configuration files are used to configure O-CU and O-DU.
1.2 Assumptions
In current release of this test specification, the following assumptions have been made:

The F1 interfaces are assumed to comply with 3GPP release specifications [2], [15], [16] and
[17].

O-CU and O-DU comply to the same version of the O-RAN Software Architecture
specifications [1].
All elements in the interoperability test and the supporting test environment, where 3GPP support is
relevant, comply to the same version of the 3GPP specification.

3.1 Terms
For the purposes of the present document, the following terms apply:
O-CU: O-RAN Central Unit is a logical node hosting PDCP, RRC, SDAP, and other control functions.
O-DU: O-RAN Distributed Unit is a logical node hosting RLC, MAC, and High-PHY layers based on a lower
layer functional split.
O-RU: O-RAN Radio Unit is a logical node hosting Low-PHY layer and RF processing based on a lower
layer functional split.
F1 interface: The interface defined by 3GPP TS [15], 3GPP TS [16], and 3GPP TS [2], to be further
interpreted as per O-RAN WG5 specification for interoperability between O-CU and O-DU from different
vendors.

7 Interoperability (IOT) Standard Test Definitions
7.1 Interoperability Standard Test Definitions
7.1.1 Standard Test Configurations
Interoperability testing is performed to validate whether the software of O-CU can interact with the
software and system components of O-DU. The message flow and IEs are compliant to 3GPP and O-RAN
Software Architecture [1]. The focus of this document is to validate interoperability of O-CU and O-DU of
same/different vendors.
7.1.2 DUT
O-DU and O-CU are the physical components considered as DUTs. Other network elements, such as O-
RU, may be real hardware or simulated based on the test requirements. In certain test cases, the O-DU
or O-CU may be simulated.
For details on the test setup and configuration, see 7.17.

Figure 7.1.2-A: DUT configuration
7.1.3 Testing Tools
In all test cases, O-RU may be real or simulated. In certain test cases, the O-DU or O-CU may be
simulated.

O-CU or O-CU Emulator: A separate O-CU or simulated O-CU is used based on the test setup.
More details are mentioned in 7.17.

O-DU or O-DU Emulator: A separate O-DU or simulated O-DU is used based on the test
setup. More details are mentioned in 7.17.

_____________________________________________________________________________________

O-RU or O-RU Emulator: A separate O-RU or simulated O-RU is used based on the test
requirement. More details are mentioned in 7.17.

Test UE or UE Emulator: An End-to-end (E2E) test requires a UE. It can be a real UE or
simulated one based on the test requirement. More details are mentioned in 7.17.

Core or Core Emulator: An E2E test requires a core network. A real Core Network (CN) or
simulated core is used in E2E setup.
7.1.4 Time Synchronization
The O-DU and O-RU components are required to be synchronized to a common system time and master
time source unless otherwise stated.
7.2 ORAN.WG8.IOT.001: Cell Setup
7.2.1 Test Purpose
The purpose of this test case is to explain the cell setup when O-DU and O-CU started separately.
7.2.2 Reference Requirements
For detailed requirements, refer to the section 9.2 and 10.1.3 in ORAN-WG8.AAD [1].
7.2.3 Initial Conditions
Following are the preconditions for this test.

Physical interface of DHCP(v4/v6) server, DNS server, CA/RA server, SMO, O-DU and O-RU is
connected.

NETCONF client is operational.

Use the default O-CU configuration files to configure all modules (NR RRC, NR PDCP, and
SDAP) in O-CU.

Use the default O-DU configuration files to configure O-DU.

O-DU is physically installed. It is assumed that when Power-ON the O-DU, the NETCONF
Server is started or when the O-DU is restarted, the NETCONF Server is restarted.

O-RU is connected to O-DU. O-RU is managed entirely by O-DU using O-RAN WG4 defined
hierarchical approach (Refer Section 5.1.2 of [24]). Fronthaul CU-plane data communication
is verified and M-plane communication using NETCONF server is operational.

O-DU and O-RU to time synchronize using one of the O-RAN Front

g O-RAN WG4 defined
hierarchical approach (Refer Section 5.1.2 of [24]). Fronthaul CU-plane data communication
is verified and M-plane communication using NETCONF server is operational.

O-DU and O-RU to time synchronize using one of the O-RAN Fronthaul Transport
Synchronization profiles (LLS-C1 to LLS-C4) defined by O-RAN WG4 specification [26].

O-CU is connected to 5GC through NG interface and O-CU is operational.

O-CU and O-DU may be configured with YANG data model or static configuration files.

7.96 ORAN.WG8.IOT.095: Verify Carrier aggregation, S-Cell
Release over D2 Interface
7.96.1 Test Purpose
The purpose of this test case is to verify Carrier aggregation, S-Cell addition/Release over D2 Interface.
7.96.2 Reference Requirement
For detailed requirements, refer to section 9.4 in ORAN-WG8.AAD [1] and sections 5 and 6 in O-
RAN.WG5.TS.D2AP [40]
7.96.3 Initial Conditions
Following are the preconditions for this test.

Physical interface of DHCP(v4/v6) server, DNS server, CA/RA server, SMO, O-DU and O-RU is
connected.

Use the default O-CU configuration files to configure all modules (NR RRC, NR PDCP, and
SDAP) in O-CU.

O-RU is connected to O-DU. O-RU is managed entirely by O-DU using O-RAN WG4 defined
hierarchical approach (Refer Section 5.1.2 of [24]). Fronthaul CU-plane data communication
is verified and M-plane communication using NETCONF server is operational.

O-CU is connected to O-DU’s. Both O-DU's are connected to same CU-UP

O-CU is connected to 5GC through NG interface and O-CU is operational.

It is assumed that when Power-ON the O-DU, the NETCONF Server is started or when the O-
DU is restarted, the NETCONF Server is restarted.

NETCONF Client is operational.

The O-DU have obtained end to end IP connectivity between O-DU and SMO. The O-DU shall
support either IPv4 or IPv6.

The PNF Registration is successful with TLS secure connection is established between O-DU
and SMO as per test case ORAN.WG8.IOT.017.

O-DU and O-RU to time synchronize using one of O-RAN Fronthaul Transport
Synchronization profiles (LLS-C1 to LLS-C4) defined by O-RAN WG4 specification [26].

Scope
Fronthaul networks have to provide flexibility to mix and match different deployment scenarios (CRAN, DRAN), functional
splits, and other mobile traffic on the same packet network. CPRI remains the preferred choice for legacy (2G/3G) support. For
4G/5G technologies and beyond, the novel LLS and eCPRI together are capable of reducing bitrate requirements on the
fronthaul for classic radios, preventing the rate explosion for massive MIMO, and enabling connectivity flexibility in packet
fronthaul.
The majority of today´s deployments are DRANs, typically using wireless microwave links or leased lines transporting packets
for S1/NG and X2 backhaul. However, CRANs enable key potential benefits, such as simplification antenna sites, full inter-
site coordination, and operational gains by centralizing processing resources at hub sites.  The flexible relationship between
radios and physical ports on a baseband together with the user data-dependent characteristics of eCPRI/LLS, allows a baseband
node to serve a larger set of radios and utilize processing capacity more efficiently.
Several important characteristics of packet-based fronthaul networks need to be met, such as
•
Efficiency – make use of the statistical aggregation possibilities in eCPRI/LLS,
•
Flexibility – allow for connectivity between all radios and all basebands,
•
Scalability – small to large CRAN deployments using the same architectural principles,
•
Resiliency – a robust network to minimize the effects of failures,
•
Observability – based on the telemetry.
•
Security – via service isolation, integrity and privacy protection.
•
Simplicity – a network easy to dimension and deploy,
•
RAN-agnostic – support of both purpose-built and cloud-native RAN networks,
•
Synchronization – providing sync for the RAN com

ecurity – via service isolation, integrity and privacy protection.
•
Simplicity – a network easy to dimension and deploy,
•
RAN-agnostic – support of both purpose-built and cloud-native RAN networks,
•
Synchronization – providing sync for the RAN components.
A service overlay network architecture enables the separation of the physical network topology from the application service
structure and connectivity. Packet-based transport can utilize protocols that have been broadly deployed and well-understood
for years for sharing network topology and characteristic information. For example, the eCPRI L2 Ethernet traffic can be
handled as a virtual overlay Ethernet service with fronthaul-specific strict service requirements. Such architecture can combine
additional virtual overlay Ethernet or IP services with tailored characteristics.
This networking concept provides ease of deployment and connection flexibility by enabling the establishment of software-
defined overlays in combination with optional traffic-engineered paths. Distributed IP control protocols on the packet
infrastructure make the network self-contained and give a fast response to failures. There is no need for multiple control planes
as extensions in the routing protocols make it possible to distribute RAN-specific forwarding information (including traffic
engineering).
The overlay service runs on top of the packet network to create virtual network connectivity. e.g., via L2 EVPN or L3 IP-VPN
services. The MP-BGP protocol and an SDN controller may drive the configuration and control of virtual networks and
services. They can fully control traffic steering and traffic engineering for the virtual service by utilizing, for example, segment
routing traffic engineering (SR-TE) capabilities of the transport infrastruc

tion and control of virtual networks and
services. They can fully control traffic steering and traffic engineering for the virtual service by utilizing, for example, segment
routing traffic engineering (SR-TE) capabilities of the transport infrastructure.
The distribution of functions to different sites for tailored services drives the need to simplify the deployment and operation of
both RAN and its related transport. A tight interaction between the two is necessary to achieve cost-efficient deployment and
operation.
Another essential new requirement is to provide a synchronization service in the new architecture. When transitioning from
CPRI to eCPRI in the fronthaul, the time distribution between the baseband and O-RU has shifted from being carried by the
CPRI frame itself to being carried by protocols like the packet-based precision time protocol (PTP) or Synchronous Ethernet
(SyncE). ITU-T has specified several PTP profiles with relevant properties for telecom. Requirements for time alignment and
frequency stability in the fronthaul network remain the same as those for CPRI-based solutions.
For the RAN to support full functionality, a performant synchronization solution must be available. With packet switches in
the fronthaul network, special attention must be given to maintaining synchronization to or between radios and ensuring

sufficient synchronization availability. The transport nodes can distribute sync and hold-over functionality located in the RAN
nodes (baseband, radio) or outside (packet nodes). to mitigate sync interruptions from e.g., GNSS-derived sources.
The packet fronthaul transport is a cornerstone for future automation, because of (1) simplified deployment and maintenance
via SDN orchestration, (2) service-aware routing and traffic engineering, and (3) compatibility with cloud-native RAN and
containerized vRAN functions.
Packet transport is not just a replacement for CPRI, but a whole transport network transformation:
•
Supports both DRAN and CRAN deployments.
•
Optimizes OPEX and CAPEX by enabling multiplexing and centralization.
•
Provides a scalable foundation for 6G-ready architectures with integrated synchronization, SDN, and cloud-native
capabilities.
The scope of the Technical Specification includes:
•
To provide functional reference architecture and nodal requirements for realizing transport services for the O-RAN
fronthaul interfaces in the converged packet-switching transport networks. The packet-switching transport consists of one or
more packet transport functions between the fronthaul radio and baseband equipment, e.g., O-RU and O-DU. Applicability to
the fronthaul interfaces other than those defined in O-RAN is not precluded.
•
To define end-to-end reference architecture for transport network solution based on a packet-switched technology and
services addressing control, user, and management traffic in support of the packet-switching fronthaul transport.
•
Transport for RAN synchronization distribution in packet-switching fronthaul.

4
Functional planes and data flows in the RAN fronthaul
In the O-RAN architecture, a single split point, known as "7-2x", is chosen as the functional split for defining the fronthaul
interface between O-DU and O-RU. The split 7-2x allows a variation in placing the precoding function either in the O-DU or
in the O-RU.  In other architectures, the split can be at different points. The fronthaul interface facilitates the transmission of
control, user, and management data between O-DU and O-RU.
The fronthaul is divided into Control, User, and Synchronization Plane (CUS-Plane) and the Management Plane (M-Plane) to
support different types of data flows. The CUS-Plane carries both real-time and non-real-time traffic, including user data and
control information required for radio signal processing, while the M-Plane handles configuration, monitoring, and
management features.
4.1
Control Plane (C-Plane)
Control Plane (C-Plane) handles real-time control and signaling information between O-DU and O-RU. C-Plane provides
instructions on scheduling, beamforming, and resource allocation to coordinate the transmission of user data. The C-Plane also
ensures that O-RU processes and transmits data according to the O-DU's instructions while supporting advanced radio features.
C-Plane messages have lower bandwidth requirements, whereas they have higher reliability requirements.
The C-Plane supports the eCPRI protocol over Ethernet networks illustrated in Figure 2, which provides encapsulation and
prioritization for control messages distinct from user data. C-Plane messages are not concatenated with User Plane (U-Plane)
messages within the same Ethernet frame. The C-Plane protocol stack may also include IP/UDP for data transmission, if
supported by both the transmitting and receiving nodes.

-
C-Plane provides low-latency and high-reliability signaling, which is necessary for 5G features such as massive
MIMO (Multiple-Input Multiple-Output) and network slicing.

4.2
User Plane (U-Plane)
User Plane (U-Plane) supports transport of user data i.e., IQ (In-phase Quadrature) samples representing digitized radio signals
between O-DU and O-RU for uplink and downlink transmissions. U-Plane is also responsible for transferring PRACH
(Physical Random Access Channel) IQ from O-RU to O-DU needed for initial UE access. U-Plane may utilize compression for
IQ sample transmission to maximize throughput and efficiency of fronthaul.
The U-Plane supports the eCPRI protocol over Ethernet networks illustrated in Figure 3. The U-Plane protocol stack may also
include IP/UDP for data transmission, if supported by both the transmitting and receiving nodes.

The U-Plane features include:
-
U-Plane provides high-bandwidth and low-latency data transfer for user data.
-
It can utilize efficient compression techniques for IQ samples transmission to maximize fronthaul efficiency.
-
It supports fragmentation and reassembly of O-RU to O-DU user data packets.
-
U-Plane supports massive MIMO and dynamic beamforming.
-
It works closely with the C-Plane to ensure data delivery aligns with dynamic scheduling and radio resource
allocations.
4.3
Synchronization Plane (S-Plane)
Synchronization Plane (S-Plane) is responsible for maintaining synchronization between O-RAN components and with
references such as GNSS in terms of frequency, time and phase. S-Plane achieves synchronization by distributing precise clock
signals from grandmaster, PTP messages and SyncE signals as required by different synchronization configurations.
The S-Plane supports PTP and SyncE protocols over Ethernet networks illustrated in Figure 4.

4.4
Management Plane (M-Plane)
Management Plane (M-Plane) responsible for non-real-time management operations of O-RU. It facilitates initialization,
configuration and management of O-RU. It supports both hierarchical model (O-RU managed by O-DU) and hybrid model (O-
RU managed by network management systems). To support different functionalities, various types of messages are carried
over M-Plane which includes configuration management commands, performance management reports, fault management
notification, and messages for software management.
M-Plane uses NETCONF/YANG as the network element management protocol and data modelling language. It requires an
end-to-end IP connectivity between O-RU and the elements managing it. The M-Plane protocols stack is displayed in Figure 5.

5
Functional Reference Architecture

Figure 6 Reference Functional Architecture for RAN Fronthaul in Converged Packet Transport Network
A functional reference architecture is a blueprint that outlines a system's functions and their interactions, providing a
generalized, reusable model that can be adapted to create specific solutions. It focuses on what the system does (the functions)
without delving into the specifics of how it's implemented (the physical architecture), making it useful for design, testing, and
development, as well as ensuring consistency across different projects or systems.
This project approaches the RAN Fronthaul transport architecture from the perspective of the Provider Transport Network
(PTN). Mobile traffic in all planes, as noted in Section 4, is considered application (overlay) data of the respective PTN tunnels
and is transparent to the PTN. In the scope of this document, transporting over the PTN the Ethernet-encapsulated traffic of the
Control, User, Synchronization planes. As a result, the PTN provides transparent bridging of Ethernet frames. For this
document, IP forwarding based on information in a packet that belongs to CUS-Planes of the RAN Fronthaul is outside the
scope of this document.
The PTN, shown in Figure 6, provides fronthaul interface service using a combination of underlying network technologies,
such as Ethernet, IP, and MPLS. Some underlay technologies, e.g., Segment Routing, allow for path engineering, thus
improving utilization of network capacity. Other technologies, such as RFC 9543 Network Slicing, support resource
reservation in combination with path engineering, thereby realizing the traffic engineering paradigm. In some deployment
scenarios, PTN can use EVPN over Segment Routing in IPv6 (SRv6), in MPLS (SR-MPLS), or IP/MPLS underlay. In other
deployme

source
reservation in combination with path engineering, thereby realizing the traffic engineering paradigm. In some deployment
scenarios, PTN can use EVPN over Segment Routing in IPv6 (SRv6), in MPLS (SR-MPLS), or IP/MPLS underlay. In other
deployments, PTN can use an Ethernet underlay network.
5.1
Provider Transport Network’s demarcation
The Ethernet Attachment Circuits (AC) provide reference points for network demarcation. TNE’s interfaces facing RU or DU
support Ethernet AC in port and VLAN modes. In the port mode, all traffic is processed regardless of any VLAN tags present.
In the latter mode, individual VLANs are treated as separate connections. That can be used with simple or multiple tags (IEEE
802.1Q [i8][i8]). Furthermore, the TNE’s set of functions includes the Ethernet OAM, as defined in Link OAM (Clause
57/IEEE 802.3 [i9]) and/or ITU-T G.8013/Y.1731 [i10] [i10], that provides essential for operating the fronthaul interface at the
required quality level.

13

5.2
Transport Network Entity functional set in the Provider
Transport Network
A TNE, which is a part of the PTN that provides transport service for the fronthaul interface, includes functions in the data,
control, and management planes. For example, a TNE that is part of the MPLS-based PTN supports a label distribution
mechanism. Label distribution can be provided by LDP [i11], RSVP-TE [i12] for IP/MPLS networks, or by the Segment
Routing extension of Interior Gateway Protocols (IGPs) for SR-MPLS [i13][i13] networks to set up LSPs. Also, labels can be
provisioned over the management plane. A TNE that is a part of an IP-based PTN includes a mechanism that provides dynamic
route information distribution, for example, by IS-IS [i14], as an example of IGP. In some environments, routing information
can be provisioned using the paradigm of the Software Defined Network using the management plane. Segment Routing,
through IGP extensions, enables path engineering for PTN. BGP [i15] can be used as the control plane of the Ethernet VPN
(EVPN) [i16], a technology that provides virtual Layer 2 connectivity between dispersed sites over an IP or MPLS network.

7
Conclusions
The specification positions packet-based fronthaul not merely as a CPRI replacement but as a transformational enabler for
future RAN architectures, including 6G, with integrated synchronization, SDN orchestration, and cloud-native support.

physically match an O-RAN site, however it is considered logically external since it pertains

7.2 Non-ORAN Fronthaul
44
Legacy Fronthaul scenarios are those C-RAN use cases where the Fronthaul traffic is transported
45
over a packet switch network while not using the O-RAN compliant encapsulation protocol that
46

34
supports 7.2x split. The two most likely legacy Fronthaul scenario in a packet switched transport
1
network are:
2

3
• eCPRI based C-RAN solutions: using eCPRI encapsulation protocol not compliant to O-
4
RAN WG4 CUS specifications [18]. i.e., a non O-RAN 7.2x split.
5
• RoE based C-RAN solutions:  CPRI encapsulated by the RoE protocol.

7
7.2.1 eCPRI based C-RAN solutions
8
An operator may choose a packet-based C-RAN Fronthaul architecture that is not O-RAN 7.2x
9
compliant. In this case the RU and DU uses eCPRI as the packet encapsulation protocol to
10
packetize the Fronthaul data but implements a non-O-RAN compliant radio message protocol to
11
support a different function split.
12

13
Following 3GPP recommendation [9], the possible function splits may include
14
• Option 6, split between MAC and PHY layers
15
• Option 7.1, 7.2, or 7.3, splits within PHY layer
16
• Option 8, split between radio and PHY layer
17

18
7.2.2 Radio over Ethernet (RoE) based C-RAN solutions
19
In this scenario an operator has an existing radio deployed at the cell site and the operator intends to
20
convert these radios to support a C-RAN Fronthaul architecture whilst implementing their 5G RAN
21
infrastructure.  In this case it is likely the legacy equipment (RRH and BBU) only supports an
22
optical CPRI interfaces.  To implement a C-RAN Fronthaul architecture in a packet switched
23
transport network the CPRI needs to be converted to an Ethernet frame at the cell site, transported
24
over the access network as packet and then get converted back to CPRI at the hub for processing
25
from the BBU. In this scenario a component called a RoE mapper is used to perform a CPRI to
26
Ethernet frame conversion at the cell site and an Ethernet frame to CPRI conversion at the location
27
where the BBU is located.
28
7.2.2.1 RoE Mapper transport
29
The design, implementation, management, and interface from the RoE mapper to the legacy
30
equipment is not in the scope of WG-9 but the expectation is the RoE mapper will present either O-
31
RAN 7.2x compliant Ethernet or Ethernet IP packets or IEEE 1914.3 Radio over Ethernet packets
32
[40] to the transport network. At this time O-RAN has not defined a CPRI to O-RAN 7.2x
33
conversion capability so implementations out in the market are based on CPRI to Radio Over
34
Ethernet.
35

36
It is then the responsibility of the transport network to transport these packets to their destination
37
with appropriate characteristics for the legacy connection to function.
38
7.2.2.2 Radio over Ethernet
39
Radio over Ethernet (RoE) is defined in IEEE Std 1914.3-2018 – IEEE standard for radio over
40
Ethernet Encapsulations and Mappings [40]. Two mapping techniques for supporting CPRI to
41
packet conversion are defined.
42

43
Structure-agnostic RoE mapper
44

ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

35
The structure-agnostic RoE mapper captures bits from one end of a constant bit rate link, packetizes
1
the bits into Ethernet frames, sends the frames across the network, and then recreates the bit stream
2
at the far end of the link. While the constant bit-rate data stream is commonly encoded with the
3
CPRI protocol, it could also be of any other protocol, provided it is within the range of data rates
4
supported by that equipment.
5
The structure-agnostic RoE mapper has two main modes of operation:
6

7
• Tunnelling mode or type 0 works as a simple Ethernet tunnel. It does not remove any line
8
coding bits and does not interpret any special characters (such as K-characters). If the source
9
data is 8b/10b-encoded, the 10-bit symbols present on the line will be tunnelled by this RoE
10
mapper as 10 bits of data. Similarly, 66-bit symbols will be sent for 64b/66b-encoded data as
11
66 bits of data. The entire stream is simply packetized.
12

13
• Line-coding-aware mode or type 1 removes the line coding bits such as for CPRI encoded
14
with 8b/10b or 64b/66b. If the source data is 8b/10b-encoded, the 8-bit symbols present on
15
the line will be tunnelled by this RoE mapper as 8 bits of data. Similarly, if the source data is
16
64b/66b encoded, the 64-bit symbols present on the line will be tunnelled by this RoE
17
mapper as 64 bits of data. To allow the restoration of the 10-bit or 66-bit symbols at the de-
18
mapper, the RoE mapper/de-mapper must have some awareness of the protocol it is
19
mapping/de-mapping; the locations of the special characters must be known a priori relative
20
to an event that is indicated in the RoE frame.
21

22
Structure-aware RoE mapper
23
In this mode only the useful information in the CPRI stream is packetized into the RoE frames and
24
different types of data (such as control words and data words) can be encapsulated into separate
25
frames for prioritized processing. Those unused fields within the CPRI stream will be ignored thus
26
bring the benefit of Fronthaul BW reduction. This mode requires full knowledge of the protocol
27
layout of the CPRI and due to the proprietary nature of CPRI will require input from the radio
28
vendor.
29
7.2.3 Non O-RAN Fronthaul logical transport requirements
30
The main use case identified by operators for non O-RAN fronthaul is 4G equipment that uses
31
CPRI between the RRH and the BBU (see section 8.4). To support this over a packet based
32
fronthaul network, the CPRI stream needs to be packetized as it ingresses the packet network and
33
the CPRI stream reconstructed as it egresses the packet network. Bandwidth, delay and jitter
34
characteristics in the packet network clearly depend on the technology used to perform this
35
function, which is outside the scope of O-RAN. To provide some guidance on support of this traffic
36
it has been assumed that it is presented as Ethernet and has similar delay and jitter requirements as
37
7.2x fronhaul traffic.

1
There are different ways packet switching could be deployed to support an Open Xhaul
2

3
• Span of the packet switching components. Packet switching could be deployed from cell

5
form the end-to-end network.
6
• The nature of the underlying L0/L1transport used by the packet switching equipment.
7
• The network protocols used at the packet switching layer.
8
• How Xhaul services are built on the Xhaul infrastructure.
9

10
9.1 Physical layout and xHaul transport options
11

16
network, and a third TNE in Midhaul network.

18

9.3 Technology and architectural choices
19
As discussed in the introduction to this section there are other packet-switched solutions and
20
potentially many design approaches available that may have the same capabilities of the
21
architecture described in this revision of the document. Future versions of this document may
22
describe alternative technologies and designs based on operator requirements and suitably mature
23
standards.
24
9.4 Standardization
25
The underlay packet-switching technologies described in this document are based on MPLS and
26
IPv6 with an emphasis on the Segment Routing (SR) control and data planes. The overlay service
27
layer uses EVPN and MP-BGP L3VPNs. The IETF is the primary standardization body for these
28
technologies. The key specification of the IETF is the “Request For Comments” (RFC). RFCs are
29
labelled with different statuses: Internet Standard, Proposed Standard, Best Current Practice,
30
Experimental, Informational, and Historic. RFCs usually begin as Internet-Drafts written by
31
Individuals, or a small group and are known as individual drafts. Depending on interest an
32
individual draft can be adopted by an IETF Work Group (WG) where it is improved and revised by
33
a wider group

ually begin as Internet-Drafts written by
31
Individuals, or a small group and are known as individual drafts. Depending on interest an
32
individual draft can be adopted by an IETF Work Group (WG) where it is improved and revised by
33
a wider group and can ultimately become an RFC. This process is well defined by the IETF, with
34
guides and considerations for the progression of a document. If the process completes, then the
35
document is published as an RFC by the IETF RFC Editor. If a document does not follow the
36
process or doesn’t meet the guidelines outlined, then the drafts will expire and never become an
37
RFC. Depending on subject matter the process of moving from an WG adopted draft to an RFC can
38
several years.
39

40
To present architectures suitable for 5G, based on modern packet-switching technologies,
41
Standards, proposed standards, best current practise and informational RFCs and current workgroup
42
adopted drafts with the same designations can be referenced in this document. All experimental and
43
historic RFCs and workgroup adopted drafts and all forms of personal drafts MUST NOT be
44

ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

52
referenced. When writing requirements around these different types of documents consideration
1
should be given to document type and their status.
2

3
Future revisions of this document MUST be updated to reflect the status of IETF drafts which are
4
referenced. If they expire, they MUST be removed and if they complete the IETF standardization
5
process, references and requirements MUST be updated to remove the IETF draft and include the
6
appropriate RFC number.

9.5 Document organization
9
The remainder of this document describes the physical and logical architecture of a packet
10
switching Xhaul architecture and how it can support 5G and legacy mobile services. It is arranged
11
as follows:
12

13
Section 10 describes the end-to-end physical network infrastructure.
14

15
Sections 11 and 12 describes two underlay packet switching architectures capable of supporting a
16
5G mobile environment. The first is based on MPLS, the second IPv6 with Segment Routing
17
(SRv6). Depending on scale and preference, operators will need to select one or the other.
18

19
Section 13 describes how IP and Ethernet services suitable for 5G are delivered on a packet
20
switched Xhaul network. The approach is common regardless of the underlay technology deployed.
21

22
Section 14 describes the QoS architecture for a packet switched Xhaul network.
23

24
Section 15 describes multicast and consideration for deployment.
25

26
Section 16 covers packet-switched orchestration and telemetry. Currently it is empty and will be
27
completed in a later revision of this document or in a separate document.
28

29
Section 17 covers TNE and transport network security.
30

31
Section 18 and 19 describes how the packet switched Xhaul architecture supports 5G and legacy
32
mobile use cases outlined in section 8.
33
10 Physical network design for packet switched Xhaul
34
Figure 10-1 shows two of the most common physical topologies seen in transport networks between
35
the access and the core of the transport network. In the first, there are four layers of transport
36
infrastructure; access, pre-aggregation, aggregation, and transport core. In the second, there are three
37
layers of transport infrastructure; access, aggregation, and transport core. Packet switches are used
38
within each layer and provides connectivity between the layers.
39

40
The way the mobile RAN and core infrastructure is arranged over these different segments varies
41
based on geography and the MNO’s RAN and mobile core designs and individual operator’s
42

10.1 Packet over fibre
11
This document concentrated primarily on a transport infrastructure built using packet over fibre
12

13
10.1.1 Access
14
A Transport Network Equipment (TNE) – Ethernet switch or IP router – resides in the cell site
15
aggregating traffic received on access ports (downlinks) from end-hosts (O-RUs, or O-DUs, as
16
outlined in Section 8, as well as other types of end-hosts, like for example 4G BBUs, business
17
CPEs, etc. in hybrid deployment models), and statistically multiplexing this traffic onto a higher
18
capacity Ethernet uplink, typically established over a dark fibre or WDM lambda, or any other
19
underlying technology (for example microwave radio link). Link speed will depend on the traffic
20
levels required by the services running in the access network. The anticipated ranges will be from
21
1…50 Gbps (downlink) up to bundles of 100 Gbps (uplink).
22
10.1.1.1 Topology
23
The physical topology employed in the transport access network is operator dependent and driven
24
mainly by the three aspects:
25
• fibre topology, its availability
26
• the traffic matrix
27
• latency and time error requirements
28

29
The main physical architectures anticipated in the transport access are:
30
• ring
31
• chain
32
• hub and spoke (called as well spine and leaf), with redundant CSR connectivity
33
• hub and spoke (called as well spine and leaf), without redundant CSR connectivity

As discussed in detail in Section 8, depending on the use case, O-DU function can be placed at the

1
Open Fronthaul Interface between O-RU and O-DU has very strict latency and timing budgets
2
(O-RAN.WG9.XTRP-REQ-v01.00 “Xhaul Transport Requirements v01.00”, November 2020 [20]).
3
The implication of these requirements on the transport network design is, the number of Transport
4
Network Equipments (TNEs) between O-RU and O-DU should be minimized, as each TNE
5
increases the latency and time error.
6

7
While each of the depicted access topology could be used for Fronthaul, topologies with limited
8
number of transit Transport Network Equipments – hub-and-spoke or spine-and-leaf – leave more
9
latency budget for delay caused by light propagation in the fiber, allowing for extending Fronthaul
10
over larger distances, comparing to the topologies with bigger number of transit Transport Network
11
Equipments (ring or chain topologies).
12

13
Ring or chain topologies can be used for Fronthaul, providing that latency and timing error budgets
14
required for particular Fronthaul deployment are maintained. For example, designing Fronthaul for
15
standard NR performance (O-RAN.WG9.XTRP-REQ-v01.00 “Xhaul Transport Requirements
16
v01.00”, November 2020 [20] Table 3), mandates maximum 100 s one-way latency between O-
17
RU and O-DU. This latency budget is consumed by the fiber (~4.9 s/km), as well as by transit
18
Transport Network Equipments (~1-20 s per node, depending on hardware capabilities and port
19
speeds). Assuming 10 s latency per Transport Network Equipment, a chain or ring with 10
20
Transport Network Equipments would completely consume entire Fronthaul latency budget (ring
21
might break, so any Fronthaul design must be prepared for link failures not only from traffic
22
rerouting perspective, but as well must take into account increased number of transit network
23
elements, leading to increased latency, under ring failure condition).
24

25
Shorter chain or ring, with for example 7 Transport Network Equipments, leaves only 30  (6 km)
26
latency budget for fiber.
27

28
Note: the maximum number of TNEs can be limited due to overall synchronization requirements
29
and the consideration of time error contributions of integrated T-BC/T-TC. Examples are given in
30
CUS specification Annex H, and will be provided in WG9 Timing and Synchronization architecture
31
solution document [22].
32

33
For Midhaul/Backhaul interfaces, there are not so strict requirements regarding latency budgets, so
34
any access topology (ring, chain or hub-and-spoke/spine-and-leaf) can be used without special
35
considerations.
36

37
Note: Hub and spoke architectures are often super-imposed over a physical ring topology using
38
WDM technology. To minimize the Fronthaul latency, direct (dark) fibre should be used in hub and
39
spoke (spine and leaf) access physical architecture carrying Fronthaul traffic. Otherwise (ring
40
topology), detailed latency analysis must be performed to confirm that latency stays within
41
mandated Fronthaul budget.

10.1.2 Pre-aggregation / Aggregation / Core transport
31
Pre-aggregation and aggregation and the core transport infrastructure can support Midhaul and
32
Backhaul requirements. Due to the delay requirements associated with Fronthaul, it is unlikely O-
33
RAN 7.2x or RoE will be seen in these portions of the network. Additionally, in most scenarios the
34
transport core will not be part of the Midhaul or Backhaul environment but may provide N6
35
connectivity to any of the following:
36
1. Peering points for mobile consumer services.
37
2. Enterprise locations for mobile enterprise solutions.

3. Inter region voice communications within the operator.
1
4. Other operators.

10.1.2.1 Physical media and topologies
3
The assumption made in this architecture is the connectivity between routers in the pre-aggregation,
4
aggregation and transport core is provided by point-to-point Ethernet connections where the full
5
capacity of the Ethernet interface is available to the router. Link speed will depend on the traffic
6
levels required by the services running and the position in the network. The anticipated ranges will
7
be from 10Gbps up to bundles of 400Gbps with the capacity provided over dark fibre or some form
8
of WDM solution.
9

10
The physical topology employed in the pre-aggregation, aggregation and transport core are operator
11
dependent and driven by fibre topology, its availability and the traffic matrix. The main physical
12
architectures seen in these segments of the network are all redundant and include ring, “hub and
13
spoke” and mesh. These are shown in Figure 10-8.
14

15
Note: This document uses the term “hub and spoke architecture” but it is used inter-changeably
16
with leaf / spine and fabric architectures.
17

18
Figure 10-8 Physical topologies anticipated in Xhaul pre-aggregation, aggregation and core
19

20
1. Ring: This architecture is commonly seen in pre-aggregation and aggregation networks
21
where traffic is being collected and aggregated from the access towards components in the
22
aggregation or transport core. Connectivity between routers is either via direct dark fibre
23
connections or via lambdas derived from a WDM system.
24

25
2. Dual hub and spoke: This architecture is most commonly seen in aggregation and core
26
transport networks but also sometimes in pre-aggregation networks. It is used to collect and
27
aggregate traffic towards common aggregation points. Connectivity between routers is
28
typically via direct dark fibre or via lambdas derived from a WDM system.
29

30
Note: Hub and spoke architectures are often super-imposed over a physical ring topology
31
using WDM technology.
32

33
3. Mesh: This is architecture is normally seen in transport core networks but can be seen in
34
aggregation networks. It is used when traffic is flowing in an any-to-any fashion. As drive
35
distances increase and connectivity becomes meshier in nature, so there is increasing use of
36
DWDM and ROADM technology to derive the links between routers.
37

10.2 Alternative physical transport solutions
2
This document concentrates packet switching over a fibre infrastructure. However, there are other
3
physical solutions that can be employed in Xhaul networks. This section outlines some of those
4
technologies and discusses their applicability in different Xhaul roles.
5
10.2.1 WDM in access network
6
The access network uses optical technology with no packet switching transport functionality. Figure
7
10-9 illustrates a passive WDM Fronthaul design but the same design principle applies regardless of
8
the WDM solution. Each O-RU directly connected to the WDM multiplexer/demultiplexer by a
9
colored optic and an optical cable. At the O-DU side in the central office, the WDM
10
multiplexer/demultiplexer performs wavelength multiplexing/demultiplexing, which realize the
11
one-to-one optical wavelength connection. The WDM solution can be passive, semi active or active.
12

13

14
Figure 10-9 WDM Fronthaul design (passive)
15

16
WG-9 has a work item underway considering WDM-based Fronthaul transport [21], consequently
17
this document does not consider this type of access network design further.
18

19
10.2.2 Passive Optical Networks (PONs)
20
Passive Optical Networks (PONs) are fiber-based point-multipoint access networks, relying on
21
TDM/TDMA for the exchange of traffic between a central Optical Line Termination (OLT) and
22
multiple Optical Network Units (ONUs). PONs also use WDM for separation of up- and
23
downstream traffic, and for overlaying of multiple different PON technologies over the same fiber
24
infrastructure called Optical Distribution Network (ODN). Note that there are two basic flavours of
25
PON;
26
1. Time or Time +Wavelength Division Multiplexing (TDM or TWDM) PONs apply point-
27
multipoint connections (one up/down wavelength pair (called Channel Pair) is shared over
28
multiple ONUs) over a point-multipoint ODN.
29
2. Wavelength Division Multiplexing (WDM) PONs apply point-point connections between
30
each ONU and the OLT (one Channel Pair per ONU) over a point-multipoint ODN.
31

32
WDM PONs are like dedicated point-point links whereas TDM/TWDM PONs have some
33
fundamental characteristics to bear in mind when considering them for mobile Xhaul, described
34
below.
35

36

ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

61

1
Figure 10-10: Typical TDM PON network. In TWDM PON multiple Channel Pairs are
2
muxed per ODN
3

4
TDM/TWDM PONs are standardized technologies (see [195], [37], [38], [39]) and are
5
characterized by generic capabilities (independently of the use case):
6
• PON line rates are shared over the ONUs and existing technologies reach 10 Gbit/s per
7
channel (up to 4x 10 Gbit/s with NG-PON2), with new variants being developed at 25 Gbit/s
8
and 50 Gbit/s. Note that some fraction is consumed by the technology-specific overheads
9
(e.g. by parity bits for Forward Error Correction).
10
• Depending on the technology the maximum distance can reach 20 km or 40 km (or 60 km
11
with a reach extender), the maximum amount of ONUs per PON port can reach 64 or 128.
12
Note that the reach (distance) and scalability (amount of ONUs per PON ODN) are a mutual
13
trade-off bound by the optical budget (many classes of optical budget exist, e.g. Class N1
14
covers optical losses from 14dB to 29dB).
15
• The max amount of traffic flows per PON port can reach 4k (independently of physical layer
16
considerations).
17
• The upstream TDMA multiplexing is controlled by a Dynamic Bandwidth Assignment
18
(DBA) algorithm in the OLT (which is equivalent to upstream shaping over the PON
19
segment). The DBA allocates the bandwidth needs per transport container (each ONU can
20
have one or multiple transport containers) and update its assigned bandwidth. The assigned
21
bandwidth is then converted into a burstiness (rate and size of bursts). Bandwidth can also
22
be (partially or fully) assigned as a fixed value. The upstream latency is influenced by the
23
DBA behaviour, with a trade-off between latency and efficiency (more frequent bursts
24
means less waiting time between bursts but more overhead).
25
• Protection of (parts of) the passive ODN and active OLT equipment by automated switch-
26
over f

3
DBA behaviour, with a trade-off between latency and efficiency (more frequent bursts
24
means less waiting time between bursts but more overhead).
25
• Protection of (parts of) the passive ODN and active OLT equipment by automated switch-
26
over from working to protecting parts of the equipment.
27
• Management and configuration of the ONUs. Note that ONUs operate at Layer 2 only (e.g.
28
for Layer 2 flow classification). An ONU can be connected to (or integrated with) a Layer 3
29
device like a residential gateway.
30

31
PON ports are terminated in the OLT node, which terminates the PON layers and acts as an
32
aggregation and multiplexing node for the multiple PON ports. Contrary to the PON layer, the
33

62
OLT’s features are not strictly standardized, although reference deployment models are defined in
1
Broadband Forum documents (See [190], [191]). Typical OLT features include;
2
• QoS-aware packet forwarding between user side and network side (unicast, multicast, Layer
3
2 switching, Layer 3 routing)
4
• Traffic management (classification, (re)marking, queuing and scheduling, policing,
5
shaping…)
6
• User-side protocol interaction (e.g., DHCP relay agent, IGMP proxy, ARP relay, …) or on
7
the contrary protocol transparency
8
• Network-side protocol support (e.g., IP routing protocols, IGMP proxy, MPLS signalling,
9
…)
10

11
The datagrams (typically IP over Ethernet) undergo several handlings when being transported from
12
end to end over a PON system. The different steps can be summarized as follows:
13

14
Downstream (OLT SNI ingress to ONU UNI egress)
15
1. Traffic Management (classification, policing, queuing and scheduling) at ingress (OLT SNI),
16
2. Forwarding (Layer 2 switching or Layer 3 routing) towards corresponding PON MAC (PON
17
port),
18
3. Encapsulation in PON MAC (according to standard, ITU-T or IEEE),
19
4. OLT PON port egress queuing and scheduling,
20
5. Fiber propagation,
21
6. ONU (Layer 2 based) forwarding to corresponding UNI,
22
7. Decapsulation of PON MAC layer,
23
8. ONU UNI egress queuing and scheduling (Layer 2)
24

chunks.section_title: Using PON for Xhaul: specific features
chunks.text:
25
Upstream (ONU UNI ingress to OLT SNI egress)
26
1. DBA processing in OLT for burst-based TDMA transmission (acts as policer and shaper),
27
OLT notifies grants to ONUs by sending a Bandwidth Map to all ONUs,
28
2. Traffic Management (Layer 2 classification, queuing and scheduling) at ingress (ONU UNI),
29
3. Encapsulation in PON MAC (according to standard, ITU-T or IEEE),
30
4. Burst generation as per bandwidth map,
31
5. Fiber propagation,
32
6. Decapsulation of PON MAC layer,
33
7. Forwarding (L2 switching or L3 routing) to right OLT uplink (SNI),
34
8. OLT uplink (SNI) egress queuing and scheduling
35

36
PONs are widely used for all FTTx use cases (Cabinet, DPU, Office, Home, …), and are designed
37
for multi-service support (residential triple play, business services, Wireless LAN access points). As
38
explained in the next section and [194], PONs have been extended with additional features and are
39
also suitable for multiple Xhaul scenario’s. PONs can act as layer 2 legs in the end-end transport, or
40
participate (from OLT upwards) to layer 3 routing.
41
10.2.2.1 Using PON for Xhaul: specific features
42
As a PON is an asymmetrical (bandwidth and latency) point-to-multipoint medium, time and
43
frequency synchronization have to be transported using native media means using media converters
44
(in OLT and ONU). The PON technology have in-built mechanisms for providing frequency and
45
phase synchronization. This will be described in [22].
46

47

ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

63
The PON DBA is being extended with a cooperative mode DBA (called Cooperative DBA or CO
1
DBA in short) for interaction with O-RAN CTI ([24], [25]) making it suitable for some Fronthaul
2
needs by improving the multiplexing while keeping transport latency low.
3

4
A specific side effect of T(W)DM PONs is the need for discovery and ranging of new ONUs by
5
means of short interruptions (up to a couple of 100’s of µs) of upstream traffic. Such interruptions
6
are likely to impact the performance at the mobile radio layer, but several ways to mitigate the
7
impact or reduce or eliminate the interruptions are being developed (ranging notification from OLT
8
to O-DU by CTI, optimization of ranging timing to minimize impact, avoiding ranging on the
9
latency-sensitive channel by means of separate dedicated activation wavelength).
10

11
10.2.2.2 Xhaul Use cases: topologies
12
PON for Fronthaul
13

14

15
Figure 10-11 PON for transport of Fronthaul flows
16

17
Points of attention for Fronthaul deployments are latency at transport level, capacity per O-RU, and
18
time synchronization accuracy (Time Error between the O-RUs). For Fronthaul the O-RUs are
19
connected to ONUs, the OLT is connected to multiple O-DUs (or O-DU/O-CUs), possibly through
20
intermediate aggregating node(s). The PON system can be on-site (e.g., cell site = event zone) or
21
reach up to the cell site (ONU at cell site).
22
The appropriateness of a PON technology depends on several points:
23
-
the considered radio bandwidth and corresponding Fronthaul throughput and the number of
24
O-RUs per PON that can multiplexed per single PON port
25
-
the obtained latency at packet transport level which depends on the DBA settings (and use
26
of CTI). The requirements for Fronthaul depend on the combination of O-DU and O-RU
27
categories, which have one-way latency budgets ranging from tens to hundreds of µs for
28
usual Fronthaul, and multiple ms for non-ideal Fronthaul (see [18]). Plain DBA is not suited
29
for usual fronthaul, for which Cooperative DBA with CTI is required. Plain DBA can
30
address non-ideal fronthaul. See 10.2.2.3 for more details.
31
-
The time accuracy between O-RUs on PON systems will be described in [22].
32

33
PON for Midhaul
34

35

10.2.3 DOCSIS Networks
11
Today’s modern cable operators deploy and manage extensive hybrid fiber coaxial (HFC) networks.
12
The HFC plant reaches 93% of American households and connects to virtually every building
13
across north America. The data-over-cable service interface specification (DOCSIS®) is the
14
protocol designed to work on the HFC network. DOCSIS suite of specifications is standardized and
15
maintained by CableLabs® [203][204], and is deployed worldwide. DOCSIS technology has
16
evolved through six generations of progressive refinement. Originally developed for delivering high
17
speed broadband to residential customers, the cable industry has made many advances in the HFC
18
technology, making it a promising option for 5G transport. The HFC plants are already extensively
19
deployed in areas where 5G will be in the most demands, especially in dense urban and suburban
20
environments. Additionally, the HFC plant is active, providing power needed for small cell radios.
21
The cable operators typically have the right of way on the strands where radios can be hung,
22
eliminating the need to obtain permits from government. Leveraging the existing HFC deployments
23
significantly reduces time-to-market and cost of deploying 5G.
24

25
10.2.3.1 DOCSIS technology overview
26
DOCSIS protocol is a Layer 2 transmission protocol that encapsulates the IEEE 802.3 Ethernet. The
27
technology supports both Layer 2 and Layer 3 services and is aware of both. DOCSIS network is a
28
point-to-multipoint access network, where the transmission of upstream and downstream is
29
controlled by the cable modem termination system (CMTS). Figure 10-14 shows a typical HFC
30
plant. The CMTS is typically located in either a headend or a hub, which is connected to the fiber
31
nodes through digital or analog fiber. From there, the communication path traverses through a coax
32
network of zero or more amplifiers to the neighborhoods. The hybrid (fiber and coax) network
33
topology is called “N+x”, where “N” is the fiber node, where the fiber ends and coax starts, and “x”
34
is the number of amplifiers traversed. The average north American plant is between N+2 and N+5.
35
The smaller the x, the closer the fiber node it is to the neighborhood, the larger the amount of
36
capacity would be available to each customer.
37

38
The traditional physical CMTS controls 50k cable modems (CMs). It is expected to scale up as the
39
CMTS moves to the cloud native architecture.
40

41

21
Functionally, the DOCSIS network can interconnect the small cells or radios as shown in Figure
22

23

24

25

26

27
The latency requirement for Backhaul is based on the application. Additional service-level
28
agreement (SLA) can be specified by the mobile operator. Midhaul latency is generally considered
29
to be less than 10 ms [206]. LLX can be implemented to ensure these requirements can be met, as
30
well as providing better latency performance, particularly for latency-sensitive flows.

10.2.4.1 Overview of Microwave and mmwave technology
12
For over 20 years, microwave has been the primary solution for the rapid and cost-effective rollout
13
of mobile Backhaul infrastructure with over 50% of mobile sites worldwide today connected via
14
Microwave (MW) or Millimetre Wave (mmW) radio links and up to over 90% in some networks.
15
The evolution from 4G towards 5G presents significant challenges to all transport technologies and
16
wireless ones make no exception.

10.3 Data Centers
4
Data center solutions, connectivity to the Xhaul transport infrastructure and orchestration are not in
5
scope of this version of document. However, it is important to note the critical role
6
Data centers play in 5G, with key components of the 5G architecture running on servers either
7
virtualized, containerized or as bare metal located in data centers. Consequently, operators need to
8
consider how data centers are connected to the Xhaul transport network and how end to end
9
transport services are built that span the DC and the WAN. At a high-level two basic approaches to
10
interconnecting DC to the Xhaul transport network are available.
11

12
10.3.1 Complete separation between DC and WAN infrastructure
13
This refers to data centers that are discrete from the WAN infrastructure with each domain
14
potentially running different underlay and overlay transport network technologies. The inter-
15
connection between the two domains is via “Data Center Interconnect” (DCIs) routers. These
16
routers reside in both the DC and WAN domains and have an awareness of the DC environment on
17
one side and an awareness of the WAN on the other. To provision an end-to-end network service,
18
the data center and the WAN are provisioned separately, using a cross-domain orchestrator to stitch
19
the two separate service environments together.
20

21
10.3.2 DC integrated into WAN infrastructure.
22
This refers to data centers that run the same underlay and service infrastructures as the WAN. In
23
this case, although there maybe DCIs to create underlay separation between the WAN and the DC,
24
it is possible to treat the network service infrastructure as a single orchestration domain with WAN
25
transport services directly configured on the Top of Rack (ToRs) devices or on soft switches /
26
routers residing on the server themselves.
27

contained in this section (section 11) and the second based on SRv6 contained in section 12. An

This section outlines a packet switched underlay model based on “Multi-Protocol Label Switching”
4
(MPLS).  MPLS data plane is based on label switching but has more than one control plane
5
technology. The first, classic approach is based on the control plane developed when MPLS was
6
first conceived in the mid 1990s and utilizes IGPs, BGP-LU, LDP and RSVP. An emerging
7
approach, very appropriate to mobile transport networks, is based on Segment Routing (SR)
8
extensions to IGP and BGP, which have been developed since around 2010 and aim to simplify and
9
minimize the number of protocols running in network, as well as reduce the state held on the TNEs.
10
This document describes scalable, multi-domain Xhaul transport architecture that can involve
11
domains with different MPLS control plane technologies (classic: LDP, RSVP, BGP-LU, as well as
12
emerging: SR, SR with Flex-Algo, or SR-TE), in order to support both brownfield (extending
13
existing mobile transport network using classic control plane with additional domains using new,
14
emerging SR control plane) and greenfield (building new Xhaul transport network) deployment use
15
cases. However, in order to avoid duplications with BBF technical reports documenting classic
16
MPLS control plane in mobile transport network designs, and to keep the size of this document
17
within reasonable limits, this document puts more focus on the new, emerging control plane based
18
on SR.
19

20
Regardless which MPLS control plane – classic or SR – is used to distribute underlay transport
21
labels, the services are overlaid on-top. The service layer is independent from the underlaying
22
MPLS transport layer and supports native Ethernet services and layer 3 services.
23

11.2 MPLS control plane
10
The MPLS control plane is used to distribute information required to deliver the packets through the
11
transport network. It typically includes following information:
12

13
• Topological information (nodes and links in transport network, including attributes, like
14
metrics, IP prefixes administrative groups, SRLGs, etc., associated with these topological
15
elements)
16
• IP prefixes
17
• MPLS transport label information
18

19
Based on the collected information, control plane responsibility is to
20

21
• calculate paths (shortest path to the destination, or path fulfilling certain administrative
22
constraints, which are not necessarily the shortest paths – for example low latency path)
23
• program data plane with information required to forward the MPLS packets through the
24
network (next-hops, MPLS labels stack manipulation rules – pop, push, swap)
25
• calculate and program in the data plane backup paths required for rapid protection
26
mechanisms (fast re-route – FRR)
27

28
In a packet switched transport network consisting of a large number of routers, a mix of WAN and
29
data centers components, the need to support traffic engineering, the underlay control plane is a
30
typically a collection of independent routing domains that interact in a collaborate fashion.

11.4 SR/MPLS control plane
5
The following section outlines the control plane requirements for SR/MPLS environment.
6
11.4.1 Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) for SR/MPLS
7
The distribution of labels, rapid convergence and distribution of traffic engineering information and
8
optional calculation of TE optimized transport planes in a single SR domain is done by a link-state
9
IGP, in the form of either IS-IS or ISPF, with suitable SR enhancements. This document separately
10
outlines the requirements for IS-IS and OSPF with support for TiLFA for fast convergence and
11
optional support for flex-algorithm for the creation of multiple transport planes optimised for
12
different criteria and potentially using different topologies.
13

14
SR/MPLS requires at least one IGP with SR awareness per routing domain or autonomous system.
15
There are two IGPs that support SR/MPLS; ISIS or OSPF. They are both link-state protocols and
16
have similar capabilities but there are operational differences which is beyond the scope of this
17
document.
18

19
The IGP provides internal connectivity within a routing domain. The size of a routing domain is
20
determined by technical, operational and organizational considerations, such as protocol scalability
21
and spans of control. In large networks, such as a 5G infrastructure, extending from the access to
22
the transport core, it is very common to see multiple autonomous systems, IGPs and segmentation
23
within the IGPs.
24

25
In an SR/MPLS environment the IGP is responsible for distributing node, prefix and label
26
information to all nodes within the routing domain and for calculating the “Routing Information
27
Base” (RIB) and the Label Forwarding Information Base (LFIB) on each TNE.  Optionally it can
28
provide fast convergence mechanisms and distribute traffic engineering attributes within the domain
29
and build multiple transport planes.  Both IS-IS and OSPF have facilities to create a hierarchical
30
routing structure within a routing domain using levels and areas respectively. They also have the
31
facility to bring external routing information into a routing domain and push its routing information
32
into other routing domains using route redistribution.
33

34
Note: There are other techniques to achieve route re-distribution between routing domains, such as
35
BGP and centralised SDN controllers.
36

37
Note: When looking at SR/MPLS IGP requirements there are sets of requirements for ISIS and
38
OSPF. Operators need to follow the requirements associated with IGPs they are using within their
39
network infrastructure.
40
11.4.1.1 Topology Independent Loop Free Alternative (TiLFA)
41
In the SR/MPLS underlay design outlined in this document, TiLFA can be used to achieve fast IGP
42
convergence in the event of a network failure.  Topology Independent Loop Free Alternative as
43
defined “Topology Independent Fast Reroute” using Segment Routing (draft ietf-rtgwg-segment-
44
routing-ti-lfa [185]) is an IGP capability supported by Segment Routing that provides a local repair
45

ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

81
mechanism that achieves 100% coverage within a routing domain against links, nodes and SRLGs
1
failures with convergence times, once failure detection has occurred, H/W dependent but typically
2
less than 50ms.
3

4
For each destination in the network, TI-LFA pre-installs a backup forwarding entry for each
5
protected destination ready to be activated upon detection of the failure of a link used to reach the
6
destination.  TI-LFA provides protection in the event of any one of the following: single link
7
failure, single node failure, or single SRLG failure.  In link failure mode, the destination is protected
8
assuming the failure of the link.  In node protection mode, the destination is protected assuming that
9
the neighbor connected to the primary link has failed.  In SRLG protecting mode, the destination is
10
protected assuming that a configured set of links sharing fate with the primary link has failed (e.g. a
11
linecard or a set of links sharing a common transmission pipe). The mechanics of the TiLFA in an
12
SR/MPLS environment at failure is shown in Figure 11-3 and upon convergence in Figure 11-4.
13
One of the key advantages of TiLFA over some other fast convergence mechanisms, not well
14
illustrated in the example below, is that the TiLFA backup path is the same as the post convergence
15
path, thus minimising micro-loops that can occur as IGPs converge.

11.4.1.2 IGP Flexible-Algorithm
5
In the SR/MPLS underlay design outlined in this document Flexible Algorithm can be used to
6
within an IGP domain to provide an IGP based traffic engineering facility.  Flexible-Algorithm is an
7
IGP based traffic engineering technique that permits multiple forwarding tables to be created in the
8
IGP based on operator programmed criteria. It is a simple, automatic way, in which a packet
9
switched transport network can be traffic engineered, using only the IGP, to create different
10
transport planes designed to meet specific operator defined criteria.
11

12
Standard ISIS and OSPF use the IGP metric on links and the “Shortest Path First” (SPF) algorithm
13
to calculate the “best” path between an ingress and egress point in the network. For many services
14
this approach is sufficient, however this approach cannot, for example, take into account real-time
15
link latency, utilization, packet loss and whether an ECMP path shares links using the same
16
underlying fibre ducts.
17

18
IGP Flex-Algo, defined in RFC 9350 [162] is an IGP based Segment Routing traffic engineering
19
capability, that enables an operator to define their own custom algorithm, based on a wide range of
20
variables including: link latency, packet loss, bandwidth, affinity and shared risk link groups
21
(SRLG), to achieve a specific forwarding aim. This is illustrated in Figure 11-5.
22

11.4.2 SR/MPLS Traffic Engineering
33
SR/MPLS supports two forms of SR policies or Traffic Engineering. Both solutions rely on the IGP
34
to gather and convey topological and resource information around the network and optionally to an
35
SR Path Computation Element (SR-PCE) via BGP-LS.
36
11.4.2.1 Segment Routing Traffic Engineering (SR-TE)
37
The SR policy consists of a list of SIDs the packet needs to traverse and is programmed into the
38
packet on the source node. The SID list can consist of a mix of prefix and adjacency SIDs. In SR
39
this form of TE allows a path to be:
40
1. Loosely source routed where some intermediate points, but not all, are specified between the
41
ingress and egress node. Paths between these intermediate points typically use the shortest
42
path, ECMP based routing determined by the IGP.
43
2.  Explicitly source routed where all intermediate points and even links are specified between
44
the ingress and egress nodes.
45

46

ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

85
In all cases, topology information and live network status within a routing domain is distributed
1
within a routing domain by the IGP with suitable extensions. In single routing domain environments
2
path computation can be performed either by individual head-end routers or via a centralised “SR
3
Path Computational Element” (SR-PCE). In multi-domain routing environments, then path
4
computation generally occurs on a “centralised SR-PCE” component that has topology information
5
for all domains being traversed. This function can be a standalone entity or be integrated into
6
strategically placed TNEs. This form of traffic engineering can support loose and explicitly routed
7
paths, low-latency paths, bandwidth-guaranteed paths, and disjoint paths. Precise TE capability
8
depends on the capabilities of the SR-PCE component.
9
11.4.2.2 IGP Flexible Algorithm
10
IGP Flexible-Algorithm is described in section 11.4.1.2. It is an IGP based traffic engineering
11
technique that permits multiple logical topologies to be created in an IGP domain based on operator
12
programmed criteria. When used in a single IGP routing domain the IGP calculates and maintains
13
the path. The ingress node simply needs to address the packet to the MPLS label associated with the
14
flexible algorithm. This removes the need for a head-end or centralised PCE path computation
15
element and also keeps SID list contained in the label stack to a minimum.
16
This works in a single IGP domain but depending on area border router and autonomous system
17
border router capabilities can be supported in multi-domain environments based on redistribution.
18

19
For flex-algo requirements for SR/MPLS, see section 11.4.1.3  and 11.4.1.4.

11.5 Scaling the MPLS infrastructure
21
In order to provide communication between two MPLS TNEs, end-to-end MPLS LSPs must be
22
available between the TNEs. This implies, that unique MPLS label towards the Transport Network
23
Equipment, which possibly resides in different routing domain, must be available. In highly scaled
24
environment the number of potential next-hops can be high, therefore care must be taken to ensure
25
that resources, especially forwarding plane resources, are utilized in an efficient way, while
26
providing end-to-end MPLS connectivity.
27

28
While the requirement for having unique label per remote Transport Network Equipment increases
29
the pressure on scaling, the benefit of unique label is faster detection of remote Transport Network
30
Equipment failure, resulting from unique underlay prefix/label withdrawal. For architectures, which
31
can use prefix summarization for remote Transport Network Equipment reachability, like for
32
example SRv6 architecture discussed in Section 12, such capability is missing, since remote
33
Transport Network Equipment failure does not influence underlay summary prefix state.
34
11.5.1 Seamless MPLS architecture
35
Seamless MPLS (draft-ietf-mpls-seamless-mpls [182]) is applicable to for both LDP/RSVP and SR
36
based control planes. Seamless MPLS is based on following architectural aspects:
37

38
• Transport network is divided into multiple smaller routing domains. Routing domains can be
39
represented by separate BGP autonomous systems, or separate IGP domains (areas). Or,
40
combination of BGP autonomous systems and IGP areas, where BGP autonomous systems
41
are further divided with IGP areas.
42
• The size of each routing domain might vary, but must be chosen in such a way, that even the
43
weakest transport device in given routing domain can participate in intra-domain routing and
44
