86
intra-domain MPLS path (SR, SR-TE, Flex-Algo, RSVP, LDP) establishment without any
1
scaling concerns.
2
• Inter-domain routing and MPLS path establishment is achieved by BGP labelled unicast
3
(BGP LU), running on top of intra-domain protocols. BGP-LU is used for both prefix
4
distribution (PE loopbacks), as well as label distribution (labels allocated for PE loopbacks)
5

6
This concept is outlined in Figure 11-6.
7

8
Figure 11-6 Seamless MPLS architecture
9

10
BGP-LU operation can be further optimized for enhanced scaling:
11

12
• BGP-LU prefixes (loopbacks of remote TNE) are not installed in the forwarding table (FIB)
13
– they are just installed in the routing table (RIB), which consumes only control plane
14
resources. On typical transport device, control plane resources scale better than forwarding
15
plane resources
16
• Service NLRIs (L3VPN, EVPN) are automatically filtered on route reflectors (not shown in
17
Figure 11-6, for diagram simplicity), and distributed only to the TNEs requiring specific
18
service prefixes. This is achieved with constrained route distribution.
19
• Only these automatically filtered service NLRIs are installed in the forwarding plane, using
20
the BGP-LU transport label of the required BGP-LU prefix (remote TNE loopback).
21
Therefore, usage of forwarding plane resources is highly minimized.
22
• Further optimization of control plane resources is possible, where TNE (PE) requests from
23
route reflector only limited set of BGP-LU prefixes. This can be achieved with outbound
24
route filtering (ORF) of BGP-LU prefixes with ORF filter automatically generated to allow
25
only BGP-LU prefixes required to resolve protocol next-hops of accepted (filtered with
26
constrained route distribution mechanism) service NLRIs.
27

28
With Seamless MPLS architecture, ingress PE uses recursive next-hop resolution, where service
29

11.5.2 Controller based network scaling architectures
2
In addition to the “Seamless MPLS” approach which is an infrastructure-based scaling technique,
3
an external controller in the form of a distributed “Path Computational Element” (PCE) could be
4
used for scaling across multiple MPLS domains. The approach aims to simplify the underlying
5
infrastructure by reducing interactions between domains at the infrastructure level and delegating
6
cross domain path determination to a distributed PCE component.
7

8
Figure 11-8 shows the general architecture with a distributed PCE layer that gathers IGP topology
9
information from their respective domain. PCE’s can exchange topology information with each
10
other using BGP-LS. In scenarios where the headend is not able to resolve the next-hop locally, it
11
may rely on PCE to provide an End-to-End Path when requested. The headend communicates with
12
the PCE using Path Computation Element Protocol (PCEP). This mechanism can helps save
13
resources on CSR’s contributing to overall Xhaul Network scale.
14

15

16
Figure 11-8 General concept of a controller-based architecture
17

18
The figure above shows network simplification and scalability by:
19
• Creating a multi domain topology, each with its own PCE Controller
20
• Removing extensive Route leaking and filtering requirements between IGP domains.
21
• Removing the need for the headend to populate its routing table with topology and routing
22
information.
23
• Use Passive Stateful PCE Path Computation Request/Response as per RFC 8231 to create
24
an end-to-end path.
25

26
Each domain may have its own path consideration and constraints that can independently be
27
implemented and communicated to the PCE/PCEs. PCEs can calculate end to end path based on
28
these constraints and communicated to the headend TNE via PCEP as shown in Figure 11-9.
29

30

ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

89

1

2

5
network size and the use-case, the SID list may exceed the platform’s label stack capacity. In those
6
cases, the SID list across domains could be further optimized by using techniques offered by one of
7
the following two architectures.
8

9
• Using Forwarding Adjacency (FA) between domain boundaries, with associated Adjacency
10
SID, abstracting the path between domain boundaries
11
• Using SR-TE policies between domain boundaries, with associated Binding SID, abstracting
12
the path between domain boundaries
13

14
Both these approaches are optional architectures that could be used to further optimize the size of
15
the label stack in controller-based solutions.
16

17
While the PCE is shown as a separate entity in the figure above, an operator may choose to either
18
have PCE functionality integrated into the infrastructure router(s) or use a dedicated device or
19
devices for PCE. As long as the PCE’s in the distributed PCE layer can exchange topology
20
information and communicate with their respective PCEP clients, the positioning of PCE
21
functionality can be a choice an operator makes based on their respective network environment.

11.5.2.1 Forwarding Adjacency architecture for cross domain scale
11
Forwarding Adjacency abstracting the path between domain boundary routers is one of the ways to
12
optimize and scale a controller based Xhaul architecture.  Forwarding Adjacency architecture is
13
based on following architectural concepts:
14

metadata.section_title: Forwarding Adjacency architecture for cross domain scale

chunks.section_title: Forwarding Adjacency architecture for cross domain scale
chunks.text:
15
• Transport network is divided into multiple smaller routing domains. Routing domains can
16
be represented by separate BGP autonomous systems, or separate IGP domains (areas).
17
Or, combination of BGP autonomous systems and IGP areas, where BGP autonomous
18
systems are further divided with IGP areas.
19
• The size of each routing domain might vary, but must be chosen in such a way, that even
20
the weakest transport device in given routing domain can participate in intra-domain
21
routing and intra-domain MPLS path (SR, SR-TE, Flex-Algo, RSVP, LDP) establishment
22
without any scaling concerns
23
• Head-end router (border router) of intra-domain LSP advertises the intra-domain LSP (of
24
any kind, i.e. SR, SR-TE, Flex-Algo, RSVP, LDP) as standard link in BGP Link State
25
(LS) topology database, with attributes similar to standard link, like for example SR
26
Adjacency-SID, administrative group (link color, link affinity), SRLG, etc. IGP
27
forwarding adjacency is established (RFC 4206) between domain border routers creating
28
abstracted topology of the routing domain.
29
•  BGP-LS (RFC 8571) is used to distribute abstracted topology. Given the fact that only
30
border routers, and only abstracted forwarding adjacency links between these border
31
routers are exported, the size of the topology database exported via BGP-LS is
32
considerably smaller. BGP-LS distribution can happen in two way, depending on the
33
overall network scale
34
o BGP-LS topology is exchanged between routers in different routing domains
35
o BGP-LS topology is exchanged between PCEs in distributed PCE layer
36

metadata.section_title: Forwarding Adjacency architecture for cross domain scale

chunks.section_title: Forwarding Adjacency architecture for cross domain scale
chunks.text:
37
The first approach is more suitable for small to medium scale deployments. In this approach, any
38
Transport Network Equipment has the detailed topology visibility of the local routing domain, and
39
abstracted (with Forwarding Adjacencies advertised as links in BGP-LS) visibility of the remote
40
routing domains. This significantly reduces the topology database stored on the Transport Network
41
Equipments, therefore, in small/medium deployments PCE might not be necessary.
42

43
The headend PE, based on the full topology database (detailed topology from local routing domain
44
+ topology abstracted with links representing forwarding adjacencies from remote routing
45
domains), performs calculation of end-to-end SR-TE paths (local constrained shortest path first –
46
CSPF – calculation). Each forwarding adjacency is represented in the resulting SR-TE label stack as
47
single Adjacency-SID associated with given forwarding adjacency, regardless of the underlying
48

metadata.section_title: Forwarding Adjacency architecture for cross domain scale

ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

91
MPLS transport used for given forwarding adjacency. At each border node, this Adjacency SID is
1
mapped to the actual transport label stack (LDP, RSVP, SR, SR-TE) used for the given forwarding
2
adjacency.
3

4
This concept is outlined in Figure 11-10.

6
Figure 11-10 Forwarding Adjacency architecture

loaded from end-to-end path computation. Distributed PCEs (Path Computation Elements) can be

13

14
network topology. In this scenario, ingress PE requests from PCE on demand path computation for
15
unresolved next-hops, as outlined in Figure 11-11.

11.5.2.2 Using Binding SID (BSID) for cross domain scale
7
As mentioned earlier, a controller-based architecture make use of the PCE to provides the SID list
8
to the headend for an end-to-end path across multiple domains. If no constraints are imposed on the
9
traffic, the SID list would consist of Area Border Routers Prefix SIDs as next hop. Traffic within
10
the domain will use IGP to get to the next hop while utilizing well established IGP routing
11
mechanism such as Equal Cost Multi Path (ECMP), metric based best path etc. At the ABR, the top
12
most SID is popped and the new next hop SID/Label is exposed, starting the routing within the next
13
IGP are or domain. The process is repeated until traffic reaches its destination. Figure 11-12 shows
14
such behaviour between IGP Domain 0,1 and 2.
15

16

17

18

19

20

21

22
Figure 11-12 Basic SID list with no constraints
23

metadata.section_title: Using Binding SID (BSID) for cross domain scale

chunks.section_title: Using Binding SID (BSID) for cross domain scale
chunks.text:
24
There may be scenarios where more explicit path considerations and constraints could be required,
25
such as using low latency path or inclusion/exclusion of certain links or node. In those scenarios,
26
rather than provide a SID list that encompasses every link/node through the path, mechanisms such
27
as Flex Algo could be used to optimize the SID list on the head end. Figure 11-13 shows a scenario
28
with latency and link/node constraints across the path. In this case operator may use Flex-Algo
29
within a domain and use the PCE controller to provide SID list to the headend accordingly. Notice
30
while the SID depth is no different from the earlier scenario Figure 11-13) and while it still only
31
contain prefix-SIDs of ABR as next hop label, the SID’s now refer to the node’s Flex-Algo Prefix
32
SID, instead of default algo SID. Due to this, the traffic behavior is also different and the next Hop
33
SID automatically uses the desired constraints-based path.
34

35

chunks.text:
ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

93

1

2
Figure 11-13 Constraint based SID list with Flex-Algorithm

In scenarios where an operator is unable or unwilling to use Flex-Algo for SID list optimization, an
5
SRTE Binding SID (BSID) could be used. A Binding SID is a fundamental component of Segment
6
Routing network that may be used to provide SID and network scaling. A BSID is a SID that is
7
associated with an SRTE policy’s active path and is a representation of an End-to-End candidate
8
path. BSIDs could be used to provide additional scale by using nested SRTE policies across
9
domains. The PCE instead of providing a full path through multiple domains, may provide the
10
headend with a path within its own domain and a BSID corresponding to the next domain. When,
11
exposed at the domain boundaries, the BSID gets translated into another set of SID List, providing
12
extensibility and scalability throughout the topology. This process is shown in Figure 11-14.
13

14

15

16

17
Figure 11-14 SID scaling using binding SID

20
link/nodes constraints along the path. The first scenario is where the PCE provides a full SID list to
21
the headend for the entire path, with based path is required end to end. The second scenario uses a
22
Binding, exposed at domain boundaries and then use the appropriate constrains based SID within
23
the domain in question.

11.6 MPLS Quality of Service
5
The MPLS data plane includes a 3-bit field in the MPLS header, the TC – Traffic Class (previously
6
EXP - Experimental) bits. These bits are assignable as a marker for QoS mechanisms in transport
7
nodes to use as a classification and marking tool. The per-hop behavior for MPLS forwarding
8
elements can be defined based on these markings. Because of the restricted size of the TC field, the
9
specific markings are not standardized, but are open for individual operators to define. For a full
10
discussion of a proposed marking scheme and QoS architecture for TNEs in Xhaul, see Chapter 14.
11
11.7 MPLS OAM
12
Basic OAM tools are Ping and Traceroute. Ping is required to test liveliness to a remote MPLS
13
underlay destination and traceroute is required to trace paths and perform hop-by-hop fault isolation
14
to remote MPLS underlay destination. The following capabilities are required on all TNEs.
15

16
[R36]: MUST support “Detection of MPLS Data Plane Failures”, RFC8029 [129]

[R37]: MUST support LSP Ping/Traceroute for SR IGP Prefix-SID and IGP Adjacency-SID with
19

11.8 IP/MPLS service infrastructure
22
For IPv4, IPv6 and Ethernet services an overlay solution is used. Please refer to section 13 for a
23
description of overlay service recommendations for a 5G Xhaul infrastructure.
24
12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based
25
This document presents two packet switched underlay technologies, the first based on MPLS
26
contained in section 11 and the second based on SRv6 contained in this section (section 12). An
27
operator wishing to implement the transport architecture outlined in this document will need to
28
select one of the two and implement the requirements outlined in the associated section. It should be
29
noted that other transport architectures are potentially available but not covered in this revision of
30
the document. This section outlines a packet switched underlay model based on SRv6.
31

32
SRv6 is based on the segment routing architecture as defined in RFC8402 [141].  For more
33
information on Segment Routing see annex A. In an SRv6 infrastructure, like an MPLS
34
environment, it is important to consider the underlay / fabric of the transport infrastructure
35
somewhat separately from the services that run on-top of the infrastructure. The emphasis with the
36
underlay / fabric is to provide an environment that will scale and support the services required by a
37
5G infrastructure. In contrast, the services infrastructure runs on-top of the underlay/fabric of the
38
transport network and supports the different components of the 5G infrastructure (Fronthaul,
39
Midhaul, Backhaul).
40
This chapter is specific to an SRv6 underlay/fabric, its data plane, control plane and how to scale it.
41
Although there are some similarities with an SR-MPLS environment, in terms of architecture, there
42

ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

95
are some key differences in requirements and particularly on how to scale the underlay
1
infrastructure, which is critical in a 5G environment.
2

3
The service infrastructure and how to support 5G service requirements for both SR-MPLS and
4
SRv6 are covered in a common services section (section 13) as the technologies used and the
5
designs have many similarities.
6
12.1 SRv6 data plane
7
SRv6 relies on an IPv6 data plane with segments defined using SIDs contained in the IPv6 header.
8
SRv6 SIDs are specified in “Segment Routing Header” (SRH) and standardised in RFC8754 [153].
9
Packet switching TNEs supporting SRv6 will need to:
10

11
[R38]: MUST support “IPv6 Segment Routing Header (SRH)” RFC8754 [153]
12

13
[R39]: MUST support “SRv6 Network Programming”, RFC8986 [156]
14

15
[D30]: SHOULD support “Compressed SRv6 Segment List Encoding”, RFC 9800 [177]
16
12.2 SRv6 control plane
17
The SRv6 control plane refers to routing and path control within the SRv6 underlay/fabric. This
18
infrastructure can extend to customer devices or stop at a Provider Edge (PE) function. Its role can
19
be summarised as learning the topology, calculation, and implementation of dynamic and explicit
20
routes across the SRv6 infrastructure and providing rapid protection and repair mechanisms.
21
In a packet switched transport network consisting of a large number of routers, a mix of WAN and
22
data centers components, the need to support traffic engineering, the underlay control plane is a
23
typically a collection of independent routing domains that interact in a collaborate fashion.
24

25

26
Figure 12-1 SRv6 underlay architecture
27

28
Figure 12-1 illustrates how a large packet-switched transport infrastructure might be designed and
29
how different components interact. It should be noted that not all these components are required,
30
and some serve the same purpose but in different ways.
31
1. Each routing domain has an IGP for internal connectivity.
32

ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

96
2. Mechanisms to calculate SR policies or Traffic Engineer paths and convey them to the
1
source nodes. Figure 12-1 shows a distributed “Path Computation Element” (PCE), with
2
“Path Computation Element Protocol” (PCEP) running between the edge nodes and the PCE
3
but there are other network-based mechanisms to calculate SR policies such as Flex-algo
4
running in the IGP or head-end calculated paths.
5
3. Mechanisms to convey routing between IGP domains. This could be provided by
6
summarization and redistribution, E-BGP between AS boundaries or via a multi-domain
7
“Path Computation Element” (PCE). One of the key differences between an MPLS and IPv6
8
based underlay is that IPv6 enables address summarization within routing domains and also
9
between routing domains. This makes an IPv6 based underlay network more scalable and
10
less complex than a corresponding MPLS solution.
11
4. Mechanisms to convey topology and network state information from the network to the PCE
12
and other central management elements. BGP Link State (BGP-LS) and Telemetry feeds are
13
recommended tools to fulfil this requirement.
14
12.2.1 Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) for SRv6
15
SRv6 requires at least one IPv6 IGP per routing domain or autonomous system.  There are two IGPs
16
that support SRv6; ISIS for IPv6 or OSPFv3. They are both link-state protocols and have similar
17
capabilities but there are operational differences which is beyond the scope of this document.
18

19
The IGP provides internal connectivity within a routing domain. The size of a routing domain is
20
determined by technical, operational and organizational considerations, such as protocol scalability
21
and spans of control. In large networks, such as a 5G infrastructure, extending from the access to
22
the transport core, it is very common to see multiple autonomous systems, IGPs and segmentation
23
within the IGPs.
24

25
In an SRv6 environment the IGP is responsible for distributing node, prefix and SID information to
26
all nodes within the routing domain and for calculating the forward tables between these nodes.
27
Optionally it can provide fast convergence mechanisms and distribute traffic engineering attributes
28
within the domain and build multiple transport planes.  Both IS-IS for IPv6 and OSPFv3 have
29
facilities to create a hierarchical routing structure within a routing domain using levels and areas
30
respectively. They also have the facility to bring external routing information into a routing domain
31
and push routing information into other routing domains using route redistribution.
32

33
Note: There are other techniques to achieve route re-distribution between routing domains, such as
34
BGP and centralised SDN controllers.
35
Note: When looking at SRv6 IGP requirements, there are sets of requirements for ISIS for IPv6 and
36
OSPFv3. Operators need to follow the requirements associated with IGPs they are using within
37
their network infrastructure.
38
12.2.1.1 Topology Independent Loop Free Alternative (TiLFA)
39
In the SRv6 underlay design outlined in this document TiLFA can be used to achieve fast IGP
40
convergence in the event of a network failure.  Topology Independent Loop Free Alternative as
41
defined “Topology Independent Fast Reroute” using Segment Routing [185] is an IGP capability
42
supported by Segment Routing that provides a local repair mechanism that achieves 100% coverage
43
within a routing domain against links, nodes and SRLGs failures with convergence times, once
44
failure detection has occurred, H/W dependent but typically less than 50ms.
45

46

ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

97
For each destination in the network, TI-LFA pre-installs a backup forwarding entry for each
1
protected destination ready to be activated upon detection of the failure of a link used to reach the
2
destination.  TI-LFA provides protection in the event of any one of the following: single link
3
failure, single node failure, or single SRLG failure.  In link failure mode, the destination is protected
4
assuming the failure of the link.  In node protection mode, the destination is protected assuming that
5
the neighbor connected to the primary link has failed.  In SRLG protecting mode, the destination is
6
protected assuming that a configured set of links sharing fate with the primary link has failed (e.g. a
7
linecard or a set of links sharing a common transmission pipe). The mechanics of the TiLFA for
8
SRv6 at failure is shown in Figure 12-2 and upon convergence in Figure 12-3. One of the key
9
advantages of TiLFA over some other fast convergence mechanisms, not well illustrated in the
10
example below, is that the TiLFA backup path is the same as the post convergence path, thus
11
minimising micro-loops that can occur as IGPs converge.

12.2.1.2 IGP Flexible-Algorithm
5
IGP Flexible-Algorithm is an IGP based traffic engineering technique that permits multiple
6
forwarding tables to be created in the IGP based on operator programmed criteria. It is a simple,
7
automatic way, in which a packet switched transport network can be traffic engineered, using only
8
the IGP, to create different transport planes designed to meet specific operator defined criteria.
9
Standard ISIS for IPv6 and OSPFv3 use the IGP metric on links and the “Shortest Path First” (SPF)
10
algorithm to calculate the “best” path between an ingress and egress point in the network. For many
11
services this approach is sufficient, however this approach cannot, for example, take into account
12
real-time link latency, utilization, packet loss and whether an ECMP path shares links using the
13
same underlying fibre ducts.
14

15
IGP Flex-Algo, defined in RFC 9350 [162] is an IGP based Segment Routing traffic engineering
16
capability, that enables an operator to define their own custom algorithm, based on a wide range of
17
variables including: link latency, packet loss, bandwidth, affinity and shared risk link groups
18
(SRLG), to achieve a specific forwarding aim. This is illustrated in Figure 12-4.
19

ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

99

1
Figure 12-4 Flex-algo example with three topologies
2

3
This enables an operator, using a single IGP instance, to build multiple forwarding tables within an
4
SRv6 underlay network based on different optimization criteria. The default forwarding instance
5
uses shortest path forwarding based on IGP metrics, but an operator can build additional IGP
6
Traffic Engineered forwarding tables based, for example on lowest latency or avoiding certain links
7
or a combination of the two.
8

9
The requirements to support flex-algorithm are all associated with the IGP requirements and
10
contained in sections 12.2.1.3 and 12.2.1.4.
11

12.2.2 SRv6 Traffic Engineering
12
SRv6 supports two forms of SR policies or SR Traffic Engineering. Both solutions rely on the IGP
13
to gather and convey topological and resource information around the network and optionally to a
14
Path Computation Element (PCE) optimized for SR via BGP-LS.
15
12.2.2.1 Segment Routing Traffic Engineering (SR-TE)
16
The SR policy consists of a list of SIDs the packet needs to traverse and is programmed into the
17
packet on the source node. The SID list can consist of a mix of prefix and adjacency SIDs. In SR
18
this form of TE allows a path to be:
19
1. Loosely source routed where some intermediate points, but not all, are specified between the
20
ingress and egress node. Paths between these intermediate points typically use the shortest
21
path, ECMP based routing determined by the IGP.
22
2. Explicitly source routed where all intermediate points and even links are specified between
23
the ingress and egress nodes.
24

25
In all cases, topology information and live network status within a routing domain is distributed
26
within a routing domain by the IGP with suitable extensions. In single routing domain environments
27
path computation can be performed either by individual head-end routers or via a centralised “SR
28
Path Computational Element” (SR-PCE). In multi-domain routing environments, then path
29
computation generally occurs on a “centralised SR-PCE” component that has topology information
30
for all domains being traversed. This function can be a standalone entity or be integrated into
31
strategically placed TNEs. This form of traffic engineering can support loose and explicitly routed
32
paths, low-latency paths, bandwidth-guaranteed paths, and disjoint paths. Precise TE capability
33
depends on the capabilities of the SR-PCE component.
34

35
12.2.2.2 IGP Flexible Algorithm
36
IGP Flexible-Algorithm is described in section 12.2.1.2. It is an IGP based traffic engineering
37
technique that permits multiple logical topologies to be created in an IGP domain based on operator
38
programmed criteria. When used in a single IGP routing domain the IGP calculates and maintains
39
the path. The ingress node simply needs to address the packet to the “locator-block” associated with
40
the flexible algorithm. This removes the need for a head-end or centralised PCE path computation
41
element and also keeps SID list to a minimum.
42

43
This works in a single IGP domain but depending on area border router and autonomous system
44
border router capabilities can be supported in multi-domain environments based on redistribution.
45
For flex-algo requirements in an SRv6 environment see section 12.2.1.3 and 12.2.1.4.
46

ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

101
12.2.3 Inter-domain connectivity
1
In a large packet-switched transport network the underlay infrastructure will need to be sub-divided
2
into multiple routing domains. These routing domains can be within an autonomous system, at the
3
IGP level, or between autonomous systems.  One motivation is IGP scalability, but other reasons
4
include fault isolation between domains and organizational, for example different groups run the
5
DC and WAN infrastructures. However, even though the infrastructure is divided, connectivity
6
between routers in different routing domains is still required to build end to end services, therefore
7
the underlay infrastructure needs mechanisms to enable inter-domain connectivity and services to
8
be built inter-domain. In an SRv6 environment, potential mechanisms for interchanging routing
9
between domains include:
10

11
1. IGP based hierarchy
12
2. Inter-domain IGP redistribution
13
3. Inter AS BGP
14
4. Controller based
15

16
12.2.3.1 IGP based hierarchy
17
Both ISIS for IPv6 and OSPFv3 have the concept of routing hierarchy in their basic designs. In an
18
SRv6 environment, route summarization or injection of a default route between IS-IS levels or
19
OSPFv3 areas is sufficient to enable EVPN or L3VPNs services to be built over an SRv6
20
hierarchical IGP infrastructure.
21

22
12.2.3.2 Inter-domain IGP redistribution
23
One or more routers are located on the boundary between two or more IGP routing domains. These
24
routers run multiple IGP instances, so have routing awareness of all the IGPs they participate in.
25
Routing information is mutually re-distributed between the IGP protocols allowing reachability
26
between the domains. This redistribution can be in the form of full routing, summarised routes or
27
even default routes. The choice is dependent on the level of awareness required between domains.
28

29
See Figure 12-5 for more detail. IGP route re-distribution in both IS-IS for IPv6 and OSPFv3 is a
30
common capability.
31

32
12.2.3.3 Inter-AS BGP based routing
33
A router in each autonomous system exchanges routing information using BGP-4 supporting the
34
IPv6 address family. It should be noted that this scheme provides better separation than inter-
35
domain IGP redistribution but typically requires separate routers in each autonomous system.
36
See Figure 12-6 for more detail.
37

38
12.2.3.4 Controller based path calculation
39
In this scenario no routing information is exchanged between routing domains at the device level.
40
Instead, each routing domain provides its topology to an SR Path Computation Element (SR-PCE),
41
which is a central SDN control element responsible for determining and finding routes to a
42
destination node on behalf of a source node. Although the SR-PCE is logically a central component,
43
for scale and resiliency reasons it can consist of multiple individual entities distributed around and
44

ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

102
serving different parts of the network. In this case the source TNE requires very limited visibility of
1
the overall network, as end to end cross-domain path computation is delegated to the SR-PCE.
2
A SR-PCE function in an SRv6 underlay transport network has three main functions.
3
1. Gather data about the topology of the overall SRv6 network underlay. Several options exist:
4
a. The SR-PCE participates in the IGP domains and directly collects each domains IGP
5
link-state database.
6
b. Use BGP Link-State (BGP-LS) with appropriate extensions for SRv6 to collect the
7
IGP’s link-state database from each routing domain. This is done through one or
8
more BGP session between the SR-PCE and a TNE in each routing domain
9
participating in the domain’s IGP. The TNEs retrieve information from the IGP
10
LSDB and distribute it to the controller using the BGP link-state address family.
11
2. Communications between the PCE and PCC (path computation client) which is the headend
12
TNE. In this document it is assumed to PCEP (path computation Element Protocol) is used as
13
the communication mechanism between the source TNE and the SR-PCE.
14
3. Path computation. The PCE uses information gathered from the various domains to compute
15
an SR policy consisting of a SID list which packets using the SR policy will traverse. This
16
SID list can be a loosely sourced routed or explicitly source routed.
17

18
12.3 Scaling an SRv6 underlay infrastructure
19
Scaling is one of the key challenges in building a packet switched infrastructure supporting 5G
20
services. Communications and support of L2 and L3 VPN services between two SRv6 TNEs relies
21
entirely on IP routing mechanisms on the underlay transport fabric. In SRv6 this is based on longest
22
IP prefix matching and forwarding, so TNEs can support routing and forwarding based on full IPv6
23
host routes, summarized IPv6 routes or default routing or a combination, derived from dynamic
24
routing protocols or statically defined. Further, different TNEs in the end to end path can use
25
different levels of route summarization appropriate to their position in the network and their
26
computation, memory and NPU/ASIC resources.
27

28
12.3.1 Route summarization and redistribution
29
Summarization within ISIS for IPv6 and OSPFv3 is part of the base protocol capability and can
30
occur between levels in IS-IS for IPv6 and between areas in OSPFv3 using “Area Border Routers”
31
(ABRs). Summarization is also a common capability when redistributing routes between different
32
routing domains and is also supported between Autonomous Systems using BGP-4 between
33
“Autonomous System Border Routers” (ASBRs).  This is illustrated in Figure 12-5 and Figure 12-6
34
and shows how PE1-4’s routing tables can be controlled through route summarization.
35

ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

103

1

2
Figure 12-5 Summarization / redistribution using IGPs
3

4

5
Figure 12-6 Summarization / redistribution using BGP-4
6

7
This approach offers considerable flexibility, as operators can choose the level of summarization,
8
ranging from no summarization to default routing between domains depending on the size of the
9
network and level of awareness required between domains. It can also offer inter-domain traffic
10
engineering support based on flexible algorithm within an IGP domain. However, there are some
11
considerations and limitations:
12
1. Address planning is critical and needs to occur upfront.
13
2. Route summarization might result in sub-optimal routing in certain designs.
14
3. Some traffic engineering scenarios cannot be achieved with route summarization alone.
15
4. A source TNE cannot rely on a host route withdrawal to detect a remote TNE failure covered
16
by a summary route. In this situation over forms of device or service verification are
17
required.
18

19

[R48]: BGP with IPv6 multi-protocol extensions (RFC1771, RFC2545, RFC2858) [45][52][57]

12.3.2 Controller based scaling
8
Route summarization and redistribution is simple and allows massive scale and allows end to end
9
traffic engineering based on flex-algo. However, some traffic engineering scenarios cannot be
10
achieved, such as path diversity and bandwidth optimization, because summarization hides
11
topological details.
12

13
To achieve more complex TE solutions, end-to-end visibility of the network is required, and a
14
controller-based solution based on an SR-PCE is used.  The SR-PCE receives detailed topology
15
information via BGP-LS protocol from each domain. The SR-PCE then has a full picture of end to
16
end reachability. When an ingress PE need to establish an end to end path it requests information
17
from SR-PCE via PCEP protocol. SR-PCE responds with stack of SIDs to establish path to egress
18
PE.

12.3.3 SRv6 scaling conclusion
18
To build an underlay transport network that is highly scalable and supports traffic engineering the
19
simplest way is to uses a multi-domain IGP that supports flex-algo and use address summarization.
20
This design might not be sufficient for all application requirements. In these instances, a PCE based
21
solution could be deployed in tandem for TE use cases that require additional network visibility.
22
12.4 IPv6 Quality of Service
23
The IPv6 packet includes a 6-bit field in the IPv6 header, the DiffServ Code Point (DSCP). These
24
bits are assignable as a marker for QoS mechanisms in transport nodes to use as a classification and
25
marking tool. The per-hop behavior for IPv6 forwarding elements can be defined based on these
26
markings. For a full discussion of a proposed marking scheme and QoS architecture for TNEs in
27
Xhaul, section 14.
28
12.5 SRv6 OAM
29
SRv6 OAM functionality is required to understand the status of the network. SRv6 OAM is
30
described in “Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) in Segment Routing over IPv6
31
(SRv6)” RFC 9259 [161]

chunks.text:
ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

113
13.3 IP Services
1
Mobile IP services will be provided by MP-BGP based L3 VPNs (RFC4364) [90]  over MPLS or
2
SRv6 depending on the underlay network technology employed by the operator. More details on
3
L3VPN are provided in annex C.
4

5
Operators that choose to implement IP services using the BGP Based L3VPN services may use the
6
following architectural design options:
7

8
13.3.1 Building flexible L3VPN service topologies
9
L3VPN services can be used to establish L3 connectivity between various mobile components. BGP
10
L3 VPN support both IPv4 and IPv6 VPNs and offer flexible connectivity models including:
11
• IP N:N multipoint services
12
• IP 1:N multipoint services
13
• IP 1:1 connectivity services
14

15

16
Figure 13-12 Flexible L3 VPN service topologies
17
13.3.2 Constraints based Traffic Steering in L3VPNs
18
By default, BGP based L3VPN use shortest path routing across the transport underlay. However,
19
BGP based VPN traffic can also get automatically steered into SR policy, such as one created by a
20
flexible algorithm or a point-to-point TE tunnel. This is achieved by coloring VPN routes within
21
MP-BGP with extended community attributes. As illustrated in Figure 13-13 this can be done in
22
two ways
23
1. While defining a VRF, define a color for all Prefixes associated with that VRF, or
24
2. When sending or receiving BGP routes, using a policy to “color” the route.
25

26

27

28

metadata.section_title: Constraints based Traffic Steering in L3VPNs

chunks.text:
ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

114

1
Figure 13-13 Import / Export of route colors for SR policy selection
2

3
In either case, the VPN route will now be tagged with a color and traffic for the destination will
4
automatically get steering into an SR policy based on the color associated with the VPN route.
5

6
An operator using MP-BGP L3VPN services for Xhaul, TNEs need to support:
7

8
[R71]: MUST support Multiprotocol Extensions for BGP-4, RFC4760 [92]
9

10
[R72]: MUST Support BGP/MPLS IP Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), RFC4364 [90]
11

12
[D38]: SHOULD support SRTE Policy configuration as RFC 9256 [160], if SRTE policies are used
13
with L3VPN services
14
[D39]: SHOULD support EVPN and L3VPN traffic steering based on “color extended community
15
BGP attributes” defined in RFC5512 [112]
16
[D40]: SHOULD support to color extended community attribute for VPNv4, VPNv6 and EVPN
17
BGP address families defined in RFC5512 [112]
18
[R73]: If using SRv6 as the underlay technology TNEs providing PE functionality MUST support
19
“BGP Overlay Services Based on Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6)”, Internet Engineering
20
Task Force, RFC 9252 [159]
21

22
14 Quality of Service in packet-switched networks
23
This chapter discusses the Quality of Service (QoS) capabilities that must be deployed to support
24
the delivery of Xhaul traffic and non-Xhaul traffic in the RAN network.
25
14.1 Xhaul transport core interface QoS
26
For the purposes of this document, the transport network domain will be considered to be
27
constructed of two interface types. Core interfaces and edge interfaces. An interface is considered to
28
be transport network core if it is interconnecting two devices inside the transport domain. An
29
interface is considered transport network edge if it is connecting to an element outside the transport
30
domain.
31

ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

115
14.1.1 Transport network core interface classification
1
Interfaces in the transport network core domain should perform classification on the outer transport
2
header only. The header in use will depend on the transport model selected by the operator. An
3
example classification scheme for MPLS TC (EXP) to queue is shown below in Figure 14-1
4

5
[R74]: TNEs MUST support classification based on MPLS TC in a MPLS underlay transport
6
network
7
[R75]: TNEs MUST support classification based on IPv6 DSCP in an SRv6 underlay transport
8
network
9

10
14.1.2 Core interface queue structure
11
The Xhaul domain must support a differentiated QoS architecture supporting priority queueing and
12
scheduling with weighted fair queue scheduler for non-priority packets.
13

14
[R76]: MUST support EF forwarding described in IETF RFC 3246 [69]  mapped to a strict priority
15
scheduler with shaping and policing to prevent bandwidth starvation of other classes.
16
[R77]: MUST support AF forwarding model described in IETF RFC 2597 [53] mapped to a WFQ,
17
WRR or MDRR scheduler for non-priority classes.
18
[R78]: MUST support the ability to manipulate queue depths
19

20
14.1.2.1 Flat queue model
21
In the flat queue model, the TNE should support a single level of queue on each physical interface.
22
This model is used for a single topology infrastructure, or a “soft slicing” where the QoS model for
23
each slice is common and bandwidth is dynamically shared between slices.
24

25
Figure 14-1 Example Xhaul queue model
26

27
The system should be capable of supporting a minimum of six queues within the core domain. An
28
example queuing model is provided in Figure 14-1which should be adapted to fit the available
29
queue and scheduling model available in the deployed hardware.
30
All deployments must support a strict priority queue dedicated to latency sensitive front haul traffic
31
(shown as queue marking 5). This queue must be serviced in strict priority over all other queues up
32
ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

116
to its shaped or policed limit. If the node is providing transit for G.8275.2 PTPoIP as a PTP
1
unaware element, then PTP packets MUST also be scheduled in this queue. If the hardware
2
supports multiple levels of strict priority queueing, and is a PTP unaware node, then PTP MAY also
3
be scheduled in a dedicated highest priority queue to minimise packet delay variation (PDV).
4
Two further latency sensitive queues are defined, one for network control (shown as queue marking
5
7) and one for other latency sensitive transit traffic (e.g. latency sensitive Backhaul or Midhaul U-
6
plane or latency sensitive business or consumer traffic) (shown as queue marking 2). These queues
7
should be configured to be serviced with a latency bound suitable for the traffic associated with
8
them. The scheduling model used will be dependent on the specific HW choice. For example, this
9
could be a guaranteed bandwidth queue with suitable scheduler weight and queue depth, or a high
10
priority queue with lower priority scheduling than that for the latency sensitive Fronthaul traffic.
11
Additional queues are defined for guaranteed bandwidth traffic (Management (shown as queue
12
marking 6), guaranteed bandwidth U-plane (shown as queue marking 3,4) and best effort traffic
13
(shown as queue marking 0,1)).
14
Additional queues may be supported if the carrier deems necessary.
15
The example queue model is show in Figure 14-1 provides example MPLS “Traffic Class” (TC) or
16
often called EXP, based classification for the queues. It should be noted that a transport based on
17
SRv6 allows the use of IP DSCP as the QoS marker, allowing for more flexibility in the queue
18
model, and that more queues may be used if the marking scheme and hardware are appropriate.
19
[R79]: MUST support a min

oted that a transport based on
17
SRv6 allows the use of IP DSCP as the QoS marker, allowing for more flexibility in the queue
18
model, and that more queues may be used if the marking scheme and hardware are appropriate.
19
[R79]: MUST support a minimum of 6 HW queues per physical interface
20

21
14.1.2.2 Hierarchical queue model
22
The hierarchical queue model provides a capability to support a segmented infrastructure “Hard
23
slicing” where the QoS model for each slice is different, or where each slice requires dedicated
24
bandwidth. (see Figure 14-2 for details)
25
Here the model the transport device must support a minimum of two levels of queue hierarchy on
26
each physical interface.
27

ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

117

1

2
Figure 14-2 Sample hierarchical queue model
3
In this model the first, or child level defines the queues needed to support the capabilities associated
4
with the slice. These might be the same as in the flat queue model or may be different. In the second
5
or parent level, a scheduler is defined to allocate the maximum bandwidth that will be available to
6
that hard slice. It should be noted that the sum of the guaranteed bandwidth to each shaper should
7
not exceed the interface bandwidth.  As with the flat queue model, example is provided which
8
should be adapted for the specific HW in use.
9

10
[R80]: MUST support a minimum of 6 HW queues per logical interface
11

12
[R81]: MUST support a minimum of two tiers of configurable scheduler per physical interface
13

14
14.1.3 Transport network core interface marking structure
15
Transport nodes should preserve the QoS marking of transported frames and packets across the
16
transport network. This should be accomplished via the use of the pipe or short pipe model
17
described in IETF RFC2983[61].
18
The specific marking structure used to define the transport QoS behaviours is left to the individual
19
providers and is dependent on the transport encapsulation implemented. An example marking
20
structure for MPLS TC values is shown in Figure 14-1.
21

22
14.1.4 Core interface scheduling model
23
Latency sensitive and network control plane traffic should be forwarded using an expedited
24
forwarding model as described in IETF RFC 3246[69]. In order to preserve minimum latency, these
25
queues should be scheduled with a maximum of one packet in each queue and be allocated a
26
priority forwarding schedule in the NPU. To prevent bandwidth starvation of non-priority scheduled
27
traffic, each priority queue should be shaped or policed at a combined capacity less than the
28
physical rate of each egress interface in the core, and with sufficient bandwidth capacity available
29

on TSN may be found in section 10.1.1.2.1.
3
Guaranteed bandwidth queues (management and best effort) should be scheduled using the assured
4

5
Weighted Round Robin (WRR), Minimum deficit round robin (MDRR) or weighted fair queue
6

7
is assigned to a guaranteed bandwidth queue, the scheduler for that queue must be configured to
8
support minimum latency to ensure time sensitive network control traffic (eg BFD) is not delayed.
9
The scheduler MUST have sufficient buffer capacity to avoid loss in these queues due to the effects
10
of micro-burst caused by the aggregation of traffic from different ingress interfaces, or speed
11
mismatch (higher to lower).
12

13

14
and encapsulation for transport. It can be assumed that there are two types of traffic that will be

17

18

20

14.2.1.1 Untagged frames
5
As per Figure 14-3(1) the Mobile Client (MC) presents a flow of untagged frames to the PE. The

10

11

12

14.2.1.2 Tagged frames (VLAN), PCP unset or untrusted
15
As per Figure 14-3(2) The RoE mapper presents a flow of VLAN tagged frames to the PE. The PE
16

17

18
PE has no knowledge of the RoE mapper encapsulation model, or priority needed for each frame,
19
all frames must be given the same appropriate treatment and transport marking, to support the
20
encapsulation mode. It can be assumed that the operator has this knowledge at the either the VLAN
21
or port level and can apply the appropriate local policy for both transport marking and PHB for all
22

17.2.1 TACACS+ Authentication
17
Typically, the default authentication used to authenticate user on the TNE is password
18
authentication using locally stored user data (username, password). In large-scale deployments, like
19
5G Xhaul deployment, local authentication database on each TNE is very impractical. Therefore,
20
the recommended solution is to use TACACS+ server, which should always be considered the first
21
and principal authentication method.
22

23
After integrating the TNE into TACACS+ authentication infrastructure, the TACACS+
24
authentication method should be preferred over password authentication using local authentication
25
database. When user authentication order is set on TNE (with TACACS+ authentication as first, and
26
authentication using local authentication database as second) the user is first authenticated with
27
TACACS+ server. If TACACAS+ server responds (either granting the access or refusing the
28
access), this response is used by the TNE to either allow or deny the user access to the device.
29
However, if TACACS+ server doesn’t respond (is unreachable), local password authentication is
30
used to grant or deny access to the device. Therefore, it is always recommended to have limited
31
number of local users defined on the TNE as a last resort for authentication. These users can be
32
used for authentication purpose in failure cases, when TACACS+ server is not available.
33

34

35
authorization, i.e., to grant access rights to certain portions of the TNE, or to certain configuration
36
or operational commands on the TNE. Additionally, TACACS+ performs accounting, which is the
37
action of recording what a user is doing and/or has done. This is commonly known as AAA
38
(Authentication, Authorization, Accounting).

17.3 Transport Network control plane security
37
17.3.1 Control plane DoS/DDoS protection
38
A denial-of-service (DoS) attack against an TNE is any attempt to disturb legitimate traffic or deny
39
valid users access the TNE by using up all the resources of the TNE. Distributed denial-of-service
40

ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

130
(DDoS) attacks involve an attack from multiple sources, enabling a much greater amount of traffic
1
to attack the TNE. The attacks typically use network protocol control packets to trigger a large
2
number of exceptions, which are packets handed over from the data plane to the control plane of the
3
TNE. This results in an excessive processing load that disrupts normal network operations.
4

5
TNE MUST have DDoS protection capability, which enables the TNE to continue functioning
6
while under an attack. It identifies and suppresses malicious control packets while enabling
7
legitimate control traffic to be processed. TNE SHOULD have possibility to customize DDoS
8
protection profiles allowing to optimize DDoS protection of network control traffic in a particular
9
deployment.
10

11
To protect against DDoS attacks, typically filters and policers for host-bound exception traffic are
12
used. The filters completely block specific types of control traffic (for example, if OSPF is not used
13
in particular deployment, there is no need to send OSPF packets to the TNE’s control plane), while
14
policers specify rate limits for individual types of protocol control packets or for all control packet
15
types for a protocol. Control traffic is dropped when it exceeds policer values. Each violation
16
SHOULD immediately generates a notification to alert operators about a possible attack. The
17
violation SHOULD be counted, the time that the violation starts noted, and the time of the last
18
observed violation noted.
19

20
[R102]: TNE MUST support protection mechanisms (filters, policer) to protect own control plane
21
from DoS/DDoS attacks
22

23
[D52]: TNE SHOULD have the possibility to customize DoS/DDoS protection parameters to
24
protect own control plane

29
Transport control plane uses various protocols to exchange information between TNEs. This
30

31
MPLS deployments), exchange service information (L3VPN, L2VPN), monitor the network state
32
(periodic OAM messages), and more (for example, determine the virtual gateway state in multi-
33
homed environment). These protocols could be divided into following groups:
34
▪ IGP (e.g., OSPFv2, OSPFv3, IS-IS)
35
▪ Multicast (e.g., PIM, MSDP)
36
▪ Protocols to distribute transport labels (e.g. LDP, RSVP)
37
▪ Other protocols (e.g. BFD, VRRP, …)
38

39
This document doesn’t mandate any specific protocol to be used. For example, one deployment
40
could use OSPFv2 as the IGP, while other deployment could use IS-IS as the IGP. However, if
41
certain protocol is used, this document mandates minimum security requirements for each protocol

that must be fulfilled.

9

4
Before a TNE can establish a mutual EAP-TLS connection with a signaling peer, e.g., with an IEEE

To validate against a trust anchor, the TNE shall be able to be provisioned with one or more trust

anchor certificates. The TNE shall ensure that all trust anchor certificates are stored in reset

16

18.1.1 Underlay transport plane
6
The transport plane determines how traffic is sent over the packet-switched underlay infrastructure.

Four approaches are outlined for constructing the underlay transport plane/planes for a 5G transport

18.1.2 Single transport plane for all slices

13

14

15

17

6

8
18.2 Quality of Service
9
Quality of Service is an important component in slicing a transport infrastructure. As with the
10
transport plane, different approaches could be taken depending on the level of isolation required
11
between slices. In considering QoS it is necessary to look at the edge QoS solution and the core
12
QoS solutions. For more info on QoS refer to section 14 and 25.
13

14
18.2.1 Edge QoS
15
Edge interfaces to packet transport networks are generally the slowest and also where congestion
16
and packet drop most often occurs. Regardless of the QoS structures implemented in the transport
17
core, it is important with slicing to support edge conditioning of traffic on ingress and scheduling on
18
egress to the transport network. This ensures that each slice gets its contracted overall bandwidth
19
and class bandwidth as it enters and leaves the transport network. When slices are presented via
20
VLANs from the mobile clients, the PE router needs a hierarchical QoS capability that can account
21
for the overall contracted bandwidth at the VLAN level and also the overall contracted class
22
bandwidth within the VLAN.
23

24
18.2.2 Core QoS
25
Within the core network different QoS strategies can be applied that determine the level of
26
bandwidth and queue sharing that occurs between different slices.

chunks.section_title: Dedicated links and queues per slice
chunks.text:
ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

144
18.2.2.1 Shared queue architecture
1
This approach follows the classic Diffserv QoS architecture. Slice traffic would be conditioned, and
2
optionally marked or remarked as it enters the Diffserv domain, in this case the transport network.
3
These markings determine the behaviour or Per Hop Behaviour (PHB) the traffic receives in the
4
transport network. The number of PHBs in the core is determined by a number of factors; the
5
number of PHBs that can be marked, the number of queues supported on the TNEs and operational
6
complexity of the solution. Typically, in an MPLS network the traffic-class field is used to
7
designate the PHB in the core. This is 3 bits, giving a maximum of 8 markings. In an IPv6 network
8
the DSCP field is used to designate the PHB in the core. This is 6 bits giving a maximum of 64
9
markings. Even with more marking options, the number of PHBs in the core is generally kept small
10
(<8) to simplify configuration, management and is generally done as a one-time set-up when a link
11
is first installed. Core PHBs are enabled using a combination of queues, congestion management
12
and scheduling techniques and are normally set-up in a work preserving fashion.  That is, if one
13
PHB is not fully utilised, the unused capacity can be used by traffic with other PHBs.
14
Applying this to slicing. Each slice has an SLA based on overall and class bandwidth it receives.
15
This is enforced on ingress at the PEs. In this QoS model, core queues are shared between slices and
16
can be considered to be a soft form of slicing, but there is protection between slices through ingress
17
edge conditioning of traffic. This architecture it is well tried, and tested, is simple and scales and
18
able to support very tight SLAs.
19

metadata.section_title: Dedicated links and queues per slice

chunks.section_title: Dedicated links and queues per slice
chunks.text:
20
18.2.2.2 Dedicated queue architecture
21
This approach uses the same Diffserv QoS architecture, except one or more PHBs is exclusively
22
dedicated to a particular slice or slice type. An example could be a high priority PHB, which is
23
dedicated exclusively to the URLLC slice. At the same time other slices can share the remaining
24
PHBs. Given the small numbers of queues normally provisioned in the core (and available traffic
25
classes in an MPLS environment), this type of solution needs to be used with extreme care, however
26
it is a model used today successfully in production networks to support private line services which
27
run in a dedicated high priority queue, while simultaneously supporting other services using a
28
shared queue architecture.
29

30
18.2.2.3 Dedicated links and queues per slice
31
This QoS approach achieves hard slicing by either dedicating core links or parts of a core link to a
32
specific slice. This can be achieved by one of the following approaches:
33
•
Using dedicated links per slice in the transport network. This could be done using full
34
physical Ethernet interfaces or using Ethernet TDM technology, such as flexE, to create
35
dedicated Ethernet channels for different slices. Within these links, class-based queuing
36
would be used to support different traffic types associated with the slice. This approach
37
offers no ability to share unused bandwidth between slices as the links are hard partitioned.
38
•
Using hierarchically scheduled bandwidth on core links. In this case core links would be split
39
using a shaper to govern the level of bandwidth available to each slice, with class-based
40
queuing within the shaped bandwidth. This approach does offer the ability to share unused
41
bandwidth between slices.
42

metadata.section_title: Dedicated links and queues per slice

chunks.section_title: Dedicated links and queues per slice
chunks.text:
43
In addition to dividing the core bandwidth up, mechanisms are required to guide slice traffic into
44
the links or shaped bandwidth associated with each slice. Slice traffic could be guided into the
45
appropriate links using a TE solution, such as flex-algo or SR-TE or alternatively the core routers
46

chunks.text:
ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

145
could be enhanced to schedule on a slice identifier within the packet. At this time there is discussion
1
on this subject but as yet nothing solid. Like with the previous example, this could support a small
2
number of slices but scaling up would be highly problematic with core provisioning, as well as edge
3
provisioning required when a slice is defined, changed or deleted. It is also a large departure in the
4
way QoS in core of packet networks has been managed in the past.
5
18.3 5G Services and slices
6
MP-BGP based L2 EVPN and L3VPNs are used to create slice instances. VPNs are very scalable in
7
terms of numbers and endpoints and allow different flexible connectivity models. This means slices
8
could be based on 5G service, customer or a combination of the two.
9
Each slice would have a VPN associated with it. By default, VPNs use the default IGP based
10
forwarding tables to forward traffic. However, VPN traffic can be directed, either by configuration
11
or using automated traffic steering techniques based on BGP “color extended community attribute”
12
to use traffic engineered paths. In this way, a URLLC slice could be directed to use a delay
13
optimised TE solution. Further control of the transport level connectivity within the VPN can be
14
achieved using Route Target filtering. For example, “Route Target” filtering could be used to stop
15
transport level connectivity between UPFs of different customers but allow O-CUs to communicate
16
with any UPF.
17
19 Energy efficiency in the context of Xhaul Packet
18
Switched Transport Network Equipments
19
Energy efficiency is becoming relevant as sustainability goal in the operation of any kind of
20
network, and in consequence, also for the purpose of Xhaul.
21

22
The O-RAN Alliance has already setup activities in regards energy efficiency in WG5 and WG10,
23
in relation to the management of the energy consumption at the radio level, enabled by e.g. the
24
possibility of handling “sleep modes” of radio elements. This work is complementary to that by
25
focusing on the transport side, specifically on which relates to packet switches solutions, as part of
26
the scope of WG9.
27

28
When dealing with Transport Network Equipments (TNEs), different approaches can be considered:
29

30
• Actions taken at architectural level
31
• Actions taken at transport network (TN) level
32
• Actions taken at Transport Network Equipment (TNE) level
33

34
The following sections elaborate on each of those approaches.
35

36
19.1 Architecture level
37
Here the purpose is the identification of actions that can positively influence the consumption of
38
energy of the Xhaul segment at architectural level. This means the identification of architectural
39
propositions resulting more efficient from an energy consumption perspective. This is much related
40
to the design of the overall Xhaul solution by leveraging on architectural approaches in the direction
41
of reducing the number of elements present in the network. Actions that could lay on this set are for
42
instance:
43

ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

146
• Topological optimizations by concentrating the number of TNEs aggregating O-RU’s, O-
1
DU’s and O-CU’s, while keeping the necessary redundancy levels to satisfy service SLAs.
2
• On scenarios requiring both packet-switched TNEs and an underlay optical network,
3
schemes favouring the reduction of elements such as IPoDWDM solutions (i.e., the support
4
of coloured interfaces on routers to avoid transponders).
5
• When feasible, the support of coloured interfaces directly on O-RU’s, O-DU’s and O-CU’s.
6

7
Any of these actions require an initial planning or a migration process. There could be structural
8
dependencies on the suitability of these approaches based on the architecture design of the operators
9
in their actual aggregation networks.
10

11
19.2 Transport Network (TN) level
12
Here the purpose is to improve the energy consumption of a network by implementing mechanisms
13
that can dynamically optimize such consumption according to network status and conditions. Some
14
events need to be identified as triggers for such optimization, that could require of smart
15
management and control capabilities to make the network adapt to the observed circumstances,
16
while reducing energy. Actions that could lay on this set are for instance:
17

18
• Concentration of traffic flows in some links during low-activity periods, then freeing up
19
some of the links for reducing the consumption on the corresponding TNEs. This could be
20
done by the transport network in an isolated manner, or as part of a combined radio-
21
transport optimization scenario. Note that additional capabilities are needed at device level
22
for taking advantage of the links becoming empty as consequence of the traffic
23
consolidation.
24

25
• Exposure of energy per path or topology based on the consumption of the participating
26
individual devices, so that upper management systems can build an overall view of the
27
energy consumption map for taking decisions (e.g., function placement, traffic consolidation
28
as before, etc).
29

30
These actions leverage on the capability of the management system to collect the necessary
31
information, decide on top of the collected data, and enforce control actions on the network all in an
32
automated manner, ensuring prompting reaction to observed and even predicted network status.
33

34
19.3 Transport Network Equipment (TNE) level
35
Here the objective is to leverage on intrinsic capabilities of the TNEs for reducing its individual
36
energy consumption under conditions that can be triggered either internally or externally (i.e., from
37
the management systems referred before). Actions that could lay on this set are for instance:
38

39
• Presence of native capabilities for supporting “sleep modes” of operation, that is, reducing
40
the consumption during periods of time according to e.g. traffic patterns.
41

42
• Possibility of switching off TNE parts, especially for modular architectures, in situations
43
where those parts do not participate of the communications. This could be simply because
44
there is no active participation, or because the consolidation of network traffic as described
45
in 19.2.
46

ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R005-v10.00

147

1
These actions leverage on the capabilities of each device, so are dependent of the particular
2
implementations for equipment vendors. There is also a great dependency on the capabilities of the
3
installed base, so brownfield scenarios can be no such efficient as new deployments.
4

5
19.3.1 TNE hardware design
6

7
Based on the hardware structure, TNEs can be grouped into two main categories
8

9
▪ fixed systems
10
▪ modular chassis
11

12
Fixed systems (Figure 19-1) are typically 1 RU or 2 RU devices, which do not have replacable
13
network modules. Modular chassis (Figure 19-2), on the other hand, are typically bigger devices,
14
with flexible hardware options (line cards, modules). This allows assembling the TNE with
15
interfaces specifically required for the particular deployment. Fixed systems, while less flexible,
16
when it comes to port type variations, due to their simpler hardware structure, are typically more
17
power efficient compared to modular chassis.
18

19

20

In both cases, fixed systems and modular chassis, components consuming energy are:
4

5
▪ Pluggable optical modules inserted into the system. Responsible for electric  optic
6
conversion of the signal. Energy consumption of pluggable optical modules can greatly
7
vary, depending on the module type. For example, 800 Gbps optical module consumes
8
significantly more energy than 1 Gbps optical module. Similarly, long range or extended
9
range optical module consumes significantly more energy than short range optical module.
10
Additionally, energy consumption might depend on the traffic load. Some optical modules,
11
the so called Power over Ethernet (PoE) optical modules, can also provide power to the
12
attached end-user equipment (e.g. small in-house O-RU), which considerably increases the
13
energy drawn by the optical module.
14
▪ Physical Layer (PHY). Dedicated chipset responsible for providing an electrical,
15
mechanical, and procedural interface to the transmission medium. Energy consumption
16
might depend on the features supported by PHY.
17
▪ Packet Forwarding Engine (PFE). Called as well Network Processing Unit (NPU). It is a
18
dedicated chipset (or group of chipsets) responsible for TN data plane, switching frames or
19
routing packets from one port to another port of the device. PFE/NPU energy consumption
20
increases with increased traffic volume (for example, 800 Gbps PFE/NPU, consumes
21
significantly more energy than 1 Gbps PFE/NPU), as well as with features supported and
22
enabled on the port (for example, enabling MACsec or IPsec encryption might increase the
23
energy consumption).
24
▪ Central Processing Unit (CPU) and Double Data Rate Synchronous Dynamic Random-
25
Access Memory (DDR-RAM). In TNEs, CPUs together DDR-RAM, are responsible for
26
handling transport network control plane, processing messages exchanged by various
27

28

29
inbound/outbound route policy complexity, etc. have effect on energy consumption.
30
Additionally, modular chassis design relies on distributed control plane, with additional
31
CPUs and DDR-RAMs in the line cards (LCs).

▪ Fabric. Dedicated chipset(s) to provide internal connectivity between PFEs/NPUs in multi
1
PFE/NPU systems. In modular systems the fabric chipsets can be distributed across multiple
2
fabric interface boards (FIBs). Energy consumption depends mainly on the traffic load.
3
▪ Miscellaneous chipsets. Some additional functions (for example, PTP handling, IPsec or
4
MACsec encryption) might be implemented via dedicated Application-Specific Integrated
5
Circuits (ASICs) or Field Programmable Gateway Arrays (FPGAs). These circuits consume
6
energy to fulfill their functions.
7
▪ Fans. Fans are used to improve heat dissipation from the device. Fans energy consumption
8
increases with the temperature. Also, some fixed systems are constructed as fanless devices,
9
with heat dissipation realized via other means (like extensive use of dedicated heatsinks, or
10
reusing itself the metal shelf of the device as a heatsinks). Fanless device design might be
11
applicable to smaller TNEs only, like for example small cell site routers.
12
▪ Power Supply Unit (PSU). Energy consumed by PSU is related to the efficiency of PSU.
13
PSU with efficiency 90% consumes less energy (10% from total energy drawn) than PSU
14
with efficiency 85% (15% from total energy drawn).
15

16
In modular chassis, the components are placed in different field replaceable modules, for example:
17

18
▪ Routing Engine (RE). Hosts main CPU and main DDR-RAM
19
▪ Line Card (LC). Hosts optical modules, PHY, PFE and LC dedicated CPU + DDR-RAM.
20
▪ Fabric Interface Board (FIB). Hosts Fabric ASICs and PHY, to interconnect PFEs spread
21
across multiple LCs
22
▪ Fan trays
23
▪ Power Supply Module (PSM)
24

25
Figure 19-3 and Figure 19-4 provides an example of energy consumption distribution across various
26
components for both fixed systems and modular chassis. Components that typically consumes most
27
energy are PFEs, or FPCs hosting PFEs. Other significant energy consumers are optics, fabric, and
28
– for modular chassis – fans. Therefore, it is most important to energy optimize these components
29
of a TNE.
30

31

32
Figure 19-3: Example of energy consumption distribution – fixed system
33

34

35
Fabric

19.3.2 SerDes energy optimization
4
SerDes is a functional block (single chipset or group of chipsets) that Serializes and Deserializes
5

6
TNE designs PHY might be placed between port and PFE to aggregate multiple lower speed SerDes

lines to higher speed SerDes line (Figure 19-5).

19.3.3 PHY energy optimization
15
After SerDes, next component in forwarding path is PHY. PHY should be automatically shut down,
16
when all connected SerDes lines are shut down (Figure 19-6).
17

18

19
Figure 19-6: PHY energy optimization
20

21
[D60]: PHY with all connected SerDes in shutdown state SHOULD automatically shut down. When
22
some of connected SerDes restarts (for example, due to pluggable optical module insertion
23
into a “used” port cage, or due to administrative change of port state from “unused” to
24
“used” for port with pluggable optical module already inserted) PHY SHOULD
25
automatically restart. This process SHOULD not impact neighboring ports.
26

27
19.3.4 PFE energy optimization
28
As visible in Figure 19-3 and Figure 19-4 the major energy consumer in a TNE is the packet
29
forwarding engine (PFE).
30

31
PFE energy can be optimized via different approaches:

1
• Flexible, fully programmable versus fixed pipeline PFE chipsets
2

3
PFE chipsets can be divided into two main categories: flexible, fully programmable (1), and
4
fixed pipeline, with limited programmability (2). Fixed pipeline chipsets consume less
5
energy (Figure 19-7), as their design is simpler – they are designed to perform pre-
6
determined functions (for example, to do the MPLS switching) with limited flexibility to
7
program other functions (for example, perform SRv6 encapsulation/decapsulation, if the
8
chipset was not designed from day one to perform this function). Therefore, to support
9
particular throughput, they require less transistors comparing to flexible, fully programmable
10
chipsets. This results in lower energy consumption. However, the tradeoff is feature
11
flexibility offered by flexible, fully programmable PFE chipsets.
12

13

14
Figure 19-7: PFE chipset evolution
15

16
[D61]: To optimize PFE energy consumption, it is recommended TNE is built using fixed
17
pipeline PFE chipsets.
18

19
• PFE chipset generations
20

21
Newer generation of chipsets, produced with 16 nm, or 7 nm (and emerging 5 nm)
22
technologies consume significantly less energy (Figure 19-7) compared to older generation
23
chipsets (28nm – 65nm).
24

25
[D62]: To optimize PFE energy consumption, it is recommended TNE is build using new
26
generation (<16 nm) PFE chipsets.
27

28

29
• Traffic Load
30

31
Traffic load might impact TNE energy consumption by about 10%-20% (TNE with minimal
32
traffic load, versus TNE with maximal traffic load). Thus, minimizing traffic load might
33
bring some energy savings. Some exemplary techniques to minimize traffic load are:
34

35
• Use efficient transport encapsulation with small overhead (for example, MPLS
36
overhead is typically smaller than SRv6 overhead)

• Compress data before transmission, where possible and applicable (for example, photos
1
and videos might be resized and compressed by the application server, before they are
2
sent to the user equipment). However, this might increase energy consumption by
3
servers hosting applications.
4
• Cache frequently used data close to end-users (for example, web cache)
5
• Use optimized multicast replication for multicast streams (for example, IPTV
6

7

8
• PFE power off
9

10
Both, administrative and automatic PFE power off bring energy savings.

19.3.6 Switching fabric energy optimization
20
Switching fabric complex contains fabric ASICs, and SerDes complexes interconnecting fabric
21
ASICs with PFEs (Figure 19-2). Therefore, in fabric complex, energy could be saved by switching
22
off fabric ASICs or fabric SerDes complexes.
23

24
There are couple of possible options for switch fabric design, when it comes to fabric redundancy in
25
modular chassis. One of the common switching fabric redundancy designs is N+1 redundancy,
26
where ‘N’ fabric interface boards provide capacity sufficient to interconnect all PFEs, and there is
27
+1 fabric interface board as spare. For example, if the node has 8 PFEs, each PFE with 500 Gbps,
28
the required switching fabric capacity is 4 Tbps. If the capacity of single fabric ASICs is 500 Gbps,
29
and single fabric interface board hosts two fabric ASIC (1 Tbps per FIB), equipping the node with 5
30
fabric interface boards (5 Tbps in total) would provide N+1 switching fabric redundancy.
31

32
In case of single fabric interface board failure, the switching fabric is still able to provide full
33
required capacity of 4 Tbps. However, when two fabric interface boards fail, the maximum fabric
34
capacity is reduced to 3 Tbps only. In order to provide protection for two fabric interface boards
35
failures, N+2 (two “spare” fabric interface boards) redundancy mode would be required.
